en: From pradhāna alone, which is composed of all powers without exception, the various effects proceed; they exist in reality as having that very same nature.
From pradhāna alone, which is composed of all powers without exception, the various effects proceed; they exist in reality as having that very same nature.
If, however, the effect were non-existent within the nature of the cause by virtue of its potentiality, it could not be produced at all, because of its lack of essence, like a lotus in the sky.
And for what reason do [the causes] grasp only specific material causes (upādāna), such as the distinct varieties of rice seeds and so forth, and not others, even though their non-existence is equal?
And everything would possess the property of arising from every [cause] in every way, because here, the absence of identity (tādātmya) is non-distinct with respect to all things.
The objection that "this is not so because of the restriction of these powers" is no answer, since causes that possess power can only produce an effect that is possible for them to produce.
But how could they possibly perform that which possesses no excellence of action, which is formless and immutable; for if it were to undergo modification, its very self-destruction would follow?
Furthermore, since the effect is thus impossible [prior to its arising], what could the cause be doing? Consequently, even the causal status of the seed and so forth cannot be established.
Moreover, this manifest world is clearly perceived as being endowed with pleasure and so forth, because its effects—such as serenity, distress, and dejection—are observed here.

Therefore, because it is seen that things arise from what is composed of that [cause] and follow its specific nature—just as there are distinctions such as jars and the like—the followers of Kapila maintain that this [world] is the Pradhāna.

Regarding this, the wise have said: "The injunction is equal even with respect to sentient beings; whatever answer you might have for that [injunction], that same answer applies equally to the wise as well."

If curds and the like already exist in every way within the essence of milk and so forth, then what remains to be produced for those things that already exist and possess a nature identical to their causes and other conditions?

That which is produced by a cause is not its effect, because of its [prior] existence, just like the cognition of the cause; therefore, the intended cause is not a true cause, because it is not something to be proven, like the self of another.
But suppose there exists some excellence characterized by manifestation and so forth, which causes, while producing it, do not incur the charge of being subject to criticism.
If he existed previously in this manner, why was no answer given? Otherwise, how could he attain manifestation from those things that are non-existent?

Since there is nothing to be accomplished beyond this, there is no grasping of material causes; nor is there birth even from that which is restricted, nor is there potentiality, nor is there activity.
Since it is produced in its entirety, there is nothing here that remains to be done; therefore, even the designation of "cause" is not tenable.
And every means that has been set forth—which turns back error and produces certainty—is not, in this case, consistent with reason.
Neither doubt nor error can be removed, since they are ever-present; nor is there the arising of certainty for that very reason. Therefore, everything [else] is in vain.
Even if a certainty regarding what has not yet occurred were to arise from a means of proof, would not all these [means] thereby become fallacious?

If it is argued that the unmanifest becomes manifest for those [beings], what is its manifestation? It cannot be the production of an excellence of form, because there is no differentiation and no connection.
There is neither cognition of that object nor the destruction of the veil over perception; for perception is eternal, and a second [perception] is impossible.
Just as, despite the non-difference of the three guṇas, not everything is the cause of everything, so too, despite the non-existence [of the effect], not everything is the cause of everything.
Since their limit is not established, those powers are not restricted; however, if they were existent, it would be logical for them to have a restriction that possesses a limit.

It is not so; let there be no [denial] of sound on account of the non-establishment of those [attributes], nor of anything else. For there is no injury to the nature of the reality as it is, when divested of all adventitious adjuncts.

For names and forms do not constitute the reality of things, nor are conceptual constructions and designations [the reality], since manifold conceptualizations proceed according to habituation toward that which is undifferentiated.
Arising is indeed the existence of a thing; it is not connected with what is non-existent, nor likewise with what is existent, but only with a conceptualizing mind that perceives it as non-existent.

That which is perceived as the form of an object immediately after [its destruction], such that "it did not exist before," is its seed; however, this [seed] does not exist when the [object] has already come into being.

And as for the view that curds and so forth exist in milk and other substances in the form of a potentiality (śakti): what is this potentiality there? If it were visible, it would be like the milk itself.
If it were something else, how could one thing be said to exist through the non-existence of another? For the existence of sattva is not the existence of rajas and tamas.

The manifest [world] is not established for us in any way as being followed by *sattva* and the other [guṇas], because pleasure and the rest are internal, and their manifestation consists in self-awareness (*svasaṃvid*).

Furthermore, within a single object such as sound and so forth, attachment and other [mental states] are clearly observed to occur with necessity, due to the distinctions between mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and innate disposition (*jāti*).

If consciousness were to fall under a single object, it would follow that it is variegated; if you say this is not so because of the influence of the unseen (adṛṣṭa) and other factors, then it could not be a follower of the object.

The form of an object possesses three aspects, yet the cognitions that know it have only a single aspect; how, then, can those future cognitions—which are distinct from the object—be logically connected to it?
For yogins, serenity, agitation, and obstruction arise with respect to a single person; yet such a person is not accepted as [the ultimate] Self by others.

Even if the manifest world consisting of the three qualities (guṇas) were established, the Pradhāna would not be proven; for that [Pradhāna] is held to be a single, eternal cause, whereas this [world] is not endowed with a single genus.
For all individual manifestations are seen to be like iron rods, their forms joined together only in succession, and their very nature is permeated by conceptual construction.

Likewise, the various modifications such as jars and the like do not possess a single common genus, nor are they established as having a single cause, due to their distinction from the lump of clay and other such factors.

Even though they are endowed with consciousness and other qualities, it is not admitted that persons have a single prior origin; if you claim that [their unity] is secondary, why is it not the same in this case as well?

Even in the absence of a primary cause (pradhāna), everything is conceptualized from that [consciousness]; through the differentiation of its powers, there arises the diversity of cause and effect and so forth.

Even in the absence of a primary cause (pradhāna), everything is conceptualized from that [consciousness]; through the differentiation of its powers, there arises the diversity of cause and effect and so forth.
Others declare the Lord to be the cause of all things that possess the quality of being produced; for it is said that what is insentient cannot, of its own accord, initiate its own effects.
Others declare that the Lord is the cause of all things that come into being; for it is said that what is insentient cannot, of its own accord, initiate its own effects.

Whatever possesses a specific arrangement of its own constituent parts is understood to have an intelligent cause, just like a jar or similar objects. Such subjects of dispute—whether perceptible by two senses or imperceptible—are preceded by an intelligent agent; thus, by way of dissimilarity, atoms are considered [not to be so].

The appropriation of the principles (tattvas) and so forth is presided over by an intelligent agent, because they possess form and other qualities, just as threads and the like are seen to produce their own effects [only when supervised].
All atoms of dharma and adharma, presided over by a conscious being, remain as initiators of their own effects through activity, like threads in a loom.
And at the beginning of creation, the linguistic usage of persons arises from the instruction of others, because it is restricted, like the usage of children.

The manifest world, beginning with the great elements, being presided over by an intelligent cause, serves as the cause of pleasure and pain for the entire world; because of such reasons as its insentience, its being an effect, and its perishability, all of this is clearly understood from it, just like an axe or similar tools.
And once his status as the creator of all things is established, his omniscience is proven without effort; for he who is the creator must be a knower of the nature and form of the effects.
An object that is the locus of dispute is clearly perceived by someone, because it is a real entity and so forth, just like the distinction between pleasure, pain, and the like.

Therefore, in this case, the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*) in the first proof, because neither the so-called "arrangement" (*sanniveśa*) called "yoga" nor a "composite whole" (*avayavin*) is established in that manner.
Because the two things accepted as being visible are not perceived, this example is also devoid of the probans.
Visual consciousness and tactile consciousness arise with distinct appearances; they do not share a single object, just like the cognitions of odor and so forth.

The synthesizing consciousness (*pratisandhāna-vijñāna*), whose nature follows conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) arising through the power of those [sensory perceptions], determines the aggregate. Therefore, this [aggregate] such as water or fire does not exist as something graspable by two sense-faculties; thus, because the subject (*dharmin*) as it has been described is unestablished, there is the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*).

If that very same kind of specific arrangement which is observed in temples and the like—whereby the cognition of an intelligent agent arises even when the agent is not perceived—is seen in subjects such as bodies and so forth, then it is proper that this [arrangement] should serve as a means of proving the desired [agent].

The logical principle is established that when a certain effect is ascertained to belong to a certain cause through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), the certainty [of that cause] arises from the perception of that [effect]. However, no such specific arrangement exists among these [living bodies] as it does in the case of various differences such as bodies and trees; there is merely the word [“arrangement”] being applied to them. When such a term is employed, it incurs the fallacy of a doubtful negative concomitance (sandigdha-vyatirekatā), since [the alleged cause] is absent in things like anthills, which are not made by potters and the like.

Is this not a futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*), since it arises from a conceptual differentiation of properties? For it has been established that the probans, such as "being an effect," is indeed a universal (*sāmānya*).
The mere entity, as excluded from what is not of that nature, establishes impermanence through identity; there is no other logical method for this proof.
Smoke, being white, is observed to be invariably concomitant with fire; however, from the mere fact of having the designation "white," there is no cognition of that [fire] even in the case of snow.
But when a general logical connection is established and a specific instance is invoked as a challenge, that is cited as a "futile rejoinder" (jātyuttara).
The possession of horns by the quarters and other such things would be established merely from their being denotable by the word "cow," if this principle were not otherwise accepted.
If, however, no contradiction can be established against this means of valid cognition, then since it is established here by reasoning, there is no dispute for anyone.

However, [the argument] that there exists a single eternal omniscient being who is the substratum of eternal cognition does not achieve proof, because the pervasion is absent due to the deficiency of the probandum in the example.
For instance, palaces, staircases, gate-towers, watchtowers, and so forth, are ascertained to be preceded by many impermanent cognitions.
For this very reason, even though it thwarts what is desired, this [reason] is considered acceptable, because it establishes that [the world] is preceded by multiple, non-eternal cognitions.
For you have asserted a necessary connection only with respect to an intelligent cause in general; however, regarding the second [type of cause], we state it quite clearly.
Because of the contradiction between succession and non-succession, eternal entities do not produce effects. Since objects possess succession, there is likewise succession in the cognitions of them.
The knowledge of God arises sequentially because it is connected with sequential objects of cognition, just like the cognition of Devadatta and others which has as its object a flame and so forth.

We maintain that things such as jars are merely an aggregation of atoms; therefore, the potter and other such agents are merely the makers of those atoms. Consequently, no property excluded from that [atom] is intended as the probandum (sādhya) by virtue of this example of atoms, which has been presented through its dissimilar instance (vaidharmya).
If it is asserted in a general sense that [the world] is preceded by an intelligent being, we have no dispute at all; for the manifold diversity [of the world] is indeed born of karma.

In proving that [the world] is preceded by a single eternal intellect, there is a lack of the probandum [in the example]; furthermore, there is deviation, since palaces and the like are seen to be constructed by many [agents].
This very same refutation should be applied as appropriate to the remaining reasons; furthermore, some slight additional point is now being elucidated.

The activity of atoms and other such entities is not established as occurring while they remain stable, because of their momentary destruction; moreover, there is a deviation [from the rule] by that very fact, since even those [atoms] possess sequential activity.

Persons whose consciousness and memory have been lost during the dissolution of the world are not [the same as those] for us, because they arise here from that very source through their birth in the Ābhāsvara heaven and other realms.

If the status of being an instructor for one who is averse [to the truth] is to be accepted solely on the basis of faith, then that aversion arises from the inability to distinguish between dharma and adharma due to a lack of discernment.
Furthermore, there is a contradiction with inference because pervasion must exist everywhere in a proof; for a reason cannot be conceived as being pervaded by a contradictory property.
A Lord is not the cause of living beings because he lacks the capacity for origination, like a sky-lotus; otherwise, everything would arise simultaneously.

Alternatively, those things that arise sequentially cannot have God as their cause, just like the cognitions of insentient beings produced by the aforementioned means. If they too were produced by Him, the designation of "means" would be useless; for since He is eternal and thus beyond treatment, such a means could never be a cooperative factor for Him.

When certain things exist, your [effect] is observed, and when they do not exist, it is never observed; why then do you not fall into an infinite regress by postulating other causes for those [conditions]?
Furthermore, by the refutation of agency, omniscience is also rejected; for it must be understood that the establishment of omniscience depends precisely upon that [agency].

Even if the proofs were not corrupted by the aforementioned defects, the oneness of the creator would still not be established, because of the demonstration of deviation. And if the single creator is not proven, what basis is there for his omniscience? If that [single creator] is proven, then the proof stated among the followers of Jaimini shines forth.
The means for establishing that [truth] has been proclaimed; it shines forth among the followers of Jaimini.
Since the causality of both primordial matter (prakṛti) and the Lord (īśvara) has been thus refuted, neither of them—neither individually nor together—is the creator of these living beings.
Since the causality of both primordial matter (prakṛti) and the Lord (īśvara) has thus been refuted individually and together, neither of these two is the creator of these living beings.

It is postulated that the "conjunction" (*sāhitya*) between these two arises from their acting together; this [conjunction] would exist either through the conferring of an excellence (*atiśaya*) or through the performance of a single purposeful action (*ekārthakriyā*). The first postulation is not tenable because those two [causes] are immutable (*nirvikāra*); nor is the second [tenable] because it would entail the simultaneity of all effects.

Now it is said that the threefold nature of *pradhāna* is established; therein, when joined with *rajas*, Maheśvara is the cause of creation. But when he again resorts to *sattva* whose activity has become manifest, then he becomes the instrumental cause for the maintenance of the entire world. When he is joined with *tamas* in the form of its manifested power, then indeed he brings about the dissolution of the whole universe. Thus, these forms such as *rajas*, *sattva*, and so forth, act as its auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*) in a sequential manner; therefore, there is no lack of sequence in the effects.

To this it is replied: At the time of the single activity of those two, does there exist the capacity to produce their other effects, or does that not exist? If it exists, then even at the time of creation, both [other effects] would come to be; likewise, if another were present, it would follow that yet another pair would arise.
For that [cause], in its form as another, cannot again be the producer of something else; and since its own nature is precisely that, how could there be a cessation of its activity?
But when deprived of that capacity, it could not produce that [effect] at all, because it would then be devoid of power, like a sky-lotus and the like.
If that which is intense and of the nature of power were the cause consisting of the subtle elements (tanmātra), it would exist at all times, because its cause, being eternal, is ever-present.

Nor is it desired by others to be produced by a non-sequential [cause]; therefore, it does not arise from anything else either. Nor is this [arising] independent, because its occurrence is only occasional.

If an entity existed by itself, it would be causeless, because it is contradictory for something to act upon itself; for it is through dependence that the occasional occurrence of entities becomes possible.
For indeed, no activity within its own self is admitted for a non-entity, since even this [non-entity], once established, is recognized as existing in that very state.
But one whose nature has not been realized does not engage in any activity whatsoever, because of being devoid of all causal power, like a sky-lotus and the like.
But one whose nature is unestablished does not engage in any activity whatsoever, because it is devoid of all causal power, like a sky-lotus and the like.

The proponents of the doctrine of intrinsic nature (svabhāvavādins) describe the birth of entities as being independent of all causes; for they do not even admit that [the entity] itself is its own cause.

The proponents of the doctrine of intrinsic nature (svabhāvavādins) describe the birth of entities as being independent of all causes; for they do not even admit that the entity itself is its own cause.
For who indeed creates the variety of the lotus filaments and so forth? Or by whom was the variegated eye-pattern on a peacock's tail fashioned?
Just as the sharpness and other qualities of thorns and the like are without cause because they occur only occasionally, so too are suffering and the rest without cause.

When the seeds, mud, water, and so forth—overcome by specific states and characterized by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) like the filaments of a lotus—are ascertained through perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*) to be the causes [of the lotus], why then is another cause for these being asked about?

How can there be restriction of place and time for entities? If these were not their causes, they would exist everywhere and at all times. Yet, since they occur only in certain places, at certain times, and in certain instances, they are restricted; they depend upon those [specific conditions] by way of excluding everything else.
Dependence upon that [cause] and functioning in such a manner is called "dependence" and "being an effect. Since such functioning is directly perceived, the reasons [cited] here are established.
This doctrine of intrinsic nature is sublated by direct perception, because the nature of the cause is ascertained through both perception and non-perception.

Or let there be no existence of means of valid cognition for the sake of establishing the existence of the reason; nevertheless, the non-existence of an object is certainly not established by the mere absence of a means of valid cognition.

Because the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is neither the pervader nor the cause of the existence of an object, due to the existence of difference [between them], due to deviation, and because it arises from that [object].
And for that entity which is not of such a nature, there is no exclusion [of others] by way of its own cessation; rather, the exclusion of another is understood through an absolute non-connection.

Non-perception by everyone is doubtful, while non-perception by oneself is inconclusive; for even though [certain things] such as dūrvā grass in a hole on the Vindhya mountain are not perceived, they nonetheless exist.

If a reason is not employed for the sake of establishing causelessness, then there is no proof lacking a means of valid cognition; therefore, your thesis is not established. And if a reason were employed for its establishment, even so it would not [establish it], because since that proof is produced by a cause, your thesis is thereby contradicted.
For instance, a reason that makes known, or a statement that illuminates it, is called a "knower of the probandum" (sādhyajñāpaka) when it serves as the cause for its establishment.
Therefore, this very probans is called an "informative" (jñāpaka) cause; however, because it does not produce the probandum, it is not manifested as a "productive" (kāraka) cause.
Therefore, other entities as well must have causes, since their arising is restricted; just as, for you, the cognition whose object is the thing to be proven arises from its means of accomplishment.
Therefore, other entities as well possess causes, because their birth is restricted; just like the cognition regarding the object to be proven, which arises for you from its means of accomplishment.
The supreme Brahman, consisting of sound, is untouched by destruction or origination; it is its transformation that is perceived as this multitude of entities.
The supreme Brahman, consisting of sound, is untouched by destruction or origination; this entire collection of entities is perceived as its transformation.

Those who assert this should also be asked: does this [word] abandon its own nature as a sound-form and assume the state of being blue and so forth, or not? If the first alternative is accepted, then there would be a loss of its imperishable nature (*akṣaratva*) due to the destruction of its prior self. But if the latter alternative is held, then in the cognition of blue and so forth, there would clearly be a cognition of the word-nature itself, even for one who has not heard it.
By which everything consisting of sound is established in its primary sense, through the designation of transformation while not abandoning the nature of sound.
Since the non-figurative oneness of blue and other [objects] is thus established, why is it that at the time of their cognition, there is no cognition of this [oneness]?

For if this [cognition] were not cognized, there would be no awareness even of blue and so forth; for if they possessed distinct properties while being of a single nature, an absolute difference would follow.

For the association with contradictory properties is indeed the defining characteristic of difference among many things; otherwise, even an imagined [difference] would not exist between individual manifestations.
And if it is maintained that the single essence of the word is distinct for every individual cognition, then all [cognitions] would occupy the same location and possess a single form.

If, however, there were a difference in this [Brahman] with respect to each individual manifestation, it would follow that Brahman is manifold, because its nature would consist of distinct and multiple entities, just like the difference between the individuals themselves.

Furthermore, if entities were composed of eternal sound, they too would be eternal; since their existence would be established as simultaneous [with that sound], transformation (pariṇāma) is not tenable.
For transformation is established in cases such as clay and the like, where one form disappears and another form arises; however, it cannot occur in that which is devoid of succession.
Furthermore, even if the world consists of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman) in the form of its effects, nevertheless, because it is changeless, there can be no sequential emergence from it.
Since it arises from a single nature as various distinct forms, how indeed can it be said that it has unfolded into the form of objects?

Because clay is perceived as having a nature that is excluded from what is not of that form, a single essence of clay is postulated here amidst the various differences such as jars, bowls, and the like. However, no such perception occurs regarding entities such as blue, yellow, and so forth; therefore, even the conceptualization [of them] as being excluded from what is non-auditory is without foundation.
Now, this reality of Brahman remains eternally undivided; yet, due to the affliction of ignorance, the world perceives it as manifold.

Even there, form is perceived by people overwhelmed by ignorance as blue and so forth, serving as the basis for rejection and acceptance. Apart from that form, how could the unperceived nature of Brahman be recognized as existing by those whose minds have emerged [from meditative absorption]?

That [unity] is not established through perception, because it does not appear as undivided; nor is there an inferential mark consisting of an effect, since production from an eternal entity is impossible. Furthermore, because the existence of the subject (*dharmin*) is not established, an essential nature (*svabhāva*) cannot be a proving factor; and apart from these, there is no other mark that establishes its existence.

Knowledge is established through the sequence of the objects of knowledge; otherwise, everything would be simultaneous. If that effect were to occur simultaneously, it would follow that consciousness is produced all at once. Even in the case of mere cognition, its form does not exist beyond that [moment]; therefore, it follows that such a cognition is equivalent to the son of a barren woman.
Even yogins whose mental continuum is purified do not perceive that form of Brahman, because their cognition is engaged with and conjoined to it.
The view of Brahman as being identical with the transformation of the Pradhāna is to be understood here as being subject to the same refutation that applies to that [Sāṃkhya] doctrine.

The vision of Brahman as being identical with the transformation of primordial matter (pradhāna) is to be understood here as being refuted by the same arguments used to refute that [Sāṅkhya] position.

Others, however, whose intellects follow poorly expounded doctrines, postulate a Puruṣa who shares the nature of Īśvara as the cause of the world; they claim that even during the dissolution of all things, he possesses unimpaired power of knowledge and is the cause of living beings, just as a spider is the source of its threads.

Others, however, whose intellects follow poorly expounded doctrines, postulate a Puruṣa who shares the nature of Īśvara as the cause of the world; they claim that even during the dissolution of all things, he possesses undiminished power of knowledge and is the cause of living beings, like a spider to its threads.
Against this [theory] as well, everything that must be said by way of refutation—just as in the case of the Lord (Īśvara)—should be stated: for what purpose does he perform such an activity as this?

If [the world] were not independent because it was impelled by another, then he might create the world out of compassion as being exclusively happy; yet, for one who creates beings afflicted by various hardships such as mental anguish, poverty, and grief, what compassion can be perceived?
Before creation, since those to be pitied do not exist, compassion itself is not possible—that through the connection with which this Creator is postulated.

Moreover, He would not bring about the dissolution of those who are always engaged in spiritual prosperity; for if His action were dependent upon that unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), His sovereignty would be lost.
And for what purpose would he depend upon an unseen cause of suffering? On the contrary, indifference toward that [cause] is appropriate for him when he is possessed of compassion.
If his activity were for the sake of play, he would not be the master of that play, because of his dependence on various means of play, just like a child.

Furthermore, regarding that pleasure which is to be accomplished through play and whatever means there may be for it—if he were capable of performing all of that simultaneously, yet were unable to do so even sequentially, then he could not have been capable at the outset; for it is not possible for a single entity to possess both capacity and incapacity without being divided.

Now, if its activity at the beginning of creation is described as being due to its own inherent nature—just as fire and other elements possess by their very nature the capacity for actions such as burning—then all things would arise simultaneously, because the causes endowed with the power to produce them would be present together.

Potencies produced by the power of their own causes are indeed restricted; they do not manifest at all times in things such as fire and the like. Otherwise, every effect would arise simultaneously, if this restriction were not admitted even for those [causes].

Even in the case of the spider, its status as the cause of its threads is not accepted as being due to its own nature; rather, it produces the web of saliva out of a craving for devouring living beings.
If his conduct were merely arbitrary, what kind of intelligence would he possess? For even a dog does not act without first considering its purpose.
Even those who are postulated as creators, such as Śauri, Ātmaja, and others, are in reality refuted by this very same method.
Even those who are postulated as creators, such as Śauri, Ātmaja, and others, are in reality refuted by this very same method.

Others, however, maintain here that the self (ātman) is the substratum of desire and the like; that it is by nature insentient (acid-rūpa), eternal, and likewise all-pervading; and that it is the agent of good and evil deeds as well as the enjoyer of their fruits. It is conscious through its association with consciousness, but not by its own essential nature. Its agency is said to consist in its connection with knowledge, effort, and so forth; while its state of being an enjoyer is the inherence (samavāya) of the cognition of pleasure, pain, and the like. Birth is designated for it as the conjunction with a particular class [of body] and with unprecedented cognitions and sensations. Death, conversely, is the separation from those previously acquired [faculties]. Life, moreover, is the conjunction of the mind with the body, brought about by merit and demerit. Violence is attributed to this [self] through the destruction of the body, eyes, and so forth. In this manner, even though the person is eternal, this process is observed in its pure form.

Others, however, maintain here that the self is the substratum of desire and the rest; that it is by nature insentient, eternal, and likewise all-pervading; the agent of auspicious and inauspicious actions and the enjoyer of their fruit; and that it is sentient through its association with consciousness, but not so by its own essential nature. Its agency is said to consist in its connection with knowledge, effort, and so forth; while its state as an enjoyer is the inherence of the cognition of pleasure, pain, and the like. Birth is designated for it as the conjunction with a specific class of unprecedented cognitions and sensations; death is the separation from those previously acquired; and life is the union of the mind with the body, brought about by merit and demerit. Furthermore, violence is attributed to it through the destruction of the body, eyes, and other organs. Thus, this process is observed even in the case of the eternally pure person.
And my cognitions are to be known by an experiencer distinct from the body and so forth, because they are cognitions, like those [cognitions] of another.

Furthermore, all these [qualities] such as desire and the rest must be dependent upon something; for, while being real entities (*vastu*), they are effects, like color. And that [substratum] is, for us, the Person (*puruṣa*). Because of the inclusion of the term "being a real entity," this [reason] does not suffer from the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of destruction; for although destruction possesses a cause, it does not possess the nature of a real entity.

All cognitions of form and so forth have both a single and multiple causes, because they are unified by the cognition "this is mine," just like the cognitions of many people regarding the movement of a dancer’s creeper-like eyebrows; otherwise, such unification would not arise, as it would be without a basis.

Because the word "self" (ātman) is considered a single term denoting something distinct from the aggregate of the intellect, sense organs, and so forth; and because it is thus ascertained to be different from established synonyms, it is endowed with the aforementioned property, just like the word "cloth."
If this living body were devoid of the vital breaths and so forth, it would become like a jar due to its lack of self; therefore, it is not the case that it lacks a self.
Every subsequent cognition is known only by that which knows the first [moment of] cognition and so forth; because it is my cognition, just like that first one.
Even though it resides in a distant location, [the soul] is conjoined with my own self, because it possesses a corporeal form consisting of earth and other elements, just like our own body.
And thus, when the permanence, omnipresence, and existence of sentient beings have been definitively established, it remains that all phenomena are not devoid of a self.

Therefore, regarding the first proof here, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because it is accepted that your own cognition is knowable by an omniscient being and others.
And its own conscious nature arises independent of an illuminator; likewise, the cognition of another [object] is an illustration that is devoid of anything to be established.
If that which is cognized by another [cognition] colored by the form of that [object] were to serve as its example, there would still be doubt regarding it being [cognized] by something else.

If it is sought to prove that desire and the like possess a substratum in some respect, and if the "substratum" is conceived merely as a cause, then [the conclusion] is already established for us. However, if you maintain that the substratum must be a support, even so, the postulation of a support is useless for that which lacks motion.
A vessel or similar object is established as the substratum for jujube fruits and the like, either by obstructing their movement or by producing a specific change [in their position].
Furthermore, it is not logically tenable for destruction, being formless, to be an effect; therefore, the qualification stated here by the opponents in their reason is redundant.

The connection [of thoughts] expressed as "may I" arises from the affliction of ignorance; for even though all things are momentary, there appears a sense of a single agent and so forth due to false conceptualization. Therefore, the establishment of reality based on this is not tenable. Even that which is distinct due to differences in capacity can serve as a single unifying basis.

If [the mind] were to have as its object a single [preceding moment], the sequence of priority and posteriority would be contradicted, because the minds directed toward form, sound, and so forth, are in proximity to their respective efficient causes.
From a single preceding consciousness, the six consciousnesses arise; they are clearly perceived simultaneously; therefore, this [argument] establishes what is already accepted.

However, it was stated immediately prior that for those things occurring in succession, there can be no single cause; therefore, a clear sublation of this [position] by inference is observed here due to the pervasion [of the reason].
The movement of the creeper-like brow of a dancer is not truly one in the ultimate sense; because it is a collection of many atoms, its oneness is merely conceptualized.

For us, words such as *buddhi*, *citta*, and so forth, do not denote something distinct [from consciousness], even though they appear as separate words; this is because they are synonyms. Therefore, the reason [you have provided] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). But was it not stated that there is a qualification [to exclude such cases]? It is replied: No, for that [qualification] is not established, since we maintain that these are indeed synonyms. By way of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), the mind (*citta*) is called the "self" (*ātman*) because it is the locus of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*); however, in terms of ultimate reality (*vastuvṛtti*), no such object [as a self] exists.
Since a single word such as "agent" (kāraka) and so forth is applied to things like the lotus in the sky, a deviation [from the rule] is also observed.

Where are words, which exist merely as conventions, not applicable? Nor do words such as "self" (ātman) and so forth possess an inherent capacity to illuminate a [specific] meaning by their very nature.

If the connection of the vital breaths and so forth with the self were established, then this undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) would be appropriate; otherwise, it is incoherent. For the absence of a son of a barren woman does not entail the consequence that his living body exists; likewise, for you as well, this consequence [of the living body existing] follows only from the presence of the vital breaths and so forth.

And thus, since the self and sentient beings are not established by any of these means of proof, the example cited for [the properties of] permanence and omnipresence is devoid of the probandum (*sādhyahīna*).
Others have postulated that the self is established through direct perception; for they hold that the "I-notion" (ahaṅkāra), which is self-cognized, has the self as its object.

Therefore, that [claim] is incorrect, because that form does not appear in the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra). For the manifestation of permanence, omnipresence, and so forth is not observed there; rather, the manifestation of a fair complexion and the like is clearly found therein. Yet the Self is not accepted as having such a nature; therefore, this [ego-sense] is not its object.
If the person were truly accessible through direct perception, then for what purpose would this dispute regarding his existence and so forth proceed?

For this ego-consciousness (ahaṅkāra) functions as having the nature of certainty; and between the cognitions of certainty and superimposition, the relationship of sublated and sublator is established.

Therefore, all [states] such as desire do not inhere in a self, because they arise sequentially, like a seed, a sprout, and a creeper. Alternatively, all internal [phenomena] have their forms pervaded by selflessness, due to reasons such as being functional entities, just like external objects such as pots.

For if they possessed a self-nature, it would follow that their causes are eternal; and since eternal things are incapable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), existence and other such properties cannot possibly arise from them.
Since the absence of self (nairātmya) is equally [denied] by others in the case of jars and other such things, we establish that very same absence of self in this living body.
And thus, since the self is not established, every process that has been formulated regarding it stands entirely without foundation, like the son of a barren woman.
Others, however, maintain that the self consists of both exclusion and inclusion, and that its nature is consciousness, wherein consciousness is characterized by the intellect (*buddhi*).

Just as the coiled state of a serpent departs and is immediately followed by its straightened state, yet its nature as a serpent persists; even so, for the Self whose nature is eternal consciousness, there is neither a total disappearance of its form nor a persistence of every [transient] state. Rather, its states characterized by pleasure, pain, and the like cease and arise, while consciousness itself persists.

For if this [self] were to undergo absolute destruction, there would be the loss of what has been done and the acquisition of what has not been done; moreover, the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth could not occur for that which is of a single, unchanging nature.
Moreover, agency and enjoyership do not reside in the states themselves; rather, because the person is the substrate of those states, it is the agent who alone obtains the fruit thereof.
This person is thus established as being of such a nature through the existence of recognition; indeed, by this very means, the doctrine of selflessness is refuted.

The notion of "I" (ahaṃbuddhi), as in "I know," refers to a knower. That [knower] must be either the Self (ātman) or knowledge that is absolutely transitory. If the Self were its object, then everything would be perfectly consistent. However, in the view that knowledge is momentary, everything becomes utterly untenable. For instance, regarding the cognition that arises: "I myself knew previously, and I myself now know"—what indeed can be conceived as the object of this [cognition]? Is it the past [knowledge], the present, or perhaps the continuum (santati)? In the first case, if the past knowledge were the object, it would be appropriate to say "I have known," but it would not be appropriate to say "I know," because that [past knowledge] does not know at the present time. If, however, the present [knowledge] were the object, it would be logical to say "I know," but "I have known" would be untrue, since this [present knowledge] did not exist previously. Therefore, it cannot be maintained that both [the past and present] are the objects of that [notion]. For neither of them has "known" previously, nor do they both "know" now. Nor is the continuum (santāna) its object, because both [individual moments] are impossible [to be so]; for it [the continuum] did not "know" previously—since it is not a real entity—and it does not [know] now. Consequently, this ego-notion (ahaṃkāra) must reside in an object other than those mentioned; thus, the Self is established as being of an eternal nature.

The knower, who is beyond the grasp of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), persists even now; because he is accessible through the notion of "I," just like the cognizer of the present moment. Or rather, this very knower of yesterday exists [today] because he possesses the nature of being a knower, just like the knower of yesterday; and thus, the probandum for those cognitions is established.
Because they are all "I-notions" belonging to a knower connected by a single continuum, all [notions] of yesterday and today have the same object, just like a single cognition.
In this regard, it is considered that consciousness is held to be eternal and unitary; if that were so, then the intellect (buddhi) would also necessarily be of that same nature.
Since both the intellects and the Puruṣa possess the inherent nature of consciousness, they are eternal and unitary; if there is any distinction, it resides in their respective objects.
Likewise, fire, by its very nature, is eternally characterized by the property of burning; it burns the combustible object brought near to it, and nothing else, nor at any other time.

Just as a clear mirror or a crystal stone assumes the reflection of whatever is placed before it, even so do the persons, who are eternally conscious and abide within the body, perceive forms and other objects brought to them by the instruments; and this, O wise one, is our view.

Therefore, because it is subject to disruption by the agitation of the one who leads [the mind], the intellect is transitory; just as fire, though eternally burning, does not burn in the absence of fuel.

In that regard, cognition is recognized as being essentially of the nature of awakening; its status as the cognitions of jars, elephants, and so forth is accepted by the world due to its apparent differentiation.
Those who follow the distinction between objects do not say that it is "that very same" cognition; nor is there a lack of recognition when a difference in objects is maintained.
Indeed, when there is ground devoid of elephants and the like, what is the basis for the distinction among those cognitions that arise as superimpositions?

If individual instances occurring in other places and so forth were the basis [for cognition], then everything would have as its objective support an entity characterized by a different place and time.
But surely, those [cognitions] do not actually possess a connection with that place; why then do they appear there in that form?

For in your view, the form does not belong to the cognition; rather, it is described as being external. Furthermore, elephants, staffs, and so forth do not exist at the location intended [by the cognition].
And if cognition, whose nature is the awakening to all objects, were always present, why is there not a simultaneous awareness of everything at all times?

If it is argued that the cognition which has sound as its adjunct is indeed the same [cognition] that has taste, color, and so forth as its object, this is not so; for you yourself have established their difference.
Even fire, though its nature is burning, does not eternally consume all combustible forms; otherwise, everything would be reduced to ashes without remainder.
It is logical that its nature as a burner of that [fuel] exists only when the object to be burned is present; for otherwise, it would follow that all objects would be burned simultaneously.

Due to their connection with blue lotuses and other objects, mirrors, crystals, and the like are momentary; they are the causes for the production of the illusion of those reflections. Otherwise, since it would be a single entity remaining the same in both states—with and without the adjunct—either it would always appear as having that reflection, or it would always appear devoid of it.
Because it is stable, indivisible, and because material objects cannot coexist [within it], the surface of a mirror never bears a reflection.
And those situated on both sides perceive the crystal stone as perfectly white; thus, even this [crystal] has not acquired the shadow [of the object].
Otherwise, it would follow that the crystal and other such objects possess distinctness and change with every substrate; this would be the case if its assumption of their reflection were real.
Therefore, this error exists regarding those [Buddhas] who possess diverse and inconceivable powers;
however, even the state of error is not logical in relation to the Buddha, because of his freedom from differentiation.
However, by superimposing upon all cognitions a commonality consisting in the absence of the nature of awareness, recognition proceeds even though there is diversity.

Even though the self is absolutely established as empty of any distinction caused by the difference between states, that which is imagined by others regarding this stable self is as follows: "Even while passing through states such as pleasure and pain, my person never abandons the nature of consciousness, substantiality, existence, and so forth."
And upon the arising of another state, the preceding one does not perish absolutely; rather, it dissolves into the nature of the universal for the sake of conforming to the subsequent state.
For the various states are mutually contradictory in their own specific forms; however, that which is of the nature of a universal is perceived as non-contradictory throughout all of them.
In that case, if there were not an absolute distinction between the states and the person, then upon the destruction and arising of those [states], those two would likewise belong to him as well.
But when there is a conjunction of contradictory properties, a difference must be absolute, just as it exists for persons by virtue of their own individual, fixed natures.

If, according to your view, the states [of consciousness] dissolve into the person (puruṣa) by their very own nature, then suffering and the rest would also be experienced at the time of the arising of pleasure and the rest.
Furthermore, when there is a transition into another form, a transition into something else is not possible; and if the transition were by way of identity, then the self would be subject to arising.
If agency and enjoyership do not depend upon a state at all, then, because of the reality of that which possesses the state, agency and so forth would be impossible.
The fact that the Self is denotable by the word "eternal" is not denied; however, its cessation does occur because it possesses modifications of its own nature.

Even a serpent undergoes crookedness and other states because of its momentary nature; however, in a permanent entity, there can be no transition to another state, as would be the case with a [supposedly] eternal person (puruṣa).
This ego-sense indeed proceeds without any objective support; for it arises only in certain instances through the power of the seed of the beginningless perception of a sentient being.
For only certain conditioned factors (saṃskāra) attain sovereignty over that which determines its own form; this does not apply to all [factors].

This same objection applies equally [to you] regarding the person (*puruṣa*) if it were otherwise; however, because the distinction of its powers exists, everything is entirely free from confusion for you.

But if the position were that [the self] has an eternal object, then all acts of ego-conception would arise simultaneously, because a potent cause is established as being constantly present. Even if it had impermanent objects, subsequent [acts of ego-conception] would be clearly manifest; thus, they pointlessly question the existence of the actual object.

Recognition can produce a latent impression (vāsanā) regarding the knower; it cannot produce the cognition "this is that" regarding what is not that, for such [a cognition] is not the cause of error. If it is claimed that the notion of "I" is not accepted as an error because it lacks sublation, that is not so, because its sublation has been demonstrated by the reasoning just stated.
How do the various delusions regarding Ishvara and other objects—such as [the belief that He is] their cause—arise for devotees, given that they exist merely as mental impressions (vāsanā)?

And when non-referentiality is thus established in the ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*), then no cognizer whatsoever exists as something graspable by the notion of "I. Consequently, among all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*) that possesses [the required] proof; and the logical reasons (*hetu*) are unestablished in their substratum (*āśrayāsiddha*), as has been illustrated according to the circumstances.

Others consider consciousness to be distinct from the nature of the intellect; they postulate that consciousness is the innate form of the Self. It alone enjoys the fruit presented by primordial matter (pradhāna); it possesses no agency at all—such is their view, according to which agency belongs to primordial matter alone.

In that case as well, how could the forms of cognitions regarding color, sound, and so forth be experienced? If a single consciousness is asserted [to be the object], then its distinct forms would be clearly manifest as differentiated.
And if consciousness were of a single form and remained constant at all times, how indeed could its state of being the enjoyer of various kinds of objects be logically possible?
Desire to see and the other [faculties] do not exist as distinct entities that serve as the basis for his experience; for if they were so, the person would be subject to birth.

For there exists no such thing as the desire to see and so forth apart from consciousness; if that [desire] were subject to arising and passing away, then that [instability] would be unavoidable for the person (puruṣa) as well.
If neither auspicious nor inauspicious karma were performed by the self, then from where would this variety of its experiences arise?
If nature bestows [the fruit] in accordance with one's desire, then this relationship between the two is established like that of the lame man and the blind man.
If this is so, and even when there is a desire for what is wished for, it is not accomplished, why is it that primordial nature (prakṛti) does not depend on anything else at all?

And if there is no modification in him at the time of enjoying objects, he would not possess the status of an enjoyer, nor would primordial nature (prakṛti) be a benefactor to him. Furthermore, if modification were to exist, his eternity would be lost; for modification is indeed a change of state, and how could that occur if he remains in the same condition?

It might be thought: "In the beginning, the intellect (buddhi) evolves assuming the form of the object; the person (puruṣa) then apprehends the object as determined by that [intellect]. And thus, through the medium of the arising of a reflection, his status as an enjoyer is established. Yet this person never abandons his own essential nature."

It is said that when a reflection arises through identity with [the original], that alone constitutes the state of being associated with emergence; however, in the case of a distinction [between them], there is no status as an enjoyer.

Primal Matter (pradhāna) proceeds toward activity by conforming to the desire to see [the Puruṣa] and other such factors; otherwise, how could that which is insentient in nature produce such a variety of diverse arrangements?
It knows how to prepare the primary ingredients, the condiments, and so forth, yet it does not know how to eat; what could be more unreasonable than this?

If it is argued that because the *pradhāna* possesses intelligence (*buddhimattva*), everything is consistent for it, then by virtue of that intelligence, sentience (*caitanya*) would necessarily follow, just as it does in the case of the *puruṣas*. For "intellect" (*buddhi*), "ascertainment" (*adhyavasāya*), "consciousness" (*saṃvit*), "the act of cognizing" (*saṃvedana*), "awareness" (*saṃvitti*), and "sentience" (*cetanā*)—all these are synonyms for sentience.

If it is thought that the intellect (buddhi) is insentient by nature, like sound, smell, taste, and so forth, on the grounds of the two reasons of having an origin and being subject to destruction; |||

These two reasons are not established for both parties when an independent proof is intended; nor is there a sublation of the opposite, even if a reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) is what one wishes to state.

Even if the word "self" (ātman) is applied to consciousness (caitanya), there is no harm to our position; however, its permanence is difficult to prove, because the sense organs and so forth must have a purposeful result. If eternal consciousness were devoid of the results of the objects of the senses and so on, then fire would have no need for fuel if it were eternal.

Furthermore, as for the fact that the eyes and other [senses] are established as being for the sake of another by means of the reason "because they are composite," like a bed, a seat, and so forth—if it is argued that their purpose is to provide a substrate for something that undergoes change, then this is merely proving what is already accepted, since we also maintain that they are beneficial to consciousness. If, however, you seek to prove that they are beneficial to something that does not undergo change, then the example is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhya-śūnyatā*), because even those things [like beds and seats] are beneficial only to that which is mobile. But if their being for the sake of another is established in a general sense, then the proof is redundant, as it is already established that they are useful to the mind.

Like the followers of Jaimini, the Jainas declare that the person (nara) is characterized by consciousness (cillakṣaṇa), consisting of substance and modes (dravyaparyāya), and having the nature of both exclusion and inclusion (vyāvṛttyanugama).
If even there the substance remains unmodified despite being conjoined with its modes, then no distinction exists for it, and thus it would not be subject to transformation (pariṇāmin).

Oneness is asserted because there is no difference in place, time, and intrinsic nature; however, difference is described due to differences in number, characteristic, name, and purpose. For example, "color and so forth" and "the jar" are distinguished by number and name. The distinction in characteristic and purpose consists in the persistence and exclusion of effects. Thus, substance and mode are not entirely without distinction; for if the substance itself undergoes differentiation through the form of its modes, [it is distinct].
Unity is the non-difference of intrinsic nature; and when that exists, difference is difficult to establish in any way whatsoever, just like the essential nature of synonymous terms.

And thus, when the non-figurative identity of substance and its modifications is established, the substance would become differentiated, just like the nature of the modifications themselves. Alternatively, all those modifications would also possess a pervasive nature, just like the substance, because their identity with the substance is established as being one and the same.
Consequently, no substance such as the self exists that remains constant; for it is non-different from its modes, just like the nature of the modes themselves.
Nor are even any of the modes (paryāyas) subject to arising and passing away, because they are not distinct from the substance (dravya), just like the fixed nature of that very substance.

Therefore, one must either accept that destruction is total (without any continuity) or that everything is permanent; for these two—exclusion and inclusion—cannot both exist within a single, unitary self.
Furthermore, there is no manifestation of a substance that possesses a perceptible form and a nature following through its various states; therefore, it does not exist, like a lotus in the sky.

Those things which are capable of various purposeful actions, which are the causes of cognitions such as "similar," and which fall within the scope of words and concepts based on conventions regarding such objects.
Only the modes (paryāyas), which possess the nature of arising and passing away, are perceived; therefore, selflessness (nairātmya) is clearly and most purely established.
Now, form (rūpa) exists as a fusion of substance and mode; for that is held to be twofold yet partless, like Narasimha.
Is it not the case that the designation "of two forms" is a basis for multiple meanings, since the word *rūpa* denotes intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)?
Even Narasiṃha is neither exclusively one nor is he established as having a dual nature; for he is perceived as being composed of a collection of many atoms.
Furthermore, others maintain that this world, consisting of earth, fire, water, and so forth, is an evolution (vivarta) of eternal consciousness, and that the Self is of the same nature as that.
Nothing endowed with the characteristic of an object of apprehension exists here; therefore, all this is observed as a transformation of consciousness.

However, their view involves a minor fault because of the assertion of permanence; for in the cognitions of form, sound, and so forth, a distinction is clearly perceived. If they were of the nature of a single cognition, then color, sound, taste, and the rest would necessarily be perceived simultaneously, and in a permanent entity, there can be no change of state.
No cognition distinct from the perception of form and so forth is apprehended; since that [cognition] differs at every moment, what remains established as non-different?
No distinction exists between erroneous and non-erroneous cognition within the person, whose nature is that of a single consciousness; how, then, can there be bondage and liberation?

What could a yogi turn away, or what could he accomplish through the practice of yoga? For how could that which is of the nature of such [false] inversion ever be abandoned? Nor could the knowledge of reality be produced, since it is always present by virtue of its identity [with that inversion]. Therefore, this entire practice of yoga would be entirely fruitless.

But some, though considering themselves followers of the Sugata, nevertheless proclaim a self under the designation of "pudgala," which is devoid of being either identical to or different from [the aggregates].

The person (pudgala) is not other than the aggregates (skandhas), because that would entail the views of the non-Buddhist heretics; nor is it non-other, because that would entail its being multiple and so forth. Therefore, its ineffability is correct.

They should be told: "A person (pudgala) does not exist at all in an ultimate sense, because it cannot be described as being either identical to or different from [the aggregates], just like a sky-lotus and so forth."
A real entity never transcends being either different or non-different; however, that which is in reality formless is conceived as inexpressible.

Since the conceptualization of difference and non-difference has a real entity as its basis, it is appropriate that identity, otherness, and so forth cannot be predicated of things that lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). For when there is a negation of a thing in the form "this is not that" regarding a real entity, that [negation] clearly expresses otherness, just as one speaks of another distinct entity. Furthermore, the negation of the state of being "not-that" is itself designated as identity; thus, a real entity does not transcend both identity and difference.
"The person is not other than the aggregates"—this indicates its non-difference; "the aggregate is not the person"—this clearly demonstrates its difference.
For the association with contradictory properties is said to be the difference between entities; does such distinctness not indeed exist between the aggregates and the person?

For in this way, the person (pudgala) is said to be inexpressible in relation to feeling and the other aggregates; whereas form, perception, and the rest are expressible as being either identical to or different from them.
The aggregates of form and so forth are considered to be expressible as impermanent; the person (pudgala), however, is not so, and therefore its distinctness is clear.
The capacity for causal efficiency is the defining characteristic of existence; this is restricted to momentary things alone. Thus, that which is inexpressible lacks the status of a real entity.
But regarding contradictions with the meaning of the scriptures, great-souled ones have exerted themselves; the varied words of the Compassionate One were intended for the refutation of nihilism.

The teaching on the bearer of the burden and so forth is given with a mind directed toward the collection [of aggregates] and the like; and the specific negation [of a self] shines forth for those who hold such views.

The teaching on the bearer of the burden and so forth is given with a mind directed toward the collection [of aggregates] and the like; and the specific negation [of a self] shines forth for those who hold such views.

Alternatively, this effort is being made in the wrong place; for by the very establishment of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and the rest are already refuted. Since there is no distinction between what has been said and what will be said regarding [the categories such as] genus (*jāti*) and so forth, momentary destruction is therefore clearly established for the purpose of negating them.

Alternatively, this effort is being exerted in the wrong place; for by the very establishment of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and the rest are already refuted. Since there is no distinction between what has been said and what will be said regarding genus (*jāti*) and so forth, momentary destruction is clearly established here for the purpose of negating them.
Some maintain that there are two categories of things based on whether they are produced or unproduced; others hold that entities are distinguished by being momentary or non-momentary.
In this regard, all entities that are produced are momentary, because they exist without dependence on anything else with respect to their destruction.

Whatever does not depend upon any other cause with respect to a particular state, that should be known as certain in that regard, because it arises from its own causes in such a manner. For just as a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is independent in producing its own effect, so too all things that are born are independent with respect to their destruction.
Even if this [effect] were to occur at another place or time while being independent, it would not follow that it is independent, because of its dependence on those [other place and time].
Furthermore, all produced things are everywhere independent regarding their destruction, because in every respect, the causes of destruction are incapable of acting upon them.
For thus, a cause of destruction is not logically the producer of a destruction that is non-different from the entity itself, since the entity is produced by its own causes.
Furthermore, when an entity has arisen from its own cause as a partless whole, its very nature cannot be made to perish again by other factors.

But if a destruction named "destruction" were produced as something distinct from the entity itself, then nothing at all would be produced in that entity by other causes; consequently, its perceptibility, causal efficiency, and so forth would persist exactly as before. Furthermore, because it remains in that same state, even its concealment and the like would be logically impossible.
It is incorrect to say that an entity is destroyed by an entity called "destruction," because the same alternatives regarding its identity or difference and so forth apply there as well.

If it is argued that destruction—which consists of both existence and non-existence and is known by other names such as "annihilation"—is produced, then its production is not logically tenable. For if non-existence were an effect, it would follow that it is a real entity, like a sprout and the like, because it would arise through the causal power of a cause despite having an unproduced nature.

In this way, non-existence is established by the rule itself through recourse to exclusion (paryudāsa); yet, there further arises a conceptual construction regarding it, such as its difference [from existence] and so forth.
Now, this negation of action certainly does not produce an entity; nevertheless, the lack of causality is established because the agent loses its status as a cause.

Is it not the case that this destruction does not exist at the time of the entity’s existence, nor before it, nor long after it, but rather immediately following the entity? And thus, being restricted in its timing, this [destruction] is rightly considered to have a cause; for the occurrence of an event at a particular time is refuted in the case of something independent [of causes].

Furthermore, because it exists immediately after a thing, it is logical that it possesses a cause; and because it comes into being after not having existed, it is regarded as just like any other moment.

Furthermore, because it lacks a cause, this [non-existence] would be non-existent, like the son of a barren woman and so forth; or else, it would be eternal like space, since there is no other alternative. If all things were non-existent, they would possess eternity due to their lack of destruction; moreover, the cognition that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are perishable would be without a basis. Even if [non-existence] were eternal, its coexistence with destruction would not be contradictory; yet, the statement that the unborn perishes does not at all conform to reason.

In this regard, what kind of destruction do opponents inquire about? Is it the very entity that has arisen as having the nature of momentary existence, or is it the cessation of the entity's own nature, known as "annihilation"? For in the former inquiry, nothing at all is contradicted.
For that entity which, being momentary, is designated as "destruction," we maintain to be caused; however, because of the absence of any other entity [to be destroyed], it is uncaused.
In such a case, however, there is no state of being produced immediately after another entity, because that which has the nature of a mobile entity arises together with its very existence.
Therefore, because destruction exists, all conditioned phenomena are not eternal; nor does it follow that the cognition "it is destructible" would be without a cause.

But because cessation (*pradhvaṃsa*) is devoid of self-nature (*nairātmya*), it does not possess the property of arising immediately after [an antecedent]; for it lacks the connection with the state of having come into being after not having existed, just like a sky-lotus and the like.
"The meaning conveyed here is simply that 'destruction occurs,' not that 'an entity occurs'; no injunction of anything whatsoever is intended."
For merely by giving someone the name "Bāleya," not every characteristic of a donkey can possibly apply to that person.
Furthermore, when an entity named "destruction" is established, nothing at all arises from that real thing; so what is it that is being negated?

Thus, destruction, which consists in the cessation of an entity, is held to be non-existent because it is a dissociation from the form of a real thing, not because it is of the nature of the absence of an entity.

In this case, even the nature of cessation is not denoted by an injunction; rather, the persistence of a positive entity is what is negated after a moment. Therefore, no established form is prescribed for it, and thus any conceptualization of it as permanent is groundless.

As for those entities such as space that are considered uncreated, they do not exist at all in terms of their actual nature, because they are devoid of causal capacity. Consequently, the conceptual alternatives of being momentary or non-momentary have no footing in them; for it is only a real entity that could be either momentary or otherwise.
For an entity whose nature is to abide for only a moment is called momentary; conversely, an entity that is pervaded by a stable nature is non-momentary.
The nature of a thing that does not endure even for a moment after its arising is called a "moment" (kṣaṇa); that which possesses such a [nature] is considered momentary (kṣaṇika).

And even though there is no difference in the object itself, the expression "this belongs to that" is not contradicted; for a denotative word exists solely through a convention established by mere desire.

However, what is intended to be expressed here is simply an entity that does not persist beyond its arising; in that regard, let either a word accompanied by a suffix or one without a suffix be employed.
But if space, time, and so forth were existent, even then they would not escape this momentary destruction, as if they had been created.

For indeed, all those things which are real are momentary, just as unconditioned phenomena were established immediately prior. Furthermore, you maintain that space, time, God, and so forth are real; however, if they were devoid of momentariness, their reality would not follow. Since stable entities cannot perform causal functions either successively or simultaneously, they are therefore considered to be non-existent.
For effects are delayed due to the absence of their causes; when a capable cause is present, by what could their delay be caused?
Furthermore, even if there exist successive auxiliary causes for that which is eternal, depending upon which it produces a multitude of effects in a sequential manner.

This is true; however, do they become its auxiliaries by being causes of its suitable form, or by performing a single purpose? If they are causes of its suitable form, then that entity would be produced by them. But since its own nature is already established at that time, it cannot be produced. Or, if its own nature were produced, its eternity would be lost. Therefore, if this "excellence" (*atiśaya*) is distinct from it, how can it be the agent?
For when that exists, there is the arising of effects; through its absence, there is non-arising. Thus, it alone is established as the cause.

Even so, by virtue of that connection, it indeed possesses the status of a cause. What kind of connection between those two is intended? It cannot be identity (*tādātmya*), because they are distinct. Nor can it be "arising from that" (*tadutpatti*), because that would entail simultaneity. And consequently, there would be the arising of effects simultaneously.
In that case as well, if there were dependence on another, an infinite regress would result; therefore, an effect cannot be produced even once, because of the lack of a [stable] relationship.

If the relation is inherence (*samavāya*), then this must also be considered: is that which is the inherencer (*samavāyin*) accepted as being a benefactor (*upakārī*) to it, or not? If the first alternative is adopted—that it is a benefactor—then that very production (*tadutpatti*) has been reached; and that too was just refuted immediately above.

Because the conceptual alternatives of difference and non-difference are each individually refuted, the two-fold excellence of that entity becomes excluded.
Since the existence of two categories has been refuted in the examinations of the person (*pudgala*) and so forth, there is no excellence of a dual nature, nor is there any that is neither.

Now, if [the entity] is eternal and does not depend upon auxiliary conditions, even so, being devoid of them, it would not be an agent, like a final cause. This is indeed its own inherent nature that it acts only when those [conditions] are present; therefore, the effect is produced only when they exist, and not at all times.
Let it be so; however, if that very nature which is considered to belong to it in its completeness is also admitted to exist when it is incomplete, then the auxiliary causes would have to be eternal.

Since those [effects] also persist when that which has a nature connected to them exists, if it were otherwise, its unitary form would be lost. Furthermore, even through such dependence, there can be no successive arising of effects; nor is simultaneity desired, because their effects are observed to arise successively.
Having performed all its effects once and for all, it ceases; if that object is of the nature of causal efficiency (*sāmarthya*), its momentary destruction is established.

If it persists in that same form, it would produce the effect yet again; how can efficacy be attributed to that which is of a nature incapable of acting? Because it is devoid of all capacity, like a lotus in the sky, all non-momentary things are non-existent, since power is the defining characteristic of a real entity.
Now, if this definition of reality characterized as causal efficiency were not accepted, then some other definition of the nature of things would have to be pointed out by our opponents.
If the relation with existence is intended as the definition of things, that is not so; for since inherence and the like are unestablished, how could one thing be the definition of another?

Every activity, such as the investigation of objects and so forth, is undertaken by one who seeks purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) and possesses an unconfused mind; it is not done out of madness. Therefore, that which is useful to someone, in some way, at some place, and at some time—it is precisely with respect to that that the determination of existence (*sattāvyavasthiti*) is appropriate. It is the momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) of an object possessing that very nature which is established; and it is with reference to that alone that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is stated as being inclusive of all cases (*sarvopasaṃhārā*).

That which is utterly devoid of causal capacity, being like the son of a barren woman, can never serve as a cause even for the mind of an omniscient being. Since its nature as an effect and so forth is not observed, the wise do not establish its existence without a basis. There is no purpose whatsoever served by proving momentariness in that regard; furthermore, any objection raised against it is fruitless.
