But surely, things such as sky-lotuses possess causal efficiency with respect to being causes of their own cognition; yet these do not exist as real entities.
This cognition regarding such things as a sky-lotus proceeds entirely without an objective basis; it arises solely from the latent impressions of one's own verbal conceptualization.
If non-existence were the cause, [the effect] would arise continuously; for non-existence, being always devoid of distinction, does not depend on anything.

If all things are momentary, how indeed can there be causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)? For the initial auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) cannot bestow any distinction upon one another. Since a thing is already established in its entirety at the moment of its birth, and since there is no such thing as a non-existent entity that has not yet been born, if a distinction were to arise from something lacking distinction, why would the effect not arise [from the very first moment]? Nor can they be distinguished by other factors, for the same objection applies equally to those. Furthermore, this would lead to an infinite regress regarding the clusters of auxiliary causes. Since they do not produce causal efficiency either successively or simultaneously, their reliance on momentariness is therefore useless. Thus, when no excellence (*atiśaya*) is produced by auxiliaries anywhere, the continuum (*santati*) must be admitted to be eternally without distinction. If destruction were causeless, it would have to exist from the very beginning; if it does not exist at first, how could it come to be at the end? If it is held that the existence of things arises from their own causes and that destruction has no other cause, then why should there be any contradiction in their destruction occurring only at certain times?

It is said: in the first stage, these [causes] do not assist one another; however, they become co-operative causes (*sahakārin*) through the performance of a single purposeful action (*ekārthakriyā*). Even though there is no mutual assistance among them, they are not indistinguishable, because they arise from the power of their own respective material causes (*svopādāna*) and are individually producers of the complex (*kalāpa*).
From that time onwards, whatever specific qualities have arisen are produced by Him, because they possess His nature and are subservient to Him.
In this world, things possess fixed and inconceivable powers that arise at every moment; they are not to be questioned, just as the power to burn resides in fire.

However, as for that destruction which consists in the cutting off of the continuum and which has no cause, there is no existence even at its end; thus, its arising is prevented. But the production of shards and the like, which possess different characteristics, does have a cause; yet even that does not arise at the very beginning, because at that time the cause is non-existent.

Momentary entities are of two kinds: some are causes of diminution, such as fire and the like in relation to cold and so forth; others are not of that nature. However, people who have not perceived the true reality imagine a contradiction even in the case of the causal relationship described first, in its various forms. But the relationship of sublated and sublator does not exist in reality at all; for that very reason, it is said that "the apprehension of contradiction" [is merely a conceptual construction].

But surely, recognition arises in the form "this is that very same thing," and while the sensory faculties are functioning, it is free from any wavering or sublation. Therefore, this sublation by perception—which is unavoidable in all arguments put forward for the purpose of establishing momentary flux—inevitably follows.

Recognition, indeed, cannot be established as perception; for while the nature of a real entity is inexpressible, recognition is associated with verbal expression. Furthermore, recognition is erroneous, whereas perception is characterized by its opposite; for recognition functions by determining non-difference even where there is difference in form.
If this [present cognition] were to have as its object a form previously prepared, then it would have arisen previously as well, because of having that same purpose, just like the previous cognition.

And thus, for this reason, it is not held that this [cognition] grasps that object; because it arises at the time of that [object's] cognition, like the cognition of another object. Since it functions toward a distinct form through the determination of non-difference, this [cognition] remains erroneous, like the cognition of a magical ball.

Furthermore, since it operates upon an object for which the action has already been accomplished—just like memory and so forth—it is not logical for this [subsequent cognition] to be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it lacks the essential nature of an instrument (*karaṇa*).

The existence at the present moment was certainly not apprehended by the previous cognition; if there is a distinction in this [present existence] that does not exist in remembrance, then: for remembrance arises regarding merely what was previously cognized as "that," whereas this recognition, "this is that very same thing," is something additional.

And once it is known that [the object] does not exist [at the time of the second cognition], those two—doubt and error—are sublated; thus, recognition indeed attains the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Even if an object has been cognized by other means, it may turn out otherwise through direct perception; however, when an object is already determined by direct perception, there is no possibility for another [means of knowledge] to arise.
For when a matter has been firmly determined by the authority of the eldest, who else could subsequently establish the opposite through other, weaker means?
If you maintain that present non-existence is distinct from prior existence, then the distinction between them has been established by you yourself.

Even if existence is non-different [from the object], how could it be apprehended by a previous cognition? For if that [existence] were not apprehended, it would follow as a consequence that the object itself was not perceived.

And when there is sublation by perception regarding the domain of inference and other means of knowledge, there would be no validity for inference and the rest due to that sublation, just as in the case of [cognitions] such as those produced by ophthalmia.

And since the correspondence with reality is equal [in both cases], why should this [scripture] be held in aversion? But in the absence of that [correspondence], inference and the other means of knowledge would not even exist as valid authorities.
Indeed, by this inference, either the universal concomitance (vyāpti) in all reasons—subsuming all cases—is sublated, or else there is a contradiction of the meaning of the thesis.

That cognition which proceeds with reference to a specific object such as the sun or moon intended [at that moment] has, moreover, as its object the sun and so forth as connected to that very time. For, since it is designated as a cognition of that [object], and because it does not have the earth or other things as its object, it is just like the first cognition, which has the sun and so forth at that time as its range.

All those things which are the substrata of [universals] such as "form-ness" (rūpatva), and whatever common substrata they possess, as well as whatever cognitions arise having them as their objects—these do not perish immediately after their production, because they possess the properties of being knowable and nameable, just like a sky-lotus.

And those cognitions which arise in succession regarding objects of dispute—there is the proclamation that all of them have a single object. For, since they are established as having the same expression due to their being based on a single uncontradicted substratum, they are like the various cognitions occurring within a single present moment.
First, in the initial reason, the illustrative example is deficient in respect to the probandum; for not every object, by virtue of being an object, exists at the same time as its own cognition.
When words such as "sun" and so forth, which arise merely from the speaker's intention, are applied to things like lamps, they are shown to be inconclusive by virtue of those cognitions.
Since birth and so forth lack intrinsic nature, momentary destruction is not at all desired; therefore, the proof set forth for the sake of establishing their non-existence is futile.
The state of being denotable by the same word also occurs in cognitions of lamps and the like; therefore, this reason is fallacious.
If grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is assumed to be sublated in those cases, why is this same clear sublation not seen even in the intended case?

Cognitions that have ascended to the status of being subjects of dispute do not have a single object as their domain, because they arise successively, like the cognitions of lightning, a lamp, and so forth. For there is a contradiction in the successive occurrence of cognitions that arise from a single object; since there is no difference in the effect produced by other [causes], it would contradict their dependence upon that [single object].
In all these reasons, the negative concomitance is doubtful, because no subverting proof has been shown for their presence in the heterologous class (vipakṣa).
In all these reasons, the negative concomitance is doubtful, because no subverting proof has been shown for their presence in the heterologous instances.
If every entity is touched by momentary impermanence, then how can there be the relationship between action and its fruit, the nature of cause and effect, and so forth?
If every entity is touched by momentary impermanence, then how can there be the relationship between action and its fruit, the nature of cause and effect, and so forth?

The moment that is conceived as the agent of wholesome and other [actions] does not persist at the time when the fruit is produced. Furthermore, the moment described as the enjoyer at the time of the fruit's arising did not perform that action, because it was non-existent previously. Thus, since the action and its fruit are not embraced by a single agent, the loss of what was done and the acquisition of what was not done follow—which is highly contradictory.

But according to the position of the doctrine of selflessness (*nairātmya*), one would understand beforehand: "After my destruction, the fruit will not exist, or it might belong to someone other than myself. Thus, a discerning person would not engage in the undertaking of virtuous or non-virtuous actions out of a desire for results, since the fruit remains far away.
Neither a future nor a past entity is capable of performing an action; even a present entity does not remain for such a duration of time.

For an entity that has not yet attained its own nature cannot serve as a subordinate part [of an effect]; nor can one that has perished, nor its continued existence, be capable of performing an action. Furthermore, if the destruction of the preceding moment is conceived as being without any continuity (niranvaya), then the subsequent production of the effect would be untenable, as it would lack a cause.

Even if destruction and arising were simultaneous, there would be no mutual dependence; nor could they exist in a relationship of cause and effect, because the operation of one does not assist the other.
Just as odors and other qualities arising in a jar do not persist when the form of the jar perishes, so too it is held that other forms [of the same substance] do not persist either.
Therefore, that whose activity is observed prior to the accomplishment of the effect is indeed its cause; it is not mere immediate succession alone.

This is the summary: If the effect were to arise from a cause that has already perished, then because that which is destroyed is indefinable, this [effect] would be without a cause. And if it were produced from a cause that has not perished, then since multiple moments would occur simultaneously, how could the momentariness of entities not be contradicted?

If a jar or the like were to exist for only a single moment, it would not be perceived by the eye; for things that have perished are not cognized, just like objects that have long since passed away. Furthermore, the relationship between cause and effect is established through perception and non-perception; yet these do not achieve proof [of momentary existence], because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of entities is not perceived.
Or who, being an established agent, coordinates this sequential progression? When this [cause] is perceived, this [effect] is perceived; but when it is not perceived, [the effect] is not observed.
Furthermore, recognition is difficult to establish regarding entities that perish in every moment; for an object seen by one person is not recognized by others.

Recognition may occur due to similarity even in the case of distinct things such as strands of hair, provided there exists a single cognizer; however, if there were a duality [of subjects], it would be without foundation. Furthermore, if no single entity exists that performs the act of synthesis (*pratisandhāna*), then how could desire and so forth, upon seeing a visible form, arise with respect to tastes and other objects?
"One moment is bound by the shackles of passion and so forth within the prison of existence, while another is unbound and liberated"—this fact is not understood.
For liberation is never possible for one who is bound; because of its absolute destruction, the moment [of bondage] is useless for those seeking liberation.

It is observed that one who has attained liberation was previously seen bound by shackles and the like; thus, it is seen that even one who is unbound attains liberation—such an instance is uncontradicted.
Bondage and liberation have a single substratum because they exist in that manner; like their worldly counterparts, therefore, everything is established most beautifully.
In this very same manner, memory and the other mental states are impossible, because there is no single substratum among things that perish moment by moment.

To this it is replied: when the existence of the causal relationship between all effects and causes is established, these [properties] are proven to be unimpeded even in things that are devoid of self.

Just as the inherent power of a seed and the like toward the production of a sprout and so forth remains fixed even when separated from a persisting self, such is the case with the state of things within the internal world.

For something is indeed capable [of producing an effect] either through a lineage of succession or directly; therefore, the relationship between actions, their fruits, and so forth, is logically established.

The established distinction of agency and so forth is intended by way of the unity of the continuum; it is accepted as merely superimposed through conceptual construction, for it is not a factor in the actual state of reality.

In the absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), that very same causal relation would have to be considered as something distinct, just as it is [distinguished] from those things occurring in other continua (*santāna*). Now, the causal relation between seeds, sprouts, and so forth is observed to be restricted; therein, not even a subtle part exists that is of the nature of a persisting continuity (*anugama*).

If earth and the other elements were not distinct [in their causal capacities], then no differentiation would be possible among seeds, sprouts, creepers, and so forth, due to their being of a single nature; thus, [the doctrine of] non-continuity (niranvaya) would be established. Therefore, enough with the efforts made by others to establish the relation of cause and effect for the sake of proving the existence and non-existence of actions, fruits, and the like.

To this it is replied: For the effect is produced in the second moment, while at that time the cause was produced in the first moment and had not yet perished. However, due to its momentariness, that cause does not exist at the time of the moment of the effect; or, if it were to persist, the effect would be useless, since it would have already been accomplished at that time.
And that which has already arisen cannot be produced again by it; for since arising consists in the coming into being of what was previously non-existent, there is no other way for it to exist.

Therefore, from that cause which has not perished—existing in the first moment—the effect arises precisely in the second moment from that which possesses the capacity. However, if the effect were to arise in the third or subsequent moments from what has already perished, it would be like the effect of a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) once destroyed, as will be explained later. Furthermore, if that [effect] were to arise in the first moment, there would be the undesirable consequence of simultaneity; yet, as in the case of a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), this is again not logically tenable.

Because that which is non-existent lacks causal capacity prior [to its production], and because the effect can only arise when there is such capacity, the simultaneous occurrence of cause and effect is clearly contradicted.

For the effect does not produce this [effect] by grasping its own cause with a pair of tongs, as it were, whereby there would be simultaneity; nor is the fruit born by firmly embracing its material cause, like a lover his beloved, whereby the two might exist at once.

Due to the necessity arising from their own causes, [things] exist during the first moment; whatever arises immediately after that [first moment] is the presence of the second moment. Those who follow conventions produced merely by the speaker's intention say that "that [second moment] produces that [subsequent effect]," even though the entity itself is devoid of activity.
What purpose is served here by an operation distinct from the time of its birth? For existence itself is the operation, since the effect arises when that existence is present.
That very necessity of immediate succession is what is designated as "dependence"; furthermore, the operation of a cause consists in its constant presence at the time of the arising of the effect.

Since the causal operation is merely postulated on the basis of its occurring only when that [cause] exists, it is better to let either that which possesses the operation or the cause itself be the cause.
For when existence is present, the sprouting of a shoot from a seed and so forth are indeed observed; however, no such thing is ever perceived to occur merely through the presence of an activity.

Even if the causality of an unseen power (*adṛṣṭa-śakti*) were to be postulated, it would not be accepted; for why should anything else also not have causality, or what distinction is there between this [unseen power] and that?
Just as an activity is held to exist without another cause, why then would other things not also be causes of the effect?
We do not perceive that which is intended to be visible in such a manner; how then can we accept its relationship as the basis [for inference]?
Just as the birth of a Buddha does not negate his status as a valid authority, why is it not likewise accepted that [the Buddha] is the cause of all phenomena?
For just as cognition is momentary, so too have all other living beings been established as being likewise; therefore, this world is devoid of activity.

The mutual causality of odor and so forth is indeed accepted on the basis of their continuous occurrence; therefore, this logical consequence of their being causes does not contradict that [accepted view].

Even though something else exists immediately prior, only a specific thing is not the cause; likewise, this restriction is accepted [as being due to its own nature], and this is equally applicable to permanent entities as well.
If it is held that whatever is occupied with a particular task is not its cause, then let it be accepted that whatever has a necessary existence in relation to something is the cause of that thing.

These two—existence and non-existence—are established through perception and non-perception, provided that the object is considered to be cognizable by consciousness possessing a form (*sākāra-vijñāna*). However, when you maintain that the object is cognizable by a consciousness devoid of form (*anākāra-dhī*), this same [argument] is equally applicable even in the case of [the theory of] momentariness and so forth. For indeed, every consciousness arises from its own preceding causes as having the nature of cognition, with respect to color-form and other objects that exist at the same time [as the cognition].
If consciousness possesses an aspect, then indeed there would be a diversity of the mind; if it were not marked by an aspect, there would be no basis for proximity [between cognition and its object].
You too must state some answer to this; whatever resolution you have in this matter shall also be ours.

If the cause did not produce the effect, there would indeed be the loss of what has been done; nor is this desired, for causality does not exist in a mere succession. Furthermore, there would be the arrival of what was not done if an effect were ever produced without its cause; yet this is not so, because of the fixed nature of causal power.
Through the conceptualization of the distinction between moments, the destruction of moments and so forth are urged; yet nothing at all undesired has been brought forward by the opponents.

For those whose view of a sentient being has not been abandoned, the conceptualization of the distinction between moments does not arise in any way due to the conceit of a single continuum. However, those who have fully awakened to reality, having understood the necessity of causes that perish at every moment, undertake virtuous actions.
The specific causal efficiency of certain mental states alone is fixed; therefore, memory and other such functions remain unimpeded in all cases.

In this context, ignorance and the other factors are considered to exist in the nature of cause and effect; bondage is held to be their presence, while liberation is the stainlessness of the intellect resulting from their disappearance.
Even in the worldly sense, these two—bondage and liberation—are not established as residing in a single substratum; for indeed, everything is well known to be momentary.
Since no excellence whatsoever exists [in such a self], this arrangement of being an agent, an enjoyer, bound, and so forth, would be contradicted; otherwise, it would entail impermanence.

In every respect, since no excellence whatsoever exists [in the self], such an arrangement of agency, enjoyership, bondage, and so forth, would be contradicted; otherwise, there would be impermanence.

The lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) regarding genus (*jāti*) and so forth, which was previously explained, is incorrect [for them]. Those who follow Akṣapāda and Kaṇāda assert that the six categories, beginning with substance (*dravya*), exist as ultimate realities (*pāramārthika*). This refutation of substance and the other categories is now stated in brief.

"It was previously demonstrated that the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) in genus (*jāti*) and so forth is illogical; the six categories beginning with substance (*dravya*), which exist as ultimate realities—thus say the followers of Akṣapāda and Kaṇāda, relying solely on scripture. This negation of substance and the other categories is now stated in brief."
Substance is held to be ninefold, distinguished by the divisions of earth and the rest; the four beginning with earth are each twofold, according to their being eternal or non-eternal.
Those atoms which consist of earth and the other elements are eternal; however, those things composed of them and so forth, being products, are perishable.
In this regard, the non-existence of eternal atomic forms has been established by proving the momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) of all things without exception.
If they were eternal, all gross objects would indeed arise simultaneously; for they have no dependence on conjunction and the like, as there is no distinction among them.

If it is not admitted that [the effect] arises from atoms when it has approached the true causal conditions, this is because it is not an object within the scope of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for apprehending an existing thing.
Because the cause of the dyad (aṇuka) is not perceived as distinct from the weaver and so forth, and because all things such as cloth are seen to consist of atoms.

Nor is existence established due to the absence of a means of valid cognition that apprehends it; for when a means of valid cognition is absent, there is no certainty regarding the non-existence of the object.

But that whole (avayavin) which is said to be composed of those [parts] is never perceived as possessing a distinction between its qualities and its parts; therefore, it is not established, as it lacks any means of valid cognition.

Is it not observed that a crystal stone appears [colored] through contact with an adjunct? Likewise, even when its own form is not perceived, a crane and the like are seen [as such]. Even when the form and other qualities of a man are not apprehended because he is concealed by a cloak, the cognition of a "man" is observed; and when a garment is dyed red, the cognition of a "cloth" [is observed].

Form and so forth are absolutely distinct from blue lotuses and the like; therefore, by the exclusion of those [latter], [form] is distinct from Caitra and others, just as a horse is [distinct]. Or, earth and so forth are absolutely distinct from form, smell, and the like, because of the difference between singular and plural designations, just as there is a distinction between the moon and the stars.

Just as threads and cloth are distinct due to their having different agents, potencies, and so forth, they are likewise distinct through the association with contradictory properties, like a pillar and a jar.

If gross objects were impossible, there would be no perception of trees and the like; furthermore, since atoms are beyond the senses, there could be no mention of "atoms. For a thing is called "extremely subtle" only in relation to a gross object; but if a single gross object does not exist, in relation to what would its subtlety be defined?
But surely crystals and the like are perceived in the form of red and other colors; yet they do not possess that nature, because that would entail the destruction of your own position.

Furthermore, no other self is perceived apart from that form; nor is it logical that they [the selves] should be cognizable by a cognition possessing a different form, as that would lead to an over-extension of the principle.
In the same way, it might also be possible that white and other such qualities are what are cognized; therefore, this cognition is erroneous, like the perception of a yellow conch-shell and the like.
There is no inferential knowledge of the person within the sheath, because that which constitutes its cause—the sheath—is perceived.
The emergence of a different color in a cloth from dyes such as saffron occurs because the previous color of the cloth is destroyed, given that the cloth is momentary.
Furthermore, from that very same [substance], depending upon water and other factors, another color arises—such as white from silver and the like, or blackness and so forth.
If the form remains in that same state, however, there can be no suppression by another, because its previous unobstructed nature persists.
The use of the genitive case, differences in number, and so forth, arise solely from the speaker's intention; therefore, it is not logical to establish the true nature of things based on them.
For instance, the existence of the six [categories] is not admitted as distinct from one another; nor is any single entity accepted as a collection of them.

If it is argued that reality is held to be the object of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that makes it known, then if the existence of the six [objects] is asserted, it follows that there must be something other than those six.

If it is argued that these six are declared to be the substrata (dharmin) and that the properties (dharma) are indeed intended to be distinct from them, then what kind of relationship is held by you [the opponent] to exist between them? Since [such a relationship] is restricted to substances, neither conjunction (saṃyoga) nor any other [type of relation] is appropriate; nor is any other relation such as inherence (samavāya) accepted by others.

And since a relationship [of cause and effect] is untenable for them, how could it be their property? If it were due merely to their production [by those things], then others would also be of that same nature.
In this way, even for that [existence], there exists a distinct case-ending; and if there were another existence for that [existence] as well, an infinite regress would result.
When another property is superimposed, the status of being a subject (dharmitā) is attained therein; and for this very reason, the status of substance and so forth as subjects is also accepted.

If the difference of the cloth from the initial threads is being established, then the futility of the proof would be unavoidable. For those other threads that have arisen in a particular state—being engaged in a specific purposeful action—are not distinct from the initial ones.

In order to make known their utility for a single purpose, and with the desire to avoid the faults of prolixity, incapacity, and futility, speakers have applied a single term to those things—desiring the brevity of linguistic usage through comprehensive designation—even though they are heard separately. However, a cloth produced at the same time as them is not established [as being identical], for it possesses different properties such as its makers, capacities, and dimensions.
Furthermore, those atoms that are produced as mutually approaching do not possess supersensuousness, because they fall within the range of other [senses].
The blue and other forms of atoms are imagined as their own inherent shapes; yet the visual and other cognitions are experienced as manifesting blue and so forth.

Even if these [cognitions] lack a defining characteristic due to the absence of a distinction between preceding and succeeding moments, nevertheless, their status as direct perception remains uncontradicted, as is the case with a beverage and similar things.
Even when all things, which consist of the exclusion of everything else, are perceived, there is likewise no certain determination of all their aspects.

Even though the defining characteristic of an object is partless and accessible only through non-conceptual perception, that which serves as the cause for the determination of its distinctions is what is cognized.

Just as there is the illusion of a single lamp due to the arising of flames of equal intensity, so too is there the perception of oneness when many subtle cognitions exist in uninterrupted succession.

If their perception is not admitted because they lack the characteristic of distinctness, then how is it observed in the case of lamps and the like? Or is a composite whole (avayavin) likewise desired [to exist]?

This much might be the case here: how is it that these atoms of blue and so forth are not understood as being the form [of the cognition]? That too is without foundation, because cognition certainly does not have something beyond its range as its object, nor does it have a single gross thing as its object, due to the contradiction between grossness and oneness.

If the gross object were of a single nature, then when it is covered by even as much as a fly’s foot, the whole would necessarily be covered due to its lack of division. Furthermore, if one part were dyed red, the whole would become red; or else, if there were the presence of contradictory properties, multiplicity would necessarily follow.
But surely, since it possesses a single nature, why is the word "all" used here? For that [word] has multiple objects as its referent, yet it is neither manifold nor a composite whole.

Now, it might be argued: "Are not those things established in common worldly usage—such as clothing, the body, and so forth—the very same ones described by you as 'wholes' (avayavin)? For everyone employs such expressions as 'all the clothing is red,' 'entirely,' 'without exception,' or 'in its totality,' [implying] that it arose merely through one's own intention. When there is such an intention to speak, we too describe it, saying 'everything would be red' and so on; for speakers are indeed free from constraints."

If that designation were figurative, it would entail a difference in the verbal expression; yet there is no distinction in the cognition between what is intended as secondary and what is intended as primary.
But surely, because conjunction does not pervade its locus, redness would not belong to the whole, nor would the whole be seen as being covered.

Now, in a substance that has no parts, what remains unoccupied? If its own nature is established [as occupying space], then difference is thereby proven; or else, by its remaining in that state, [the existence of parts is proven]. Therefore, the occupation of multiple locations is not possible for a single entity. Consequently, the manifold nature of cloth and other objects is established as distinct from their atoms.
But the world, not knowing the true nature of reality, conceives of a single lump; depending on that which it has thus imagined, what is here called an atom is [merely] a conceptual construct.

Or rather, this perception remains independent of any objective sign (nimitta) when it is established in such a state, just as the word "Lord" (īśvara) follows conventional usage even in the case of one who possesses no wealth.

Threads, hands, and so forth do not at all inhere in a single composite whole, because they are multiple, just like mats, huts, houses, and so on. Alternatively, if the substance under discussion is held to be dependent upon multiple parts, then its existence is untenable due to its unity; this is a subverting proof [based on the analogy] with atoms.

For that [universal] would have to exist in another part of the whole either by means of the very same form that it possesses in one instance, or by some other form, since there is no third possibility. In that case, its existence elsewhere cannot be conceived by means of that same form; for if it were already embraced by that [first instance], it could not otherwise exist there.
Just as an infant does not remain in the lap of one nurse while already held in another's, so too a substance that has been embraced by one [cause] does not resort to another.

For if that which has a nature connected to it were to exist even where that [connection] is absent, it would follow that it occupies the same location as that [connected object], and it would be identical to it due to its lack of distinction. If it were to exist by means of a different nature altogether, then a single entity existing in multiple locations could not be established; for a difference in nature constitutes a difference in the thing itself.

If it is argued that its mode of existence in those [categories] consists of inherence (*samavāya*), then surely this same inquiry applies to that [inherence] as well, and thus it rushes forth with the very same vehemence.

Alternatively, if it were to exist by its entire self, multiplicity would follow; if it were to exist by way of a single part, it would be undesirable, for it would then not be one, nor would it exist anywhere at all.

Whether an argument proceeds independently or by way of a reductio (*prasaṅga*), it does not truly hold unless that [subsistence] is itself perceived. Furthermore, subsistence—whether in its entirety or in part—is nowhere observed; because of its impossibility, both substance and the other categories would be non-existent. Or, if such [subsistence] were observed somewhere, it could not be excluded from substances and so forth. On the other hand, if it is not observed therein, the question regarding its distinction is not appropriate. At most, one might say that "there is no subsistence," but that is not correct, because it is established through perception by means of the cognition "this is here. If that is not accepted as perception, let some subverting argument be stated; otherwise, even the cognitions of color and so forth would not be perceptual.
It has already been established through non-difference that there is no occurrence [of the object] here; nor is there a cognition of "it is here," because its form does not appear [in consciousness].

This point is elucidated by the two terms "entirety" (*kṛtsna*) and "part" (*ekadeśa*): Does its existence [in the parts] occur without parts (*niraṃśatvena*), or does it occur in some other way? This is observed, for example, in the case of a bilva fruit and the like contained within a vessel, or in the case of Caitra and others seated upon many seats.
In some cases, sounds are dependent [on something else] due to reasons such as perishability, like a jar or a lamp; and that [substratum], they claim, will be space (vyoma).

The cognition of "prior," "posterior," and so forth, which is based on factors distinct from actions and substances such as the sun [and other celestial bodies], is like the perception of a jar and the like; since this [cognition] is distinct from the cognitions of wrinkles, grey hair, roughness, movement, and so forth, that which is its cause is indeed asserted to be time.

Direction is inferred in this manner from cognitions such as "prior" and "posterior"; and the inference of the mind is held to arise from the sequential nature of cognition. Furthermore, cognitions of color and so forth, which arise sequentially, depend upon a cause distinct from the eyes and other [senses], just like a chariot and similar objects.

Since sound is accepted as having its cause in the primary elements (mahābhūtas) such as those that are appropriated (upātta), it is established that sounds are dependent upon them; thus, the first [argument] is not a proof.
However, their co-inherence in a single, all-pervading, and eternal space is established; for there is no deficiency in their concomitance, as they likewise extend to [all things] simultaneously.

The cognition of "prior," "posterior," and so forth, is based on mental attention arising from specific conventions; it does not derive from time or space. Since these two (time and space) possess a partless, unitary nature, a sequence such as priority and posteriority is impossible. If it is argued that this [sequence] arises from the difference between their respective correlates, then surely those two (time and space) would be rendered useless.

We also accept that the mind (*manas*) is distinct from the eye and the other [senses]; for that which is the cognition arising immediately after the six [sensory cognitions] is the mind. However, if the mind were eternal, cognitions would result in simultaneity; therefore, the reason stated here [for its non-eternality] results in the subversion of your desired position.
I consider this Sūtra to have been composed for the sake of establishing or refuting the mind as taught by others—the Sugatas—either as possessing mental images (sākāra) or otherwise (anyathā).
I consider this Sūtra to have been composed for the sake of establishing or refuting the mind as taught by others—the Sugatas—either with its own form (sākāra) or otherwise (anyathāvṛtta).
By the negation of substances, all qualities, actions, and so forth that depend upon them are likewise considered to be discarded.
By the negation of substances, all those qualities, actions, and so forth that depend upon them are likewise considered to be discarded.
When the relatum has been discarded, where and for whom could there be inherence? Nevertheless, this specific negation is stated once again.

If it is maintained that in a large substance there is only a single [universal] such as "blue," then when that [substance] is manifested by light entering through a hole, why is there not a manifestation and perception of this [universal] as well?
Furthermore, blue and other such [colors] are not held to exist through spatial division; since they are manifested by that [perception], they are therefore divided atom by atom.

Number does not appear in cognition as something distinct from elephants and so forth that are excluded from what is not of that nature; nor is it accepted as being perceptible, for it does not exist therein.

However, this cognition of "one" and so forth regarding jars arises from a mental attention based on a convention established by desire; it occurs just as it does regarding cognitions and the like. Since they [the jars] lack substantiality (adravyatva), no distinct number exists in them; therefore, that cognition is certainly not figurative (bhākta), because it is unerring (askhalitatvataḥ).

If it is argued that the cognition of "one" regarding qualities and so forth arises from their inherence in the same substance due to their oneness, then [the same would apply to other cases]. Alternatively, if the cognition of "one" regarding qualities and so forth is postulated as arising from their inherence in a single object, [then the same logic applies].

Granted that there may be such a cognition of pervasion and so forth in a single instance of knowledge; however, what cause does this cognition require with respect to these [other instances], or with respect to the six categories and so on? This cognition, being secondary (gauṇa) due to inherence in a single object and the like, is consequently erroneous, just like the notion of fire in a child.

Furthermore, it is established that the cognition of number arises from something other than those [cognitions], because it differs in character from cognitions such as "elephant" and so forth, just like the cognition of a blue garment and the like.

Through means such as mental attention to conventions established by desire, the accomplishment of what is desired occurs therein; or else, the number [of faculties] in the intellect and so forth would be determined by that very same [means].
And if it is described that the accomplishment of number depends upon cognition, why is it not accepted that such cognition arises merely through the application of convention?
As for that which is called "dimension," distinguished by categories such as large and long—is it not considered to exist in the object in that same way, simply due to a difference in its form?

Just as a long garland of palaces is perceived as something great, yet no measurement corresponding to that [perceived] form is actually constructed there; so too, if it is designated by way of inherence in a single object, then neither "greatness" nor "length" exists as intended properties within the abode itself.
The palace is intended as a metaphor for yoga; that quality [of yoga] is immeasurable. It has no further series, nor is it the basis for figurative application.
But as for the conceptualization of distinctness and so forth that is employed in the practice of abstraction—is it not considered to be based on the state of having a nature distinct from its cause?
For just as cognition, pleasure, and so forth, being mutually distinct, are designated separately even without any other [category] as their constituent part, so it is with others.
Those conjunctions and disjunctions which others postulate as inherent in substances and as the causes of the cognitions "conjoined" and so forth are useless.

It follows that seeds, water, earth, and so forth would always be producing their effects, because they lack any distinction [from one moment to the next] and because conjunction is impossible. However, it is understood that the field, seed, water, and so on, are dependent [on other factors], for they constantly produce their own effects, like a staff, a wheel, water, and so forth. That entity which is depended upon by them shall be "conjunction"; and because it possesses qualifying attributes, it is understood to be indeed distinct [from its constituents]. For when it is said, "Bring the two conjoined things," one looks toward those two [objects] and, excluding everything else, brings precisely those two.
This distinction in cognition—that "this object is continuous" and "this object is discontinuous"—by what does it exist, if those two [qualities] do not exist here?

This cognition of an interval which concludes [it] to be without interval, and that other cognition of non-interval even where there is an interval—this twofold false cognition (mithyābuddhi) follows the nature of its primary object (pradhānārtha). And here, that primary object must be stated; when it is stated, those two [cognitions] are established.

If this cognition "he is one with earrings" arises, what is its cause? It cannot arise from the mere existence of the man and the earrings, for that would entail its occurrence at all times. The negation of a state observed in one place is appropriate in another; but since conjunction is observed [to exist], how can it be denied? Therefore, the reality of the entity "Caitra without earrings" must indeed exist, because the application of negation and affirmation proceeds through such distinctions.
It is said that water and other elements are not undifferentiated by virtue of their momentariness; even though they exist, they depend upon another state, such as the absence of obstruction.
If water and the other elements were dependent solely upon conjunction, then the effect would either arise immediately after the conjunction or it would not arise at all.
For when a particular state has been reached through uninterrupted succession from birth, this [cognition] perceives and grasps those two objects in such a manner.

A cognition that arises either interruptedly or otherwise serves as a causal sign (nimitta), just as the knowledge of a house and the Vindhya or Himalayan mountains occurs with or without an interval.

Not every false cognition follows the primary object; some arise from internal derangement even without regard for similarity, such as the perception of two moons in one whose mind is directed elsewhere. Or, in this case, the primary object exists as something produced in an uninterrupted stream.
This cognition "he is Kuṇḍalin" arises with respect to both the person Caitra and the particular state of being born as a ring, just like the cognition of conjunction between Caitra and a ring.
Such a specific state, observed elsewhere, is denied in other cases; for instance, in the case of "there is an earring on Caitra," conjunction is not [the relation], because it is not perceived.

The cognition of a "joined" object does not arise from conjunction with something else as conceived by opponents; for it is like the cognition of a "joined" [pillar] in relation to palaces and the like, which arises through the nature of a joined-cognition. Or alternatively, because it arises when multiple objects exist, it is like cognitions whose objects are distinct, multiple threads and so forth. Even when there is disjunction, these two types of valid cognition should be explained accordingly. Furthermore, the objection that "the subsistence of one thing in many is not logical" serves as a refutation.

That which is postulated as the cause for designations such as "prior" and "posterior"—namely, priority and posteriority based on space and time—is not [intrinsic]. Just as colors such as blue and so forth are designated as such due to their established sequential occurrence, even when distinguished from other limiting conditions (upādhi), so too are others [designated] in that same way.

If it is argued that all things such as number and conjunction are not distinct from the substance itself, because they function as qualifiers of that substance—just like a staff or other such attributes—then this merely proves what we already accept, for these are described as having only conventional existence (*saṃvṛtisat*). This is because that which is conventionally real cannot be defined as being either identical to or different from [the substance].
Now, the indeterminability of a collection and so forth is refuted, because it possesses determinate properties, just like color, sound, taste, and the rest.

Because it lacks intrinsic nature, its properties—being conceptually superimposed—are not established as fixed in reality, just like a lotus in the sky. Even when stated in that manner, there is an inconclusiveness (anaikānta) due to examples such as the sky-lotus; for both non-difference and difference are established only with respect to real entities.

If it is thus argued that number and so forth are indeed distinct from substance, then the reason [adduced] suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished substratum (āśrayāsiddhatā), because number and the rest themselves are unestablished.

But if it is argued that substance itself is spoken of in that way as being differentiated by aggregation and so forth, then a difference [of substance] based on its own essential nature would be established, which is contradictory.

Impression (*saṃskāra*) is said to be of three kinds: that called velocity (*vega*), that termed mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and that characterized as elasticity (*sthitasthāpaka*). None of these is tenable in its entirety. Because all things are momentary (*kṣaṇika*), no action whatsoever exists that could serve as the cause for a continuum, which would then require an impression termed "velocity."

The mental impression (*saṃskāra*) called "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*), which consists of the latent tendency (*vāsanā*) of the mind, is logical; it is not a quality of the self (*ātman*), because that [self] has been refuted.

However, a nature consisting of "stabilizing" (sthitasthāpaka) is not tenable due to the doctrine of momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga). Since a persisting object is impossible, if such a thing exists, its stability arises solely from its own nature.
The subsistence for a single moment arises solely from its own cause; and the continuation in a series occurs through the influence of each preceding moment.

This [entity] does not arise otherwise; therefore, what could it be that establishes it? Nor is its causality observed; it might be either a *saṃskāra* (impression) or something else. Furthermore, this quality (*guṇa*) intended as the establisher of things like cloth is accepted only for what has already arisen. Thus, the very name "quality" or "impression" is in every respect impossible.
Since the mind, its conjunction, and the self have already been explained in detail previously, the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*)—as endowed with the characteristics asserted by others—is not tenable.

Since the mind, the conjunction, and the self have already been explained in detail previously, the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) is not tenable as something endowed with the characteristics described by others.

In entities that perish moment by moment, the projection of karma and so forth is impossible; for once [an entity] has perished in the place where it was born, it is impossible for it to reach anything else.

In entities that perish moment by moment, the projection of karma and so forth is impossible; for once they have arisen, they cease in that very place, since it is impossible for them to reach another location.

For others have declared that the time of an action is indeed distinct from the time of its origination, even in the case of objects such as lamps and the like, which are desired to perish very rapidly.

For instance: contact with the cause, the manifestation of the universal, then motion in its own parts, immediately after that, disjunction, then the destruction of the conjunction, and finally the destruction of the substance—thus, even in an entity such as a lamp-flame, a duration of exactly six moments is accepted.

When separation from and contact with two points of space—prior and posterior—are possible, either a mover or something else is postulated as the substratum of action. For that which remains for even a single moment of birth is never of a mobile nature; for such a thing, a transition to another location, even by the measure of a single atom, is impossible.
If the object were stable, however, all actions such as going and so forth would be impossible; this is especially true in all its states without distinction.

If that [entity] were by its very nature of the form of a goer and so forth, then motion and the rest would exist at all times; thus it could not remain motionless for even a single moment. For, since it has not abandoned its previous nature, motion and the rest would necessarily occur even when they are not present, just as they did at the time of their initial arising.

Furthermore, if that [entity] were by its very nature in the form of "not-going" and so forth, then non-going and the rest would exist eternally; it would not possess even a single moment of movement. This is because, even while motion and the like occur, it remains essentially immobile, since it has not abandoned its prior form, just as in a time when it is immobile.
If, however, this [self] were to come [into existence] at one time and be otherwise at another, there would be a state of difference due to its association with mutually distinct natures.
It is determined that those two selves are absolutely distinct, because they possess contradictory attributes, like a moving object and a stationary one.
Action, which is considered to be perceptible, is not distinct from the substance; yet even that [action] is not perceived, and its existence does not withstand logical scrutiny.
Whether [the entity] be unstable or stable, there is likewise the impossibility of motion and so forth, because separation from and reaching of a prior and subsequent location are incompatible.
However, because objects that are similar yet distinct are perceived in different locations through uninterrupted succession, there arises the illusion of motion, just as in the case of a lamp.

However, because objects that are similar yet distinct are perceived in different locations due to their arising in uninterrupted succession, there is an illusion of motion, just as in the case of a lamp.

When substance and the other categories have been refuted, universals (jātis) are also rejected; for all those [universals] are postulated as residing within the three categories [of substance, quality, and action].

When substance and the other categories have been refuted, universals (jāti) are also rejected; for all those [universals] are postulated as residing within the three categories [of substance, quality, and action].

In this regard, this "genus" (*jāti*) is accepted by others as being of two kinds: first, that which is a universal (*sāmānya*) alone, called "existence" (*sattā*), because it persists across all [entities]; second, that which is a universal such as "substanceness" (*dravyatva*) and so forth, which is designated as a "particular universal" (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*), because it serves as the cause for a cognition that persists within its own substrates and, by distinguishing its own substrate from all heterogeneous classes, serves as the cause for a cognition of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). Therefore, it is established that these [latter] alone possess the nature of being causes for the cognition of exclusion.
However, certain particulars alone are the causes of differentiation; those which reside in eternal substances and are described as "ultimate particulars" (antyaviśeṣas).
By the power of which cognitions arise for yogins regarding atoms and so forth; this [atom] is distinct from that, thus [the atoms] are each individually relied upon.
The universals such as "existence" and "cowness" are established through direct perception, because cognitions such as "existent" arise whenever the operation of the sense organs is present.
Their existence is also established by the force of inference, since the cognition of their specific qualities must arise from some other cause.

The specific cognitions produced by words such as "cow" with respect to cows, elephants, and so forth, are caused by an object distinct from convention (*samaya*), shape (*ākṛti*), the individual body (*piṇḍa*), and the like. This is because, while having "cow" and so forth as their objects, they are different from the word and the cognition [of those terms], just as in the case of the cognitions and sounds "with calf" or "with goad" applied to those very same things. The qualification [against] the cognitions of a hare's horn and the like is made because of the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Furthermore, the statement of its own nature (*svarūpa*) serves as an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). Moreover, the recurring cognition regarding cows and the like arises as something distinct from the individual body, because it is a qualifier, just like the cognition of "blue" and so forth. Cowness (*gotva*) is a different entity from the cow, because it is the object of a distinct cognition, like color, touch, and so on; and because it is spoken of as "its" (*tasya*), just as Caitra is distinct from his horse.

This undertaking is essentially pithless, being a mere description of a formal process; for there exists here no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever that makes it known. Indeed, cognitions such as "existent" and so forth are not established as occurring immediately following the operation of the senses; rather, they arise from the habitual application of linguistic convention (*saṅketa*).

Just as in the case of the *dhātrī* plant, *abhaya*, and others, a capacity for curing various diseases is observed both individually and collectively; yet among them there exists no single commonality that possesses such power. This is because the alleviation of disease is perceived through differences such as being slow or quick, and so forth. No excellence whatsoever can exist in a universal (*sāmānya*) due to variations in factors like the patient's constitution (*kṣetra*), whereas such excellence is eternally present in the *dhātrī* and other substances by virtue of their uniform nature. Likewise, even though they are absolutely distinct, some things become causes for a similar conceptual cognition (*pratyavamarśa*) and the like due to their restricted power, while others do not.

When there is a desire to express the suitability for a mere function, a convention is established for those [entities] by the word "existent" (*sat*), or for another [word] according to one's preference. For instance, users establish a linguistic convention such as "cow" for that which is suitable for various functions in the form of carrying, milking, and so forth. These cognitions of "existent" and the like, arising from the mental attention toward that convention, are observed to occur immediately after the operation of the senses, and not otherwise.

At first, consciousness arises indeed in a non-verbal form; from that comes the engagement with conventions, from that the derivative [conceptual] cognition, and from that, those [subsequent cognitions].
For one whose mind has gone elsewhere, there is the perception of the mere object; it proceeds from that very [perception] through the exclusion of all adjuncts.

Even in the case of the first type of cause, futility is present; for those [logicians], the manifestation of the convention is indeed desired as the concomitant factor, which possesses positive and negative concomitance.

If that [unique particular] were excluded from the subject (pakṣa), the example would be devoid of the property to be proven (sādhya). It is not so, for those causes—such as the goad and so forth—are directly [perceptible], like external objects. Indeed, there is no operation of names or conceptual constructions regarding the "braying of a donkey" (*khalabhaṇa*); for every unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) has a form that transcends the range of speech.
Relying upon that which is conventionally real and mounted upon internal mental measures, they proceed toward external forms such as the goad and so forth, having determined them as external objects.

The absence of action, quality, and designation is described as the reason [for non-existence]; however, the qualification "of the cognition of non-existence" (abhāvapratyayasya) is purposeless. That too is incorrect, because if it were a cause, it would possess substantiality, and since it possesses causal capacity, the cognition of non-existence would follow [as an object] even in the case of existence (*sattā*) and other categories, without distinction.

Furthermore, the distinctness [of the cognition] is unestablished, for the cognitions of the body-form and so forth are not established as being different from those cognitions; therefore, this reason is also unestablished.
Since the inclusive cognition (anvayī pratyaya) manifests as the individual instance of the word, the universal (jāti) is described as being devoid of the forms of color, shape, and syllables.

If the universal were also of the nature of blue and so forth, what difference would there be between it and a quality? Furthermore, a single, recurring [universal] characterized as blue and so forth is not perceived. Even if it were appearing, if it is not perceived through its distinction, then how could the cognition and the verbal expression function toward the individual by its power? This cognition of the universal is accepted by others as being of a determinative (ascertaining) nature; and since non-apprehension would otherwise follow, its non-perception is not tenable.

Even if it were established that [the cognition] has another cause, the universal would not be proven; for it would lack a single persisting nature and would be devoid of permanence due to its arising sequentially.
What other cause does the word *padārtha* depend upon among the six categories, and what is the reason for the notion "it exists" which persists even in the case of *sattā* (existence) and the rest?

If [the reason] is based on the characteristic of another property, then there too the notion of "existence" exists; since it would then have that other property as its cause, it would result in an infinite regress and thus lack a substratum (adharmitā). Therefore, this reason is held by these [opponents] to be inconclusive (vyabhicārī); moreover, its pervasion (vyāpti) has not been established through a universal application (sarvopasaṃhārāt).

That which was indicated immediately after that has been refuted by this very [argument]. Regarding that general proof, [objections] such as the establishment of what is already accepted apply equally.

Furthermore, in cases such as "the cooker" (pācaka), a specific cognition arises; likewise, there is the cognition of absence regarding an absence. This occurs even without a single recurring [common] factor. Consequently, the reason [adduced by the opponent] is inconclusive (anaikāntika) with respect to all these aforementioned instances, including those whose forms are created by desire, or those that have perished or not yet arisen.

There is no basis whatsoever for the cognitions of "cook" and so forth. If you claim that action (*karman*) is the basis, then surely that action differs with each individual. Since there is no persisting entity (*anvayin*) among distinct individuals, a persisting cognition would not be logical; thus, a single universal (*sāmānya*) that conforms to all individuals is postulated. If action—which is devoid of such persistence—is imagined to be the cause [of the cognition], then why are the individuals themselves not accepted as its causes? Furthermore, the cognition of "cook" and so forth would not occur regarding one who has ceased their activity, for opponents do not accept that action is always present like a universal. If it is argued that past or future action serves as the occasioning condition for the cognition and the word "cook" in those cases, that is not so, because such action is non-existent.

If it is argued that the cognition [of action] arises from the connection with the action related to the universal of "action-ness" (kriyātva), then even when the action has perished, [the cognition would persist] because of the indication of its permanent cause by that [universal].

But it does not exist there when the activity has ceased, even though it was previously characterized; for that genus which is apprehended as permanent is [defined] by its exclusion from its own substratum.

For indeed, the universal (jāti) such as "staff-bearer" or "bracelet-wearer" does not exist at all times within its definition; even when one is separated from the staff or the like, the cognition of them as "staff-bearers" and so forth still occurs with respect to those individuals. Alternatively, if it is argued that another universal, such as "cook-ness," exists [independently], then through its connection with that [universal], the cognition of "cook" and so forth would arise even in one who has just been born. If it is not the case that the cognition of "existent" and so forth arises [immediately], then that [universal] must be inherent (samavāyinī). If it were so, then that [cognition] would not occur there later either, because there is no difference in the conditions. Furthermore, if it is claimed that this inherence does not occur between the two due to a deficiency in their nature of being connected, how could such inherence exist later, given that their identity (tādātmya) remains unchanged?
If indeed the individual manifestation were unstable and could attain excellence, then the deficient nature of the genus would never cease.
And the primary means of an action such as cooking is considered to be "the cook" and so forth; and that primacy exists even in relation to another cook.

What indeed is this so-called "predominance"? It is not power (*śakti*), because it lacks logical connection; for this very reason, it cannot be conceived as consisting of substance, action, quality, self, and so forth.

The cognition regarding "cooks" and the like consists merely in the exclusion of what is heterogeneous; it depends upon the distinction of linguistic conventions. Therefore, words and cognitions do not function toward a division [of objects] without a single, recurring [conceptual] factor that conforms to the convention.

Likewise, the cognition of non-existence is not contradictory with respect to non-existent things; nor is a recurring sound [contradictory], because both follow from the application of a convention for that which lacks a real referent.

"This is the prior non-existence of the jar," "this is the destruction of the jar"—it is only by means of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of those [positive] entities that cognition apprehends various absences. If you argue that its recurrence everywhere is due solely to a universal residing in those adjuncts, this is not so, because there is a difference [in nature] based on their respective substrata. The cognition "jar" and so forth is appropriately inclusive of those [entities]; however, the notion "absence is not presence" is of a different character. Indeed, a cognition such as "cow" or "horse" is not held to arise merely through the power of the universal *Being* (*sattā*). Otherwise, one would have to postulate a single universal that serves as the means for all [cognitions].

If it is maintained that cognition in all cases does not conform to its objective mark (*nimitta*), then why is number and so forth accepted as the basis for cognitions such as "army" and the like? If this is so, why is this cognition not accepted as occurring with respect to these very particulars themselves—cognition which follows the manifestation of the distinctions of conventions fashioned by desire?

For when there is the cognition of difference, there arises the desire to establish a convention; from that comes its creation, then the hearing of it, then the mental application toward it, and from that, the cognition of it. Through positive and negative concomitance, this alone is determined to be the capable cause; for any other [cause] would lead to an infinite regress.

For it is assumed that a correlate must be similar; thus, one postulates another object [as the cause]. However, since cognitions are indeed distinct, it is better to rely on this much alone: namely, a restriction of capacity (*sāmarthyaniyama*). For such a restriction is preferable to postulate here, and it is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) among those whose capacities are known.
Furthermore, positive concomitance (anvaya) is not found in universals because they never exist [as individuals]; nor is negative concomitance (vyatireka) possible for eternal entities.

It is not logical that "quality-ness" (guṇatva) and the like are the cause of cognitions of non-substances and so forth; nor, consequently, is "inherence in many" the cause of the cognition of a universal (sāmānya).
Furthermore, multiple inherence is found even in [qualities] such as number; for just as in the case of universals, there would arise cognitions of "universal" with respect to them as well.

The universal "jar-ness" and so forth resides only in jars and the like; it does not reside in absences. Therefore, how could there be a cognition [of jar-ness] with respect to them? For it is not logical that a cognition or a verbal designation should apply elsewhere based on something residing in a different substratum. [For example,] "elephant-ness" and so forth do not apply to a white horse (*karka*), nor even here is there a common substratum for the same object. [One might argue: "The taste is cold and heavy"—such a cognition would arise from a common substratum. But here, even this is not the case, for an absence does not reside anywhere at all.

If it is argued that the relationship of qualifier and qualified also exists here, then surely that [relationship] is postulated only when another underlying relationship exists. The status of qualifier and qualified is postulated by relying upon the proximity (*āsatti*) between those two; in the absence of that [proximity], it cannot be established, as it would lack a basis.

Furthermore, such statements as "this is the prior non-existence of the jar" are merely constructed by conceptualization, like the attribution of bravery and so forth to an imaginary being. Wherever the relationship between qualifier and qualified is based upon real entities, another underlying relation must necessarily be postulated.
In this context, the cognition "non-existence, non-existence" alone has been taught; furthermore, a universal residing in a limiting adjunct exists only within its own substrata.

Nor is any other persisting entity desired among them; for if it were so desired, it would not be distinct from the six categories, nor do cognitions of non-existence arise apart from these six objects.

In an object whose form is produced by desire (i.e., imagined), no universal (*jāti*) exists; because the manifestation (*vyakti*) is impossible, the universal’s deviation [from its locus] is established. If it is argued that cognition has as its object an eternal universal even regarding things past or yet to arise, then this universal would be perceived in isolation. But it is not so perceived. Or, if it were perceived in isolation, it would not belong to manifestations; for the universal is not manifested by them, just as the Himalaya is not manifested by the Vindhya mountains. Indeed, this [universal] is not bound to those [manifestations] through dependence on their production, nor through dependence on cognition, because it is eternal and is apprehended in isolation. Since there is no possibility of depending on the contact of its own substratum with a sense organ and so forth, it would either be perceived at all times or never at all. Whether it is capable or incapable of producing cognition within itself, its nature must remain exactly as it was once; for since that nature is permanent, who indeed could shake it? It is truly unshakable due to its stability.

"Cowness is a different entity from the cow, because it is the object of a distinct cognition, like color, touch, and so forth; and because of the statement 'it belongs to that,' like Caitra and his horse. To this, the charge of fallacy is made by means of "cook-ness" and the like. In this same manner, all other fallacious arguments (kuhetu) are to be refuted.

Furthermore, regarding what is said about the universal’s existence in many [individuals]: what is this "existence" (vṛtti) considered to be? Is it its staying (sthiti), or is it simply its manifestation (vyakti)? First, its staying—defined as the non-deviation from its own nature—is inherent to it by its very essence. An underlying substratum (ādhāra) is not capable of producing that [staying], such that it could function as a "supporter" (sthāpaka). Nor is there for it any obstruction to movement, like that of a jujube fruit [in a bowl]; since it is devoid of action (niṣkriyatva), a substratum is therefore not postulated. If it is argued that its "staying" is its inherence (samavāya) [in the individuals], that very point is being examined. That [inherence] is intended to consist in the relationship of locus and located (āśrayāśrayitā) between things that are inseparable (ayutasiddha).

An "substratum" (ādhāra) may serve to obstruct the movement of things such as water; but what is the use of postulated substrata for universals (sāmānya), which are devoid of motion? If a thing is already capable of producing its own cognition, what is the use of causes of manifestation (abhivyakti-kāraṇa)? And if it is incapable of producing its own cognition, what is the use of causes of manifestation? If that which was previously incapable is made capable by manifestors, then the entity (bhāva) would necessarily be impermanent, just like a jar manifested by a lamp.
Furthermore, the specific universals such as "jar-ness" and so forth must either exist only in their own substrata, or they must subsist everywhere like the highest universal (mahāsāmānya).
In that case, when an object appears in another location, how is it that they are seen as possessing activity within that [new location]? This is not understood.
For they do not arise together with it because of its eternity, nor do they abide there; and since they lack prior pervasiveness, they do not come there, and thus they are inactive.

If, due to the connection with the sense-faculties residing in their own substrates, there were apprehension of that [universal] in one instance, it would be perceived everywhere, because its essential nature is undifferentiated.

If it were non-different from that which is already known, then it too would be apprehended; or else, like that [known object], there would be no apprehension of it, or there would be a difference [between them].

These cognitions of "tree" and so forth do not arise from universals (jāti) imagined by others, because they possess succession, conformity, and other such properties, just like the cognitions of "cook" and the like. Furthermore, the fact that an eternal entity cannot be a producer is understood as a subverting argument; indeed, everything that was stated in the refutation of conjunction (saṃyoga) serves as a subverting argument here as well.
Thus, this [theory] of an absolutely distinct genus has been refuted; however, that which is accepted by the followers of Jaimini shall be rejected within the context of the *syādvāda*.
Thus, this [theory] of an absolutely distinct genus has been refuted; however, that which is accepted by the followers of Jaimini will be rejected within the context of the *syādvāda*.
Furthermore, those final moments which are imagined as distinct entities through the exclusion of eternal substances—those too are impossible in a single moment.
Furthermore, those final moments which are imagined as specific distinctions through the exclusion of eternal substances—those too are impossible in a single moment.

When the intrinsic nature of atoms, space, the directions, and so forth, remains unmixed, it is then characterized by its distinctness from these others. If, however, those things whose other-natures have become intermingled were to exist again, then even when they are not in a state of mutual exclusion, their characteristic of distinctness would not be unerring. How, then, could there be a characterization of distinctness among those particularities? If you say it is "by itself," then why do you not hold this same view regarding atoms and the like as well?

For just as impurity exists inherently in dog-meat and the like, and others become impure through contact with it, so too should it be understood here. Just as a lamp exists inherently as an illuminator of jars and other objects, and its nature as illumination is fixed, so it is in this case as well.

Now, it might be argued that this impurity is merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*) and not ultimately real (*tāttvika*). How then could it possibly arise either from itself or from another? Alternatively, even if it were ultimately real, these impure states arise due to factors such as dog-meat and the like; they are certainly not eternal, because they lack birth [from themselves]. Furthermore, momentary objects such as jars, ornaments, and so forth, acquire the nature of producing cognition through the influence of lamps and other conditions. There is no notion of distinctness among them that arises from the power of some specific [intrinsic] difference, because they arise sequentially, just like pleasure and other mental states.

Now, it may be argued that this state of impurity is merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*) and not ultimate (*tāttvika*). How then could it arise either from itself or from another? Alternatively, even if it were ultimately real, these impure states arise due to factors such as dog-meat and the like; they are certainly not eternal, because they are produced. Furthermore, momentary objects such as jars, ornaments, and so forth, acquire the nature of producing cognition through the influence of lamps and other conditions. There is no notion of distinctness among them that arises from the power of some specific [inherent] difference, because they arise sequentially, just like pleasure and the like.
The existence of the notion "the cloth is in these very threads" and "the mat is in these vīraṇa-grasses," and so forth, leads one to understand the relation of inherence (samavāya).

In such instances as "the cloth is in these very threads" and "the mat is in these vīraṇa-grasses," the relation of inherence (samavāya) is understood from the existence of the cognition of "being here."

In its absence, what indeed could be the basis for this cognition? No cognition of a particular [object] is observed to be devoid of another cause.
