Furthermore, because the cognition "here" is not distinct, it does not differ from the case of conjunction; thus, when all things exist, this [space] is perceived as one alone. And because no cause is perceived, it is eternal, just like the category of existence (*bhāva*); for no cause whatsoever for it is apprehended by any means of valid cognition.
This very cognition belongs only to others; it is not perceived by them as something worldly, due to their attachment to their own tenets.

For the cognition "this is here" occurs only when there is a characteristic of diversity between that which serves as the locus and that which is contained within it, as in the case of bilva fruits in a bowl. However, no such characteristic of diversity is perceived between the threads and the cloth; therefore, cognitions such as "this is here" do not arise with respect to them.
In this work composed according to one’s own will, just like among imagined objects, this application of a cause does not hold up against an opponent.

"The branches are in the tree" and "the stones are in the goat"—this is worldly cognition, arising from the perception of proximity to those parts that remain designated as "goat. However, the cognition that "those two [the tree and the goat] are in them [the branches and stones]" is said to transcend the world; for one understands identity in the form "color is in the pot" or "action is in the pot. Indeed, words such as "color" and "pot" denote all possible states; they are applied in such a manner to denote specific instances thereof. Relying upon those [general terms], cognition proceeds toward these [specifics] in that particular form. This is not due to inherence (*samavāya*), because no distinction whatsoever is perceived among all things.

If inherence were one and the same in all things, it would follow that even in the case of potsherds and the like, there would be the cognition "this is a cloth. It would further follow that "cowness" and other such universals exist even in elephants and the like; consequently, these [elephants] would possess the form of a cow, just like a brindled cow (*śāvaleyavat*). As for the claim that "the cloth exists in the threads because of inherence," since that [inherence] also exists in the potsherds, why is it not the case that [the cloth] is perceived there as well? If you say that it does not reside in the potsherd, surely it is admitted that it resides in the threads. If it resides [in the threads] by way of inherence, why does it not exist in the potsherd in that same manner? For that which is called the "inherence of the cloth in the threads" is indeed the inherence of the jar in its potsherds; thus, the cognition of that [cloth] would be limitless.

In this way, that very same inherence which exists in elephants and so forth as "elephant-ness" and the like, is also present in their respective substrata as the distinct universals such as "cowness."
The restriction of the container and the contained exists even when there is identity; for it is just as [the distinction between] substance and its class-properties, or action and its nature.

Because one observes the continuity of cognitions arising from inherence (samavāya) with respect to the notion "here," it is understood that this inherence is one and the same everywhere. However, because one observes the exclusion of the causes of cognitions—such as substance-ness and so forth—it is determined that there is a restriction regarding the classes (jāti) such as substance and the rest.

Just as, for example, although the conjunction between a vessel and its curd is one, a restriction of the container and the contained is observed; so too here, such a restriction is accepted. Even though inherence (*samavāya*) is a single entity, it is not contradicted among the categories such as substance and genus, due to the difference in the capacities of the manifested and the manifestor.

If this [universal] were one, then the restriction of the container and the contained would indeed be difficult to establish. Substantiality is held to reside only in a substance; how could that be due to inherence? Furthermore, that very same inherence exists in qualities and so forth as well; for this [inherence] is indeed one and the same for both, owing to its connection with qualities, universals, and the like.
Otherwise, this [Yoga] would indeed be distinct according to its qualities, genus, and so forth, just as Yoga differs with respect to each individual due to the difference between practitioners.

The exclusion of causes such as substantiality (dravyatva) and the like is not tenable, because the causes for [the respective] cognitions do exist; therefore, there can be no restriction [of those cognitions] either.

Therefore, its state of being dependent, its location, and so forth, are designated as arising from that very [inherence] alone; thus, it is not logical for inherence to be the regulator of those [properties].

Even the distinction between the capacity of the manifested and the manifestor arises from inherence (samavāya), and not from anything else, because the production of eternal entities is logically impossible.
For it is not the case that jars and other such things, when produced, become capable of generating consciousness simply because lamps and the like exist.
Furthermore, the single conjunction between the bowl and the curd was previously refuted; nor is that [conjunction] restricted, for otherwise it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
If this [space] were eternal, then all things such as jars would necessarily be eternal; for their inherence in their substrates would never cease to exist.

If it is argued that actions and the like perish either through the disjunction of their own constituent parts or through their destruction—just as a lamp perishes through its conjunction with fire and so forth—that is not so; for their inherence in their own substrates is always maintained. Indeed, if those [substrates] were to undergo destruction, the destruction of this [inherence] would also be certain.

For it is difficult to maintain that a relation exists when the related entities have ceased to exist; indeed, even upon the destruction of the conjoined things, the conjunction does not fail to persist. Just as there is the continued existence of the conjoined things even in the absence of the conjunction, so too would it be for the inherent things (samavāyins) if the inherence (samavāya) were to exist.

Even upon the destruction of one related member, inherence (samavāya) persists because of the continued existence of the other related member; if you say this is not so because it is a conjunction (yoga), that is not correct, due to the difference between the two.

If this is so, then regarding those inherent entities such as jars that perish: does that inherence which was postulated as their very mode of subsistence remain in place because it resides in other related things, or is it something else entirely, like the multiplicity of conjunctions? It cannot be the first case; for if inherence, whose defining characteristic is precisely that [of being a single, eternal relation], remains as it was, then jars and the like would necessarily persist just as they did before. If they do not persist, then that inherence which constitutes their mode of subsistence could not remain anywhere—unless it were merely a name, since it would be so. Therefore, because they exist even prior [to the destruction of the jar], they would not be "subsisting" in their substrate any more than they are afterwards; for thus, their subsistence is unreal.

Furthermore, like conjunction, disjunction, multiplicity, and so forth, inherence would persist only when another related entity exists. Indeed, just as with conjunction and the rest, there would be a multiplicity of this [inherence] as well; thus, if its existence were established in such a manner, many inconsistencies would arise.

Alternatively, like conjunction, disjunction, and plurality, inherence would persist only when another related entity exists. For in that case, just as with conjunction and the like, there would indeed be a multiplicity of this [inherence]; and if it were so for the primary [inherence], many inconsistencies would arise.

If no limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) exist from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), then what would be the objects of such cognitions and verbal expressions as "the man with a staff," "white," "he moves," "there is," or "a cow"? They cannot be considered causeless; nor is it possible for those two [cognition and expression] to function without distinction across all things.

If no limiting adjuncts (upādhis) exist from the perspective of ultimate reality, then what would be the objects of such cognitions and verbal expressions as "the man with a staff," "white," "moves," "exists," or "the cow is here"? They cannot be considered causeless; yet their occurrence in all things without distinction is impossible.
It is said that there is no object whatsoever for these cognitions and words; rather, their basis is the seed situated within the internal dimension alone.
For whatever object is expressed by whichever word, that [object] does not exist at all; for such is the true nature of things.

Since the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), the universal (*jāti*), its connection, and the possessor of the universal (*jātimat*)—as well as the form of the cognition (*buddhyākāra*)—do not, in reality, apply to the referent of a word (*śabdārtha*).
In that regard, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not expressed by words, because it lacks pervasion over the time of the convention and the time of practical usage.

These [particulars], whose nature is that of individuals, do not follow one another in their mutual form, due to differences in place, time, action, capacity, appearance, and so forth. Therefore, the object perceived at the time of the convention is not seen during linguistic usage; nor can an object for which the convention has not been grasped be understood from a word, just as in the case of other things.
Even those things such as the Himalayas and so forth, which appear to be undifferentiated by space, time, and other factors, have been established as having distinct atoms and as being momentary.

It is impossible to conceive of this convention (samaya) with respect to either what has been born or what has not yet been born. A convention regarding what has not yet been born is not tenable as a real entity, like a horse's horn. Nor is it possible [for a convention] regarding what has already been born; for how could a convention be established there through the recollection of words previously grasped, when that [object] has long since passed away?

Furthermore, when another [cognition] of that same class arises by the power of that [preceding one], there is no extension of the convention (*samayābhoga*) therein, and the similarity is merely conceptualized.
The cognition of heat and so forth that arises from sounds such as names does not appear clearly, unlike the sensory cognition of those objects themselves.

Neither is the connection of that object with the word logical, nor is it [logical] in the cognition produced by it; for when the cognition exists, the object does not appear, just as taste does not appear in the perception of color.

In this very manner, the refutation of both the individual (vyakti) and the form (ākṛti) is established, since others also maintain that these two have the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) as their very nature.
Since the negation of substance and so forth, as well as of their conjunction, has already been stated, it is not tenable that these two are established as the actual referents of words.

Since the [relations of] genus and connection have already been refuted in detail previously, other threefold categories of word-meanings, such as immediate succession and so forth, are not postulated.
As for the claim that the individual, the configuration, and the genus constitute the referent of a word, that is impossible, because all of them are devoid of intrinsic form.

The form of the cognition, residing within the cognition itself, does not follow from the object nor from another cognition; furthermore, it does not produce the intended object, and thus it cannot be said to be [the object] in reality.
Those others who explain the meaning of words as being "existence" (*asti*) and so forth in a different manner are already refuted by these [arguments]; nevertheless, it is stated once more.

"The definition of that which is to be conveyed by words is that all words possess a real referent (astyartha); they say this is the same for words such as 'cow' as it is for [words denoting] the unseen force (apūrva), deities, and heaven."

Some assert that the meaning of a word is either a collection (*samudāya*)—whether it be a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) or a simple aggregate (*samuccaya*)—or else it is a relation (*saṃsarga*) that is unreal.

Either that reality which is devoid of unreal adjuncts is the basis for words, or else the word itself, having attained the state of being identified with its object (abhijalpa), becomes the denotable entity.
When the form of the word is unified with its object through the connection "this is that," they call that word *abhijalpa*.
Alternatively, some maintain that the meaning of a word is that object which, though it is the content of cognition and based upon an external thing, is understood as being the external thing itself.
In brief, every word is a cause of intuitive flash (pratibhā) through repeated practice, just as it functions in conveying meaning for children and even for animals.

In this regard, is this denotable object "existent" (asti) intended to be the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), or the universal (*jāti*), or a connection (*yoga*), or something else, or perhaps a reflection (*pratibimbaka*) in the intellect? These previously mentioned faults apply even when the mere meaning of "existent" is to be established; for without a distinction [among these], linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is not possible.

The cognition of the mere existence of an object qualified by the word "cowness" would occur; however, that view maintains that there is no cognition of distinctions such as the horn, shape, blue color, and so forth.

But in that case, there would be the denotation of both the object possessing those [qualities] and of the distinctions themselves; and if that were so, the aforementioned fault would apply there, for no other object is perceived.
Even when denoting a collection, the expression of distinct classes is clear, because austerity, caste, action, and so forth are denoted in their entirety.

Furthermore, regarding substances and so forth whose intrinsic natures have been determined, any relation [between them] based on conjunction (*yoga*), as well as any universal (*sāmānya*) that might exist, has already been refuted previously. Because it is logically untenable for the referent of a word to take the form of particulars, universals, and so on, a form of the word that is unified with the external object is not possible. This "mental discourse" (*jalpa*) exists only within the intellect due to its distinction from external conjunction; therefore, what difference is there between this and the position of the intellect itself? Moreover, the view that the form of the cognition is the word-referent has already been rejected, because that which is non-different from the cognition lacks pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*).

Furthermore, if intuition (*pratibhā*) has as its object the external thing which is the referent of a word, how could there be diverse intuitions regarding an external object that is fixed as having a single nature? Alternatively, if these [intuitions] are without an object because they exist merely as mental impressions (*vāsanā*), how could there be either comprehension or activity directed toward external objects? If you maintain that [intuition] consists of one’s own form through the superimposition (*adhimokṣa*) of an external form, then the referent of the word becomes unreal, since activity occurs through such an error. Nor is it logical for that [intuition] to be seedless, as that would lead to the over-extension (*prasaṅga*) of [cognition] everywhere. If the seed of this [intuition] is the mutual difference (*itaretara-bheda*) among things, then this is our very position.
Whether all this is indeed momentary or not so; if it were momentary, there would be no possibility of continuity (anvaya), and sequential cognition would not otherwise be possible.

By this very [argument], the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*) is also refuted as being accessible through words; for if the word and its object do not exist, where could there be an intention to speak, or where could there be hearing?

Furthermore, how could there be a function [of a word] based on similarity when it is not enjoined by the word? By this, the [objection that] names and so forth function through similarity—like the case of the *yamalaka*—is refuted.

If activity proceeds from two [cognitions] that establish an external object through a form conjoined with the inference of the speaker's intention, then that is precisely our own position once again.

Now, how can it be said by you that a word effects the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), when in this [cognition] nothing but a negation is perceived in the manifestation? Rather, from words such as "cow," "gavaya," "elephant," and "tree," the verbal cognition proceeds by way of a determination in the form of a positive entity (*vidhirūpa*).
If this word "cow" has already fulfilled its purpose by excluding other things, then let another sound be observed as the producer of the cognition of "cow" regarding the cow.

Is it not the case that words have cognition as their fruit, and yet one thing cannot have two fruits? Or how can there be a single fruit for both the cognition of an exception and the cognition of a positive injunction?

Prior to hearing the word "cow," there would have to arise for one who hears the word "cow" the cognition "it is not a cow," because it is for the purpose of negating that which is not a cow that the sound "cow" is employed.

Those who accept that the denotable object is the universal, namely the cessation of suffering (*agonivṛtti*), have clearly stated by this very statement that "cowness" (*gotva*) is indeed a real entity (*vastu*).
Since non-existence is of the nature of another existence, by virtue of which everything is established, let it be stated that the existence therein consists of the exclusion of horses and the like.

A particular (*viśeṣa*) whose nature is unique (*asādhāraṇa*) is not desired by you, because it is devoid of conceptualization (*nirvikalpanāt*). Furthermore, if that were the case, it would follow that the brindled cow (*śābaleya*) and others would not be universals (*asāmānya*). Therefore, that form which is established in each and every one of them must be the cause of the cognition "cow," for such a thing exists.
If the meaning of a word is conceived as being merely of the nature of a negation, then emptiness would be something other than what is expressed by the word "non-existence."

And in that case, the cognitions of "horse" and so forth would involve the apprehension of a portion of the self [of the object]; therefore, the claim that the exclusion of others (anyāpoha) is the denotable meaning is accepted in vain.
For the universal, which is the nature of a real entity, will be the form of the cognition, constructed as the meaning of a word.

And that cognition, which arises regarding the objects of words, has the form of a real entity; therefore, among those [objects], only a real entity should be postulated as the denotable, being a cognition that does not exclude [other things].
Even though an external object does not exist, just as the meaning of a sentence is a mental intuition (pratibhā), so too should the meaning of a word be; why then is apoha postulated?
Furthermore, the exclusion from other cognitions is not perceived within a cognition; for, by the mere production of its own form, it does not bear any other part.
If exclusion (*apoha*) were the denotable object, then all words—both those expressing distinct universals and those expressing particulars—would be synonyms.
Since exclusions (apohas) are non-entities, they lack the nature of being either mixed or characterized by unity or plurality; thus, even their differentiation does not exist.

Alternatively, because it is subject to differentiation, it is like a specific, non-common portion of an entity; however, if it were a non-entity, there would be no plurality, and thus it could not escape being mere synonyms.

But surely, the distinction of exclusion (apoha) will be established through the distinctions among horses and so forth? No; for its distinction does not arise either from itself or from something else.
For even those substrates with which it is associated do not divide it in its essential form; that it should be divided by external factors to be excluded (apohya) is an excessive conceptualization.

In the same way, a distinction of this [negation] based on a distinction of its substratum is also not tenable; for even in the case of a real entity, a distinction is not admitted merely through a distinction of its relata. How much less could that which is unreal, unconnected, undifferentiated, non-exclusive, devoid of any acquired particularity, and entirely indefinable, ever be excluded?
Furthermore, no one at all is able to cognize cows and the like as having an essence consisting of exclusion (apoha) when their similarity [to other things] is not already established.

Furthermore, without the recurrence of a single common property, one is unable to define even the things to be excluded, such as horses and the like; thus, their exclusion (apoha) cannot be established.

The operation of words and logical marks does not occur apart from positive concomitance (anvaya); yet there is no exclusion (apoha) without those two, nor is there positive concomitance in that which is unique (asādhāraṇa).

Furthermore, since exclusion (*apoha*) itself is not established, where can concomitance (*sāhacarya*) be said to exist? And when that [concomitance] is not perceived, there can be no validity for those two [the reason and the thesis].
Nor can there be comprehension from those two by mere non-perception; for since everything is unperceived, comprehension would not be distinguished [from non-comprehension].
Furthermore, if the conceptualization of apoha were possible even in the absence of similarity, why is this "non-cow" (ago) apoha not likewise postulated for both the cow and the horse?
The difference from a spotted cow is equal for both a black cow and a horse; if no other universal is admitted, then where could the exclusion of the non-cow (apoha) apply?
Nor is the exclusion of the non-cow first determined by the sense organs; nor does the operation of words occur elsewhere—having seen what, then, would that [term] be applied?
By the aforementioned argument, even inference does not exist here; therefore, the experience of its [inference's] relationship is likewise not possible.
Furthermore, how can it be understood that [the object] is not denoted by the word "cow," given that the word "cow" was not observed there at the moment of experiencing the relationship?
In that case, everything other than a single lump of cow-dung would have to be the object of exclusion; therefore, the universal cannot be the denotable meaning.

If a cow were already established, it would have to be excluded by the exclusion [of the non-cow], and that exclusion would consist in the negation of the cow. In that case, one must state that very cow which is being negated by the negative particle (*nañ*). If that [cow] were itself of the nature of the exclusion of the non-cow, there would be mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). If the cow is already established, then the postulation of an exclusion for the sake of exclusion is useless.
If the non-cow is not established when the cow is established, then in its absence, how could there be a cow? Furthermore, there can be no relationship such as locus and located between two absences.
Furthermore, a unique particular (asādhāraṇa-vastu) is not apprehended as possessing an exclusion (apoha); or else, how could a relationship between a real entity and a non-entity be conceived?
By its mere existence in its own nature, something cannot be a qualifier; that by which the qualificand is colored through its own cognition is a qualifier.

Furthermore, from words such as "horse" and so forth, there arises no cognition of apoha; for in this context, the cognition of the qualified object is desired, and a cognition of the qualified object does not occur when its qualifier is unknown.

Furthermore, a cognition that is of one nature cannot make something else—which is of a different nature—its qualifier; and how could that [object] be called a qualifier with respect to a cognition that is of a different nature?
Otherwise, if the conceptualization of a qualifier were to apply even to that which is qualified, then anything whatsoever could be accepted as a qualifier.

Furthermore, since the qualified object is of a nature accessible only through non-existence, it lacks substantial reality; therefore, for you, there is no real entity that can be expressed as qualified by an exclusion (apoha).

Although words and logical marks do not function with respect to anything devoid of exclusion (apoha), nevertheless, the cognition that arises is necessarily supported by a real entity (vastu) in order to be understood.
Furthermore, a unique particular does not appear within the intellect, nor is its apprehension tenable because it is free from conceptual construction.
And it is a rash assertion to claim that the qualified object is not apprehended by the word; therefore, a universal must be accepted as the objective domain of both cognition and verbal expression.

And when individuals cannot be the objects of exclusion because they are not denotable by words, then it is the universal that must be excluded; and from its exclusion, [the universal] would lose its status as a real entity.

Exclusions (apoha) cannot be excluded, because there is no exclusion of a non-existence by another non-existence; therefore, the exclusion of other exclusions is manifested from a real universal entity.
And if the non-existence of non-existence were different from it, it would indeed be an existence; if it were not, then the consequence of its being white follows for you.
Even if other words might have something as their object of exclusion (apohya), for the word "existent" (sat), no distinct entity is admitted as its exclusion, since it denotes non-existence itself.
In that case, there would be the great difficulty of attributing existence even to what is non-existent; if that [existence] is not established, neither being nor non-being can be proven.

Nor can a distinction or even a state of existence be attributed to exclusions (*apoha*) based on a difference in mental impressions (*vāsanā*), for such [distinction or existence] is not admitted in the case of a non-entity.

Even a difference in words based on that [exclusion] cannot be established by you; for a word that is not common [to others] is not expressive, because it has never been observed [to be so]. In that case, when a universal is postulated as the exclusion of other words, a difference between words is not conceived, precisely because it lacks the nature of a real entity. Just as this applies to expressers, so too does it apply to the mutual relationship between the expressed and the expresser; furthermore, it has been demonstrated that there is no difference [in the object] based on the difference of what is excluded.

In your view, there can be no relationship of signifier and signified between the two exclusions (apohas), because they are non-entities, just as in the world there is none between a sky-flower and a hare's horn.

If one were to say that [the reason] is inconclusive because rain is seen even when there is no cloud, [we reply: in our position, this is indeed a real entity; but how could it be so in your position?
For one who does not accept that the meaning of a word has a positive form, even negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) would not exist, for the latter is preceded by the former.

If it is here accepted that words such as "blue lotus" and others—which denote variegated objects—have as their denotation merely an exclusion (apoha), then the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyatva*) and grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) cannot be established. For when there is the exclusion of non-blue, there is no exclusion of non-lotus; nor is the latter [the exclusion of non-lotus] present therein [in the exclusion of non-blue]. Therefore, there can be no qualifier and qualified. Furthermore, those two [relationships] could not belong to the two words themselves if they were independent of their denotations.

Furthermore, there can be no grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) between two exclusions (apoha) because they are distinct; if it were claimed that such coreferentiality exists by virtue of their objects, what kind of "inherence" (ādheyatā) could there be between those two?
A unique object is not apprehended, and for you, there is nothing else [to be apprehended]. Of what use is the identity of two words when that identity is not being apprehended?

Furthermore, no connection with gender, number, and so forth exists for the exclusion (apoha); nor does it exist by way of the individual instance (vyakti), because that [instance] is itself inexpressible.
Furthermore, in the case of verbs, the exclusion of anything else is not perceived; for there exists no object of negation there that takes the form of a relative negation (paryudāsa).

For even when "no" is uttered, there is the negation of a negation; however, that which is not negated—such as "he cooks"—remains in its own essential form. Furthermore, since the exclusion (*apoha*) is already established, it would follow that the cognition of it as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), as well as its representation as having the form of past time and so forth, would be without any basis.

Furthermore, in a mass of meanings such as positive injunctions (*vidhi*) and the like, there is no determination of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). Moreover, when a negative particle (*nañ*) is joined with another negative particle, what kind of exclusion could possibly result? Since particles such as "and" (*ca*) have no connection with a negative particle, there is no exclusion there either. Furthermore, in the case of a sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), the exclusion of other things cannot be designated. In words such as "non-exclusion of others" (*ananyāpoha*), the denotable object (*vācya*) itself cannot be determined; and as for words such as "knowable" (*prameya*) or "cognizable" (*jñeya*), how indeed could there even be an object to be excluded?

And when there is the conceptualization of an object to be excluded (apohya), it is better to simply postulate a real entity; furthermore, because the form of cognition is denied, no internal object is denoted. Nor, therefore, can there be the status of being "excluded," so that exclusion (apoha) is not established in their case. Moreover, for words such as "thus" (evam) and so forth, no object to be excluded can be determined.

What object is conceived as being excluded by the word *sarva* (all)? For there would be nothing that is not a "universal name" (*asarvanāman*) which could be negated. If it is argued that "one and so forth" are the non-universals (*asarva*), then the exclusion of meaning (*arthāpoha*) follows [absurdly], because the parts (*aṅga*) are already excluded and the whole (*aṅgin*) is not desired separately. In this way, regarding the meaning of a word for a collection, if one excludes the individual members (*samudāyin*), then since no other [meaning] is desired, all words would likewise become meaningless. Furthermore, those words such as "two" and so forth which are intended here to refer to a collection, they would not be of such a nature if "one" and so forth were excluded. And as for that exclusion (*apoha*) called "non-cow" which is said to be the meaning of the word "cow"—is it a positive entity (*bhāva*) or a negative non-entity (*abhāva*); and if it is a positive entity, is it a cow or a non-cow? If it is a cow, there is no dispute, for the meaning is then characterized by a positive injunction (*vidhi*). If a non-cow were the denotation of the word "cow," that would be an extraordinary skill in the meaning of words! Nor is a negative non-entity appropriate, because commands (*praiṣa*) and the like would be impossible; for no one understands a negative non-entity from the word "cow."

Why is it maintained that the meaning of the word "cow" is the exclusion (*apoha*) of the non-cow? For by what means has "non-cowness" been attached to the cow such that it must be excluded? Furthermore, regarding this exclusion of the non-cow which is said to be the meaning of the word in the case of a cow—is it accepted as being distinct from the cow or non-distinct? If it were distinct, would it be dependent (*āśrita*) or independent (*anāśrita*)? If it were dependent, it would follow that it is a quality (*guṇa*), and therefore the word could not denote a substance (*dravya*). Consequently, since the word "cow" would denote only a quality, there could be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in expressions such as "the cow goes" or "the cow stands. Alternatively, if this [exclusion] were entirely independent, what would its referent be, by virtue of which it is designated as "non-cow" for the purpose of negation? Moreover, if you maintain that this exclusion of others is non-distinct [from the cow], then it follows that it is simply the cow itself; what more is there to say beyond that?

This exclusion (*apoha*), which is the individual manifestation, may be either one or many. If it were one, yet associated with many individual cows, it would simply be "cowness" (*gotva*). Even if it were many, it would entail an infinite number [of exclusions], just like the individual bodies [of cows]; therefore, its status as a denotable object is not tenable, precisely because it is as differentiated as the individuals themselves.

Furthermore, is this *anyāpoha* (exclusion of others) intended to be denotable or undenotable? If it is denotable, is it so by way of a positive form (*vidhi*) or through the negation of another? If its denotability is by way of a positive nature, then your extremist view must be abandoned—that it has been described that "in all cases, the meaning of a word is this exclusion of others. If, on the other hand, the *apoha* is expressed by means of the exclusion of [other] exclusions, then by desiring it thus in each instance, there would result an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Moreover, if you maintain that this *apoha* is indeed undenotable, then your statement that "a word effects the exclusion of others" would be contradicted.

Moreover, for one who attributes oneness, permanence, and individual inherence to "exclusions" (apohas) that are devoid of any defining characteristics, it would be like a cloth woven without a thread. Therefore, only in those words where a negative particle is joined does the aspect of the exclusion of others occur; elsewhere, only the word's own nature is understood.

Because they do not fully understand the exclusion of others (anyāpoha), these people of wrong views, being themselves ruined and evil-minded, ruin others as well. For exclusion is of two kinds, by way of relative negation (paryudāsa) and absolute negation (niṣedha); and relative negation is also twofold, through the distinction between the nature of cognition and the nature of the object.

Those causes of a single unifying cognition (*ekapratyavamarśa*) which were stated previously—objects such as "fearlessness" and the like—are by their very nature distinct from one another. Relying upon them, a reflection of the object appears in a conceptualizing cognition; even though that reflection lacks the actual nature of the object, it is determined as being "the object itself."

Because it is distinct from other appearances, because it is the cause for attaining a real entity excluded from others, and because it leads [to that entity] by means of an unconnected object; or because, through a delusion, there is a determination (*adhyavasāya*) of that very thing as being identical with its result—the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) which is excluded from what is of a different class—it is for these reasons that the name "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) is applied to it in a justified manner, even though it refers to the particular characteristic itself, since it possesses the state of being differentiated from others.
And this is a non-presuppositional negation (prasajya-pratiṣedha), such as "this cow is not a non-cow"; indeed, this exclusion of others (anyāpoha) is understood with extreme clarity.
In this regard, this first type of exclusion (apoha) is established by means of words, because a cognition that determines an external object arises from a word.
When a cognition arises from a word through the production of a reflection having that form, this relationship of signifier and signified is born, consisting of cause and effect.

When this direct form has been thus established, even a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) is understood by implication. Since there is a relation with entities such that "it is not of that nature, but of another nature," the comprehension of an entity as excluded [from others] also occurs precisely through the force of the meaning (*artha*). Therefore, this too is figuratively designated as the word's own referent (*svārtha*); however, this twofold apoha is not said to be directly denoted by the word.
When a word is said to "denote" its own meaning by performing the exclusion of other meanings (arthāntaravyavaccheda), this is not contradictory.

Because it produces a reflection that functions through the determination of an external object, it is designated as "speaking. However, this [cognition] does not touch the specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*) in its differentiated form; apart from the aspect consisting of that [mental] representation alone, it possesses no act of denotation.
And it is only the movement of that reflection which is followed; by implication, there is a separation from other things, because it does not possess the nature of anything else.

Like the statement regarding eating during the day, this [statement] also possesses two results; for there is no positive concomitance (anvaya) that is devoid of negative concomitance (avyatireka), whether directly or by implication.
Because this word directly effects these two: the denotation of its own meaning and the exclusion of other things.
And such an appearance is held to be the universal "cowness" (gotva), because it is determined as being identical throughout all [individuals], such as the brindled cow and others.
And because of the determination "it is a real entity," it is also called a "real entity"; for that cognition has indeed arisen instantly as an error from its own seed.
And that very exclusion (apoha), which is the meaning of the word in its form, is called a universal (sāmānya) and a real entity (vasturūpa), because it is determined as such through delusion.

Furthermore, it is not logical for this [universal] to have an ultimately real nature as a common entity; for how could that which is non-different in form from the cognition itself become a separate object?
Although this form is not distinct from the nature of the cognition, nevertheless, its external form is determined by those who are deluded.

It does not follow that it is independent of objects, because it arises from them through a causal succession; furthermore, it has been established that it possesses no substantial reality in its own right.
Apoha, consisting of a mental reflection, arises even from a word; this very thing, called intuition (*pratibhā*), is for us the meaning of the word itself.
For that [cognition] does not possess any other aspect beyond the mere production of its own nature; therefore, the exclusion of one cognition from another is perceived through that [nature].
Just as for that which does not exist there is no ultimate difference, so too is there no non-difference; therefore, they would be synonyms.

For non-difference is indeed the state of having a single form; but how could that exist in things that are formless? Furthermore, if the object were a single entity, its various expressive words would become synonyms.
Just as oneness is constructed by conceptualization even in the absence of form, so too is differentiation; therefore, how can there be synonymy [between them]?
In reality, however, words are neither synonymous nor non-synonymous; for it has been explained that there is no single external object corresponding to them, nor is there a plurality.
However, if even multiple [entities] are observed to perform a single function, then a single Vedic word is applied there by superimposing a single property.

Just as in the case of the eye and other [senses], which have the single result of visual consciousness, if someone were to apply the term "hearing" [to them] even in the absence of a single common factor that accompanies them all.

Although the function of jars and the like—such as the holding of water—and the cognition directed toward them are two distinct things, they are said to be "one" because they are the cause of a single unifying reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśa*). Nevertheless, by virtue of being the cause of that [unified] cognition, the objects themselves are non-different.
In this regard, words such as "jar" and so forth, which express universals, are the sole causes for the production of a mental reflection that is excluded from those of a different class.
Likewise, because it performs many functions, the one is spoken of as if it were not one; this is conceptually constructed based on its manifold exclusion of what does not perform those functions.
Just as visible form is also characterized by resistance, or as sound is known to arise immediately after an effort, yet is inaudible [to the ear].
In some cases, a word is applied by way of the distinction of its non-cause, as for example, "sound" is [distinguished as] "arising from effort," or "honey" as "produced by bees."
In some cases, a scriptural statement is made here based on the exclusion of its effect and its cause, such as "form is not audible" or "lightning is not produced by effort."

Through such distinctions, exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) based on differentiated objects are conceptualized, and likewise, words are established as being grounded in those [exclusions]. Therefore, because words function through differentiation to express unmixed objects according to convention, they are not synonyms for us.
Because their scope is extensive or limited, and because they are inferred from their respective conventions, there is no contradiction in these [words] expressing both generalities and particulars.
And those exclusions of objects, being constructed by mere conceptualization, do not in reality differ according to the difference of the excluded or the substratum.
For their external form is merely imagined and not real; moreover, difference and non-difference are established in reality only with respect to an actual entity.

Due to the power of conventions regarding objects that are distinct from their own seeds, conceptual constructions (vikalpas) arise, determining those forms; yet they do not attain a single nature, nor are the objects—which consist of specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa)—divided into fragments. Rather, it is this conceptual construction that floats [over them].

Even in the absence of a single underlying property, the objects of exclusion and the exclusions themselves are understood through their distinctness by means of different conceptual reflections (*pratyavamarśa*).
For it has been established that, although things are by nature distinct, only certain ones are useful for a single unifying cognition, while others are not.

The particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the mere thing itself, excluded from what does not possess its form; this positive concomitance (*anvaya*), when established with effort, is not contradictory.

For in that [particular] which possesses a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) distinct from smoke, there exists a specific characteristic excluded from non-fire as well. Just as that [specific characteristic] which is distinct from smoke exists here in the kitchen, therefore a specific characteristic distinct from non-fire exists here too.

That which is distinct from non-existent things such as a human horn and so forth is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); like a cognition, a lamp, and so on, it is excluded even from that which is permanent. Likewise, this particular characteristic of sound and so forth does not have a non-existent nature; thus, through this specified distinction, there is indeed a positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

And that very same [cognition] is proclaimed as the universal characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) when its differentiation is not intended; it is not anything else, for we do not accept another [definition].

If there is a difference between a *bāhuleya* cow and a horse based on their offspring being brindled, since that quality is equally present in both, why does "cowness" (*gotva*) not exist in the horse as well?
If it is maintained that its very self is capable of manifesting that [cognition], then even in the case of a similar reflective awareness, that [cow] alone is capable, not the horse.
And where such a reflective awareness exists regarding a given object, there the exclusion of the non-cow (*agopoha*) proceeds even in the absence of a universal "cow" (*gojāti*).

An object that is not distinct from the cow is determined by the senses; however, that superimposed reflection is understood through self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*). Having perceived this [reflection], a person employs a word for it; thus, its experience of the relationship [between word and object] is clearly established thereby.
And where such a reflective awareness does not exist regarding a thing, its being denotable by the word "non-cow" is clearly understood there.

Cows and non-cows are established through distinct conceptual determinations (*pratyavamarśa*); however, the word alone is unestablished and is employed according to one’s whim. For the apprehension of another object does not depend upon a distinct cognition of the thing itself; therefore, this fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) has no basis here.

Although its external reality is not cognized, this verbal cognition—due to intense cognitive distortion—determines its own internal reflection as having an external form. This much alone is accomplished by words; words do not even touch the object itself. Nor is any object denoted as qualified by *apoha*.
Furthermore, regarding that which was stated by the author of the definition—that [words] denote qualified objects through the exclusion of other referents—the intended meaning therein is as follows:

Those entities which are distinguished by being "this or that" through a cause or an instrument, and which are determined as distinct and unmixed with those of different classes—such as trees and the like—the striking of them produces a sound that superimposes their existence; because it generates such cognition, this constitutes the negation of [an external] genus and so forth.
He calls those which evolve within the intellect "internal"; and their distinction by way of cessation has been stated immediately thereafter.
It is said that through the exclusion of other referents, a certain part of that entity is understood; that very [part] is the reflection.

Because it relies on the perception of a real entity that is excluded from other objects, and because of the superimposition [of that exclusion] upon what has been apprehended therein, a portion of that [entity] is designated.

The meaning of "cause" and the meaning of "instrument" are as before; therefore, if a thing were not distinct from that which is of a different genus by virtue of its own nature, it would not be so [distinct].

The cessation of suffering is its distinctness, and that [distinctness] resides in the self itself. Even when a difference is expressed, mere non-existence does not cease [to be what it is]. Furthermore, even when there is the state of being a qualifier for that [non-existence], the cognition of the real entity is not lost. This qualifier, though produced by conceptual construction, exists even where there is no actual difference. Therefore, having extracted that property, it is established as if possessing a difference, whereby it indeed becomes a qualifier for that [entity], just like a staff or similar objects.

Those who contemplate reality say that the meaning of a word is a mental appearance (*pratibhāsa*). However, the world, not discerning the distinction between the perceived object and its conceptual construction, considers it to be external. Therefore, through the process of cognitive determination (*adhyavasāya*), it is the individuals themselves that are expressed by words; yet, in ultimate reality, it has been established that there is no expressible object for words.

And thus, because individuals are denotable by words, they possess the quality of being excluded; however, there is no exclusion of the universal, nor does even that which is excluded possess the nature of a real entity.

For in this way, a non-entity is not excluded by the statement "non-entity is not a non-entity"; rather, since an entity does not have that [non-entity] as its nature, it is precisely that [entity] which is intended to be excluded.

That which is not of the nature of something is indeed called its exclusion (*apoha*). It is neither an entity nor of the nature of a non-entity; thus, in that exclusion, there is no substantial reality.

When it is argued that things are not produced by primordial matter (prakṛti), a Lord (īśa), or other such causes, then indeed no thing is established as being produced by primordial matter, a Lord, or the like.

Therefore, there is no difficulty whatsoever in the fact that even the non-existent possesses the nature of being; for when that [non-existence] is established, existence exists, and that very existence is established as non-existence.

The exclusion of the non-cow is held to be the cow as something distinct; therefore, this [cow] is indeed a positive entity, and the consequence of it being neither a cow nor a non-cow does not follow.

Even regarding objects that lack real existence, there exists a latent impression (*vāsanā*) produced by the mind alone, as if fashioned by various distinctions of conceptual construction. Consequently, through the diversity of these latent impressions, both differentiation and the appearance of a positive form (*sadrūpatā*) are attributed to exclusions (*apoha*), just as they are to things constructed by imagination.

Just as this exclusion of other objects (*arthāntarāpoha*) has been established as the denotation [of a word], let it be understood that the exclusion of other words (*śabdāntaravyapoha*) is exactly the same.

Because they are determined as real entities, the two types of exclusion (apoha) are not non-entities; this is well-established on the conventional path, while on the ultimate path, it serves to prove what is desired.

In the ultimate sense, there is nothing whatsoever that is either the signified or the signifier, because among entities that are subject to momentary destruction, there is an absence of pervasiveness.

If that relationship of signifier and signified is refuted only as being conventional (*sāṃvṛta*), while relying on the ultimate reality (*tāttvikī*) wherein both cessation and origination are non-entities, even so, the fault of inconclusiveness (*vyabhicāritva*) remains unavoidable; for this applies to objects constructed by conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) and to the words that denote them.

For there exists neither a universal to be denoted by them nor a denoter of that [universal]; nor does the word possess the nature of a denoter, since its specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is subject to momentary destruction.
Therefore, those two—the reflection and so forth—must be accepted as conventional; for their deviation from [the nature of] those [objects] remains unavoidable and established.

For one who does not accept that the meaning of a word has a positive form (*vidhirūpa*), the mind indeed arises from the word as having the appearance of that [positive object], while determining the object. When words denote their own meanings, the exclusion of others occurs by implication; for me, this is also the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), since it is preceded by that [denotation].
The impossibility of a positive injunction has been stated because universals and the like are impossible, and because words and conceptual constructions have real entities as their objects.
From words such as "blue lotus" and the like, only a single reflection is apprehended—one that is excluded from what is non-blue, non-lotus, and so forth.

We do not maintain that the denotable object is a thing possessing the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*); for since there is no exclusion other than that which is excluded from others, we hold that there is no further exclusion [of that exclusion]. This fault of dependence (*pāratantrya*), which applies to a universal (*jāti*) as it is taught by others, is not applicable here; for when the meaning of a word is stated as "pure" (*avadāta*), [the exclusion] is not distinct [from the thing itself]. Therefore, the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya*) and grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) are established without contradiction when the exclusion (*apoha*) is the word-meaning.

From the word "blue" alone, a specific reflection arises, floating over [the objects] such as the cuckoo, the blue lotus, and the bee. Then, by means of the exclusion (*apoha*) of the cuckoo, collyrium, and so forth, that [reflection] is established with certainty by the word "lotus" as having a specific object. In this way, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and other relations remain uncontradicted; however, on the opponent’s view, the establishment of all these [relations] is extremely difficult to achieve.

For in this way, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is expressed in every respect by a single word; and when it has been thus denoted, why would there be a cognition of another particular (*bheda*), for the sake of which another word would be employed here in reality? If it were not expressed in every respect, it would follow that it is manifold.

If the blue universal or the quality of blueness is already conveyed by the word "blue," then the other lotus universal must be determined by the auditory perception of the word "lotus. This being the case, because of the difference between the two [referents], just as in the case of the words "bakula" and "lotus," grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth become utterly untenable.

If a substance connected with a quality and its genus is what is intended to be expressed by the word "blue," then the mention of the word "lotus" would be redundant. For that very thing which is connected with those two [the quality blue and the genus lotus] is the same thing that possesses the genus of the lotus; since this is already stated there by the word "blue" alone, the expression "blue-lotus" is redundant.
If the words "blue" and "lotus" were to have distinct substrata, then [the lotus] possessing the genus "lotus" would be something other than that which is connected with the quality and its genus.

Now, one might object that the word "blue" does not denote a substance as being connected with the nature of "lotus-ness," but rather as connected with its quality and its genus. [Response: It is true that the nature of being conjoined with lotus-ness is distinct from those two (the quality and the genus). However, that which is connected with "lotus-ness" is indeed connected with those two as well. That [substance] is expressed by the verbal cognition of the word "blue" and is made the object of that verbal cognition here. Therefore, the cognition [of it] is in its entirety, not in parts; thus, the word "lotus" would be meaningless.

If there is no conceptualization of "wholeness" or "parts" regarding that which is free from division, it is because of a failure to understand the meaning of the sentence; for this is precisely what is intended here: by the very first word, it is manifested in its entirety; not a single aspect of its nature is omitted, and it is expressed exactly as it is.
In this very manner, the utterance of other words [denoting the same object] is not fruitful; in that case, their expression would certainly result in mere synonymy.

For us, however, an external object is not established by means of a word; nor is it held that cognition arises from a word having an external object as its domain. Because, after those two [word and cognition] have made the object their own through their entire nature, any subsequent word or cognition regarding it would merely result in synonymy.

The reflection, however, is produced by the word only in a sequential manner; yet it appears as a unity and as something external due to delusion. Grammatical coreferentiality and other such relations exist in accordance with the reflection; in ultimate reality, these words are considered to be without an object.
Furthermore, this connection with gender, number, and so forth does not even exist for individuals; it is caused by conventions established by whim and is not real.
The terms *taṭas*, *taṭī*, and *taṭam* do not indicate a difference in the nature of the object, because all cognitions of it there appear as variegated.

Or, if they were to follow the speaker's intention, they would not have those [external objects] as their referents; for by the power of that [intention], they would be of a single form, whereas the object is not of a single form.
If the establishment of gender were based on persistence, production, and dissolution without distinction, it would follow that there is no differentiation of gender.
Regarding that which is called non-existence, the lack of designation, or the insubstantial: what connection with persistence and so forth can be imagined for things that are non-existent?

Their arising is considered "production" (*prasava*), and their destruction is considered "dissolution" (*saṃstyāna*). However, the essential nature (*ātmarūpa*) of entities is designated as "stability" (*sthiti*). In that case, since there is no destruction within arising, why is it called "origination"? And since there is no stability consisting of a self-nature, how can it be described as "birth"? Furthermore, since the other two [arising and destruction] do not exist within dissolution, how can it be designated by such terms as "disappearance," "destruction," or even "vanishing"? Likewise, regarding stability, by what cause could it be said to have both "stability" and "intrinsic nature"? Alternatively, if their form were entirely undivided, they would possess a single characteristic.
If these [qualities] such as femininity and so forth are considered to be like "cowness" and the like, then by the refutation of the universal (sāmānya), those of that nature are already discarded.
Or rather, it is agreed that among those [universals], "birth" and "existence" are themselves universals; for it is not logical for further universals to reside within universals.
How could non-existence, indefinability, or worthlessness be [the object of cognition]? Therefore, this establishment of the three genders is merely conventional.

Even number is conceived as merely conventional (sāmāyikī), for it is posited according to one's intention (vivakṣayā), even when distinguishing between difference and non-difference, as in the cases of "wife" (dārāḥ) and "forest" (vipinam).

Now, if words such as *dāra* (wife) are applied to both the individual and the genus, they function by taking on the number of either the individual or its constituent parts. The word *vana* (forest), however, expresses many individuals qualified by the number of the genus, or else it expresses the genus as residing in many individuals.
But surely, by this rule, every single statement is destroyed; if there is no intention to speak elsewhere, let that very intention be its basis.

There is no number even for the universal (jāti), nor for the individual entity (bhāva) as qualified by it; how could there be [a number] through a connection with that which is connected [to it], or even from the connection itself?
If it were argued that even a single tree is called a "forest," and indeed many are so called only because of their relationship [to one another], then that [relationship] exists here as well.

And that [cognition] which rests upon many individuals resides in even a single one; since the cause for it is the same, the cognition of a "forest" would arise with respect to that [single tree] as well.

Therefore, based on positive and negative concomitance, this restriction of words such as "one" and so forth arises from the speaker's intention, not from the object itself, because [the word] deviates from that object.
The connection with [specific] times for ritual action and so forth has already been refuted; therefore, these [words] are merely conventional and do not even apply to individual instances.
Or, if exclusion (apoha) is said to be determined as having the form of an individual, then its connection with gender and so forth exists by way of that individual.
A word is employed for the purpose of establishing the intended object of the intellect; therefore, the exclusion of what is not intended is established by implication alone.

Not everything is indeed desired, because that would result in the non-restriction of all objects; therefore, it is perfectly clear that there must be something to be excluded by words such as "cook" and the like.

For instance, when "he cooks" is said, it is understood that he does not remain indifferent, nor does he eat, nor does he play; thus, the exclusion of other [actions] is apprehended. Therefore, there is indeed indifference, and yet there is another distinct action; for whatever is intended as a fixed object to be excluded, it must be of the nature of a relative negation (paryudāsa).

"But that which is 'cooking' remains unprohibited in its very own nature"—this statement of yours is mutually contradictory. If this "remaining in its own nature" is the negation of another form, then the restrictive particle (*eva*) employed [in the phrase "in its own nature"] would be meaningless otherwise.

What kind of "accomplishment" can there be for an exclusion (*apoha*) that is devoid of any defining characteristic? For there is no accomplishment whatsoever of things such as a sky-lotus. If it is argued that it appears as having defining characteristics because of the mental determination (*adhyavasāya*) that "it is a real entity," then what follows? Is its possession of properties identical to those of real entities thereby established?

Therefore, the cognition of being something to be accomplished, as well as the conceptualization of it as "thus" and so forth, follows as a consequence because it shares the same form as real entities; that [cognition] has those [entities] as its cause.
In the entire mass of objects such as injunctions and the like, non-existence and so forth are negated by implication, but not by the word itself—that which is not intended to be expressed.

When a negative particle (*nañ*) is joined with another negative particle, there arises a negation (*apoha*) of that same kind as is perceived when all four [negatives] are present. For when a negative is employed, the meaning of the negative is understood as the affirmation of something; by a third negative, its absence is established; and when a fourth is used for the sake of further negation, it makes known the exclusion of other things once that [third] has been intended.

For when it is said, "It is not that he does not cook," it is understood that "he cooks"; indeed, the connection with indifference and so forth is understood by the third [negation]. But in the fourth, he is determined to be "one who cooks" as distinct from those [other states]; therefore, here, the exclusion of other [possibilities] is equal to that of an affirmative sentence.

Whatever meaning, such as conjunction (*samuccaya*) and so forth, is intended by the word "and" (*ca*) and others, by that [word] there occurs the exclusion (*vyapohana*) of its opposite, such as option (*vikalpa*) and so forth.

The exclusion of others (anyanivṛtti) in the meaning of a sentence is indeed easily understood; for it is said that the meaning of a sentence is simply certain word-meanings joined together. And those things which are of a different class from them are clearly the objects of exclusion. These very same [things] constitute the meaning of the sentence as well, for there is nothing else that exists apart from them.

Whatever is considered by those of dull intellect to be a ground for doubt is precisely what is refuted by that [scripture]; otherwise, its utterance would be fruitless. For why would he, being free from doubt regarding anything, ask a question? Or how could one whose mind is sound utter a word that does not produce a refinement of understanding?
That which is called "form and so forth" as being cognizable by visual cognition and the rest—this is indeed something superimposed by someone, and it is this that is negated.
Blue and other forms are not perceived solely by means of a consciousness dependent on the eye; rather, they are perceived even by a single, eternal consciousness dependent on the ear.

Having observed that words such as "knowable" (*prameya*) and "cognizable" (*jñeya*), when situated within a sentence, serve as the basis for cognition even at other times [when used alone], the conceptualization that arises upon the perception of those words in isolation follows the lead of that original sentence, despite the shifting differences in their referents. Such a conceptualization indeed occurs even from words like "jar" (*ghaṭa*). Therefore, words such as "jar" are equivalent to words such as "knowable."

And regarding the conceptualization of the excluded (apohya), it has been stated that it is better to conceptualize the actual entity itself; this [objection] is refuted because [the cognition] necessarily excludes others. For in that case, only that which is intended to be expressed is conceptualized as the entity. Therefore, there is an exclusion of what is not intended to be expressed, but not of everything that might be intended.

The negation of the form of cognition, however, is not possible because it is self-cognizable; for there exists a manifold superimposed [form] that is without an external objective support. There must necessarily be accepted some fixed nature residing within the cognition itself with respect to each object, and that very thing is what we call the "form" (ākāra), the "reflection" (pratibimba), the "appearance as that" (tadābhatā), the "marking" (ullekha), and the "manifestation" (pratibhāsa); the difference in terminology is of no consequence.

For words such as "thus" (*evam*) and so forth, there exists no corresponding [negation] such as "not thus" (*naivam*) and so forth; that which is to be excluded is clearly characterized by a different mode [of being].
And since this [exclusion] exists even in every word brought forward in common usage, its referent—this "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha)—is what is intended to be expressed.

"All phenomena are selfless," or "all persons have gone [to their end]"—in such cases, a collective sense is understood, while a certain portion is excluded. Alternatively, it may be intended that only certain external things, such as jars and the like, are selfless; and when someone understands it thus as a mere going [of some], that error is dispelled.
Furthermore, a negation of all parts is certainly not intended in that case; this [objection] results in the negation of its own meaning, and is therefore stated out of ignorance.
Exclusion (apoha) is neither an entity nor a non-entity, characterized by neither difference nor identity; it is neither dependent nor independent, and in reality, it is neither one nor many.
Thus, it does not exist in reality in the manner that it is determined; therefore, from the perspective of its determination as a real entity, it is neither an existent nor a non-existent.

All [concepts] such as difference and non-difference are established as existing in reality; yet the referent of a word is devoid of intrinsic nature, and therefore these [concepts] are without foundation.

A word directly effects for us the exclusion of other referents; however, once its own meaning has been denoted, that exclusion is understood through the force of implication (*sāmarthya*). It has been demonstrated at length that "it is not of the nature of that [other], but of the nature of another. Therefore, this [objection] is raised here by one who is ignorant of the opponent's position: "By whom was 'non-cowness' attributed to a cow such that it must be excluded? For this is not excluded by the word in its direct sense.

By which word is the state of being denotable questioned? Is it by this [term "exclusion"] regarding exclusion (*apoha*), or rather by "jar" and so forth? In the investigation of whether the meaning of a word is an exclusion or a positive injunction (*vidhi*), that which appears as "exclusion" is understood in this way: for the cognition "the reflection is indeed the word-meaning" is direct; however, the negation of positive categories such as universals (*jāti*) is understood through implication (*sāmarthya*). Words such as "jar" and "tree" express that very same reflection directly through their production [of the mental image], but they exclude what is other than the object. Therefore, there is no fault regarding the positive injunction, nor does an undesirable consequence follow. Furthermore, the fault of the position that [exclusion] is not denotable does not apply to us, because we do not accept that [position].
Oneness, permanence, and so forth are merely conceptual constructs and not real; therefore, to mock this [position] is indicative of great erudition.
By the force of the restrictive particle itself, the exclusion of others (anyāpoha) is also understood; for where one's own nature alone is understood, a restriction would otherwise be useless.
But for one who does not even accept that an external object can exist otherwise [than it appears], how can exclusion (*apoha*) be asserted in the case of words such as "the son of a barren woman"?
Since non-existent things lack form, words that denote universals and the like cannot even be suspected [of denoting them]; they are established as indicators of nothing but the appearance itself.
That reflection which appears, constructed solely from the latent impressions arising from empty verbal discourse devoid of objective referents, is what is expressed by words.
These words, which directly illuminate only those [particulars], are accompanied by doubt because they depend upon convention, just like the expression of imagined objects.
Since these sounds do not establish the production of distinctions and so forth that have been accepted by others, it should be understood that they are exactly like those [other cases].

For the impossibility of linguistic convention regarding difference and so forth has already been established here; nor is there futility, for the two reasons do not possess a doubtful negative concomitance.

But surely, even on the theory of apoha (exclusion), how is the establishment of a convention possible? And how can it be effective, for it is not established for both [parties]—neither for the speaker nor for the listener. Indeed, their respective cognitions cannot be mutually experienced; nor is that which was perceived during the convention observed during the actual usage.
Even though it exists in the cognition of its own respective manifestation, it is equal for both [the subject and the object] in the determination of the external object, because of that.
Just as one whose vision is impaired by cataracts speaks of two moons to someone like himself, so too is all verbal usage considered to be [of that same nature].
And this pervasiveness of it is accepted as being based on conceptual determination; for these cognitions produced by words are indeed false appearances.
And this pervasiveness of it is intended as being based on conceptual determination; for these cognitions produced by words have a false appearance.

The perception and inference that others have stated for the sake of establishing the limiting adjunct (upādhi) are not established as such, for they possess those very characteristics [which we have refuted].
The perception and inference that others have stated for the sake of establishing the limiting adjunct (upādhi) are not established as such, for they possess the following characteristics:

Perception is free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous. Conceptual construction is a cognition associated with verbal expression; it consists in the nature of being a cause for designation, and not otherwise.
That which is capable of connecting word and meaning in forms such as "tree" arises as if accompanied by verbal expression, even when words are not actually employed.

Due to the continuity of the latent impressions from the cultivation of the meanings of names in past existences, even one newly born becomes proficient in what is to be done through connection with that [continuity].
And that [cognition] which is clearly experienced at the time of reflection, imagination, and so forth, as if permeated by words, cannot be denied.

And through the determination of that [non-existence], the status of word and object is erroneous; because of the impossibility of any other [connection], this [status] would be possible even though it is non-existent, despite its appearance as such.

Others define conceptual construction as that which is capable of being associated with universals and the like; however, this is not tenable, because universals and such have already been refuted and are never perceived.
Since universals and so forth are not perceived, and their connection does not appear, how can a synthesis with an object be possible, as in the case of milk and water?

For the purpose of explaining what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, this well-known conceptualization is declared to be twofold, based on the expression of two [levels]: the higher and the lower.
And this application of names and so forth proceeds by immediately implying its own cause; therefore, it is not a discussion of something irrelevant.
Or, it is so called because all names, universals, and so forth are joined by means of it; thus, conceptualization is described as a cognition associated with verbal expression.

Alternatively, it is simply the conceptual construction established in our own system that is presented; for the application [of the term] is based on the principle that "in every case, an object is expressed by means of its name."

By means of those [words], however, the instrumental case-ending is experienced as fulfilling its purpose; for the meaning "this is such-and-such" is determined through the name by way of genus and so forth.

Nor should it be thought that this [definition] lacks pervasion (avyāpti) because of the existence of a genus denotable by arbitrary words; for the separate mention [of "genus"] is due to conventional usage.
But surely, because it expresses the exclusion of others (anyāpoha), a genus-word (jātiśabda) is merely a word of intention (vivakṣāśabda), since it is dependent upon the speaker's intention.
It is true that this has been stated by the knower of logic in accordance with worldly convention; for it is only to this extent that a word enters the path of linguistic usage.

However, those [factors] such as birth and so forth are not here separate entities as they are in the world; it is for the purpose of establishing this that the passage beginning with "But others... has been described.

Even for those who rely on the conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) consisting of the association with universals (*jāti*) and so forth, a cognition that is necessarily associated with verbal expression (*abhilāpinī*) must be admitted. Otherwise, because there would be no association—just as in the case of two distinct entities—the conceptual construction could not be postulated at all, since [the object] would be perceived independently. Or else, this entire universe would consequently become something that cannot be engaged in linguistic practice (*avyavahārya*). Therefore, this world is considered to be the object of linguistic practice precisely because it is conjoined with the forms of universals and the like. The association with universals and the like is invariably concomitant with the association with words; and thus, the statement "it is called such" becomes fruitful.
Therefore, since there is no dispute among proponents established in all philosophical systems, this conceptual construction is considered by me to be provable without effort.

Having accepted all this description of names, classes, and so forth, he here employed the mention of "our own" and "others' opinions" in this manner. Others, however, said that there is no difference at all between them and us; thus he spoke the subsequent sentence beginning with "But others," and so on.
In this manner, the *Nyāyamukha* treatise is to be explained by way of this direction; for, due to its connection with the term "knowledge" (*jñāna*), it is cognition that is intended there.
Alternatively, a qualifier is a distinction by which a word effects the exclusion of others; and by this [qualifier], it effects the exclusion of universals (*jāti*) and so forth.

If conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is considered to be of such a well-known nature, and the negation of identity with perception (*pratyakṣa*) is thus described, then even though it is denotable by words such as "perception," it is not contradicted; for the absence of conceptual construction in perception does not consist in its being denotable by a word. Otherwise, form, smell, and so forth would become conceptual. Therefore, this position held by other dull-witted people has no foundation: "If perception is denoted by the word 'perception,' how can it be understood that it is free from conceptual construction? How could that be tenable?"
