Perception is clearly experienced as being free from conceptual construction, because even when the mind is attached elsewhere, there is still the sensory cognition of blue and other objects.
For that very conceptual construction does not apprehend that object, because it abandons the expression of "past" and so forth, and because it achieves the association with its name.

At that time, there is no other conceptual construction associated with that name, because the object of perception is not cognized [simultaneously] and because the simultaneous occurrence of both is undesirable.
Therefore, conceptual cognition is experienced as coexisting with [sensory] knowledge; thus, it is clear that this sensory consciousness is free from conceptual construction.
If it is thought that cognitions arise only in succession, yet there is the misconception of simultaneity due to their rapid occurrence, like [the whirling of] a firebrand;
At that time, there exists no conceptual construction of a visible object accompanied by the attachment to manifest cultivation; thus it has been stated by the Blessed One.
Error, the conceit thereof, and its manifestation are continuous; therefore, the simultaneity of the cognition of objects is clearly established.

In states such as the vision of a dancer, everything is perceived simultaneously; even when there is an intervention by many [moments], that is an illusion arising from rapid succession. Since the occurrence of cognitions regarding a vine, a palm tree, and so forth, is extremely swift, why does the conceit of simultaneous occurrence not apply here as well? Furthermore, in a pure mental construction, no sequence could be determined; for the rapid succession of all cognitions is minimal due to their long duration [of persistence]. Therefore, in every object, there would be no apprehension of sequence, but rather an appearance of simultaneous apprehension, just like the cognition of sound and other objects.

Even in the case of a whirling firebrand, the illusion of a wheel arises all at once; it does not result from the synthesis of successive visual perceptions, because [the wheel] appears with complete clarity. For synthesis is performed by memory alone, and not by perception, since a past object cannot be apprehended by seeing. Furthermore, whatever is the object of this [synthesis] is not vivid, because it has already perished. Therefore, it follows that this appearance of a wheel would not be vivid.

Alternatively, if for any given entity there exists no cause for its establishment in a specific form, it is not established as such by the wise. Just as a white horse (*karka*), lacking a dewlap and other [cow-features], is not [established] as having the nature of a cow; and there is no apprehension of an object qualified by qualifiers [if they do not exist]. The basis for the establishment of a conceptual state (*savikalpaka-bhāva*) is the sense-faculties (*akṣa*); otherwise, the opposite case, such as a brindled cow (*śābaleya*), would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Nor is the reason (*hetu*) unestablished, because of the negation of genus (*jāti*) and so forth; and since there is no determination through differentiation, such a qualifier does not exist at all.

Even the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a word is not at all the denoter [of its own form], since the status of being the denoted and the denoter has been refuted for the specific characteristic. Therefore, it is only that which is superimposed (*adhyāropita*) that is accepted as the denoted and the denoter; and perception apprehends the object as it is, without superimposition. This is because [the specific characteristic] exists when the specific characteristic exists, and it is absent when that is absent; and because even when there is an intervention or other such conditions, that [perception] likewise undergoes cessation.
For the nature of blue and other [objects] cannot be conventionally designated, as it does not partake of anything else; therefore, the cognition of them is not associated with verbal expression.

Granted, let it be that name and so forth are not its apprehended qualifiers; nevertheless, the reason’s lack of establishment (asiddhatā) does not cease at all, because: If there is no apprehension of [the jar] in a form distinguished from other objects, then there would either be the apprehension of the object-in-general, or non-apprehension, as in the case of a jar [when not distinguished]. If there is no apprehension of [the jar] in a form distinguished from other jars, then there would either be the apprehension of the jar-in-general, or indeed non-apprehension of the jar.

If it is held that determinate cognition (*savikalpaka-vijñāna*) apprehends an object as distinguished from other objects of apprehension by means of its positive existence, then it would be like the cognition of a tree or similar things.
There exists no particular whatsoever that is not associated with a universal; if it were unmanifest during perception, it would not be apprehended because it lacks distinctness.
To claim that cognition whose object is qualified is not conceptual construction is audacity; for the state of being qualified (vaiśiṣṭya) is impossible without a relation to a qualifier.
Cognition is held to have a qualified object because it apprehends an entity as excluded from both similar and dissimilar things; it does not [arise] from a connection with qualifiers.

For difference has been said to be "distinctness" (vaiśiṣṭya), not the connection with a qualifier; even when one says "it is distinct," it is not perceived as being permeated by that verbal expression.
When that [object] is apprehended as being distinct from its own nature and all other things without exception, a conceptual construction arises accordingly.
Others maintain that the universal is unqualified by any particular; therefore, it is likewise [the object] grasped by non-conceptual cognition.
For that universal is understood as being distinguished by its particularities; therefore, the cognition that grasps it must be conceptual (savikalpaka).
If a particular is apprehended as being without distinction, it is called a universal; therefore, it is not logical for that particular to be qualified by a universal.
These [elements], indeed, when perceived through their states of disequilibrium and equilibrium, fashion within themselves the existence of universals and particulars.

If this state of being unequal and equal is held to be differentiated, then the particularity of the universal remains established by virtue of that very differentiation. Alternatively, if this [state] is undifferentiated, how can there be a non-confused status? For there is no other possibility for their existence than through mutual exclusion.

Apart from the nature of the specific particular (*viśeṣātman*), there is no other characteristic of difference. If [the cognition] does not touch that nature, how can it be said that those [particulars] are apprehended? And even if it touches that nature, since they are distinguished from other differences, it follows that the cognition regarding them would be conceptual (*vikalpaka*).

From that which is indefinable (the non-existent), the universal and the particular are nevertheless perceived; therefore, even those two must be graspable by conceptual cognition according to you. If it is argued that they are not qualified by the non-existent, then what difference is there between them and that [non-existent] itself? If it is not so, then why is their qualification by it not admitted?

For this distinction of the entity is indeed not of its own nature; and since the universal is not of the nature of non-existence, why is that [entity] not qualified by it for you? Therefore, whatever cognition whatsoever arises regarding the particular (svalakṣaṇa), having as its object that which transcends the path of words, all of that is non-conceptual (nirvikalpaka).

For there exists an initial non-conceptualizing awareness (*nirvikalpaka*), which is a mere observational cognition (*ālocanājñāna*), resembling the consciousness of infants or the mute, and arising from the pure object itself. At that time, neither the particular (*viśeṣa*) nor the universal (*sāmānya*) is experienced; rather, it is the individual entity (*vyakti*) alone, which serves as the substratum for both, that is apprehended. Subsequently, however, that cognition by which the object is again apprehended through its attributes such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth, is also accepted as being of the nature of perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Even when there is conceptual construction again and again, whatever realization occurs is accepted as entirely direct perception, in accordance with its connection [to the object].
For it is not the case that because objects do not appear to those who have just entered an inner chamber from the heat, they are therefore no longer apprehended by the sense faculties.
Just as people first recognize someone by their mere appearance and later perceive them in their true nature, so too do they [recognize objects] through the properties of genus and so forth.

If someone were to form a conceptual construction after having looked and then closed their eyes, that [cognition] would not possess the status of direct perception, because it does not follow from the [sensory] connection.

That is incorrect; for if that cognition is directed toward the particular (svalakṣaṇa), it is indeed devoid of verbal expression even when grasping universals (jāti) and so forth. And thus, it has already been established previously that this particular is indeed inexpressible; and the cognition operating upon it is necessarily non-conceptual (nirvikalpaka).
If only the genus were apprehended, there would be absolute distinctness of the qualifier; however, this is not accepted by the opponents as it has been stated.
For if the qualifier were absolutely distinct from the qualified, how could it then produce in the qualified a cognition corresponding to itself?

It is not logical that a single cognition should be the knower of both the specific and the universal natures; for if it were otherwise, there would be no distinction between the prior [cognition] and the subsequent one, as both would be conceptual.

If it is argued that because there is no absolute difference [between the first and subsequent cognitions], the subsequent cognition has already been reached by the first through its nature as a genus and so forth, then the latter, because it apprehends an object already known, would be equal to a memory-cognition.

When there is an apprehension in the form of various indistinct universals, if the object is not yet ascertained, then certainty arises progressively. Just as inference has as its object the exclusion of superimposition (*samāropa-vyavaccheda*), so too does certainty have as its object the exclusion of superimposition.

Cognition does not possess the status of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of having the elimination of superimposition as its object; for if that were so, it would follow that even inference and memory would be valid cognitions. [Objection: It is accepted that inferential cognition is a valid means of knowledge because it prevents superimposition arising immediately after perception. [Reply: That is not the case for you. For in cases such as "the cow," "white," or "moving," no superimposition is experienced in the cognition immediately following perception that needs to be negated.

Generality (*jāti*) and the other categories do not exist as identical, different, or both; for if they did, conceptual cognition would attain the status of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). This is because there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*), because they appear as distinct, because they do not manifest as differentiated [in a single cognition], and because identity and difference are established through mutual exclusion.
Even non-conceptual knowledge possesses the power to give rise to conceptualization; therefore, by means of that [power], it becomes a factor for all worldly transactions without exception.

If [you argue that] non-conceptual [cognition] is capable regarding conceptualization because of the difference in objects, [we reply: it is not so, because of its non-conceptual nature, like the cognition of color-form and the like, or like the eye and other sense organs.
Therefore, there is no contradiction here between these two [cognitions] and conceptual construction; nor is their object different, because they both determine that same object.
In reality, however, conceptual construction proceeds without any objective support; it has no object whatsoever that could be differentiated in any way.
The mutual causality of cognitions such as those of form, sound, and so forth, certainly exists; therefore, this example that has been cited is one whose probandum is unestablished.
Even a clear deviation is observed in this case, due to the causal relationship between the cognitions of fire, smoke, and so forth.

This [qualification "non-erroneous"] was formulated for the purpose of excluding cognitions such as that of a tuft of hair; for that [cognition] is not accepted as valid cognition because it is erroneous.

Some maintain that even this [cognition of a double moon] is mental; however, this is not so, because it arises from the state of the sense faculty, since its modification is observed to follow the modification of that [faculty], and because it would cease like the error of a snake and so forth even when the impairment of the sense organ has not perished, given that it appears with clarity.

The state of being manifested by that [object] is not directly established [as a cause], for it is deviant; yet, indirectly, it is established because of its concomitance with that memory-cognition. In the world, the fact that an effect undergoes modification when its cause undergoes modification is clearly seen even in cases arising through a lineage, such as mules and the like. All mental errors cease through investigation; thus, there is no deviation [of the rule] regarding these [errors] due to cognitions of generalities (sāmānya). By their very nature, these do not operate upon the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a real entity. If it is argued that their cessation occurs in this manner, the same applies to the case of two moons and so forth. If it is argued that there is no cessation of existence [for the error of two moons], that is equally true for cognitions of generalities. Furthermore, for those who are attached to the doctrines of the Lord (*Īśvara*) and other [deities], there is no cessation of their errors even upon hearing millions of arguments; on the contrary, they themselves say, "These are not valid arguments," and thus those dull-witted ones persist.

The state of being manifested by that [object] is not directly established for one whose mind is non-erroneous; nor indeed is an intervention established, for no such thing is perceived in between. Even one whose mind is attached to another object perceives a double moon and so forth; therefore, there is no arising through a mediated succession. When the withdrawal of cognitions of the general nature of things is possible, cessation is certainly possible even for the intellect of the Lord, according to his own will.

Others declare that cognitions such as those of a yellow conch-shell, even though they are erroneous, possess the status of valid cognition because they are non-contradictory with regard to purposeful action.

Therefore, there exists no [cognition] that corresponds to an unascertained form; even in that case, the attainment of causal efficiency [is required], otherwise an over-extension would follow. Furthermore, since cognition appearing as hair-locks and the like possesses a state of correspondence with light and so forth, its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is difficult to avoid.
Furthermore, a shape distinct from color is not tenable; nor is it accepted that there is correspondence with the color as it appears.

If validity were postulated while disregarding the form [of the cognition], on the grounds that it is non-discrepant with purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), then how would all that has been stated—namely, "for the determination of an object is of that very form"—not be contradicted? Therefore, the possibility of such non-discrepancy arises from the cause that is the maturation of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).
The same reasoning that establishes the non-conceptual nature of mental and sensory consciousnesses also establishes the non-conceptual nature of pleasure and the other feelings.

If they do not experience themselves, how indeed could they possess self-awareness even with respect to another? If it is argued that these [cognitions] become cognizable by a consciousness residing in the same object, [we reply:]...

If external objects are perceived in uninterrupted succession, why is pleasure and so forth not experienced continuously at that same time? If it is claimed that these are experienced only by a mental consciousness (*mānasa-cetas*) and not by the [sensory] mind, then that [mental consciousness] cannot exist at that time, because its arising is described as being successive. If you argue that while its *arising* is not admitted to be simultaneous, its *duration* (stability) is, we say no; for its stability has been refuted by the proof of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*). If you claim that the illusion of simultaneity arises from rapid occurrence, that too has been rejected; for there would be no clear manifestation in the domain of memory. Furthermore, if that illusion is imagined to take the form of pleasure, pain, indifference, and so on, then it follows that the existence of pleasure and the rest must be characterized solely by that [illusion]. Moreover, when yogis perceive the pleasure and so forth of others through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), they would themselves become afflicted, since their experience would be identical to theirs. For you, the existence of suffering within oneself is not what constitutes "experience"; rather, it is the cognition having that as its object. And such cognition exists in the continuum of another. This same logic applies to the inference of another's suffering; for inference is described as having an object, not being without a domain.
Pleasure and the like are perceived simply as pleasure, pain, and so forth, but they are not perceived as "cognition"; therefore, they are not cognition, unlike a jar or similar objects.
If this is so, then even the notion that "there is knowledge" is not our position; for since it exists in the mind, at that time non-knowledge would also necessarily follow in that case as well.

It is evident that [the mind] is of the nature of luminosity; if it were not so, the same consequence would apply to pleasure, pain, and the like. Why then should all this [luminosity] not be identical? We shall now sufficiently describe the cognition of the yogi—which arises from the cultivation of reality, is free from conceptual construction and error—by means of pure proofs.

In this system, the apprehension of the object is held to be the fruit of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); alternatively, self-awareness (svavitti) is the means of valid cognition, while its conformity (sārūpya) or even its capacity (yogyatā) constitutes the fruit.
If it is argued that, just as there is no cutting of a *palāśa* tree when an axe has reached a *svadira* tree, so too in the world there is no identity between the axe and the act of cutting;

The establishment of the relationship between the probandum and the probans does not depend upon a formal arrangement; for such an arrangement is indeed not tenable within a cognition that is devoid of form.
Therefore, a distinction exists as something conceptually constructed, like that between a bow and its arrow; however, this relationship of producer and produced is not accepted here.
And when the joint of a wood-apple or similar fruit is being split, the axe-blade is said to enter; therefore, oneness is established therein.

But once a fixed order has been established, it may indeed be conceived otherwise; for the rule of structural arrangement is described as consisting of the relationship between that which is produced and that which produces.

For it is held that the immediately preceding [cognition], having functioned as the result of delimitation, serves as the cause for the subsequent cognition which is the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa), while the latter is the result. If it is argued that self-awareness (svasaṃvitti) is the result, that is not tenable because it has been refuted; furthermore, if the means of knowledge consists in the form of the object, the consequence follows that the [means] and the [result] would have different objects.

It cannot be denied on the grounds that it would lead to the consequence of knowing everything; nor is there a difference in meaning here, for self-cognition is also considered to be the cognition of an object.

If it is argued that "the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) produces an effect distinct from itself because it is an instrument (kāraka), like an axe," then [we reply] that another fruit [of the axe] is considered to be useless. According to the reasoning already stated, there is no fruit other than [the cutting] for an axe or the like; furthermore, its status as an instrument is not established if one intends it to mean "that which produces" (janakatva). If, however, one intends it to mean "that which establishes" (sthāpakatva), there is no contradiction whatsoever. Therefore, the reason (hetu) is inconclusive (anaikāntika), since no contradiction has been demonstrated.

If it is argued that cognition cannot possibly possess a common form with the object because it is of a different category—just as taste is not the same as color and so forth—then we have already explained all such points while following the principles of logic (*nyāya*) in our detailed analysis of the distinction between the grasped and the grasper. Furthermore, this other point is clearly established therein.
For if there were identity in every respect, cognition would become non-cognition; yet if there were similarity in some respect, everything would be a cognizer of everything.

However, in the doctrine that external objects truly exist, the possibility of similarity (sārūpya) must certainly be admitted; this is the meaning for which that [similarity] has been elucidated. For in the position that cognition possesses an appearance, even though the mind is distinct from the object of apprehension, there may still be a figurative (bhākta) perception due to the reflection’s conformity with that [object]. But for one who maintains that cognition is not the locus of similarity to the object, even this mode of perceiving the external does not exist at all.

However, in the theory that external objects truly exist, the possibility of similarity (*sārūpya*) must necessarily be admitted; this is the meaning for which that [theory] was elucidated. For in the view that cognition possesses an appearance, even though the mind is distinct from the object of apprehension, there may still be a figurative perception due to the reflection possessing that same form. But for one who maintains that cognition does not possess similarity to the object, even this aforementioned mode of perceiving the external does not exist at all.

Inference is held to be of two kinds by way of the distinction between that for oneself and that for others. Inference for oneself is the perception of the object to be inferred from a mark possessing the three characteristics. Furthermore, inference for others is said to be the statement of the mark possessing the three characteristics. Consequently, an object that possesses only one, two, or two [of the three] characteristics is considered a fallacious mark (*liṅgābhāsa*).

Inference is held to be of two kinds by way of the distinction between that for oneself and that for others. Inference for oneself is the perception of the object to be inferred from a mark possessing the three characteristics. Furthermore, inference for others is said to be the statement of the mark possessing the three characteristics. Consequently, an object that possesses only one, or two, or two [of the three] characteristics is considered a fallacious mark (*liṅgābhāsa*).

Indeed, the status of being a sound reason is observed precisely in the impossibility of [the probandum] otherwise; it does not exist even for that which possesses the three members [of the syllogism]. Therefore, reasons characterized by the three marks are impotent.

That which possesses the property of being otherwise impossible (*anyathānupapannatva*) is accepted as the logical reason (*hetu*); that object has a single characteristic, or it does not have four characteristics.
Just as in the world a man who has three sons is called "one who has an only son" because that one son is a truly excellent son, so too should it be understood here.

The relationship of inseparable connection (avinābhāva) is never found in [the three types of] reasons possessing the three characteristics; rather, it is observed only in those reasons that possess the single characteristic of "impossibility otherwise" (anyathāsambhava).

Only that which possesses the property of being otherwise impossible (*anyathānupapannatva*) has the status of a logical reason (*hetu*). Let there be two types of examples (*dṛṣṭānta*), or let them not exist at all; for they are not the cause [of proof]. Where the property of being otherwise impossible does not exist, what is the use of the three [characteristics]? Where the property of being otherwise impossible exists, what is the use of the three?
"He is dark because he is his son, just like the other [sons] seen to be dark"—this reason, possessing three characteristics, does not lead to certain knowledge.

In that regard, there is a reason consisting of a single characteristic and devoid of the two types of examples: "Because existence and non-existence are somehow perceivable, they are both of the nature of being."

"Because it is designated as being the moon, the hare-marked one is not non-moon"—this is called another [type of] reason characterized by two features. "This pain of mine is known to be caused by the falling of this insect, because its arising is obtained through contact with that falling insect. "The eye possesses an ever-superior power regarding the effect of perceiving form, because it is employed toward that [object], or else because of the seeing of it. "In some way, the self, pots, and so forth, are non-existent, because they are not perceived in any way, like the horn of a donkey. "And even the horns of a hare and so forth are in some way existent, because they are perceived in some way, just like the self, pots, and so forth. "Or it is understood that 'your father is in that house,' because of hearing your father’s voice here in this dwelling. "Even in the case of things such as sound or a lamp, their status as indicators is observed through 'impossibility otherwise' (anyathānupapatti), even though they do not possess the property of being a feature of the subject (apakṣadharmatva). "Therefore, let for us the reason characterized by a single feature be the primary means of comprehension; what is the use of other [features] such as 'being a property of the subject' (pakṣadharmatva), which are merely imagined?"
Is this characteristic of the reason understood in a general sense, or with respect to the subject whose specific nature is sought to be known, or else with respect to the illustrative example?
If, when that [reason] has been stated in a general sense, its presence in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) were thus to be made manifest, it would not bring about the intended proof.

Just as the non-deviation of "visibility" [from impermanence] is established by its absence in destruction generally, yet that [visibility] is not a means of proving it in the case of sound; if it is argued that its existence in the subject (dharmin) is what is being made known, then in that case, the very same three-fold nature (trirūpatā) of the reason is attained even in your own view.

Since positive and negative concomitance are understood through the principle of "impossibility otherwise" (anyathānupapatti), its presence in the subject (dharmin) constitutes the basis for the property of being a characteristic of the subject (pakṣadharmatva).
The teachers have also pointed out such a concise definition: "The property of the subject (grāhyadharma) is the reason (hetu), provided it is pervaded by a portion of that [property]."

Now, this characteristic of the reason is understood only with respect to the subject (*dharmī*); for it is from that same means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) [that the reason is known], and not from that [same source] that the probandum (*sādhya*) is established. For if the probandum is not apprehended, there can be no certainty regarding the reason either; therefore, the reason is useless if the probandum is established by some other means. Furthermore, there is the fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) in the ascertainment of the probandum from the reason; for if one of the two is not established, the other cannot be ascertained either.

Even if that [pervasion] were established in the example, there would be no cognition of the probandum regarding the subject (dharmin); for its pervasion has not been ascertained through a universal induction (sarvopasaṃhāra).
Furthermore, as for this reason stated here—"because it is somehow perceived"—there is no object at all that is doubtful in this regard; thus, [the reason] is fruitless.
For the identity of that [nature] with the entity is certain to everyone; how then can its being "to be proven" be asserted in this way?

Even in the doctrine of the identity of all things, some [aspect] is clearly manifested by the self through distinctions such as modification and essence. Even those who rely on the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) residing in all things, they too rely on qualifiers such as "in reality" (*tattvataḥ*).
Otherwise, the fact that [the object] is somehow apprehensible would not be established; for if conventional usage were what is to be proven, a well-known example would be available.
The state of being designated as "the moon" also persists in the similar instance (sapakṣa), whether it be in a certain boy or in camphor, silver, and so forth.

If the reason were based on the actual nature of the thing, yet deviated from what is commonly recognized, there would be the fallacy of being "uniquely inconclusive" (asādhāraṇatā) in proving the state of being the moon.
No distinction is observed between that which is produced by a falling insect and that whose arising is obtained through contact with a falling insect.

Indeed, the qualification "of this" must certainly be applied to the effect [as a qualifier] of the reason; otherwise, the presence of deviation (*vyabhicāritva*) would result as something difficult to avoid. However, if the probandum (*sādhya*) possesses the three characteristics (*trirūpa*) due to a previously established example (*nidarśana*), then the conventional usage of "being an effect" may occur even when that [qualification] is forgotten.

First of all, the existence of the eye as a substantial entity (dharmin) is unestablished; and it is not proper to provide a proof for that [existence], because it would entail the fallacy of proving what is already unestablished (asiddha).
However, even when form and other [objects] are present, visual cognition does not arise; therefore, it is understood that at times those [objects] alone are not the cause.
The arising of sprouts and the like, produced by their own specific causes, does exist; thus, in that very example, the difference [between the two cases] is extremely clear.

Furthermore, if one attempts to prove that things such as jars lack the nature of reality, the same faults observed previously—namely, the futility of the reason and its lack of established proof—are seen to apply.

Moreover, there is here also a clear illustration by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-nidarśana*): for that very same intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of those [entities] becomes their counter-example (*vipakṣa*). Even when attempting to prove the existence of a self (*sātmatva*) in things that are soulless (*nirātman*), there is the proving of what is already accepted, non-establishment [of the reason], and likewise the attainment of a dissimilar instance.

Even that connection with the father which is established regarding the house based on hearing the word "father"—in that case, the three-featured reason (*trilakṣaṇahetu*) is manifest. For, in some instances, a voice previously perceived as connected to the father is not experienced [at the time of inference]; if it is not so experienced, the non-establishment of the reason (*asiddhatā*) is unavoidable.

In a case where something has been previously perceived and is not perceived [again] at that same place, there the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is clearly observed. But a word does not in any way make known an external object, because it lacks the impossibility of being otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*). Rather, it indicates [the object] through its distinctness (*vailakṣaṇya*). And when that distinctness is to be communicated, it is very clear: for a word is not employed unless there is the presence of the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*). A lamp, however, is not an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of blue and so forth by virtue of being a logical mark (*liṅga*); rather, it is so called because it produces that which is capable of generating cognition. When the indicator is in the form of a logical mark, one considers the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and so on; otherwise, why would this [set of criteria] not be demanded of the eyes and other sense organs? Even by way of "impossibility otherwise," the quality of being visible (*cākṣuṣatva*) is not a prover. Therefore, those [reasons] characterized by only one feature are impotent due to their lack of the property of the subject. It is observed that those stated as having only one form actually possess two forms, and those stated as having two forms actually possess three forms by virtue of the property of the subject. If it is argued that [all requirements] are implied by "impossibility otherwise" alone, that is not so; for in the case of words and the like, even if [the property] were desired otherwise, that [impossibility] would not exist.

Because the reasons such as "being his son" possess a doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatireka*), the presence of the three characteristics [of a valid reason] is not established, since there is no contradiction with heterogeneous instances (*vijātīya*).

For even in the case of his being that person's son, a change [in the expected state] is possible through causes such as karma, food, and so forth, in every way and particularly so. Indeed, neither an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), nor an effect (*kārya*), nor the non-perception of a perceptible object (*adṛṣṭi*) possesses infallibility (*avyabhicāritā*) with respect to anything other than itself.

But surely, non-deviation is observed in other cases as well: for instance, the blooming of night-lotuses and the rising of the ocean are seen as signs of the moon’s appearance; from the presence of sunlight, the existence of shadows on the opposite side is inferred; from the sight of a firebrand in the darkness, smoke is perceived at a distance; and from the rising of the Kṛttikās, the proximity of Rohiṇī is postulated.

Therefore, in this case, those other qualities such as cognition and the rest, which are inferred to be of the same nature as the property of the cause, are considered to have arisen at that very same time. From such a rule, the establishment of the cause from the effect occurs; otherwise, if no relationship were possible, there would be no understanding of anything at all.

That specific wind which is the cause for the rising of the Kṛttikās is indeed, through its continuity, the cause for the proximity of Rohiṇī. Therefore, the cognition of the causal property is considered to be the cognition of that [effect]; there is no other independent cognition of it here whatsoever.

Inference proceeds from the mark known as the reflection; it is logical that this inference has the original object (*bimba*) as its domain, whereas other [inferences] arise from the mark of an effect (*kārya*).
Since two things cannot exist simultaneously in one place, there is no real entity in the reflection; therefore, how could its being an effect be logically tenable from an ultimate standpoint?

Although this reflected image of a material form lacks substantial reality, how could the consciousness appearing as that reflection be without reality? It is precisely that [consciousness] which serves as the inferential mark here, for it is intended as the effect; indeed, through the predominance of the original object (bimba), this [consciousness] proceeds without an external support.

Others also describe statements such as the proposition (*pratijñā*) as being for the sake of another; however, because it is not a constituent part of the proof (*sādhana*), the proposition is useless.

Because it lacks a necessary connection, that [statement] is not directly capable of establishing the object; nor is it appropriate even indirectly, because it does not indicate what is relevant. If this [statement] is desired to be a member of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*) by virtue of its status as a "statement of the example" (*dṛṣṭāntapada*), due to its pointing out the subject matter of the property to be proven (*sādhya*) and the means of proof (*sādhana*), then is there not indeed a deviation (*vyabhicāritā*) here on account of statements such as "concession" (*abhyanujñā*)? Furthermore, it would be fruitless in cases where the subject matter is already pointed out.

If there is no formal establishment of the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and so forth due to the non-employment of a thesis (*pakṣa*), then the three-fold nature (*trairūpya*) of the reason—which is based upon that [establishment]—does not exist either.

In the actual statement of the proof, there is no conceptual differentiation of the similar class (sapakṣa) and so forth; however, they are thus divided in the treatise for the sake of conventional discourse.
Furthermore, that [objection] is not contradictory if it relies upon the subject matter at hand; for the first section (pūrva-kāṇḍa) does not state a proof even for the opponent.

For the property of being a feature of the subject (pakṣadharmatā) consists in its occurrence in that which possesses the specific quality sought to be known; the similar instance (sapakṣa) exists because of its similarity to that, and the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa) because of the absence thereof.

Furthermore, since the reason has not been stated if the thesis is not expressed, the statement of the application (*upanaya*) cannot serve to establish the existence [of the subject in the reason]. Moreover, because the mere presence [of the reason] was stated previously and the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is revealed afterwards, the purposeful object is already established; thus, the reflection (*pratibimbaka*) is useless.

Since the proof is established by the very power of the statement of the three-featured reason, there is no possibility of doubt regarding its opposite; therefore, the conclusion (nigamana) is redundant.
A single meaning is established by the very statements that are interconnected; therefore, the conclusion (nigamana) need not be stated separately for the sake of establishing that connection.
Some explain that inference is of two kinds, distinguished by being "seen through particulars" (viśeṣadṛṣṭa) or "seen through generalities" (sāmānyaparidṛṣṭa).

When a specific relationship has been perceived through direct observation between two particular instances—for example, when a cognition is formed regarding cow-dung fuel and its specific location—and one goes to that very place at a later time and perceives that same fire again and again, following that previous cognition, then it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it cognizes an object whose existence was previously doubted. This is what is called "perception of particulars" (*viśeṣadṛṣṭa*), as recorded by Vindhyavāsin. However, when the difference between fire and smoke must be stated in an inference based on generality (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*), the sun is cited as an example of something that moves with absolute certainty.

Therefore, since the all-pervasive momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) has been established here, no inference of that very same [entity] as it was previously can possibly occur. If that identity is merely conceptualized through the desire to express the unity of a continuous series (prabandha), then that [series] has no stability whatsoever, nor does its substantiality possess any reality.
Furthermore, you do not admit that cognition can be without an object; yet, if its object were merely a conceptual construction, it would clearly be objectless.

Even when the individual form (*vyakti*) perishes, the generic form (*ākṛti*) of those two certainly persists; otherwise, since the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) would apply, that [form] too would surely not exist. For what reason have you stated this rule: "The relationship is perceived through direct perception only between two specific individuals"? Why is an inference made subsequent to one previously seen through inference not accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), for what difference is there from the former? If it is argued that this is not a valid means of knowledge because it apprehends an object already known, then why is the same not seen to apply to the previous [inference], which is like a memory? If it is argued that its superiority lies in its removal of a doubt that arose in the interval, is this not equally the case here as well? Therefore, the perception of the universal (*sāmānyadarśana*)—which takes the form "it is that very same thing"—removes doubts such as "does it exist or not? and is thus free from further expectancy.
Some of evil vision, however, while expressing their own intention through these very words, declare that inference is not a valid means of knowledge.

Because it is preceded by a logical mark (*liṅga*) possessing the three characteristics (*trirūpa*), inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*) is not tenable as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For indeed, that which is produced by something that destroys what is desired is false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*). Furthermore, even if the [three] characteristics are present, it is not a cause of inferential cognition (*anumiti*) when there is no actual inference; thus, just as a logical mark has two characteristics, it lacks the three characteristics, and therefore there is no inference. Moreover, because contradiction with inference, contradictory reasons, and non-erroneous contradictories (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) are possible in every case of proof, [inference is untenable].

When the potencies of things differ due to variations in state, place, and time, the establishment of those things through inference is extremely difficult. Even for one who has ascertained the potency of a thing, that potency may be obstructed in relation to a specific causal function when it comes into contact with a particular substance. An object that has been inferred with great effort by skillful inferents may be demonstrated in an entirely different way by others who are even more proficient.

Inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*), however, is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to the speaker, because it is a mere restatement; therefore, he does not himself apprehend the object through it. Even with respect to the listener, this [inference] is established as being for one's own sake (*svārtha*) alone. For what difference is there between the cognition rooted in the listener’s own perception? The speech is not "inference for the sake of others" from the perspective of the listener, because it is a cause of the cognition within the listener’s continuum and because it makes [the object] known. Just as a sense faculty does not directly manifest the inferable object, so too this [speech] is not like that, because it lacks the knowledge of the relation of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*). If it is argued that its status as "for the sake of others" is in view of the exclusion of others (*paravyāvṛtti*), that too is incorrect, because it would follow that even inference for one's own sake (*svārtha*) would be for the sake of others.

Is it not the case that the definition of a reliable [cognition] is its being preceded by a logical mark possessing the three characteristics? And since validity has that as its definition, why is it denied on that basis?

False cognition is considered "identical" only in relation to the opponent's prima facie position; it is not said to be so produced in reality because it destroys what [the proponent] desires. For, according to the actual state of things, that cognition is certain and non-contradictory; therefore, it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for that which is the opposite of what the proponent desires. Consequently, there is contradiction (*viruddhatā*) in the reason (*hetu*), and the probandum (*sādhya*) is unestablished in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). By this very same method, in the second case, the reason is unestablished (*asiddhatā*).

Logicians declare that only that which is ascertained as being related through identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*) is a valid means of proof for establishing a conclusion. In such a means of proof, there is no contradiction with inference or other defects; for such a proof can never occur without those two [types of] internal reasons. Two mutually contradictory properties cannot coexist in a single entity; therefore, the possibility of a "non-deviating contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) is not tenable.

For those who have practiced the definitions [of the logical marks], when there is a correct determination of the mark (*liṅga*), inference proceeds; otherwise, it is not called inference. Since the potencies of entities differ due to differences in state, place, and time, the establishment of things through inference is therefore not very difficult to attain. Even an object that has been inferred with effort by skilled inferents cannot be established otherwise even by others who are more proficient.
For neither an essential nature nor an effect exists without an essential nature or a cause; since [otherwise] they would result in being causeless, there can be no inference without them.

Because the statement of the three-featured logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*) indicates what is connected [to the object], that which was called "inference for others" (*parārthānumāna*) is stated with respect to the listener. Thus, the status of being an inference is adopted in a secondary (*gauṇa*) and conventional (*sāṅketika*) sense; therefore, by virtue of indicating what is connected, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If inference were not a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), then your contradiction would be fruitless, for no discourse whatsoever could convey the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*).

If it is claimed that the worldly mark (*liṅga*) is accepted [as valid], but not that which is imagined by others—[we reply: surely even the world understands causes and so forth from effects and so forth. Indeed, that very thing has been sufficiently stated by the proponents of logic (*nyāyavādin*) as well. When that is already admitted by the world, what have you yourself rejected?

And what can another person understand by means of this which is not a valid means of knowledge? Furthermore, what kind of cognition could that be which is produced by something that is not a valid means of knowledge?

If inference were a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then one would not say that it is not of the nature of speech; for just as that [speech] reveals [its object], so too should this [inference] be. Since it does not reveal an unknown object, it is held by you to be invalid (*apramāṇa*). But your [inference] is not like that, because it indicates [the object] through the speaker’s incapacity [to state it directly]. Is this not so?

If inference were a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then one would not say that it consists of speech; for just as that [speech] reveals [its object], so too should this [inference] be. Since it does not reveal an unknown object, it is held by you to be not a means of valid cognition; yet, because it indicates [the object] through the speaker’s lack of incapacity, your [position] is not [tenable].
But surely, since other means of valid cognition such as verbal testimony and so forth exist, for what reason has the definition been stated for only two means of valid cognition?
But surely, since other means of valid cognition such as verbal testimony and so forth exist, for what reason has the definition been stated for only two means of valid cognition?

It is said: No means of valid cognition other than these two is tenable, because of the impossibility of the definition of a means of valid cognition; and even if it were possible, it would be included herein.

Others have declared that verbal cognition (*śābda*) is the knowledge of an imperceptible object arising from the knowledge of words; and that [knowledge] arises from a sentence that is either authorless (*akartṛka*) or uttered by a trustworthy person (*pratyayin*). Furthermore, this [verbal cognition] is certainly not perception, because its object is imperceptible; nor can it be inference, because it lacks the defining characteristics of that. For it is well-established that the subject (*dharmī*), as qualified by a property (*dharma*), is the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*); and there can be no inference so long as [the cognition] does not have that [qualified subject] as its object.

And whatever subject (dharmin) is postulated here, that alone is its object of cognition (prameya); nor is there a determination of its being a property (dharmatva) when that [subject] has not been ascertained.

If it has already been apprehended prior to the property-of-the-subject (pakṣadharmatva), what is the use of subsequently knowing the property-of-the-subject and so forth, through which inference would otherwise be established?
Nor is the concomitance of a word with its object of cognition established; for it is through their respective functions that the concomitance of all things is perceived.
Wherever there is smoke, there is clearly the positive concomitance (anvaya) of fire; however, it is not certain in this way that wherever there is a word, there is an object.

It is not the case that this [word] does not reach that place or that time; for if it were due to its being eternal and all-pervasive, that would be the same for all words. Consequently, because [the word] is seen everywhere and because its absence is never perceived, it follows as a logical consequence that all meanings would be understood from every single word.

Therefore, verbal cognition, like perception, should not be considered inference, because it lacks the three characteristics [of a logical reason] and because it excludes such an object [as that which is to be inferred].
Because it gives rise to unshakable knowledge through the injunctions regarding the Agnihotra and other rites, its status as a valid means of cognition cannot be denied.
In that regard, since the possibility and the meaning of a sentence without an author are untenable, the first definition of verbal testimony (śābda) is declared to be impossible.
Since the nature of being capable or incapable persists at all times, that consciousness which was to arise then would either always exist or never exist at any time.

Just as defects such as hatred and delusion are causes of falsity, so too are qualities such as compassion and wisdom known to be causes of truth. In the absence of a person who is their substratum, neither of these two can possibly exist; therefore, it follows that speech which does not rely upon a person is rendered purposeless.

If it is argued that meaning is not understood [from words] because of this, then it must arise from interpretation (*vyākhyāna*). For a person is seen to be independent when explaining a meaning according to his own will. If the capacity to illuminate the real state of things were inherent in him by nature, then the comprehension of the meaning would occur even for one who does not know the convention (*samaya*). A lamp is naturally an illuminator; it does not depend upon a convention. And if another convention were present, there would be a comprehension of a different meaning. Indeed, even when a convention exists, a lamp does not illuminate smell, taste, and so forth; nor can that capacity [to illuminate those] be produced [by convention].

Therefore, since the cognition of meaning is impossible [from such a source], how could there be any stability in it? That [cognition] is properly understood as conventional (*sāmayika*), for it does not differ from the words of men. Logicians do not perceive any distinction between these two; however, this [notion of stability] is unshakable only for the Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*) who are ignorant of the path of logic.

Because the status of being a reliable authority (āpta) has not been accepted, even the second definition of verbal testimony is not tenable; or, if it were accepted, that very person would remain undetermined.

Generally, it is observed that confidence in a person is derived from their speech; yet, if that speech is intended for the comprehension of something beyond the senses, then there is no confidence elsewhere due to the absence of such trust. For even if one has previously lacked confidence, there is certainly no rule that it must persist once confidence has been established in a single instance.

Or what obstruction could there be even to words regarding external objects, such that those who communicate them would possess the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? There is no identity [between word and object] because they are apprehended by different senses and so forth, nor does [the word] arise from it; nor is non-deviation possible for anything else, because of the possibility of error.
This desire to speak is inferred even from all [uttered] words; for that cause [of speech] is ascertained through perception and non-perception.

If it is observed that when one who is deluded intends to speak of one thing, another sentence is uttered, then even this [sentence]—though intended in that way—is not produced from that very [intention] due to its commonality with other instances. The distinction between speech uttered by the deluded and the non-deluded is perfectly clear; the wise are fully able to determine it from the context and other such factors.

Those who do not understand the distinction among those [smokes] based on the diversity of their causes possess this fault; however, there is no such fault regarding the logical mark (*liṅga*) itself. Even for smoke, whose nature is sometimes doubted because it may exist otherwise [as something other than fire], its status as a logical mark for fire would not be established even at the time of certainty.
Even for them, the mere intention to speak is contradicted, because inference exists with certainty for the purpose of establishing [the existence of] life and so forth.

And when the intention to speak is to be understood, the three-fold nature [of the reason] is indeed quite clear, because that [intention] is to be proven in the person as the subject by means of the speech as the effect: "This man possesses the intention to speak of the meaning of 'pāda' (foot/tree), because he is a user of the word 'vṛkṣa' (tree), just as I was in previous states."

Therefore, where the three-fold nature (*trairūpya*) and so forth of words are rejected by others, we do not at all accept their status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). However, where this [three-fold nature] is intended for them, it is clearly present there; indeed, when the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*) is the probandum (*sādhya*), the possession of the three characteristics (*trailakṣaṇya*) has been demonstrated. Such being the case, the status of verbal testimony as inference would be established—just like smoke and the like—by virtue of its being accompanied by the three-fold nature and the existence of such an object.

Therefore, where the three-fold character (*trairūpya*) and so forth of words are rejected by others, we do not at all accept their status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). But where this [three-fold character] is accepted by them, there it is clearly present; for when the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*) is the probandum (*sādhya*), the possession of the three marks has been demonstrated. This being the case, the nature of inference would belong to words—just as it does to smoke and the like—because they possess the three-fold character and because such an object exists.

When a forest-dweller, questioned by city-dwellers as to what a gavaya is like, replies with the statement, "As is a cow, so is a gavaya," this is well-known as the nature of comparison (*upamāna*) among the followers of Śabara; however, because it is not distinct from verbal testimony (*āgama*), it has been described otherwise [by others].

When a forest-dweller, questioned by city-dwellers as to what a gavaya is like, replies with the statement, "As is a cow, so is a gavaya," this is well-known as the nature of analogy (*upamāna*) among the followers of Śabara; however, because it is not distinct from verbal testimony (*āgama*), it has been described otherwise [by others].

When, having seen a cow in the forest, one beholds a gavaya that possesses many common bodily parts and a rounded neck, then the cognition of that gavaya—which apprehends its mere form and is specifically conceptual, such as "this animal has a form similar to a cow"—is held to be perception, provided that the operation of the sense organs is present. This is because it arises from the genus (jāti).
In that case, although that knowledge arises after one has remembered the cow, it would nonetheless fall within the range of the senses because of the proximity [of the cow] residing in the gavaya.
For resemblance, like a universal, is fully present in each individual; since it is perceived even when the counter-correlate is not seen.
Furthermore, the reality of similarity cannot be denied; it consists in the connection of another class of entity with many common constituent parts.
Within that very same state of affairs, whatever cognition arises—namely, "this cow-individual is equal to a beast"—that is the simile.
Therefore, that which is remembered, as qualified by similarity, would be the object of knowledge for analogy; or else, it is the similarity itself, which is based upon that [remembered object].

When the similarity has been perceived through direct perception and the cow has been remembered, comparison (upamāna) possesses the status of a means of valid cognition, because that specific [similarity] cannot be established by any other means.
Just as when a place is perceived and fire is being remembered, inference does not lose its status as a valid means of knowledge because its object is specific.

It is not possible for cognition to be established as perception at that time, because it lacks the operation of the connection between sense organ and object. Nor can it be an inference, because the three characteristics [of a logical mark] are untenable; for here, the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and so forth cannot be established in any way. Indeed, the similarity residing in the cow was not previously grasped as a property; and that which is being grasped in the gavaya cannot serve as an inferential mark for the cow.

Because it is a part of the very meaning of the proposition, the cow cannot serve as a logical mark; and because there is no connection, the gavaya likewise does not attain the status of being a mark for the cow.
And that cognition is not invalid, because it reveals an object not previously known; for prior to seeing the gavaya, its similarity [to the cow] was not apprehended.

Its status as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is not intended [by us] because of the non-existence of an object to be cognized (prameya). If it is argued that similarity consists in the connection with many common parts (sāmānya), [we reply: universals (sāmānya) have already been refuted; how then could there be a plurality among them? And if the connection with those [parts] were the means of valid cognition, then there must exist something that establishes it. Furthermore, the reality (vastutva) of the universal and its being graspable by perception would follow, because it is a cognizable object other than non-existence, just like a unique particular (asādhāraṇa-vastu).

For those who assert that a universal is an entity relegated to the category of non-existence, there is the fallacy of the unestablished (asiddhi) regarding the first probandum, and the fallacy of the thesis being a part of its own meaning (pratijñārthaikadeśatā).

In this way, however, it is logical that there: certain parts of the gavaya are the causes of a cognition identical [to that produced] by the parts of the cow's form. Thus, when that gavaya is seen, a memory arises in him regarding those parts of the cow's form which have been seen many times before. For this very reason, no such cognition occurs with respect to horses and the like due to similarity to that [cow]; otherwise, what would be the difference when the gavaya is seen?

Since this [subsequent cognition] merely illuminates an object already known, it is therefore not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); how, then, could there be the existence of another means of valid cognition?

Or let there be a real entity that constitutes similarity; yet, like a universal (*sāmānya*), it is perceived right before one even when its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*)—the cow—is not seen. Thus, its nature as being of the form of memory (*smṛti-rūpatva*) is by no means set aside. Furthermore, while similarity within the cow is known merely by its existence (*sattāmātreṇa*), it has not been determined in this way: "The similarity [of the cow] is with the gavaya. Therefore, analogy (*upamāna*) validates [this], which is why it differs from memory.
Even if it was not previously grasped by that very name, it was indeed grasped in its own essential nature, which is designated as its "self."
Name-and-form is not the reality of things, for if it were, then even those who have fully realized the truth of the self would remain ignorant when it is not grasped.

And if the status of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were established by this much alone, there would be no limit to the number of means of valid cognition, since they could also exist in other ways.

When a row of trees or the like is perceived, from the sight of one tree and the subsequent cognition of a second tree, there arises the ascertainment: "This is that [same tree]. If it is argued that this is not a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) because it depends on similarity and so forth, or because it apprehends what has already been apprehended, then the same objection applies to analogical cognition (*upamāna*) as well.

And when a gavaya is perceived, if a cognition of its dissimilarity to a horse and so forth arises, why is that not another type of valid cognition? If you say it is not so because it is included within non-existence (abhāva), it is not thus, for it rests upon a positive entity (bhāva). Or, if you claim it is a case of mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva), then the same would apply to cognitions of similarity.
For just as the distinction of similarity is cognized there, so too is the distinction of the commonality of all parts understood.

If [an object] were to be apprehended through the connection with a commonality of some parts, then it would follow that its true nature consists in the connection with the commonality of all its parts.

Some maintain that analogy (upamā) is the cognition of the relationship between a name and its referent, occurring when one who has heard the statement of extended application perceives an object possessing a similar nature.

Even in that case, the unconfused comprehension of the connection between the name and its referent occurs only if that extended application statement (*atideśavākya*) is heard at that very time. Thus, because it merely grasps an object already apprehended, comparison (*upamāna*) lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), just like memory, due to its lack of an instrumental function.
Then, even though she had not actually been born, she nevertheless acted; how was it that she then recognized him as the one whose name she had heard from me?
For instance, when one perceives a gavaya without having heard its name, no one is able to know that "this is the name he has heard."
If the object of comparison has been employed, then upon the apprehension of similarity, one understands the relationship by virtue of its having a specific object.
For he knows that relationship through scripture as having a general scope; however, he understands it as having a specific object by relying on analogy.

Surely, elsewhere it is not [the case] that the cognition of a relation [occurs] through a name; for its cognition of another object would be untenable due to the fallacy of over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

For no one, upon hearing the name "Citrāṅgada," understands that word at a later time to refer to someone wearing a beautiful crown; therefore, that name was previously known by him through conceptual reflection (*vikalpa*) as an external object, designated as a "universal" (*sāmānya*). Even when the *gavaya* is perceived, he recognizes [the name] in that very same [conceptual] form, and—failing to distinguish between the visible object and its conceptual construction—he conceives of it as being external.
And one should practice in this way: that conceptual constructions and verbal expressions whose objects are specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) have been refuted at length.

Even though that [similarity] is their object, it is indeed nothing but inference; for its being produced from a three-featured mark (*trirūpaliṅga*) is understood as follows: "That which is similar to a cow is the object of the word 'gavaya'," just like the gavaya present in the intellect at the time of grasping the convention.
If even a Buddhist were not to exist in that state, what occasion would there be for making this commitment? And how could this [commitment] be comparable to a cow?

It has already been established previously that there is no relation existing apart from the related entities themselves. At the time of the initial convention, the word was apprehended by the auditory consciousness; meanwhile, this animal standing before one is perceived by the visual organ. Since these two have been cognized separately, their conjunction cannot be a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*). Rather, like the [simultaneous] perception of fragrance and sweetness, the cognition of the connection with that name does not transcend the nature of memory (*smṛti*), because it arises from the synthesis of what was previously apprehended.

Furthermore, cognitions resulting from the application of names and yogic practices, which arise from infinite means, occur even among ordinary people and others, regardless of any similarity [to the original object].

"The king, whose feet are covered by the white parasol, is situated in their midst"—this is declared according to a specific instruction. When that [object] is seen at a later time, the cognition "his name is such-and-such" arises; at that time, this is another means of valid knowledge (pramā), because it does not depend on similarity or other such factors.

Another [opponent] seeks to establish the existence of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) other than perception and inference by the power of inference: "Perception is conjoined with a means of valid cognition distinct from inference, because it is a means of valid cognition, just like inference; and inference likewise [is so]. This is not so, for this reason is unestablished (*apratibandha*), since a sublation (*bādhā*) is revealed. Furthermore, in this way, your own fourfold classification of the means of valid cognition would be contradicted. Whatever solution you offer there will serve as the solution here as well.

Another [opponent] seeks to establish the existence of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) other than perception and inference through the power of inference: "Perception is conjoined with a distinct means of valid cognition other than inference, because it is a means of valid cognition, just like inference; and inference likewise [is so]. This is not so, for this reason is unestablished (*apratibandha*), since its sublation (*bādhā*) has been revealed. Furthermore, in this way, your own doctrine of the fourfold nature of the means of valid cognition would be contradicted. Whatever resolution you offer there will serve as the resolution here as well.

When an object known through the six means of valid cognition cannot be otherwise accounted for, and one postulates another unseen factor [to explain it], that is cited as presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).

When an object known through the six means of valid cognition cannot be otherwise accounted for, and one postulates another unseen factor [to explain it], that is cited as presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).

In that regard, the power of burning in fire is inferred from the act of burning known through direct perception; and the possession of that same power in the sun is inferred from its movement. The powers of all entities are established by the presumption (arthāpatti) based on their effects; these powers are understood as something unprecedented (apūrva), even without the prior apprehension of a [direct] relationship.

Neither a prior connection nor any other [connection] between these [reasons] and their effects is apprehended at present, such that the two—namely, the property of the subject (pakṣadharma) and positive concomitance (anvaya)—might exist here.

Or, if the position is that [the sense organs] such as the ear possess a [specific] capacity, whatever reason is employed will all result in being unestablished in its locus (āśrayāsiddha), because the subject (dharmin) itself is unestablished.
Upon hearing such statements as, "He is fat and does not eat during the day," the resulting cognition of his eating at night is called *śrutārthāpatti* (presumption based on what is heard).

The meaning of the word "night" and so forth is not understood from the sentence concerning the day; nor is there a connection between the meanings of the words "day" and so forth with the act of eating at night. Since there is no such distinction [of relation], that sentence cannot be the means of cognizing it. Furthermore, because it is occupied with another object, one cannot postulate a second meaning. Therefore, this [sentence] is understood through another sentence present in the mind. Consequently, even though that sentence has not been heard, if it is understood, its means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) must be stated—whether it be perception or one of the others. However, perception is certainly not admitted for a sentence that has not been uttered. Nor is it inference, for this [sentence] has never been seen together with that [unseen] instance. If, however, you maintain that it is a logical mark (liṅga) despite the relationship being unperceived, then by the mere utterance of [any] sentence, there would be comprehension of all sentences. Because it lacks a relationship, it does not differ from any other [sentence].
The capacity of a cow to be apprehended by the cognition [of it] as being similar to a gavaya is understood through the power produced by the force of comparison.

Thinking that denotation could not otherwise be established, one first understands the expressive power [of words] through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), since there is no other way for it to exist. Then, by means of yet another presumptive testimony, the permanence of the word is ascertained; for that which is impermanent cannot maintain continuity in the process of linguistic convention and usage.

The proof of Caitra’s existence outside [the house] which is described here—arising from a house qualified by the absence of Caitra as determined by the non-operation of means of valid cognition (pramāṇābhāva)—one should cite that as another instance of presumption (arthāpatti) originating from non-existence (abhāva). Even though it is distinct from inference, this [presumption] differs from inference because the property of the subject (pakṣadharma) and other such factors are not constituent parts of it. How can the absence in the house be the property of the subject (pakṣadharma) with respect to the object of knowledge (prameya), whether it be the person qualified by the external location or the location qualified by him? For in this case, the absence in the house of one who is alive is postulated as the property of the subject; yet that cognition does not arise without first cognizing his existence outside. However, an absence in the house that is pure and devoid of the qualification "being alive" is not a prover of existence outside, since such an absence is observed even in the case of those who are dead.

In that case, there is no such thing as "potency" (śakti) over and above the potent object itself which could be understood through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti); for the potent object is indeed directly perceived (adhyakṣa).

Whatever cause of burning and so forth is observed, such as fire and the like—apart from that, what other power (*śakti*) could there be, free from doubt or error? For, since it is precisely that [power] which is employed in the various effects, the entity itself would be a non-agent [if the power were distinct]. Even when there is employment [of the power], it is not different [from the entity]. Indeed, the definition of power is an essential nature (*svarūpa*) capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). And this entity, being of such a nature, is determined through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

There is no means of valid cognition whatsoever for the establishment of any other characteristic; even if it were known, there would be no purpose in it, because its function is accomplished by the form [of the object] itself.
For that perception of sound and so forth depends upon other causes; even when another [cause] is present, it does not occur due to the absence of its specific cause, just like a sprout and the like.

And birth occurs continuously in a location not occupied by the substratum [of fuel], just as [the movement] of the sun is perceived through its pervasion of different locations, like that of a flame and so forth. This [perception of movement] does not otherwise follow for that which is of a stable nature; for it [the stable entity] has no reaching of another location, and any other [independent] power [to move] has been refuted.
Regarding the matter that "Fat Devadatta does not eat during the day," there is no certainty; because of the presence of hatred, delusion, and so forth, a person might speak otherwise.
If, however, another sentence with its own meaning were to be implied by [the first] without regard for the course of the meaning, then that would be an implication of a different statement.

Alternatively, it is maintained that the comprehension of the object there occurs by way of the act of approaching; or rather, let the comprehension of the object arise from another means of valid cognition.

A person associated with eating at night is understood to be desired [as the subject], because of his fatness despite the absence of eating during the day, just like another [person who eats at night].
Since corpulence is determined through positive and negative concomitance to exist when food exists, there is a cognition of the object in reality by means of that which is connected to it.
For how can a sentence, which is devoid of all connection, be understood? Otherwise, everything would be understood from a single sentence.
For if there were no relation, or if it existed but was not ascertained, this sentence being understood would result in being invalid.
The validity of that which is connected [to its object] is established; otherwise, it would be by royal decree! How, moreover, could the validity of perception exist without such a connection?

Now, if [a cognition] were to be understood as being unrelated [to its object], why would there not be comprehension of anything else? For when a thing is devoid of relation, no distinction whatsoever is observed. Indeed, even in the case of perception (*pratyakṣa*), validity is established solely on the basis of relation; for validity consists in correspondence (*saṃvāda*), and that arises from the fact that [the cognition] acquires its very nature through the object.
Agreement with that [object] is not tenable for what lacks its cause or for what is causeless; otherwise, there would necessarily be agreement with all things.

Alternatively, the intention [of the speaker] appearing as a second sentence is inferred; by this, it is held that the understanding of the negative concomitance (vyatireka) arises from the positive sentence (anvaya-vākya).
When the validity of analogy has been refuted in detail, the validity of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) arising from it is likewise precluded.

In the case of the means of knowledge known as comparison (*upamāna*), it is held that "cowness" (*gotva*) is its objective basis (*ālambana*). And it is considered that an object is apprehended by its own existence alone and is the producer of its own cognition. Therefore, what need is there here for another power (*śakti*) for which one would have to look? The status of presumption (*arthāpatti*) as a means of knowledge is dependent upon comparison.
Even in the absence of non-difference, the communication of meaning by words is not contradicted, just as the movement of the hand and so forth serves as a cause [of understanding].
Just as vibration is the cause of a uniform reflective judgment, so too the capacity of words to convey meaning is not contradicted.
Indeed, those actions which are observed to reside in perceptible substances—their eternity is accepted, just as that of color, on the basis of recognition (pratyabhijñā).
And because of the absence of a manifestor, these [sounds] are not perceived continuously; for that which is your producer is itself considered by you to be the manifestor.
