For if their capacity were not thus obstructed, that cognition would occur constantly; but upon its separation from them, it would never occur at all. Consequently, manifestors [of sounds] are logically consistent as being the causes of those [cognitions], whereas recognition has already been refuted regarding the case of permanence.

However, Caitra’s presence outside is not logically established by his absence from the house, because that absence can be accounted for otherwise—namely, by the suspicion of his death. If it is argued that his absence from the house serves to establish his existence outside through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), this is not the case, for even there no certainty exists; for one who does not perceive Caitra in the house, there is no valid means of knowledge (*pramā*) belonging to a person of limited vision that establishes a connection with his being alive in any way whatsoever.

Now, when his being alive has been ascertained by means of sound and so forth, and his absence from home has been determined by his non-perception there, then this [non-apprehension] possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge.

Even then, his non-connection with the house is ascertained through the perception of his non-perception; therefore, his existence outside is determined solely by means of an inferential mark (*liṅga*). For one who is not in contact with the house is necessarily outside, just as a man standing in the courtyard of a house is seen by those standing at the door. A person inside the house serves as the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) here. Therefore, this presumption (*arthāpatti*) does not differ from inference (*anumāna*).

Even then, the fact of being unconnected with the house is determined through perception and non-perception; therefore, in that case, his existence outside is ascertained solely from the inferential mark (*liṅga*). For one who is not in contact with the house is necessarily outside, just as a man standing in the courtyard of the house is seen by those standing at the door. A person inside the house serves as the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) here. Therefore, this is Presumption (*arthāpatti*), and it does not differ from Inference (*anumāna*).

Where the five means of valid cognition do not arise with respect to the nature of an object, there the means of valid cognition known as non-existence (abhāva-pramāṇa) functions for the purpose of cognizing the existence of that object.

Where the five means of valid cognition do not arise with respect to the nature of an object, there the means of valid cognition known as non-existence (abhāva-pramāṇa) functions for the purpose of awakening one to the existence of that object.

The non-arising of perception and the other means of knowledge is held to be the absence of valid cognition (pramāṇābhāva); that [absence] is either the non-modification of the self or a cognition directed toward another object.

Furthermore, the non-existence of things is cognized through the absence of valid cognition; and this [non-existence] is divided into four kinds, according to the distinctions of prior non-existence and so forth.

And these distinctions cannot belong to a non-entity; therefore, it possesses substantiality. That which is the non-existence of effects and so forth is precisely the existence of causes and so forth.

Alternatively, since it is itself the object of the cognitions of both inclusion and exclusion, it should be understood as a real entity, like a cow and so forth, and because it is an object of knowledge.

If you ask how non-existence can be a means of knowledge (māna), what would the object of knowledge (prameya) be in this case? For just as the object of knowledge is indeed non-existence, so too should the means of knowledge be accepted as such.

Because it is denotable by the word "non-existence," non-existence is distinct from perception and the other [means of knowledge]. For the non-existence of the means of knowledge is like the non-existence of the objects of knowledge. Or rather, non-existence is measured by a means of knowledge corresponding to its own nature; because it is an object of knowledge, it is therefore separate from that which consists of existence.
Thus, in this context, the transformation of an eternally existent entity has been refuted; its existence as something occasional, being the opposite of that [eternity], is not tenable.
If what is intended here is merely its negation, then its status as a real entity would always be understood, since that negation does not exclude it.

Or, let it be granted that there is no transformation of this [consciousness]; even so, its deviation [from the object] remains. For in states such as sleep or fainting, the object may still be present even when that [consciousness] exists. Furthermore, when other cognitions are present, one perceives something else distinct from it. If you claim that this [consciousness] is intended to exist in the form of the cognition of a jar and so forth, then what distinction has been stated between this and the second position? Thus, these two positions have been indicated by you through an alternative formulation.

When consciousness occurs with respect to one object, the non-existence of everything else would be understood—even of that which is invisible—by relying on the absence of a second [perceived] entity.
If non-existence is perceived when there is proximity of other causes for that which has a form suitable to be similar to it, yet there is no cognition of anything else distinct from it; |||

The non-existence of perception itself is established only when there is the appearance of an object capable of being perceived; this being the case, it should be so designated, and not for other [types of] perceptions which are fallible. How can a cognition that has arisen regarding another object be known? If you hold that cognition is not perceptible and is known only through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), then since that [presumptive cognition] is also of the nature of knowledge, how is its own apprehension achieved? If you say it is explained by another presumptive testimony, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) follows. If the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*) and likewise the absence of an object of cognition (*meyābhāva*) are both included within perception, then in that case, why do they not belong to you [as well]?
For the non-existence of the effect and so forth is indeed an existence [constituted] by the cause and so forth; and that, having a nature distinct from others, is apprehended by perception itself.

In an entity that is eternally of the nature of both existence and non-existence by virtue of its own form and the form of others, some aspect is known by some people at some time. And when the operation of perception and other means of knowledge occurs, it is the positive aspect of the thing that is grasped; whereas when there is a desire to grasp the negative aspect, the operation [of those means] does not arise.
Indeed, the very intrinsic nature of things is held to be differentiated; thus, it exists as that [differentiated] self, and it is perceived by means of that self through direct perception.

That which is capable of causal efficiency is called "existent," and that which is otherwise is called "non-existent. A coexistence of these two within a single locus is not tenable due to their mutual contradiction. If it is argued that [an entity] is capable with respect to its own effect but incapable with respect to another, then indeed this duality of form does not exist at all within a single real entity. If, however, it is maintained that what is incapable of one thing is simply a different [entity] from what is capable of another, then two distinct entities would result; thus, there is no duality of form for a single entity.
If the reality of non-existence has already been accepted previously, for what purpose is its formlessness described once again?

For it is not logical that a formless [cognition] should possess the status of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) upon the loss of its cognitive nature; for that [status] is characterized by the awareness of the object of cognition (prameya).

The perceiver regards that very mass of light and darkness as space, because there is neither existence nor perception of anything else. Even the distinction from all other sounds is understood through the non-perception of their effects; and that [non-perception] is established ultimately through the self-awareness of other cognitions.
And thus, since its nature as a real entity is established, its being denotable by the word "non-existence" remains uncontradicted even when it is included [within the category of existence].

Or, if it is argued that "non-existence is measured by a means of valid cognition corresponding to itself," in this case there is the fallacy of proving what is already established, for such correspondence exists [in our view as well].

Or, if it is argued that "non-existence is measured by a means of valid cognition corresponding to itself," in this case, you are merely proving what is already established, for such correspondence indeed exists.

"When this exists, that necessarily comes to be; when this does not exist, that does not come to be. Therefore, because it necessarily arises from that, this is declared to be a logical principle (*yukti*). The Sage Caraka stated that this is indeed a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), for it is not inference (*anumāna*), since no corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*) can be found here. When an object is known through a certain perception, and its non-existence is understood from the absence of that perception, this is considered "non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*). This too is a distinct means of valid cognition, because it does not depend upon a corroborative instance or other such factors. For even regarding the non-existence in a corroborative instance, it is established by this very [means] alone.

"When this exists, that necessarily comes to be; when this is absent, that does not come to be. Therefore, it follows from this that [the effect] must exist; this is what is called "reasoning" (*yukti*). The sage Caraka stated that this is indeed a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it is not inference (*anumāna*), since no corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*) can be found here. When an object is known through a certain perception, and its non-existence is understood from the absence of that perception, this is considered "non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*). This too is a distinct means of valid cognition, because it does not depend upon a corroborative instance or other such factors. For even in the case of a corroborative instance, non-existence is established by this very [means of cognition].
The cognition of the absence of the relation between cause and effect is not restricted; for in this case, there is no distinction between the probandum and the means of proof.
Apart from the state of being conditioned by that [cause], there is no other nature of cause and effect; apart from the non-perception of what is perceived, no other non-existence is apprehended.
But when establishing the fitness for the conventional usage of that [word], there exists an object known at the time of the convention which serves as the illustrative example.
But when establishing the capacity for the conventional usage of that [term], there exists a known object as an illustration at the time of the convention.

The members of a collection are the causes for the establishment of that collection; the cognition of the possibility of a hundred and so forth arises from a thousand as an effect-sign (*kāryalinga*).
The members of a collection are the causes for the determination of that collection; the cognition of the possibility of a hundred and so forth arises from a thousand through the mark of the effect.

The members of a collection are the causes for the establishment of that collection; the cognition of the possibility of a hundred and so forth arises from a thousand as its effect-sign (*kāryaliṅga*).
Tradition, intuition, and the like are for the most part subject to deviation; it is not possible for such things to possess the status of valid cognition, as that would lead to over-extension.

Tradition, intuition, and the like are for the most part subject to error; it is not tenable that such things possess the status of valid means of knowledge, as this would lead to an over-extension of the definition.
Tradition, intuition, and the like are for the most part subject to deviation; it is not possible for such things to possess the status of valid cognition, as this would lead to over-extension.
Or rather, this effort is made in vain, since objects are established as being of only two kinds: perceptible and imperceptible.
Or rather, this effort is being made in the wrong place, since objects are established as being of only two kinds: perceptible and imperceptible.

Indeed, that other [object] which is of the nature of both or neither is not tenable; for within a single cognition, action and non-action regarding one and the same thing are contradictory. An object is called "perceptible" (*pratyakṣa*) by the wise when it directly produces knowledge; conversely, that which is the opposite of what has been described is considered "non-perceptible" (*parokṣa*). First of all, verbal testimony, analogy, and the like do not have the first type of object (the perceptible) as their domain, because they would then be included within perception or else be redundant, like memory. Even if they have the non-perceptible as their domain, how could it be the object of all [cognitions]? If this [non-perceptible] were not directly [known], it would not be like a perceptual object. Even if there is comprehension through dependence on another [means of knowledge], what is its [verbal testimony's] role? Is it based on something connected [to the object], or otherwise? If it were not so, there would be no appearance of distinction. If it arises from something unconnected, the consequence is a lack of restriction (indeterminacy). Furthermore, pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not possible if there were only an appearance of distinction. As long as a cognition has a non-perceptible object, relies upon a connected entity, and does not apprehend its specific distinctions, it is clearly inference (*anumāna*).

For that other [object] consisting of both or neither is not at all tenable; for it is contradictory for activity and non-activity to belong to one and the same thing in a single cognition. Indeed, an object is called "perceptible" (*pratyakṣa*) when it directly produces knowledge; conversely, that which is the opposite of what has been stated is considered "non-perceptible" (*parokṣa*) by the wise. First of all, verbal testimony, comparison, and the like do not have the first type of object (the perceptible) as their domain, because they would then be included within perception or else be as useless as memory. Even if they have the non-perceptible as their domain, how could it be the object of all [cognitions]? If this [non-perceptible] were not directly [known], it would not be like a perceptible entity. Even if there is comprehension through dependence on another [means of knowledge], what is its [verbal testimony's] role? Is it based on something connected [to the object], or otherwise? If it does not appear as distinct [from the other means], then it is not so. If it arises from something unconnected, the consequence is a lack of restriction (indeterminacy). Furthermore, pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not possible if there is only an appearance of difference. Cognition that has a non-perceptible object, which relies upon a connected entity and does not grasp its specific differences, is clearly inference.
Indeed, an object consists of multiple natures, just like a variegated gem; if that is the case, what contradiction could there be for [the properties of] existence and so forth by their very nature?
But surely, an object consists of multiple natures, just like a variegated gem; if that is the case, what contradiction could there be for existence and the other [categories] by their very nature?
An entity that is not comparable to another entity does not differ from a sky-flower; if it were devoid of such incomparability, its distinction from those [other entities] would not be established.

For in every way, if this entity is intended to be incomparable with another entity, its very status as an entity (vastutva) is necessarily lost. For when an entity has ceased to exist, what other possible state could there be for it, except non-existence, like a lotus in the sky? Therefore, one who desires that this entity be incomparable to a sky-flower must accept the universal called "entity-ness" (vastutva-sāmānya) and its similarity [to other entities]. Otherwise, why would that cognition not occur regarding the teeth of a crow, but rather be restricted to existing things alone? If you say this restriction is due to similarity (sārūpya), then that very thing is our "universal. By this, the power inherent in their own nature (svabhāva) has been described. Consequently, absolute difference is not possible for anything; for everything is distinguished from others by its form as an entity.

If an object were devoid of dissimilarity from the things taken as its limits of comparison, then that object would not be distinct from them; it would be non-different from them, like their own nature. Indeed, dissimilarity is defined as being distinct in its own form from those [other] things. To say that there is dissimilarity and yet it is not distinct is a mutual contradiction. Therefore, by one who accepts the distinctness of objects in some way, dissimilarity must be accepted; for this reason, they also possess the nature of particularity (*viśeṣa*).

This single entity is held to possess many forms; these [forms] exist as being apprehended by inclusive and exclusive cognitions. Because they are inclusive, the former are proclaimed as "universals" (sāmānya); because the others are exclusive, they are designated as "particulars" (viśeṣa).

If the universal and the particular were of a mutually identical nature, there would be a confusion of their essences; thus, in reality, this dual form is not tenable. Even if they were of a mutually distinct nature, a plurality [of separate entities] would follow; even in such a state, the dual form is not tenable.

Even though there is a single essential nature, a distinction between properties is established here; and there is no contradiction in their existing as distinct, just as in the case of the potencies of causal factors. Furthermore, it is not the case that what is observed is untenable; for even when the universal and the particular are of one essence, a distinction is seen that conforms to worldly practice.
But surely, if there is a single nature, a distinction of properties cannot be established; for it is an unconstructed differentiation that is designated as "manifoldness."
The multiplicity of powers is constructed merely by the speaker's intention; for even here, if they consist of a single reality, no distinction is logically tenable.

That which is sung as "it is that very same thing" is called "one"; however, that which is manifold in nature is not that [which is one]. Furthermore, the state of being that and the state of not being that are mutually contradictory; this [contradiction] cannot in any way be conceived within a single entity.
For injunction and prohibition are mutually contradictory; they cannot be established together in a single place by anyone with a sound mind.

Because an entity is excluded from many things—both similar and dissimilar—and because it is turned away from this or that [other], its various properties (dharma-bheda) are spoken of. Therefore, even for a single entity, it is logical that it possesses an imagined multiplicity of forms; however, it is not consistent for a single real entity to possess even two actual natures.

Indeed, as for those such as Narasiṃha who are described as having a dual form, even their possession of two forms is not real. For that [form] is by nature an aggregate of many atoms and does not possess a single form; indeed, that which is variegated is not one, like a collection of jewels of various kinds. If there were unity, there would be no appearance of diverse forms due to duality; nor would there be a lack of obstruction when even a portion the size of a fly’s foot is covered.

Those atoms are the causes of the recognition that is interwoven with the aspect of the Man-Lion (Nṛsiṃha), because they arise as distinct cognitions by their very nature. In this very manner, variegated gems and other such things are explained; for multiplicity is indeed contradictory with unity.

The capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsamarthatva*) is defined as "reality" (*vastutva*). If that [capacity] were pervasive, then everything would perform every function. If a single object is the producer of a certain effect due to its possession of that capacity, and if that capacity is indistinguishable in another [object], then how could that other not also be a producer? If it is maintained that "blueness" and so forth alone constitute the pervasive reality, then white, yellow, and other colors would also necessarily produce the effects accomplished by blue. Consequently, everything born from a single source would be devoid of a second nature; thus, for us, there would be no universe that is manifold in form, since nothing would be distinct from anything else. If that [capacity] is not what constitutes reality—just like the "existence" (*sattva*) in the system of Kaṇāda (the Vaiśeṣika)—then for you, a single entity could never possess multiple forms, because they are distinct. Furthermore, the association with contradictory properties is the defining characteristic of the difference between things. Even if one desires them to be different in some way, there would be no difference between blue and yellow. Since the state of being pervasive and the state of being otherwise [non-pervasive] exist in both the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*bheda*), how is it that there is no clear distinction between the two?

Just as one may grasp whichever color one desires from a variegated object, so too, because an entity is manifold, there is no fixed determination of its difference or non-difference. However, when a variegated entity is apprehended simultaneously, then all distinctions such as "other" or "non-other" completely dissolve.
Of an object possessing multiple forms, a particular form is intended according to the speaker's wish; there is no other way for words [to function] than through simultaneous or successive operation.

In this way, neither multiplicity nor unity is established, for it has just been refuted. Multiplicity consists of manifold forms, which cannot coexist with unity. For as many real aspects as there are in that object, so many distinct objects must have arisen; thus, unity does not exist therein.
If [an entity] were other than a single thing, it would be devoid of identity with it; for that [otherness], like a flower in the sky, would not be capable of causal efficiency.

The form [of a universal] that is capable [of functioning] does not reside in other things; this has been explained through the differences in the perception of effects and appearances. Furthermore, the fact that it does not have the nature of those [other] things is logical because of its non-connection with them. However, there is no lack of distinction or lack of substantiality, since the defining characteristics of a real entity (vastu) are present.

If one conceives that even that [non-entity] is a real thing because it is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-yogya*), then its "similarity" would consist merely in the exclusion of what is incapable; such similarity is thus a conceptual construction (*vikalpita*). Consequently, even though there is absolute difference, a conceptualized equality exists: an entity is similar to other entities, yet it is distinguished from a sky-flower.

Now, if that very nature by which an entity is distinguished from other entities—both those of its own class and those of a different class—is indeed the same as that by which it is similar [to those of its own class], then it would be perceived as equal even to those of a different class, because that nature is not distinct [in either case]. Yet, it is not perceived in that way. Therefore, that nature by which this entity is dissimilar to those of its own class, and that nature by which it is similar [to them], constitute a difference between those two intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*).
It is understood that this [object] is identical by virtue of that very nature, because it is the cause of a single reflective awareness through its exclusion of others.
For only certain things are the causes of a single unifying cognition, due to a restriction of their causal capacity despite their difference, just like the sense organs, nectar, and so forth.

Now, how can the eye produce the cognition of blue and so forth if it is held to possess only a nature that is excluded from blue and the rest? Just as the ear is not the producer of that [cognition] because it is distinct from the blue and so forth which are the producers of the cognition of blue, let the eye be regarded in the same way. For what other entity could be a producer that is turned away from the producer itself? Therefore, it is certain that there is also a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) among things.

Otherwise, since there would be no distinction, why is it not accepted that even hearing and so forth are producers of that [cognition], just as the eye is a producer of the cognition of color and other objects?

The exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of the eye and other [senses] from being producers is not established, because they are considered to be producers by their very nature (*ātman*) without distinction. Furthermore, the exclusion of entities from their own nature is not tenable; for if there were a turning away from one's own nature, it would follow that they lack intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*). If their exclusion from another producer is described, then it must be stated that they possess a nature that does not produce that [other thing], and this is indeed acceptable to us. For a producer is not described as such by its own nature alone; rather, all those [entities] are restricted in that regard, having arisen from their own respective causes. If these [causes] are producers of one [effect] because they are followed by a single essence (*ekātman*), then since that same essence exists in each individual [cause], what is the use of other auxiliary causes? If you say that one is not a producer due to the deficiency of certain specific qualities (*viśeṣa*), then surely they are incapable because of their difference; or if there is no difference, how could they be deficient? Just as even when there is a specific quality, everything is not the cause of everything, so too there would be a restriction despite the non-distinction of multiplicity (*nānātva*). Even given difference, some thing may be a producer due to the restriction of its own nature. But if there is a positive concomitance (*anvaya*), why would one [entity] be both the producer and the non-producer of the same [effect]? If you say that difference also exists here, let it be; but is that difference of that very entity itself? For difference is not something other than its positive concomitance; indeed, difference is not the causal factor. That alone is a real object (*bhāvika artha*) which is capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyākṣama*). And that which persists [through change] does not produce the effect; therefore, the effect is not born from that which persists. The conceptual distinctions and identities (*bhedābheda*) are imagined only with respect to that essence toward which a person acts. Otherwise, there would be difference through the essence and similarity through exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). The entity certainly exists, yet it does not persist [unchanged], because otherwise it would follow that there is activity [toward it] at all times.
In the description of the very variety created by conceptual construction, what excellence indeed has been proclaimed by the Brahmins, the Nirgranthas, and the Kāpilas?

When a necklace is fashioned from the breaking of a golden pitcher, then there is sorrow for one who desired the former object, joy for one who desires the latter, and indifference for one who desires the gold itself; therefore, an entity consists of three aspects. Without the existence of arising, persistence, and destruction, these three cognitions would not occur.
There is no sorrow without destruction, no happiness without arising, and no equanimity without stability; therefore, there is a commonality of permanence.

This [position] of ours is also not tenable, because there is no common substratum; for arising, persistence, and destruction do not have a single object as their locus, since they would necessarily occur simultaneously, which is impossible for mutually contradictory states. However, this [explanation] is entirely consistent if momentary destruction is accepted. For how could grief arise for someone regarding the destruction of a golden vessel if there were no continuity? On the contrary, joy arises at the birth of the earring, which is of that same nature as the previous form; but there is no persistence of anything whatsoever.

When one of deluded intellect perceives two states consisting of gold as being identical in their subsequent nature, he then considers them to be permanent. Since the nature of gold remains constant, its forms—such as a necklace and so forth—are also seen [as such] throughout prior and subsequent states; otherwise, there would be a perceived multiplicity.

When one of deluded intellect perceives two states consisting of gold as being identical through their common nature, he then considers them to be permanent. Since the nature of gold remains constant, even its forms such as necklaces and the like would appear as that same [gold] throughout prior and subsequent states; otherwise, multiplicity would be perceived.
When stability is conceived through the similarity of the persistence of gold, then even some Buddhists accept that an entity possesses different states.
When stability is conceived through the similarity of the continuous succession of gold, then even some Buddhists accept that an entity possesses different states.

Just as gold does not abandon its essential nature even when there is a difference in its states throughout its various stages, so too this entity does not abandon its substantiality (dravyatva). Otherwise, cognition of the past and the unborn would be without an object; and how could the Protector have taught that consciousness is based on a duality [of subject and object]? Furthermore, how could a past action, being devoid of existence, be held to yield a fruit? And how could there be a distinct cognition by yogis regarding the past and the future? Therefore, the past and future are not objects consisting of the exclusion of substance (dravyāpoha), because they possess the form of being included within the time-periods (adhvan) and the like, just like the present.

And one should not think in this way: "From where does this distinction of time-periods (*adhvan*) come? This division of the time-periods is merely postulated on the basis of activity (*kāritra*). For that which is engaged in activity is called "present"; that which has fallen away from activity is "past," and that which has not yet attained it is "future. Furthermore, the activity of phenomena (*dharma*) is the projection of a fruit, but it is not its producer. There is no such projection by past [phenomena]; therefore, activity is impossible for them.

They must accept that this activity (kāritra) is either different from the phenomenon (dharma) or is of the very same nature as it; for there is no other real possibility. If it were different, then present phenomena would lack intrinsic nature (asvabhāvatā) prior to or after [the activity], just as the activity itself lacks it due to its being a cause or being conditioned (saṃskṛta). Otherwise, the consequence of permanence would follow because the intrinsic nature would always remain established; for indeed, no characteristic of permanence exists apart from this [nature].

The causality of an eternal entity has already been refuted on the grounds of its contradiction with both successive and simultaneous action; for conditionedness (*saṃskṛtatva*) clearly finds no footing in what is eternal. Furthermore, if one describes "activity" (*kāritra*) as something distinct from the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, an unavoidable contradiction with one's own established tenets (*svasiddhānta*) results.

Even if the activity (*kāritra*) were non-different from the dharma, because it would not be distinct from the dharma itself, it would follow—just like the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of the dharma—that it exists at all times. Consequently, this distinction between the time-periods (*adhvan*) could not be established on its basis; for there would be no distinction in its loss, its attainment, or its non-attainment.
Alternatively, because it is not distinct from its activity, the dharma would be like the activity itself: it would possess only that which is in the middle, excluded from what precedes and follows.

Activity does not exist at all times, yet the phenomenon (dharma) is described as existing always; and activity is not other than the phenomenon—this is clearly the work of the gods! If it is argued that the endurance of that [activity] also depends upon another activity, then surely this same objection applies everywhere.

Even if a particularity (*viśeṣa*) were observed to be distinct from the essential nature (*svarūpa*), as in the case of resistance (*sapratighatva*), this would not be of any benefit to the subject under discussion. For no such thing as resistance or the like is considered to be an occasional property of a persisting entity; rather, it is held that the entity itself arises in such a manner.
That which is not distinguished from others is called "existence" (bhāva) itself; by the word "of that nature," it refers both to the mind and to its latent predispositions (vāsanā).

Now, it is described as being inexpressible in terms of either identity with or difference from [the entity], just like a continuum (*saṃtāna*) and so forth. In that case, activity (*kāritra*) would indeed be merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*). Furthermore, because it is a conceptual construction (*kalpita*), it is of no use anywhere; for it is only a real entity (*vastu*)—like a continuum—that is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Moreover, since its presence is not ultimately real (*bhāvika*), the establishment of the three time periods (*adhvan*) based upon it cannot be established as ultimate reality.

The capacity to project a fruit, which is called "activity" (*kāritra*) and falls within the range of verbal expression—how can that be merely nominally existent (*prajñaptisat*), given that it is the capacity itself that constitutes a real entity? Furthermore, as for this form (*rūpa*) which is held to perform effects such as burning or cooking—is it accepted that this very same form exists in its past and future states? If it is indeed that same thing, how can there be non-activity, activity, and even the cessation of activity for that which possesses a single, undifferentiated nature? For how could these mutually contradictory modes possibly apply to a single, indistinct entity? If it is argued that the entity is not indistinct across the time-periods (*adhvan*) because it abandons one state and assumes another, then do these states differ from the entity itself? They cannot, for if they were separate, the entity would lose its status as the agent. Indeed, it is through the actual existence of those very states that the existence of the effect is perceived.

How can they admit the non-difference of a substance across its temporal stages (*adhvan*), when those [stages], having not existed, come into being and then perish, while that [substance] is their very essence? And if it is the agent by its own nature during the middle stage, then that same nature must exist in the other two states as well. In that case, how can action and the cessation of action be attributed to it in those two states? Furthermore, if its agency were by means of another form, then its lack of agency would follow once again. If fire and so forth in the past and future states were considered different, then this fault of confusion (*sāṅkarya*) and the like would have no basis in this position. Therefore, it is established that this [substance], having not existed, arises now as fit for causal efficiency, and having existed, does not remain; thus, its nature is one of non-continuity (*ananvaya*).

Only that which is capable of causal efficiency is a real entity; and that [efficiency] does not exist in those two [past and future things] which you assert to exist. Therefore, the production of an effect from them is impossible.

This past entity, having come into being after not having existed, is clearly established as present, just like any other [present thing], and also because it occurs only occasionally (*kādācitkatayā*). If it were causeless, it would have to exist eternally or not exist at all, since it would be independent of anything else. An object is called "present" when its existence is restricted by a cause. Others maintain that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) such as form (*rūpa*) possess characteristics like birth (*jāti*), duration (*sthiti*), and so forth, in order to distinguish them from things like cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*). In that regard, what specific distinction does "birth" produce that it can be designated as "the producer of this"? Is it something other than that form which is yet unborn? If it is non-different [from the form], then no excellence (*atiśaya*) can be produced, because it already exists prior to its production, just as it does after production. If it is different, there is no excellence [belonging to the form], because they are distinct and unconnected; furthermore, this would entail the fallacy of the effect being previously non-existent (*asatkārya-prasaṅga*), since that excellence was previously absent. The same defects regarding aging (*jarā*) and the rest follow by implication, whether one considers them to be different or non-different from the entity's stability or destruction.

These [factors] such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth, which initiate their own effects by way of a restricted capacity (*sāmarthya*), possess that very nature both before and after [the effect]. Since they exist in a state of capable form, why do they not then initiate their corresponding activity? And if that activity were initiated, there would be an infinite regress of time-periods (*adhvan*).

Furthermore, are entities such as the past and so forth momentary or not? If the former, then for those two [time periods], that same state of having immeasurable paths (adhvan) would result. That moment which is being born is the present; that which, having arisen, has perished is the past; and that which is yet to arise is the future.

Moreover, if those [entities] were non-momentary, your established doctrine would be contradicted; for in the Siddhānta, it is proclaimed that "all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāras) are momentary. If they exist, there is also sublation by reasoning, because they must necessarily be subject to momentary destruction. Just like present things, their causal connection was previously established here.

These past and future [entities] must either be capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) or not. If they possess the reality of such capacity, they would be present, just like anything other than them. But if they lack the state of being present, then, being devoid of all power, it follows that the past and the unborn are like a sky-lotus and the like. Furthermore, all unconditioned things such as space (*ākāśa*) are subject to the same inquiry; since they are postulated as non-exclusive [of the definition], they too cannot be the basis [for the distinction]. The restricted power of causal efficiency in entities arises from conditions. If there were no cause [for this restriction], everything would be applicable everywhere. The birth of a restricted power for causal efficiency is produced by conditions; there is no other characteristic of a present entity. And yet, according to you, that [power] exists in its entirety in past and future things as well. Why, then, does the status of being "present" not follow for these too?
Therefore, this effort toward union with heaven or liberation is fruitless; for not the slightest result achievable through exertion is perceived here.
Now, if it is not admitted that they possess the capacity for causal efficiency, then for this very reason their non-existence follows, like a flower in the sky.

The reasons, however, are properties of an entity; they do not share in the proof [of the subject] when it is unestablished. Alternatively, they are contradictory because of the establishment of its present existence, which subverts the subject.

That form which, having existed, has ceased, is declared to be the past; that which is to be when the totality of conditions is present is the future. It has been established that if [form] were to exist [as a substance], it would follow that it must be present; for the defining characteristic of the present is merely its state of existing.
Having superimposed upon this [present entity] its past and future states—such as its being "form" (rūpa) and so forth—it is described in that way, but not according to its actual reality.
That which was stated by the Seer of Reality—that consciousness arises in dependence upon a duality—is taught with the intention of referring to the mind together with its object.
For there is no objective referent at all for cognitions such as those of an eternal creator god and the like, because they are devoid of the forms of dharmas such as words and names.
It is called "consciousness" (vijñāna) merely by virtue of its following after awakening; and that [awakening] is conceived as its non-inert nature due to its luminosity.
A ripening cause is not admitted to yield its fruit once it has passed away; rather, the fruit is held to arise from the continuum of consciousness that has been perfumed by it.
Referring to that very latent impression within the continuum of consciousness, it is designated as "karma" by way of metaphorical attribution, just as one speaks of the "destruction of the root."
Thus has it been revealed by the Teacher for the sake of destroying the view of annihilation; otherwise, how could the teaching in the *Śūnyatā-sūtra* be interpreted?

Yogins discern that form which constitutes the causal relationship of the present, whether it be mediated through a succession or immediate; they subsequently follow it with conceptual cognitions that, though pure worldly consciousnesses, do not have [that form] as their actual object. Based upon that continuity—both past and future—of causes and effects, the teachings concerning the past and the future proceed. For the Tathāgata, whose stream of cognition is free from the entire web of conceptual construction, these teachings proceed quite effortlessly, without exertion.

Yogins discern that form which constitutes the causal relationship of the present, whether it be mediated through a succession or immediate; they subsequently follow it with conceptual cognitions that, though pure worldly consciousnesses, do not truly possess that object as their domain. Relying upon the past and future continuities of those causes and effects—both what has been and what is to be—the teachings concerning the past and future proceed. For the Tathāgata, whose stream of cognition is free from the entire web of conceptual construction, these teachings proceed entirely without effort.
If no persisting entity whatsoever exists here, then there would be no future world, because of the non-existence of one who goes to that future world.
If no persisting entity whatsoever exists here, then there would be no other world, because of the non-existence of one who goes to the other world.

Since the body, the intellect, the sense organs, and so forth perish at every moment, it is not logical for them to possess existence in another world, nor is any other [permanent entity] admitted. Therefore, just as fermented acids, wine, and the like arise from specific primary elements (*bhūta-viśeṣa*), so too does cognition either arise or become manifest from those very same elements.
And it is this particular arrangement of earth and the other elements that is designated by the terms "body," "senses," and so forth; for no other reality exists.

There is no causal relationship between the two minds under dispute, because they reside in different bodies, just like the cognitions of a cow and a horse. Nor are these cognitions considered to be produced by the intended consciousness, because they possess the nature of cognition, just like cognitions connected to a different continuum.
A mind possessed of passion at the time of death does not effect a connection with another mind, due to the nature of the cognition of death, just as in the case of one free from defilements.
"Therefore, it is logical that knowledge arises from the body itself, which is presided over by the prāṇa, apāna, and other vital breaths; this is what was declared by Kambalāśvatara."

To claim that consciousness exists during the embryonic stages such as the *kalala* and so forth is reckless; for since the sense faculties have not yet arisen, no object can be apprehended there. And it is not logical for cognition to have any form other than the apprehension of an object; therefore, its existence even in states such as fainting is untenable. Nor does cognition persist at that time in the form of a potentiality (*śakti*), because the subsistence of potencies is not possible without a substratum. Since a self as the support of cognition does not exist, the body alone must be its support; and when the body finally ceases, what would be the support for the functioning of cognition?

If another body is observed arising immediately after that [previous one], how can it be understood that [the person] exists? Furthermore, how could that consciousness—which has proceeded in a different body—be connected to a single continuum, like the minds of elephants, horses, and so forth? Therefore, one must either accept some transmigrating person (*puruṣa*) who is a single substratum of cognition, without beginning or end, or else embrace absolute nihilism.

In this regard, there is no "other world" (paraloka) here that exists as something distinct; rather, it is merely a certain state within the continuum of the elements and consciousness—both the material cause and its effects—that is designated by a fixed limit. Since this continuum is beginningless and endless, the terms "other," "prior," and "here" are applied to it just as those addicted to immediate pleasures imagine an "other world" consisting of another place and so forth; we speak of it in the same way. If, however, you deny an "other world" as something separate from that [continuum], then your proof is futile, because there is no dispute regarding its non-existence [as a separate entity]. Surely, since the continuum is not a real substance (*avastu*), no transition to another state is possible; how then could a "world" established therein be real? It is not that the word "continuum" refers to the moments themselves as the possessors of the stream; rather, they are indicated collectively for the sake of brevity, just as one speaks of a "forest."

Because it cannot be conceived as a unity, it is held to be devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*); it is indefinable in terms of identity or difference, like a row of sky-lotuses. Furthermore, how could that [consciousness], which is beginningless and endless, ever attain establishment, if this mind were considered to be without a cause due to its primacy? [If it were caused,] would it arise from an eternal cause, or be eternal in itself, or else be produced solely from the elements (*bhūta*), or perhaps born from another cognition? Regarding the initial consciousness at conception and so forth: it is not logical for it to be causeless; otherwise, its existence would be entirely accidental. Nor is it created by an eternal mind, time, space, God (*Īśa*), the self (*Ātman*), and so on; for if it were, it would follow that it exists eternally, yet such [causes] do not exist. It is a rash assertion to claim that consciousness is a single, eternal nature, since a clear distinction is perceived between the cognitions of form, sound, and other objects. Its production does not come from the elements—earth, fire, water, and so on—nor is there a manifestation of all cognitions [from them], because that would entail their simultaneous occurrence. For those others [the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas] maintain that those four elements are of a stable nature; however, the dependence on auxiliary causes (*sahakārī*) in the case of a stable entity has already been refuted.
Now, if even your opponents assert that this [world] is indeed momentary, how is it that their own admission is not contradicted by this being the case?

Granted that this [position of yours] may be refuted; nevertheless, it is accepted as being logical: that all things are determined to be momentary by every means of reasoning. If, out of a passion for logic, you have no regard even for your own position, then let this supreme logic be accepted: that the elements themselves do not exist.
If, out of devotion to logic, you maintain impartiality even toward your own position, then let this supreme logic be accepted: that "elements themselves do not exist."
Neither can they have the nature of a composite whole, nor is their being of the nature of atoms logical; for the impossibility of [the existence of] atoms will be explained hereafter.
Relying solely upon the manifestation of consciousness, this fourfold great element is conceptualized; it is like a dream or an illusion.

It is not logical for something other than that [object] to be the cause when there is no appearance of it; rather, a preceding cognition that has the appearance of a real entity would produce the subsequent one.

The consciousness of another continuum is held to be its cause; if so, is it its material cause (*upādāna*) or its cooperative cause (*sahakārin*)? If it is intended to be the material cause, then in the stream of consciousness of a son, there would follow the specific impressions (*saṃskāra*) of learning and so forth belonging to his parents. For this is the established nature of the material cause and its effect, as determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) within one’s own continuum. If, however, the consciousness of another continuum is conceived as a cooperative cause for that which has arisen by the power of its own material cause, there would be no contradiction whatsoever.
Therefore, the initial consciousness therein arises from the power of its own material cause, because it possesses the nature of consciousness and other such reasons, like the present mind.
Since other causes have been rejected and the state of causelessness has been established, it follows that this [world] cannot be a phenomenon determined otherwise [by such causes].
The consciousness at the moment of death is capable of giving rise to its own effect, because it belongs to one possessed of attachment, just like the preceding consciousness.
Why is that form, which produces a determinate consciousness while maintaining itself unbroken both before and after, not considered the agent?

Furthermore, in the opponent's position, it is established that such cognition arises from the body alone. How, then, can the two examples be proven to be endowed with the property to be proven (the *sādhyadharma*)? [Objection: But was not the causality of the body already refuted earlier, because [cognition] occurs simultaneously with the mind, and because there is no additional [cause]? [Response: It cannot be denied that the cognition of memory, passion, and so forth is determined by the cultivation of mental application (*ābhoga*), virtuous thoughts, and the like. Since memory and the rest arise through the specific decrease or increase in the practice of learning, arts, and so on, and since when attention (*manaskāra*) is deficient one does not grasp other objects of knowledge, the fact that cognition is the cause of cognition does not fall into the category of the unmentionable. As for the reason "because it exists in a different body," that reason is unproven (*asiddha*). What kind of existence could there be for an incorporeal mind in bodies that do not fall [into its domain]? (Verse 1906)

An object may serve as a support for things such as water by preventing them from falling; but what purpose is served by supports for cognitions that possess no motion? If it is postulated here that their existence or activity consists in identity [with the body], that too is untenable, for it is not logical for you that cognition should have the nature of the body.

For if there were identity, why is it that the mind—such as passion, hatred, and so forth—is not perceived by others in the same way that the body is clearly perceived by them? The mind is perceived only by oneself, whereas the body is perceived by both oneself and others; those two things which are thus distinct must be differentiated, like an actor and the stage upon which he performs.

But from the standpoint of non-dual knowledge (*advayajñāna*), this reason is not established; for [the mind] perceives its own respective manifestations, just as in the case of [visual distortions like] *timira* and so forth. Since the body-mind complex is observed to perish immediately after its arising in an uninterrupted succession, why is its momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) not accepted if it possesses that very nature?

If it is claimed that cognition functions there [in the body] because it arises based upon it, or because it is inseparable from it, even so, there would still be a lack of consistency. For even a cognition existing in a prior state, though perishing moment by moment, certainly effects a continuous reconnection while functioning within the body. If it is argued that there is no difference in those cases due to their belonging to a single continuum, then let there be no difference in other cases either, since they too belong to a single continuum.

How can the consciousness of one whose outflows are exhausted be considered non-reconnecting? If you say it is because of the tenets of another school, no; for those tenets are not accepted as authoritative.

Furthermore, for those wise ones here who maintain that the Jinas attain a non-abiding nirvana and that there is a finality in those two vehicles, even if you rely on the tenets accepted by your opponent, your example remains unestablished and yet endowed with the property to be proven.

Furthermore, because no subverting argument has been stated, the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is doubtful; and due to the possibility of the existence of heterogeneous instances (vijātīya), there is deviation (vyabhicāra).

It is not reckless to say that consciousness exists during the stages such as the *kalala* (embryonic stage); for even when the sense faculties have not yet arisen, why should there not be cognition there? The claim that all consciousness arises through the power of the sense faculties and their objects is understood to be rash, because it is otherwise in cases such as dreams. Furthermore, its nature is determined to be different from the apprehension of external objects; therefore, its existence is logically established even in states such as fainting.

Nor does the mind persist in that state merely as a potentiality; for it is held that at that time, cognitions exist only in their own actual form. How then do you [establish] the certainty that "the mind does not exist" during states such as sleep or fainting? If you say it is because of the absence of sensation, then from what source does that [certainty] arise? If such a certainty were to occur for you in those states in the form, "I do not know the mind," then the existence of the mind is thereby established. It might be thought: "If consciousness exists in these states, why is there no memory of its specific form upon waking? That is not a valid reason, because of the impossibility of clarity and other such factors. Memory would not arise, just like the mind of a newborn infant.

If this is so, how is its existence in these states determined? It is understood from the very reason previously described. Furthermore, if the mind is not admitted to exist in states such as dreaming and fainting, then there would either be death in those cases, or else an absence of death upon awakening. Mental cognition is independent because it does not depend on the eyes and other [senses]; it functions solely by the power of its own material cause (*upādāna*), just as in dreams and similar states.

For instance, conceptual constructions do not depend upon sense organs and their objects, because they occur even in the absence of those operations, as in the case of [mental images of] sky-lotuses and the like.

Even when those two [the object and its cognition] are absent, the conceptual construction that arises regarding the past and so forth is determined to be exactly the same, insofar as it is colored by an unreal object. For it has been established in detail that, because objects appear within conceptual constructions through the mediation of words, their true nature as real entities does not manifest.
Even during states such as deep sleep and despite physical deformities of the body, there is no alteration in the mind or the intellect; therefore, these two are not dependent upon it.

Even when there is a very slight impairment of the eyes or other senses, such as cataracts, the cognition dependent upon the eye and so forth arises indeed as something distorted. Yet, even upon the destruction of that body, the mental cognition—which does not depend on those [senses]—continues by the power of its own material cause and remains uncontradicted.

Since even the intellect of the mind alone is thus non-contradictory, we do not exert ourselves to prove the existence of another body. Nor can its existence be denied, because it is based on the unseen (adṛṣṭa); this [intellect] may exist for one with weak vision, just as smoke and other such things are not seen by those with poor eyesight.

Even though it resides in different bodies, because it conforms to their specific characteristics, the prior cognition is connected to a single continuum, like a continuous stream. Furthermore, even in those born at the very moment of birth, there occurs an inclination toward suckling at the breast and an aversion toward injury; this is inferred from effects such as crying and suckling. Moreover, all of that consists of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and that [conceptualization] is accompanied by the association with names (*nāman*).
In this present life, no name-and-form exists without the eye; and if those [faculties] were absent in another existence, it would follow that they are utterly annihilated.

This [perception] arises through the power of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) from the repeated practice of reciting their names; because it has the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it appears at present as if it were a conceptual construction itself.
That conceptual construction which arises for them from the ripening of the latent impressions formed by the repeated practice of verbal designations—that is what constitutes their "other existence."
If their activity proceeds solely through the power of habituation to names, then why do they not possess distinct speech or memory like that of eloquent speakers?
Due to the intense impairment [of the faculties] and because they are distracted by the process of maturation, this functioning of theirs would not occur, as in states of derangement (sannipāta).
But for those great-souled ones, even the slightest injury is not heard of; their words are clearly manifest, and that tradition is distinct.

These [afflictions] such as passion and hatred are intense due to the force of habituation; this is ascertained through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Those which arise for the first time in this life, being devoid of prior habituation, what could be their cause if there were no other existence? For their arising does not occur merely from the presence of an object, because they do not arise even when the object is present if analytical discernment (*pratisaṅkhyāna*) exists, whereas they are seen to become powerful upon the cessation of that discernment. Furthermore, because they increase through error even regarding objects that have perished or not yet arisen—for instance, by superimposing qualities such as purity, "mine-ness," and permanence onto women and the like—the afflictions such as passion proceed with those very forms, even though the objects do not possess such characteristics. Even in this life, these afflictions such as passion continue to exist solely without such external objects, due to the power of similar habituation, just like the subsequent ones.

When objects present themselves, however, there arise pleasure, pain, and so forth; therefore, the afflictions such as attachment and aversion are born from the ripening of homogeneous latent impressions (*vāsanā*). For those who are hostile to analytical discernment (*pratisaṅkhyāna*) and are subject to improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*), these afflictions arise according to their strength. (1955) Objects, however, are not directly the causes of attachment, aversion, and the like. For if that were the case, a single affliction would occur for everyone toward a single object, just as the cognition of it does.
Nor is this their [the Buddhas'] conduct established through the perception of another's conduct or through hearing it from others, because their conduct is observed to be inconsistent.
Even wild boars, deer, and other animals, though they have neither seen nor heard of such occurrences, undergo transformation indeed upon contact with the movement of their own kind.
The qualities unaccustomed to cyclic existence—wisdom, ethical discipline, compassion, and so forth—proceed by their own very nature, and not like intoxication and the like.

Nor does their occurrence arise through the influence of phlegm (*balāsa*) and the like, because, as before, deviation is observed in every respect. Therefore, since these [cognitions] are preceded by practice and do not exist at first, that very [practice] is established as being from another birth; thus, the Nihilists are defeated.

If what is to be proven is that [the cognition] is preceded by practice in this very life, there is sublation by perception and scripture. If it is to be proven that it has as its cause practice in another life, the illustrative example is devoid of the probandum. But if the probandum is stated without qualification, this reason is contradictory, because it likewise excludes the possibility of having practice in another life as its cause.

The state of being the probandum (sādhya) exists only in a general sense, and there is no contradiction in the reason (hetu); for this [reason] has no contradiction with that [general property], by which it would exclude it.
The probandum is indeed established in a general sense, and there is no contradiction in the reason; for this [reason] has no contradiction with that [general property], by which it would exclude it.

If the four elements do not exist apart from cognition, then why does this [world] appear so clearly and distinctly? Even though it appears in such a way, if you admit its non-existence, what proof could you possibly have for the existence of the mind itself?

If the four elements do not exist apart from cognition, then why does this [world] appear so clearly and distinctly? Even though it appears in such a manner, if you admit its non-existence, what proof could you possibly have for the existence of the mind itself?

What is the nature of this external object that appears as it manifests? Is it of the nature of atoms (*paramāṇu*), or is it characterized as a composite whole (*avayavin*)? First of all, the form of atoms is not perceived; for there is no cognition of those which are partless, multiple, and appearing as a single mass. Indeed, atoms would have to appear as devoid of any distinction of parts; otherwise, they could not possess perceptibility, since they do not impart their own form [to the cognition].

Even through their association with literary compositions, they shine by their very own nature; they do not abandon their partless form, nor do they ever enter into those [limited] states. If their form were subject to the ultimate limit of decay, how could they not be material? For if they were material, they would be like sensations and the like.

Just as there is the delusion of permanence due to the arising of subsequent moments similar [to the preceding], so too there is the delusion of grossness when there is the apprehension of an uninterrupted series of homogeneous moments.

If perception were to produce [its result] solely by the power of its own operation, how could reflective cognition (*parāmarśavijñāna*) have those things as its objects? Furthermore, how could entities be determined through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) as being momentary, or how could atoms be understood as yellow, white, and so forth? For that which consists of an accumulation of subtle parts is not initially perceptible to the eye because of its grossness (*sthūlatva*), just like a mountain and the like. If it is argued that here too there is an inference regarding their being either combined or uncombined; yet, grossness is indeed a property of real entities (*vastudharma*), and it is not established in either of these two subjects (*dharmin*). For there is no gross composite whole (*avayavin*), nor are the atoms of such a nature. Now, if it is said that the form existing as an extension in space is thus described, even so, there is doubt because it appears in a deluded cognition. If it is argued that this is not so because of its truthfulness, provided that its difference [from error] is not proven; then what excellence does this [perception] possess if it is merely the correspondence with the effect? Indeed, even when there is a correspondence with a cognition manifesting the effect, it is stated that this is possible otherwise, due to the restriction of causal capacity (*sāmarthyaniyama*).

When a form that is similar is perceived, yet one that is dissimilar is not perceived at all, then what is not possible regarding the dual nature of atoms? Since every entity consists of both a universal and a particular nature, atoms are traditionally held to be dual-natured because they possess both a similar and a dissimilar essence. Among these, the form that is common is the object of sensory cognition; therefore, it is logical that cognition has a single aspect with respect to the atoms themselves. However, the dissimilar form is asserted to be the object of the direct perception of yogis. Thus some of poor intellect imagine this confused doctrine.

For how indeed could two forms be logical for a single entity? In that case, two distinct entities would result, each possessing its own separate form. If, however, they were of a mutually identical nature, then their duality of form would be contradicted; furthermore, a distinction between them would be perceived by the sense organs, such as the eye.

Therefore, even for that which is non-existent, there is cognition—just as in the case of the form of a conch-shell appearing yellow; moreover, apart from the association with contradictory attributes, there is no other definition of difference.
Granted that atoms may not be established by means of valid cognition and that there may be doubt regarding them, how could those who possess discernment arrive at a certainty of their non-existence?

If the form of an atom situated in the middle, which faces one atom when conjoined with it, remains the very same when conceived as facing another atom—even though that other atom is located at a distance and established in immediate proximity—then, this being the case, the accumulation of mountains and the like would not be possible. Alternatively, if a different form is admitted for the atom when facing another atom, how indeed could there be a single atom under such circumstances?

Regarding that atom which is asserted by others to be devoid of any division of parts, this very analysis is applied; therefore, there is no possibility of it being non-undesirable [to refute]. When they accept that the parts themselves possess the nature of atoms, then their own thesis necessarily falls away. Furthermore, because this is a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) argument, there is no fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) here; for unity is refuted on the strength of the "conjunction" and other properties admitted by the opponent himself. Thus, in all these positions, it is not tenable for it to have a single nature. Since a single nature is not established, a multiple nature is likewise impossible. Therefore, to the wise, the atom is determined to be non-existent, because it is empty of both a single and a multiple nature, like a lotus in the sky.
Furthermore, because an atom is impossible, the composite whole does not exist; for that [whole] is accepted by others as being composed of atoms.

Cognition perceives neither that which is without appearance, nor that which is with appearance, nor even that which has another thing as its appearance; it does not perceive an external object in any way whatsoever.
Consciousness arises as something distinct from insentient forms; this very non-insentience is its self-awareness.

However, its self-awareness does not occur through the relationship of action and agent, because it is a single entity without parts, and the threefold nature [of action, agent, and object] is untenable for it. Thus, since it has the nature of consciousness, its self-awareness is indeed logical; but how can there be awareness of another, namely an external object, by means of that [self-awareness]?
For that form does not belong to anything else such that it would be experienced by another upon the cognition of it; because, in the ultimate sense, all entities are distinct.
Since it arises in the form of consciousness, it is logical that cognition is what is cognized; but how can an object, which has not arisen as consciousness, be cognized?

In the view that cognition possesses an appearance (*nirbhāsijñānapakṣa*), although those two [the object and the cognition] are distinct in reality, there may still be a figurative apprehension [of the object], because the reflection possesses the same form as it. However, for one who does not accept that cognition is colored by the form of the object, even this mode of external apprehension does not exist at all.

It might be thought: just as swords, fire, and so forth cut, burn, and perform other such actions upon elephants, wood, and the like—even though they do not possess the same nature as those objects—so it is in this case as well.
This is inconsistent, because those [causes] exist as such established causes of production; knowledge, however, is not a producer in that manner.

The nature of consciousness as the determination of that [object] is tenable only if a determination in the form of cognition is possible for the object of apprehension. Otherwise, it must clearly be stated that "cognition has the nature of determination," yet no such apprehension of the object has been demonstrated.
Nor does one deserve the objection as to whose discernment that is; for that discernment is its very nature, just as being continuous and so forth is the nature of pleasure and the like.
The capacity to illuminate exists in external objects, but not in the self, because of the absence of such power; yet, the causal power of all entities is not subject to such questioning.

Now, is it not the case that the cognition of an object is designated as nothing other than knowledge itself? When that [cognition] is the very self-nature of [the object], what other operation could there possibly be?

If the nature of the experience of an object consists of that [experience] itself, and that [nature] is of the essence of cognition, then it would be logical for cognition to possess the nature of experiencing the object; yet that is not the case. For, because of the consequence of abandoning the accepted [object], even if that [cognition] possesses the nature of experience by its own nature, the awareness of the object is not established.
For in that case, there exists no basis for proximity on the part of the external object, as there is in the theory of cognition with forms (sākāravijñānavāda) regarding the reflection of the object.

If, because it is by nature insentient, there is no self-experience for this [cognition], then, due to the absence of the awareness of knowledge, its experience would likewise be for the sake of another.
The so-called experience of an object is designated as nothing other than cognition itself; if that [cognition] were of an unestablished nature, what further establishment could there be for it?

If that object were experienced by another cognition while its own experience exists, then since it is already established, when would it ever be established again through a lack of establishment? If it is unestablished in the awareness of itself at the time of the arising of the cognition of that cognition, yet established in the awareness of another—this is indeed a fine saying!
If its experience is also unestablished, then the first one is likewise unestablished; in that case, if another consciousness were to arise, an infinite regress would result.

Furthermore, the movement from one object-domain to another would not occur, yet such movement is observed. If, during the movement to another object-domain, that final cognition were established neither by itself nor by another, it would remain unestablished; and if that one is unestablished, all others would likewise be unestablished. Consequently, the entire world would be plunged into blindness. However, if the final cognition is established by itself, then the establishment of the others is certain as well, because they possess the nature of cognition (*jñānatva*). Otherwise, these others would lack the nature of cognition, just like a jar or other material objects.
The eye is the illuminator of that form which produces consciousness; however, because [the eye] is not itself of the nature of cognition, what comparison can there be between it and that knowledge?

That of which cognition is the very essence and whose cognition is certain, that [object] is non-different from it, or else it is not distinct from it—just as the self-nature of the cognition of blue, or as a second moon [is not distinct from the first]. And this is the cognition of the cognition of blue, because of the cognition of the form of blue.

If the nature of cognition is not the supreme self, how can there be an awareness of the form of blue when cognizing blue? If there is no non-difference between those two, [such awareness would be impossible].
All this is cognition, and it does not have an external object as its domain; for the cognition of blue is like the self-cognition of itself.

Primarily, it does not grasp the object because it is established in its own intrinsic nature; nor does it do so figuratively, due to its lack of coloring by the form of the object. This is the proof directed against those who maintain that cognition is like a pure crystal, unmarked by the forms of objects.

Let it be, then, that consciousness possessing similarity [to its object] is the cognizer of the external; yet, because that too is impossible in every respect, the status of being a cognizer is not tenable.

Because it is not distinct from cognition, there could not be a multiplicity of forms; consequently, there would be no established state of the awareness of objects by virtue of that [cognition]. Alternatively, because it is not distinct from the forms, cognition itself would become manifold; otherwise, how could the oneness of these two be conceived?
If there were identity in every respect, then knowledge would become non-knowledge and so forth; if there were similarity in only some respect, then everything would be the knower of everything.
How can a cognition that has one form be the knower of something else? Otherwise, everything would be cognizable by everyone, and the cause would not be a restricting factor.
For just as your cognition is in reality formless, yet perceives unreal forms while [perceiving] everything real exactly as it is; so too [is the case for us].

This nature of consciousness and mental factors is indeed unique: the experience [of them] is not primarily possible for others in any way whatsoever. Based on their dependence upon the same causal complex (*sāmagrī*), their relationship as cause and effect, and so forth, there might indeed be a figurative experience of an external object. However, for an entity that is devoid of form (*nīrūpya*), there is no dependence upon the same causal complex; nor is there anything else [by which it could be known]. Therefore, there is not even a figurative experience of such an entity.

Alternatively, it is designated as "knowing" because it perceives a non-existent form; for due to delusion, it does not know it in its true nature, since that [cognition] is indeed objectless. If you also say that consciousness is the knower of such [an object] only through delusion, then it is clearly established that your [consciousness] is pervaded by being objectless.
"It is with form, yet it is formless; it is logical that it does not perceive anything else"—such a reflection does not even occur regarding the Buddhist consciousness.

In the perception of another's passion and so forth, because it arises from a resemblance to that [passion], the existence of an obscuration follows according to the view of those who maintain direct apprehension (*aupalambhika*).

Like a wish-fulfilling tree, the Sage—though unmoved by all the winds of conceptualization—indeed brings about the fulfillment of the aims of the world. Therefore, they call the Jina, the knower of all, "invisible," because the performance of every task of an omniscient being occurs without effort (*anābhoga*).
