If cognition possesses a form such as white and so forth, how can that [external object] be its experience? If cognition possesses a form such as white and so forth, what means of valid cognition is there for an external object?
The appearance of blue and so forth is established as being of the nature of cognition because it is reliable; it arises from a cause of the same class, just like [the cognition of] awareness itself.

Whether the attainment of an external object or the capacity for such attainment is intended [as "correspondence"], that correspondence is unestablished for one who denies external objects. If, however, the cause of a cognition is held to be its determination by purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), even so, such correspondence can be established even for a cognition that lacks an objective basis.

Just as the capacity and restriction of external things like water and so forth are accepted, so too are these [restrictions] in cognitions, because they do not differ from consciousness. This [restriction] is also clearly evident through inferential appearance; it is common [to all], yet the form of fire and such things is not identical to that [consciousness].

If it is argued that the cognition of another's mind—[inferred] from reasons such as its being an object of knowledge—is distinct from internal experience because it appears as separated by space, even here there is the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāritva*) due to the nature of this consciousness; for this is likewise [seen] in cases such as the double moon perceived by those with diseased eyes.

Otherwise, if it is argued here that only an external object is what is cognized, [we reply: this appearing form is surely not of the nature of that [external] object. And because it appears in such a way, it is known by consciousness; however, the intrinsic nature of the external object does not appear there at all. How indeed can that which does not appear be cognized? Furthermore, the claim that one knows it "otherwise than it is" is a mutual contradiction. For this very reason, the self-cognizability of cognitions is difficult to establish, since we observe that cognition occurs as the appearance of its own nature. Therefore, this intellect is deluded; it does not conceive of the object as it truly is, but conceives it otherwise than it exists, and thus it perceives itself as something else.

Now, that form which is the grasper must be distinct from that which is grasped; for when that [object] is cognized, it is not cognized [as the grasper], just as the grasper of taste and so forth [is not cognized when taste is]. Likewise, the object of grasping is not necessarily cognized by one who is reflecting upon its grasper, just like the grasper of taste and so forth. Both [subject and object] are to be proven as mutually distinct from each other, like taste and so forth; or else, because they are not known in a single form, they are like the cognition of another mental continuum. Cognition does not grasp its own part, because it is a cognition [already] arisen, like its own causal capacity; and there is a negation of its being an object of grasping, for the latent impression (*vāsanā*) is devoid of both [subject and object]. The cognition of Caitra would not be a cognizer of the object-part of the cognition arising from it, because it is a cognition, just like [a cognition] arising from another body.
Because non-distinctness has not been previously established here—as demonstrated [above]—there is no proof [of it] regarding [the states] from the lack of awareness of a single form up to the end.
Is it not stated by this very [verse], "connected with the external object," that the cognition of the form of the apprehended occurs without the experience of the apprehender?

Nor do I remember that "some object was grasped by me at that time. [Rather,] people remember the arising of the apprehender as devoid of the form of the apprehended. Therefore, if there were non-difference [between them], there would be remembrance of the apprehended as well; but in that case, it is only this [apprehender] that is remembered when there is the existence of the memory of the apprehender. Thus, their difference is established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka). And in this way, these reasons are also well-established in the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin).

For one whose apprehension is not established, the cognition of an object is not established; therefore, there is no awareness of the apprehended object apart from the experience of the apprehender. Just as yellow and other colors are perceived by those with diseased eyes, so too is the object of cognition [perceived] when extracted from the portion of the apprehender; it is not otherwise.

And that memory regarding an external form has its specific details unperceived; however, it does not apply to a form distinguished from everything else, because the conditions for such repeated practice (abhyāsa) and so forth are impossible.

If it were held that memory occurs only when [the object] has been grasped in this manner and not otherwise, then memory would not be experienced as resembling pure crystal; nor is it the case that memory is perceived [as such]. Furthermore, because of cognitions such as "yellow conch," the two latter reasons are clearly inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); this same direction applies to other proofs as well.

Therefore, because it possesses the nature of cognition, the mind—which has become the subject of dispute—is non-dual, due to its separation from both the state of being an object of knowledge and that of being an agent, just like a reflection.

But surely, even in the case of a reflection, cognition is held to have an objective support (sālambana), because one's own face and so forth are seen in that way when the rays of the eye are turned back.

Because that [face] is not seen directly, one's own face and so forth are likewise not perceived; this is because they are seen with a difference in location relative to the means of perception, just like any other object.

The nature of consciousness is luminosity (*prakāśatva*), and that [luminosity] has no locus within an object of apprehension (*grāhya*), because it would be impossible for it not to appear [as such]. Therefore, its pervasion [of consciousness by luminosity] is certain. We do not accept that the objective status of the apprehended aspect resides in a subsequent cognition that is capable [of cognizing it], as that would not be ultimately real (*tāttvika*). By this, our means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established. Thus, the proof of Cognition-Only (*vijñaptimātratā*) has been clarified by the wise; we have followed that direction in determining the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

The nature of consciousness is luminosity (*prakāśatva*), and that [luminosity] finds no support in an external object (*grāhya*), because it is logically impossible for [consciousness] to lack manifestation and so forth; thus, its pervasion [by luminosity] is certain. Therefore, we do not accept that the objective status of the "object-aspect" (*grāhyāṃśa*) resides in a subsequent cognition that possesses the capacity [to grasp it], as that would not be ultimately real (*tāttvikī*). By this, our means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established. Thus, the proof of Cognition-Only (*vijñaptimātratā*) has been clarified by the wise; we have followed their direction in determining the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Others here, however, whose intellects are defiled by ignorance, have declared: "This [world] is not logically established as being mind-only, because it contradicts the sacred scriptures."
Others here, however, whose intellects are defiled by ignorance, have declared: "This [world] is not logically established as being mind-only, because it contradicts the sacred scriptures."
For that [Veda] stands as the authority for all, by virtue of not being human-made; since human utterances are subject to falsity.

For regarding those things expressed as human speech, it is indeed suspected whether defects exist or not; but since there is no author in the case of the Śruti, for us there is no suspicion of defects whatsoever.

First, it is maintained that such an author was never seen at any time; having no previously perceived relationship [to his work], he is now known only through ignorance. Even though devoid of inference, he is postulated to exist; yet there is no scripture (āgama) for his establishment, nor any other [source]—whether human-composed, non-human-composed, or uncreated. Because it is itself not a means of valid knowledge (apramāṇa), a human-composed [text] cannot inform us of him. For even the words of Manu and others possess truth only because they were composed by him. How could one who is unrelated [to the Veda] and hostile to it be a speaker of truth? Therefore, we do not have any scripture regarding an author of the Veda, even if it were composed by someone else. If anyone resembling an author of the Veda were seen at present, then by that analogy (upamāna) an analogy for the author might exist. If nothing whatsoever could be established as validly known without an author of the Veda, then the author would certainly be understood through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti). But is there anything in the Veda that is not possible without him? Indeed, while he exists, much—including its own validity—is not established. Since he is inaccessible to the five [means of knowledge], he is known only through non-existence (abhāva); thus, his existence is difficult to attain, being sublated by the absence of any means of valid knowledge.
The authorlessness of the Veda is desired for the purpose of removing its lack of authority; however, since that [authorlessness] is a non-entity, it cannot be established by means of proofs.

Whatever argument a logician might offer to prove the human origin [of the Veda], the Veda’s lack of human origin is established by refuting that very argument. For when two positions regarding the nature of reality—such as those of Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*) and atoms (*paramāṇu*)—are presented, the failure to establish one does not automatically establish the other. Even after the proof for Primordial Matter as the cause has been refuted, the thesis that the world is produced from atoms must still be proven by means of a different reason.

Whatever proof is stated for the purpose of establishing the side of existence, when that is thoroughly refuted, non-existence itself is established by its own force. Having performed the refutation of whatever proof is asserted by opponents regarding the two limits—the prior and the posterior—the proponents of the Veda have accomplished their purpose.

Even for those who do not attempt to prove it, the establishment of that which is the nature of a real entity—namely, its permanence—occurs of its own accord once the two preceding positions have been refuted.
The prior limit of the Veda is characterized by its being composed by a person; the subsequent limit consists in its destruction, for its absence [of these] is indeed eternity.

If it is held that the very fact that the Veda is not first produced and does not subsequently perish constitutes its eternality, then that is indeed what is intended by "eternality"—namely, being uncreated and being indestructible. However, since these two consist in mere non-existence, they do not require any means of their own proof.
For one who asserts, on the basis of inference, that the meaning of Vedic statements is false, his position is overturned by the power of Vedic knowledge.

And because it is equivalent to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), that which is Vedic is far more powerful; it cannot be sublated by inference in any way whatsoever. Since the scripture itself is established as being placed on the same side as direct perception, its status as "far more powerful" constitutes a sublation of inference.

Because it is independent of examples and free from defects, scripture possesses a lightness of operation that inference does not have. Therefore, when there is doubt regarding a matter based on both scripture and inference, the determination must be made by scripture alone, as it is more powerful.

Even though the Veda makes its meaning known by saying "it is authoritative for me," it cannot be rendered false by a speaker of untruth through mere malice. Neither hatred nor lack of approval renders it non-authoritative; nor is its status as authority established by personal liking or consent. Even those who hate the Veda do not utter anything that constitutes a reason for its lack of authority; those who merely prattle such things could not be considered speakers of truth. How can those who are distant from the Veda perceive the cause of its falsity, when they are constantly engaged in its retention, study, exposition, and ritual performance? For those who are experts in a particular field and whose interests are bound up with it are the ones authorized to know the merits and defects inherent therein. As for those wicked people who hate the Brahmanas and are cast far outside the Veda—how can they shamelessly prattle about the merits and defects of the Veda?
Furthermore, since the permanence and omnipresence of sound are established by auditory recognition, who could possibly determine its opposite?
Therefore, the oneness [of the self] at all times and in all places is established by direct perception and recognition; that [oneness] sublates this [notion of difference].

If it is argued that there is recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) even though flames and the like are momentary, we say no; for in that case, what is recognized is the universal (*sāmānya*), which for us is indeed eternal. As for the cognition of difference (*bhedabuddhi*) regarding any particular aspect due to some limiting condition (*upādhi*), there is no recognition there, as it has been determined by that very cognition of difference.

The cognitions of the individual instances of the word "cow" (go-śabda), though distinct by virtue of differences in place, time, and so forth, all have a common object; they do not have various objects as their domain. [Thesis: All [cognitions] arising as "cow" have a common object, because they arise as "cow," just like a cognition presently arisen. Or: This word "cow" was manifested by yesterday’s cognition of the word "cow," because it has the word "cow" as its object, just like that which is produced today. Or: This [present cognition] knows that [same word], because it has that as its cause, just like the previous cognition. Or: Both [cognitions] must have one and the same object, because they are cognitions of one [thing], just like a single cognition. Or: All cognitions of "cowness" (gotva), though distinct by place, time, and so forth, must be produced by a single word "cow," because they are cognitions of a cow, just like a single cognition. Or: The word "cow" uttered yesterday exists even today, because it is accessible through the cognition of the word "cow," just like the sound uttered today. Or: The word being heard today as "cow" was heard by me yesterday, for the very reason stated above, just like the sound uttered yesterday. Or: Whatever expressive word is stable, it endures for a long time, because it functions as a cognition of an object dependent upon the experience of a relationship [between word and meaning]; whatever is such is seen to be stable, like the universal aspect of smoke. But what is unstable does not cause comprehension by depending on the knowledge of a relationship, because it serves as a cause only for that moment, like the light of a lamp or lightning. Therefore, the position that words are non-eternal is contradicted by all these firm, established inferences; thus, words are established as eternal.

If the oneness of jars and other such things is [the object of your argument], then since that is already accepted by us regarding the universal (*jāti*), you are proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). If, however, you intend this line of reasoning to establish the oneness of individual instances (*vyakti*), then it must be stated that this contradicts what is observed, for the distinction between individuals is well-ascertained through all means of valid cognition, beginning with direct perception.

If the relationship were artificial, it would cease upon the cessation of its usage; because it would be restricted to that single individual instance, it could not be universal. Due to the confusion with other earthy substances, existence, and the possession of a tail, there could be no certain determination of "cowness" (gotva) without an abundance of usage. Therefore, the word is non-artificial and never perishes, because of its eternal relationship with an eternal [object], like space or an atom.

The word "cow" (go), when heard once, has as its object many universals present before it; it does not immediately attain the capacity to denote its own specific meaning [the universal *gotva*] in abstraction. Through repeated hearings, this word—excluding qualities such as being a living being, actions such as whiteness or moving, and properties such as having a dewlap or a tail, as well as individuals like the brindled cow (*śāvaleyādi*) or the hornless one (*khaṇḍādi*), each based on their own specific causes—eventually attains the status of denoting the abstracted universal *gotva*.

Who could destroy this [sound], which remains stable for such a duration, later on? Its destruction cannot be further imagined through any other cause, as is the case with jars and the like, which are understood to perish due to being cut by weapons or through decay; no such cause exists for sound.

Furthermore, although there is a difference in place, time, and speakers, the phoneme *ga* and others do not possess that difference, because the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of it therein is perfectly clear.
For even when there is a difference such as rapidity and so forth, another distinct individual cow is not clearly perceived as being produced, separated from other individual cows.

The letter *ga* does not exist as an absolutely distinct substratum of the universal *gatva*, because it cannot be defined by a cognition other than that of the individual *ga*, just like the *gatva* postulated by others.
Moreover, this [sound] is to be proven as being a color (varṇa), just like the letter *kha* and so forth; and since no counter-example is observed, nothing seen here can serve to refute it.

Just as the nature of the phoneme, its eternity, and so forth, are accepted by both parties even though they are imagined, so too should they be admitted for that which is established [as real]. Therefore, due to the oneness of the phoneme, a single cognition arises; yet the existence of distinct cognitions occurs because of the difference in the manifesting agents.

Surely, for one to whom both [the sound and its quality] are audible, there would be two distinct cognitions; but since, according to you, they are beyond the senses, how can there be a cognition of their specific differences through the sounds?
When a word is perceived by the auditory organ as refined by the *nāda*, some declare that its cognition occurs through contact with that [refinement].

Or rather, there is no apprehension of those [qualities] in the sound; yet, cognition of them arises by virtue of that [sound], and through the imitation of the mental impressions (saṃskāra), magnitude and so forth are also perceived.

Just as those whose minds are deluded by the disorder of bile perceive sweetness as bitter and white as yellow, so do they grasp objects erroneously; just as those running at great speed or traveling in a boat perceive mountains and other things as moving due to their own motion; and just as those whose eyes are smeared with frog-fat perceive bamboo joints as snakes—perceiving the generality and its substratum through the smallness or largeness of the individual instances even without grasping the specific cause—so too, without perceiving that which resides in the manifestor, there will be an error regarding the manifested.

However, a distinction such as shortness and so forth in the letter itself contradicts its eternity and other such qualities. How can that which exists eternally be inherently measured by a specific duration? Therefore, it is the utterance of it that should be understood as having a duration of one *mātrā*, or two *mātrās*, or three *mātrās*; the phoneme (*varṇa*) is not itself measured by a *mātrā*.

Indeed, the manifestation of sound through articulated noises (nāda) is not tenable; for such manifestation would have to occur either through the refinement of the sound itself, the sense organ, or both. In that case, if the sound were being refined, it would be perceived by everyone. For there can be no partial refinement of that which is partless and all-pervading.
Nor can there be a restriction of refinement based on a difference in substratum, because sound is without a substratum, just like space, the self, and so forth.
Moreover, if space were the substratum, then since it is partless, there could be no refinement of its specific locations, even though sound reaches every part of it.
For it is not possible to perceive in its entirety that which is established throughout the whole of space as being refined by only a single part.

Moreover, on the view that the auditory organ is space, because of its omnipresence, there would be an equal reach [of the organ] to all sounds; thus, it would follow that sounds, even when at a great distance, would be perceived here. Furthermore, in this way, the auditory organ of all living beings would become one; therefore, at the time of hearing by one person, everyone would hear as well.

Furthermore, because it is partless, the region of space cannot be the auditory organ conditioned by merit and demerit (dharma-adharma) for the sake of establishing the two-fold determination [of hearing and not hearing].

Furthermore, the auditory organ, once refined, would perceive all sounds; for the eye opened toward a jar does not fail to perceive a cloth [in its vicinity]. This same consequence must apply even in the case of the recollection of an object, because the mental impression (saṃskāra) exists in the same location [as the sense organ] without distinction.
And its refinement occurs through the introduction of the steady wind and the wind of the atmosphere; when the obscuration is removed, it is perceived in that location, as is observed.

The states of being conditioned and unconditioned are not established by the oneness of the word; and if they were admitted to be a single state, they would either be known by everyone or not known at all.
The faults previously stated for each [of the two views] would apply to both when they are combined; therefore, a manifesting agent (vyañjaka) is not in any way tenable with respect to sound.

The author of the Bhāṣya has explained the subsequent [point]: that the distinction in hearing arises from the refinement of the auditory organ, and this distinction in hearing is established separately for each listener according to the specific state of their respective organs.

Just as a lamp or similar object is held to be the manifestor of a jar or the like, so too sound would be [the manifestor] only through the assistance of the eye, by way of refining the auditory organ.

Nor is there any objection here as to "in what form does the refinement occur," for this is equally applicable even to the case of production; moreover, the capacity [for such refinement] is likewise beyond the reach of the senses.
Since power is eternally to be inferred from its effects, why is it questioned? In that regard, the only proof perceived is the mere fact that [the effect] occurs when that [power] exists.

Therefore, it is by means of this very supersensuous power that these [manifesting causes], acting upon the supersensuous power inherent in the sense organ, flash forth as the causes of manifestation.

However, for those who hold that this sound is perceived by the ear without reaching it, since non-reachability is equal in all cases—including distant or obstructed sounds—then the perception and non-perception of sounds located far and near would be identical; there would be no sequence [of hearing], nor would the occurrence of intensity, faintness, and so forth be possible.

Therefore, let this hypothesis also be examined from the perspective of a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*): "The air within the body, struck by effort, moves out—of this there is no doubt. It conforms to the conjunctions and disjunctions of the palate and other [articulatory organs]. And because it possesses velocity, it necessarily persists as long as that velocity lasts. From its movement, conjunctions and disjunctions with its own constituent parts and with the stagnant air inevitably arise. Having reached the space of the ear, it imparts a capacity to the auditory organ (*śrotra*) in degrees. Since the cognition of sound occurs only when that [capacity] exists, an imperceptible refinement (*saṃskāra*) is postulated. Like the power of production (*utpatti-śakti*), that too is nothing more than what we already accept. In the same way, its specific variation would also arise from the perception of the specific [sound].

Even the obstruction by walls and such is possible for the wind (mātariśvan), as is its impact upon the location of the auditory organ, because it proceeds with intense velocity. Furthermore, because that [wind] possesses a gradual progression and a nature of waning speed and intensity, it serves as the cause for the sequence, sharpness, and dullness of the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*).

We do not necessarily accept that the auditory organ is space (*ākāśa*), nor is space partless, because that has been refuted by the Jainas and the Sāṅkhyas. Therefore, the auditory organ—whether it be a specific portion of space or a distinct entity—is established in each individual person as something known through the presumption (*arthāpatti*) based on its effects.
Although [the auditory organ] is all-pervading and unitary, nevertheless, it is only that person whose substratum is refined by sound who perceives the word.

Furthermore, even if there were a refinement of the sense organ, that [refinement] would occur only in the location of its physical basis; therefore, the ear whose concha has not been refined will not hear the sound.

Since the sound has not reached the location of the ear, there is no refinement of the auditory organ; therefore, the restriction of refinement is established by means of the distinction between the physical bases [of the various sense organs].
Indeed, for one who maintains that there is only a single sense-organ, an organ that has received refinement upon a single substratum would have to be the cognizer in all bodies.

The arising of cognition is held to occur within specific regions of the bodies of men; therefore, because of this spatial separation from the primary cause, the refinement of the auditory organ is deficient.

Furthermore, although our self is partless and perceives everything in its entirety, there is no fault in saying that it experiences [sensations] only within the body. It is for this very reason that the distribution of deafness and other such conditions occurs: that very same body, being governed by one's own merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), is not an object of experience for another. Just as a person, while remaining in that very place, does not receive enjoyment if he has been deposed from his lordship, so too a deaf person does not hear when others are hearing.
Furthermore, the parts of the names that serve as the substrata for the auditory organ and the sounds do not themselves exist in a single location; nevertheless, this [theory] is not defective.
For the manifesting breaths possess distinct constituent parts and locations, as well as differences in their genus; by that very fact, the refinement (saṃskāra) is established as distinct.
Just as the wind, impelled for one purpose, does not perform another, so too that which is capable of producing the impression (*saṃskāra*) of one phoneme will not produce another.
Just as one phoneme is not produced by other articulations such as those of the palate and so forth, likewise, the projection of one sound is not caused by the currents of another sound.

Therefore, since both production and manifestation are established through the presumption of an effect, there would be an equal difference in capacity everywhere, whether in the case of effort or the desire to speak.

Alternatively, the notion that the ear consists of the quarters (diś) should be formulated in accordance with the Veda; for nowhere in the Veda is the ear said to consist of ether (ākāśa) or the like. Indeed, the statement "the quarters are the ear" is made in reference to the [cosmic] dissolutions; and that is a declaration of its merging into its primary cause (prakṛti), just as in the case of the eye and other organs.
"Just as the eye of this [person] should cause the sun to go to the Bherukata [region], so too the ear, whose nature is light and whose essence is space, consists of the knowledge of that [light]."
Space is one and all-pervading, established as far as the sky extends; when delimited by the cavity of the ear, it becomes the sense of hearing, like a portion of space.
Whatever logic Kaṇabhuj employs in conceiving of space as having parts is equally applicable to the quarters of space; however, it is the scripture that provides the distinction.

Therefore, that portion of the substance of space which is governed by merit and demerit, delimited by the cavity of the ear, is the auditory organ (*śrotra*), and it is this that is refined (*saṃskriyate*). Even if the refinement pertained to the object, then only a single person would perceive it; however, due to the difference in the capacities of men, it is not perceived by everyone.

Just as this [sound], even while being produced, is not perceived by all [hearers] due to the distinctions of direction, place, and so forth—despite its existence in relation to everyone—in the same way, the sound is heard only by that person whose auditory organ is refined by the sounds located near him, and by no means by those situated at a distance. Since the production of sound has been refuted, it is concluded from the impossibility of any other explanation that there arises a specific refinement [of the auditory organ] from the manifesting sounds (*dhvani*).

And here, the state of being manifested by that [object] is what makes known the existence of the power; this is accepted as being like the power of hearing, for the intellect is indeed withdrawn there.
But in the case of two [successive] impressions (*saṃskāra*), that pair of faults is indeed futile; for due to the deficiency of either one of them, the sound would not be perceived by all [hearers].
Just as the single sun is perceived as having many forms simultaneously in water and other media, yet there is no actual division in it, so too should sound be understood.

Because it is dependent upon the manifesting sounds (*dhvani*), the word-sound is perceived only in their location. And those sounds do not have the capacity to pervade the sky without interruption; therefore, because they are separated by intervals, the [word-sound] is not perceived everywhere. Since the sounds occupy different locations, the hearing is restricted to them. Because the intervening spaces are not filled, a sense of separation is perceived. Furthermore, because those sounds occupy only a small portion of space, there arises the notion that the word-sound itself is non-omnipresent. Due to their movement and velocity, from whichever direction those sounds come, the hearer perceives the word-sound as if it were coming from that very direction.
He asked: "By what cause are distinct reflections perceived simultaneously, one for each individual vessel?"

To this we reply: when the visual light, being turned back by the solar radiance shimmering in the water, reaches its own [original] location, it perceives the sun as manifold; since its form is divided according to the vessels, how then can there be any actual multiplicity in it?
Just as when the eye is slightly closed by a finger, even a single object is perceived as distinct due to the differentiation of the visual function, so it is for us.

But others, seeking to establish the arising of a reflection (*pratibimba*), raise this objection: "If it is that very [face] which is perceived, why is it not seen above? Why is it not seen below in wells and the like, apart from a reflection? And how could one facing east, while looking at a mirror, become one facing west?"

For those who see the sun in water, the eye functions in two ways: one part directed upwards and the other downwards. There, because the upward ray is not in a straight line with the physical locus [of the eye], the self does not reach the sun directly; rather, it perceives the sun as it is presented through a continuous series by means of a downward movement. Because of the identity [of the visual organ] between that upward movement and the downward one, it conceives of the upward function as if it were downward. Thus, the sun is perceived as being right below, even though there is an intervening space.
Thus, through the function of the outward-turned mind, one who perceives the face presented by the inward-turned function understands it to be "inward" due to delusion.
Or, even though the reflection exists in many locations, its multiplicity does not exist at all, because it is apprehended by a single uniform cognition.
The claim that [the object] is differentiated by difference of location is inferential; however, the perception "that very same [object]" is the sublater of that [inference].

Just as Devadatta, though moving through different locations one after another, does not become divided, so too the word-sound is not divided. And just as a single entity, once its unity is known, is seen again and again without being divided by the difference in time, so too the word-sound is not divided by difference of location.

If you argue that there is no contradiction because of the difference in perspective (paryāya), then let it be seen that this is also due to its pervasiveness (vyāpitva); for whatever property is observed to be established is accepted by all.

Just as there is a cognition of "largeness" in the sky when the mud is large, or a cognition of "smallness" when it is small, so too is the cognition regarding that which is absolutely uncreated. Therefore, it is only here—in the application of words based on external adjuncts—that there is a delusion of cognition. Indeed, grossness and subtlety are not perceived as residing in the word itself. The conceptualization of largeness and smallness is actually the intensity or dullness of the cognition; and this [cognition] occurs just like a cloth: it is intense when illuminated by a great light, and dull when illuminated by a faint light, even in the case of an object such as a jar. Thus it is established that all properties such as length and so forth are attributes of the sound (dhvani).
A word does not become expressive of its meaning through a relationship with an unseen purpose; for if it were so, then every previously unknown word would likewise manifest its own meaning.

Furthermore, the perception of a relationship is not possible for that which is impermanent; if the establishment of knowledge of a relationship is to occur, there must certainly be persistence over a period of time.
When a relationship has been known with one thing, another cannot be the communicator; for when the relationship has been known with the word "cow," the word "horse" is not its denoter.
Furthermore, if some other [entity] were by its very nature the awakener, then in the absence of a causal basis, there could be no certainty as to what that entity is.
Since the conventional usage "this is a cognition" is established, such [a usage] might indeed apply to listeners; however, it is not tenable for speakers.
Without knowing it, how could he intend to utter that sound at the very beginning? If he knows it, then it must necessarily have been apprehended by him previously.
Fire is illuminating even though it is new, because it is subordinate to direct perception; and because its similarity is not perceived, it is non-expressive even by way of that [perception].

And on the basis of similarity to which single [word] could another be postulated as its denoter, when there is equality with the preceding words due to their having no observed connection [with the meaning]? If it is argued that the preceding word was seen to possess the meaning, how can it have such a long duration? For a word is not recognized as possessing a meaning if it has not been perceived two or three times.
At that time, it is meaningless for those who do not understand other words; yet it is a marvel that the very same word becomes meaningful for those who hear other words.

First of all, it is not possible to establish a relationship [between a word and its meaning] without uttering the word; nor is there any purpose in a relationship for that which has perished as soon as it was uttered. Therefore, because it has perished before the relationship could be established, the former [word] is useless; how, then, could the latter be understood as having a meaning when no relationship has been formed?

Who could ever perform at once anywhere those actions pertaining to the utterance of sounds, the establishment of linguistic conventions, and worldly transactions, since they are by nature sequential?

Because men separated by place, time, and other factors do not hear other words [used for the same object], not even a single word with an artificial (conventional) relationship can be established beforehand. Even when its relationship is being explained, the same objection applies: for it is impossible to explain [the relationship] regarding things that are destroyed, non-existent, or present [only at the moment of utterance].

Which word is meaningful? Let it be stated whether it is the word heard by the listener or the one uttered by the speaker. Since the word previously heard [by the listener] cannot be uttered [by the speaker], he does not speak a meaningful word; rather, he would utter something similar. Yet a word similar to a meaningful one is not possible for the listener in that context. Because there is no apprehension of a meaningful word, that [similar word] is not itself meaningful. This same consequence would apply when the speaker becomes a listener.

Therefore, the relationship between word and meaning must be accepted as indeed eternal; it is not logical for it to be conventional, because that is impossible in every respect. There is no inherent capacity between the signified and the signifier of one another; if there were comprehension for people through convention, it would be like a wink of the eye.

Is the convention (samaya) made for each individual person, or for each utterance, or was it made once at the beginning of the world by some single being? Furthermore, would the relationship [between word and meaning] be distinct for each instance, or would it be one? If it were one, it could not be something produced; if it were distinct, there would be a cognition of difference.

Because of the difference between the cognitions of the speaker and the listener, linguistic usage becomes impaired; for the relationship [of the word] in the mind of the speaker is one thing, while it is another in the mind of the listener.

Regarding the relationship between the speaker and the listener, what [relationship] can the speaker establish? For that which was previously perceived by him, he does not produce for the listener; and that which he produces as something new has never been perceived before as a means of communication. If it is argued that this is the same even in the case of a jar and other objects, we say no, because the universal (*sāmānya*) is well-established. Although an individual whose capacity is already known cannot be produced [anew], that which is produced has its capacity for the effect not yet determined. Nevertheless, the capacity for utterance and so forth is established through the form (*ākṛti*); and since that form has no beginning, the relationship [of the word to its meaning] is likewise without beginning. If you also admit that the universal of that [form] is eternal, then our own position is proven; however, there is no possibility of a dual nature [both eternal and non-eternal]. Indeed, the relationship is simply the capacity (*śakti*), and no difference in this capacity is perceived. Since it is inferred from its effects, it conforms to the differences in those effects. Furthermore, the existence of the capacity is postulated because it cannot be explained otherwise; and when the purpose is accomplished by one alone, the postulation of many is not desired.

And at the time when the relationship is being explained, when a word such as "cow" is uttered, some understand the object through their cognition of the relationship, while others do not. In that case, if the relationship did not exist, no one would apprehend the object; yet if it did exist, there would be universal understanding, which is not the case because it is not grasped by everyone.
For a relation, being a signifier, requires knowledge of its own nature; therefore, even though it exists, it does not manifest [its object] if it is not itself apprehended.

Furthermore, it is observed that an existing object is sometimes not apprehended; however, the existence of something absolutely non-existent is not established for anyone. Existence and non-existence are contradictory states and cannot coexist in a single entity. Nor is there an equal degree of contradiction between being known and being unknown; for knowledge resides in a person, and due to the difference between persons, there is no contradiction. Moreover, the knowledge residing in one person is not negated by the lack of knowledge in another person.
A white object situated near the blind is not perceived by those who are blind; yet it is perceived by others. Thus, its existence or non-existence does not depend upon them.

However, there is no contradiction therein due to the distinction between the capacity and incapacity of men; for indeed, in this case, there is no cause for the perception [of difference] other than the connection [itself].

In this very same way, the perception of conventional usage through the sense faculties is identical for all; those who possess it understand the object from that [perception], while others do not, like the blind.

For all those who lack direct knowledge [of the relationship], the relationship is established through the well-known status of each preceding member; thus, there is no such thing as a beginningless relationship.

The production [of words] through repeated utterance is not tenable from the perspective of worldly convention (*vyavahāra*). At the beginning of creation, there is no such action, for such a time is not admitted [by us]. Indeed, the entire world is held to have never been otherwise than it is now. Furthermore, a so-called "great dissolution" (*mahāpralaya*) is not known to exist in an ultimate sense (*pāramārthika*). What is called "dissolution" is actually night, because all activities are withdrawn; and what is termed "creation" is day, because all exertions are set forth. Alternatively, dissolution may take the form of the destruction of a region or the destruction of a lineage. However, we possess no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for a dissolution that consists in the total annihilation of everything.

Nor is there anyone—be it Īśvara or another—who possesses unimpaired memory, is eternal, and is capable of performing creation and dissolution, such that he could establish a relationship [between words and their meanings].
Surely, because the sequence is impermanent, the expressive word would be impermanent; for it is accepted that the word is the expressive unit, and the cognition of it depends upon that sequence.

Because they are omnipresent, phonemes do not possess an inherent sequential occurrence. Since sequence is an effect produced by impermanent sounds, it must therefore be perishable. Furthermore, its dependence on a person would arise from the force of that person’s intention to speak; consequently, the permanence of phonemes you maintain would be rendered fruitless.

Furthermore, phonemes are not known to be expressive when devoid of sequence; thus, it follows that the word-status belongs to the sequence itself. However, for those for whom the word is something over and above the phonemes and is devoid of sequence, this postulation of the eternity of sound serves as the basis for its meaningfulness.
First of all, it does not follow for us that the sequential order (ānupūrvi) is a word; for this [order] is not observed to be an illuminator when it has another entity as its substratum.
This [cognition] is merely a property (dharma) of those [phonemes]; no separate entity is admitted. In this way, the phonemes, as they are perceived, would be the conveyors of meaning.

Furthermore, the sequence is not something produced, because it is adopted from what was previously established; for no speaker adopts a sequence independently. Just as it has been uttered by others, so does he intend to speak it. Since another person likewise [adopts it], its beginninglessness is like that of the relationship [between word and meaning].
Therefore, this permanence may exist conventionally even though there is no immutability; for we must diligently refute the independence of persons with respect to each successive [moment]. (2288)

Even for the phonemes, this will not be established even if they lack immutability; for while the phonemes exist eternally, the emergence of their sequence arises from linguistic usage. Just as the construction of jars and other objects occurs despite the eternity of atoms, for in the absence of those [eternal constituents], the construction would be rootless and could not be perceived.
If your intention is certainly such that you say "I speak what has been said by another," then the consequence is the [absurd] permanence [of speech]; and you have no other defining characteristic.

Just as the characterization of conventional usage for jars and the like is established by way of their genus (*jāti*), so too will it be established for sequential order (*ānupūrvī*) and the rest by means of their genus.

The universals (jāti) of the palate and other articulatory organs are established in all persons; the speaker, having characterized those [articulations] by means of them, emits the sounds. And their distinct universals are the causes for the manifestation of words; they operate as many as there are phonemes, or else the individual instances (vyakti) associated with them do so.

In that regard, the sequential order of the sounds would be preceded by the sequence of conjunctions and disjunctions of the palate and other articulators; and both [the sounds and the universal] would be eternal by virtue of their respective universals (*jāti*).

Just as the parts of actions such as revolving are characterized by universals (jāti) and so forth, so too would there be a sequential continuity belonging to the palate, the sounds, and the phonemes.

Or rather, it is precisely because of the subtlety of individual instances that the properties of the genus are determined; and by virtue of that, even though the phonemes are all-pervasive, they are perceived in a sequential order.
Thus, by following all the qualities of the sound (dhvani) which are established as eternal, the phonemes (varṇas), while conforming to them, become the means for the cognition of different meanings.
The sequential order of phonemes, as well as those which are short, long, and protracted, are known to be divisions of time conditioned by sound.

Time is one, all-pervading, and eternal; though it is undivided, it is perceived as divided. Like a phoneme, it is manifested by something in some particular object. Its status as a factor for communication occurs when it is manifested within phonemes; however, because its essential nature exists elsewhere as well, it is eternal.
Therefore, there exists no such perishable property belonging to a word; thus, for those who maintain the eternity of phonemes, the word is established as eternal.

Even in the case of another's dharma, it is stated to be a constituent part, like the speed of a horse and so forth; and regarding its eternality, there is the validity of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) for all [the Vedas].

Furthermore, there is a contradiction with one's own words and so forth in the proof of the non-eternality of sound. Every thesis (*pratijñā*) is uttered for the purpose of communicating the meaning to be proven (*sādhyārtha*). And it has been established that this [thesis] does not express its own meaning as something non-eternal; therefore, because the eternality is understood through the cognition of the meaning, there is no sublation by the [thesis] itself.

And it must be stated: what is this sound that is being proved to be perishable? Is it composed of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), or is it material (*paudgala*), or is it a quality of space (*ākāśa*)? Or is it something other than the phonemes (*varṇa*), consisting of resonance (*nāda*), or having the nature of air (*vāyu*), or being inexpressible? Or is it the *sphoṭa* consisting of words and sentences, or the similarity [of sounds], or the exclusion of others? Let these things be impermanent; for us, there is no permanence in them. [Otherwise,] there would be the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣatva*) or a reason whose locus is unestablished (*āśrayāsiddhahetutā*).

Now, if our desired position were correct, then for you this pair [of "sound" and "sound-ness"] would be merely sound itself; or else, if it were said that they are merely the word, then in that case, sound-ness would likewise be merely sound. And since that is impermanent, it contradicts the fact that for everyone, it is accepted as eternal. For whatever universal exists here, it is conceived by everyone as eternal.

If impermanence is said to be absolute perishability, then for us [the Mīmāṃsakas], the thesis would have an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇa*). If, however, you accept some kind of designation as "impermanent" even from the state of non-manifestation, we reply that this is indeed accepted by us, for that very nature is held to be manifest.
And when the reason is here conceived as being based solely on the sense faculties, a deviation [of the reason] is now perceived through the example of "genus" (jāti).

Just as when the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) is unestablished for the opponent, no logical reason (*hetu*) is obtained, so it is likewise with positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
In that case, even if the "reductio ad absurdum" (jāti) were unestablished for the proponent of the proof, it would nonetheless remain a non-reason so long as it has not been refuted.

An investigation must be carried out as to what kind of entity [the universal] is, given that it is perceived by the senses; this investigation is clear regarding whether it is non-different from or different from the individuals, and whether it is manifold or not. In that regard, the faults of being uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*), unestablished (*asiddha*), lacking a probandum (*sādhyahīna*), or lacking a similar instance (*sapakṣatā*)—along with other defects—should be stated according to the alternatives proposed and in consideration of the proponent.

"Knowledge following immediately after an effort is the proof for being produced and impermanent; yet even there, there is an inconclusiveness (anaikāntika) because of the three—cessation through deliberation (pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha), cessation not through deliberation (apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha), and space—which are distinct from momentary things. For the cognition of 'cessation through deliberation' refers to destruction preceded by intelligence, while their cessation not through deliberation is that which is not preceded by intelligence. And both of these two, because they are indestructible, are held to be unproduced."

They say that destruction is established by its own nature (*svabhāva*) and is without cause. For from wood, through contact with fire, there arises a series of embers; yet destruction is inherent, residing in the mere fact of birth. It is subtle and unperceived because it occurs within a homogeneous continuum. When a heterogeneous cause falls upon that homogeneous continuum, it is then manifested as a gross [destruction] by means of a heterogeneous effect. Since a heterogeneous continuum is produced from that cause, destruction is clearly manifested even though it was not being produced [by anything else].
It follows immediately after such efforts as the striking with a hammer; therefore, since it is seen to be uncreated, the [proposed] reason would be inconclusive.

Even space (*ākāśa*), though eternal, is manifested when it is covered by earth and water through their removal by means of digging, sprinkling, cutting, and so forth. Since cognition is observed to occur there as well immediately following effort, the reason you stated—that its manifestation [proves its eternity]—is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Even the alternative [view] regarding the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) here results in the fallacy of the probandum being absent from the meaning of the scripture. Even in the view that the individual is what is indicated (*lakṣya*), there is the conceptualization of it as either different or non-different from the universal (*jāti*). If it were different, the locus (*dharmin*) would not be established; if it were non-different, it would not be established for others [who do not accept such identity]. Furthermore, even though it is without distinction, for me that entity is neither non-eternal nor eternal. For its part called the "universal" is considered eternal, while the other is perishable. Indeed, it has been previously demonstrated that a single entity possesses a variegated form.

If impermanence is conceptualized in this way, then [the argument] suffers from the fallacy of proving what is already established (*sādhyahīnatā*). But if it refers to something other than that, then the fault lies with you; such is the direction of the refutation.

Even if the eternality of the relationship between words and their referents has been established, the Veda’s status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with respect to the meaning of sentences is not at all proven here. For the understanding [of the Veda] arises from human convention, just like the notions of *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, and so forth; even though the meaning is without a [Vedic] basis, it has been arbitrarily constructed by ritualists (*yājñika*). Moreover, because it is a composite whole, its human origin is like that of a story; and since there is no trustworthy person [to guarantee it], the Vedas lack the status of a valid means of knowledge.

The eternity of the Vedic sentences must be asserted on the basis of the principle that no [new] relationship can be established [between word and meaning]. While such a notion might possibly apply to words like *vṛddhi* and so forth, because their usage has an observable purpose, this conventional understanding is not tenable in the case of the Veda; for by whom has the supersensuous relationship between heaven, sacrifice, and so forth ever been perceived?

Nor is it devoid of meaning, since the cognition of that meaning arises from it. Such a counter-argument (*pratisādhana*) must be stated regarding its being a composite whole: "All study of the Veda is preceded by the teacher's own study, because it is designated as 'Vedic study,' just like the study performed today. This would apply to the *Bhārata* as well, but it is sublated by the memory of its author; whereas in the case of the Veda, there is no such memory, and any [memory] that exists is based merely on explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).

The past and future times are devoid of a creator of the Vedas, because they are time, just as the present time is observed in the world. It should be understood that Brahmā and others are not the authors of the sciences (vidyās), due to reasons such as their being human beings, just like ordinary or extraordinary men.

Therefore, it is clearly established that the Vedic word is not false; for, being independent in its own meaning, it is like the cognition of a word-meaning from a word. The conviction produced by this [Veda] is valid because it arises from an eternal sentence, just like the cognition arising from the very nature of a sentence itself. The authority of the conviction generated by an injunctive sentence (*codanā*) is established just like the conviction arising from the words of a trustworthy person (*āpta*). For this conviction is not produced by a sentence composed by an untrustworthy person, since there is no contradiction in it even across differences of time, place, and circumstances. Once the Veda is established as both a means of knowledge and authoritative, the assumption of an beginningless succession of pupils and teachers serves to ensure its faultlessness.
Therefore, while the Veda is like light—the eye for all the world—others indeed suffer an obstruction born of unrighteousness (adharma), just like owls.
Therefore, while the Veda is like light—the eye for all the world—others indeed experience an obstruction born of unrighteousness (adharma), just like owls.

All this is merely the manifestation of false pride on the part of the twice-born; it has occurred by chance like the accidental carving of letters by a woodworm, for they possess no sound doctrine whatsoever.

All this is merely the manifestation of false pride on the part of the twice-born; it has occurred by chance like the accidental carving of letters by a wood-boring insect, for they possess not even a single well-spoken word.

For even if the agent is absent, this [cognition] would not attain the status of having a real object, because of the deficiency of its causes and qualities, just like a false cognition when there is an absence of defects.

In the case of human compositions, it is suspected whether qualities exist or do not exist; therefore, [in the case of the Veda] the consequence would be meaninglessness, for we have no suspicion of qualities whatsoever.
Therefore, because there is no reliance on the causes of truth or falsity, and because of the absence of wisdom, compassion, and so forth, that duality does not exist.

Consequently, [the Veda] would result in pointlessness, like sentences such as "six cakes" and so forth; provided that meanings connected with action and factors of action are indeed understood, this comprehension would arise from the narration of human affairs, like the story of Urvaśī and others. Even if it lacks [intrinsic] purpose, for you, its status as a source [of knowledge] follows from its very nature.
Even in the absence of defects, truthfulness is not established because of the existence of something else; for there is also a further category known as "meaninglessness."

Now, if it is argued that the Veda, being inherently established as capable of generating the cognition of true objects, is therefore considered to have true meaning—[we reply: if this were so, then that cognition would occur continuously at all times, because its cause is eternally present, just as it was at the moment intended [for its production]. Or else, at the time of a single cognition, everything produced by it would occur simultaneously, since that which is capable as a cause is the very same as the cognition intended to be produced.

Furthermore, because its power to produce knowledge would be utterly destroyed, this Veda could not be eternal; or else, if that power remains, cognition would arise again [repeatedly]. Moreover, if it were to depend upon auxiliary factors such as explanations and the like, then because those factors exist sequentially, the cognition of it would also be held to be sequential. But this is not so; for what kind of dependence could there be on the part of that which is already capable? If it becomes capable through connection with them, then what room is there for your [alleged] eternality in this case?

If that which was previously incapable is made capable by them once again, then this [knowledge] would be subject to human agency, for it would have man as its basis, being a constituent part of cognition.

Indeed, even while existing, this Veda does not produce knowledge for us so long as it is not illuminated by persons acting as lamps. Therefore, one should not postulate its lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*) as the cause of knowledge regarding an existent object; for this knowledge proceeds from the explanation of men. Thus, even if present, the Veda’s lack of human authorship is useless, since the desired result—knowledge—is dependent upon persons.
If this [consciousness] is always capable, why does it require anything else? For if the single cause is capable, then for you, knowledge would indeed arise from that alone.

In this world, independent persons providing explanations of the Veda according to their own whims cannot be restrained by anyone at all. Therefore, it is suspected that these individuals, corrupted by defects such as delusion and pride, might even provide a contrary interpretation of the Śruti. Furthermore, not a single human being among them is accepted as a seer of supersensuous objects; for knowledge regarding the connection between sacrifices and heaven is certainly not possible without [Vedic] injunction. Since, according to you, there exists no direct seer of supersensuous matters, only he who perceives through the eternal Word (the Veda) truly sees.
The Veda, being devoid of intention, does not always express its meaning by itself; rather, it depends upon the human exposition, which is like a staff for a blind man.
And being drawn by her, he might even fall onto a wrong path; therefore, it is not logical that the Veda, like the eye, should be the means of perception.
Moreover, if it were to produce cognition independently, its validity would clearly not even be possible, because it would depend upon the observation of a person.

For validity is indeed established because [the scripture] is the cause of cognition according to reality; however, if it were dependent upon human interpretation, its status as a means of valid cognition would not be sound.
Thus, when the Veda is not established as authoritative, the lineage of disciples and teachers, even if postulated as beginningless, cannot be considered free from defect.

Since not even a single person among them is considered to possess supersensuous vision, this beginningless tradition is merely a succession of the blind; for a blind man led by a blind man certainly does not find the right path. Nevertheless, its beginningless conceptualization is utterly fruitless.
Furthermore, there is no authoritative evidence for the claim that this meaning was not composed by Manu, Vyāsa, and others who were knowers of the truth of the Vedas from another source.

Or let it be that validity arises merely from a constant connection with a real object; yet no one can ever ascertain that supersensuous conjunction (*yoga*). Since those objects are supersensuous, the conjunction residing within them is likewise supersensuous. Furthermore, all these men are by their very nature always incapable of perceiving what is beyond the senses.
And that scripture does not say, "This is my connection with the meaning"; rather, a connection with the meaning devised by humans does not differ from [ordinary] human composition.
Just as the falsity of a human work is suspected, why should that same suspicion not also apply to what is merely imagined by men?

Therefore, even if the Veda were established as authoritative, this beginningless succession of disciples and teachers, though imagined [as such], has become a "succession of the blind. [Objection: But surely, regarding heaven and the like, a cognition arises from the words concerning the *agnihotra* and other rites that is free from doubt and the like, just like an unshakable perceptual cognition. How could the Veda, by producing such a cognition, fail to possess the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? For no one understands a doubtful meaning from such a statement.

It is not so, because doubt arises [regarding them], just as it does regarding contradictory or irrelevant statements. For discerning people do not perceive any difference between these [Vedic statements] and others. Indeed, the certain determination of existence or non-existence with respect to supersensible matters is not possible [through perception]. If it is argued that certainty comes from Vedic statements, why should it not be obtained from other sources as well?

This unshakable conviction arises among those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) whose intellects are overwhelmed by faith; for others, it is the same as that which arises from other sources. For instance, an unshakable conviction likewise arises among the Buddhists and others regarding the production of suffering in states of woe resulting from sacrifices involving the slaughter of living beings. Furthermore, no sublation of this conviction is observed at present; if it is suspected that such a sublation might occur somewhere or at some time, that suspicion applies equally to the Vedic statements as well.

If the Veda were to reveal its own meaning by itself, independent of conventions dependent upon human will, then it would rightly be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For in that case, even when its innate meaning is being explained otherwise by those whose intellects are afflicted by defects such as delusion and pride, it does not abandon its own nature; because it swiftly produces a cognition directed toward that very object, and it does not illuminate any other meaning intended by persons. However, if there were dependence on human will, it would not differ from a human composition (*pauruṣeya*), for its illumination would then be contingent upon that [will]; and that [will] could even be erroneous.

Furthermore, just as the truthfulness of the non-human [Veda] is accepted as its natural state, why is its falsity not likewise suspected? For its truthfulness indeed arises from its being the cause of the cognition of true meaning by itself; in the same way, its being the cause of the cognition of falsehood is also naturally suspected.

Furthermore, if you are indeed insistent that the Veda is a source of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then let effort be directed toward its having a faultless author and so forth. For this [Veda], being composed by a faultless author and illuminated by faultless commentators, shines forth in this world as a means for knowing things as they truly are.
For indeed, the well-ascertained true words of those endowed with wisdom, compassion, and other virtues—even though they are of human origin—are causes for the knowledge of reality as it is.
It is not the case that something produces knowledge of reality simply because it is not man-made; for forest fires and the like are seen to be causes even of false cognition.
For a red lotus is indeed perceived when there is light from fire; if it is argued that fire and so forth [are the cause] because they are produced, then that reason is not tenable.
Or rather, is the artificiality of objects the basis for false cognition? For if that were so, smoke would not be a correct indicator of fire.
And thus, even though the Veda is not of human origin, it cannot be established as the basis for correct knowledge; therefore, the postulation of its existence is entirely in vain.

Consequently, the demonstration of its being non-human in origin, its manifest eternity, and its eternal connection with word-meanings have been described as entirely futile. Even if that were granted, its status as a cause of knowledge corresponding to reality is not accepted; this has already been explained in detail immediately above. Therefore, we pay no heed to refuting this [position], for who would take the trouble to refute that which is irrelevant to the subject at hand?

For it is the fact that scripture is the cause of knowledge of things as they truly are that is the subject under discussion here; and it has already been established that this is not proven even by the absence of human authorship. Whatever personal assertion is made here, something brief shall be said so that the paths of those with subtle vision may be expanded by it.
Even with the cessation of the means of valid cognition, the object of cognition does not cease, because they do not possess the status of being pervading causes with respect to it.

Although that [creator] is inaccessible through the five means of knowledge, he is nevertheless understood through non-existence alone, just as the author of a Vedic text whose author was unknown is known through the narrative and other such passages.

Although that [creator] is inaccessible through the five means of knowledge, he is nevertheless understood through non-existence alone, just as the author of a Vedic text is inferred from the text itself when the author of a story or similar work is unknown.

The fact that [the Veda] is inaccessible to all beings is, however, always doubtful; for it is even suspected that someone might know it through some means of knowledge. For by whom could it be clearly ascertained that all living beings within the three worlds are entirely incapable of comprehending this [Veda]? Thus, your own [reasoning regarding] inaccessibility is fallacious; for the non-existence [of such knowledge] has not been ascertained by the mental states of other persons.

And those who study the Vedas are considered by direct perception to be their authors; for it is not logical that they should be mere manifesters, since manifestation is impossible for eternal things.

The arising of things that possess a perceivable nature occurs when there is the operation of those [causes]; if they were already present even prior to that, their perception would necessarily follow.

The Veda is determined to be capable of producing those effects, such as linguistic usage and the like, because it exists when they function, just as a seed and so forth exist when a sprout and the like arise.
Because they consist of a sequence of phonemes, like dramas, narratives, and so forth, inference also establishes the human origin of the Vedas.

Otherwise, its nature as a sequence would not exist, because it is eternal and all-pervading. Furthermore, there can be no sequence of manifestation, since manifestation is impossible for that which is eternal.
The validity of scripture, analogy, and presumptive testimony has already been refuted; therefore, it is not appropriate to introduce them here.

The authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatā*) of the Veda is desired for the purpose of removing its lack of authority; and since that [authorlessness] is a real entity (*vastu*), it must indeed be established by means of proofs. This independence of the scripture is asserted because it does not depend on human activity; and that [independence] is either a property residing in the thing itself or the very nature of the thing as such.

Whatever proof is stated for the purpose of establishing the existence of an entity, even when that proof has been refuted, non-existence does not establish itself by its own power. Even when the proof for its existence is absent, there would be no certainty regarding its existence; yet from the mere absence of that proof, there is no certainty regarding the exclusion of its existence. This is because, even upon the cessation of means of valid cognition, the non-existence of the object is not established. Therefore, in both cases, there can be no establishment of the thesis that "it does not exist."
"Because it is formless, like sound"—even when this is stated, the perishability of sound is not established, due to the deviation [of the reason] in the case of pleasure and so forth.
Even if those arguments previously stated by opponents regarding the two ends [of the Veda] are refuted, these proponents of the Veda still fail to achieve their purpose.

If eternity is intended to be established by [the two reasons of] being uncreated and being indestructible, then since these are merely negative in form, they apply equally even to that which is indefinable (nirupākhya). Therefore, just as the eternity of the sky is not real, so too its validity is not established in the case of the Veda either.
Even the negation of being produced and being perishable is not established; since it has been stated that [the reason] is absent in the proof, that permanence is not established.

If permanence is not intended by these two [reasons] which consist of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), then those two, being of the nature of that [excluded] absence, depend upon their own means of proof. Since that permanence which is of the nature of a real entity cannot be established by those two, its establishment does not occur of itself once the two preceding positions have been refuted.
Furthermore, regarding that proof which has been demonstrated as possessing the three well-established characteristics, even your father would never be able to refute it.

For that person who is described in the Veda as "indestructible" (na hi śīryate) is clearly sublated by inference; this has been established in the context of the doctrine of selflessness (*nairātmya*). Furthermore, other things such as birth and so forth, which were also mentioned there, have been proven to be sublated. And that inference, having its logical connection (*pratibandha*) previously demonstrated, is the sublater.
What dull-witted person would consider that [cognition]—which is bound to a real object—to be sublated by a mere trivial word, or by the cognition arising from it?
Why do you not accept that even the cognition arising from the words of a person regarding a supersensible object is equal to direct perception?

Because it is independent of examples, there is an absence of defects due to its non-empirical nature. If it is suspected that even this [scripture] is subject to sublation because it relies on human beings, then such a suspicion does not cease even in the case of the Veda; for its capacity to cause false cognition would be inherent.
Even though this word "immeasurable" conveys its meaning, it cannot be spoken by a virtuous person out of mere malice.
Thus, regarding all things beyond the senses, every word possesses equal strength and weakness; for what reason, then, do you have this exclusive attachment to one alone?
The wise declare that the very principle just described is the reason for the lack of authority of the Vedas; therefore, they may be considered speakers of truth.

It is not at all surprising that the cause of falsehood remains unrecognized by those who have been rendered dull-witted by the constant contemplation of the Vedas born of false attachment; for indeed, no fault whatsoever is perceived in such matters as the marriage of one's mother by those rogues, the Persians and others, who are ever devoted to such customs.
Direct recognition, however, has already been refuted; moreover, because it is an error and involves conceptual construction, there is no certainty regarding permanence on this basis.

Furthermore, the cognition regarding sound is for the most part of a changing nature, as seen in the observation: "This is the utterance of a parrot," and "This is that of a maina. If you claim this is due to a difference in the manifesters (*vyañjaka*), we shall address the refutation of [the theory of] manifestation later. Moreover, by this very logic of yours, all this would become one; consequently, there would be no such thing as a manifester or a manifested object. For when a single entity is indivisible, the conceptualization of difference is contradicted. Furthermore, your distinction between "these words are human-made" and "these are not made by any author" could not even be established, since it depends upon recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
Some [Vedic words] are indeed unitary, because their manifestation occurs in a sequence; they are accepted as non-human (apauruṣeya), being endowed with a fixed order.
Surely this human dharma, consisting of the sequence of manifestors such as the palate and so forth, might therefore sometimes undergo a reversal.

This recognition can indeed occur with respect to phonemes (*varṇa*), even though they are perishable, provided that one considers the universal (*sāmānya*) to be what is recognized—or rather, [one recognizes] them specifically as such. However, in those aspects where a cognition of difference arises, such as in [the variations of] fast, slow, and so forth, there can be no recognition.
But when reasons are employed for the purpose of establishing the oneness of sound, no necessary connection (pratibandha) is established, because they do not contradict anything of a different class.
Even the portion consisting of the generality of smoke is not [the probandum]; thus, it would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

If even [the word] *gādi* were to result in oneness, then the proof of what is already established would apply to the desired [universal] *jāti*; for the exclusion of what is not that nature (*atadrūpaparāvṛtti*) is indeed non-different and merely conceptual. If, however, there were an oneness of individual instances (*vyakti*), there would be inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*), because the difference between phonemes is ascertained through direct perception and other means in each respective application.

The distinction between [cognitions] such as those that are pleasant or unpleasant is established through direct perception; because cognitions occur in succession, their difference is proven, just as in the case of a young girl [perceiving different things]. Indeed, the cognitions of individual instances of the word "cow," though distinguished by place, time, and so forth, do not have a single object, because they appear as distinct, just like the cognitions of taste, color, and other qualities. Furthermore, the appearance of distinctions such as the musical notes *ṣaḍja* and others is determined by direct perception; nor can it be claimed that this is merely due to a manifesting agent (*vyañjaka*).
All these cognitions of the word "cow" occurring yesterday and today do not have a single object, because they arise sequentially, like the cognitions of color, smell, and so forth.
Otherwise, all cognitions would have a single object; furthermore, there would be a contradiction regarding their sequential occurrence, given the presence of a capable cause.
