It has been established previously that, by their very nature, things possess a restriction of power such that they are apprehended as a single unit despite their difference. Furthermore, because of this unified apprehension, [the notions of] the oneness of the word and so forth do not arise; rather, people perceive the frequent usage of a single word. Because the relationship [between word and meaning] resides in multiple individuals, it is logically consistent; therefore, the universal does not become one with the individuals.

In reality, however, no relationship exists between a word and its object, because they are distinct and because [the word] is not produced [from it]; therefore, such a connection is merely superimposed by those who are deluded. For this entire established status of word and object has already been explained in detail; it is entirely subverted because a pervasion [between them] is impossible.
The eternality of "cowness" has been rejected, as has its relation; atoms, space, and so forth have also been cast aside, for they do not serve as reasons or examples [for your position].

Let it be granted that the denotation of an abstracted "cowness" is understood only after a long time, due to its being determined by people under the delusion of its having a single form. However, since in reality it is momentary, it does not remain stable even for that duration; why then is its continued existence even later admitted? Furthermore, it has already been demonstrated that there is no cause for the destruction of even things like jars; so how could such a thing apply to sound?

The subversion of recognition has been established previously: "Due to differences in place, time, and the manifestor, the property [of the sound] varies; through the distinctions of *ṣaḍja*, *ṛṣabha*, *gāndhāra*, *pañcama*, and so forth, the individual manifestation of the *go* (cow/sound) is clearly perceived as distinct through direct perception. However, this establishment of difference based on the difference of the manifestors is not tenable. It will be stated later that there is no such thing as an "individual manifestation" (*vyakti*) in the case of eternal things.

Furthermore, a universal *gatva* is asserted to exist as something distinct from the letter *ga*; since it does not actually exist in usage, the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) is unavoidable.

Even for that which consists of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), there is no common substratum for "g-ness" (*gatva*). If you say, "It is exactly so," it is not thus, because it results in the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*). Since there is an absence of any phoneme *ga* that is excluded from non-*ga*s, of what substrate (*dharmin*) could the property (*dharma*) of being "indeterminable by a cognition other than that of *ga*" belong?

Every valid inference depends upon what is established for both parties; therefore, the example and so forth are included, and thus the example suffers from the non-establishment of its locus (*dharmyasiddhi*).

And all this effort of yours is for the sake of establishing the oneness of the letter *ga*; in that regard, the contradiction by perception (*pratyakṣabādhā*) has been stated by you as being difficult to avoid.

These cognitions of the letter *ga*, whether belonging to yesterday, today, or the present, do not have a single object because they occur sequentially, just like the cognitions of taste, color, and so forth. Therefore, this single letter is not established as existing eternally for both [parties]. Its eternity is merely imagined, being constructed through the exclusion (*apoha*) of what is not that.

At the moment of perceiving the sound, the air-currents situated at the edge of the ear that effect the refinement of the auditory organ are not themselves perceived. When the sound is cognized through the auditory organ refined by the resonance (nāda), the cognition of that [resonance] as being in contact with it is sublated by direct perception.
Just as knowledge directed toward bitter, yellow, and other such forms with respect to sweet and other things would be without an object, so too would the cognition of a word be.

Indeed, no word other than those distinguished by speed, medium, and so forth appears; and since it does not possess that nature, how could the cognition of it as having that nature not be without an object?

Otherwise, the statement that "one knows that very object" is contradictory; for if there is the cognition of a different form, how indeed can that object be said to be known? For if consciousness is formless, then according to you, that external form must certainly exist [within it]; yet since the external is not of the nature of that [consciousness], how can it exist in such a way? Even in the view that consciousness possesses a form, an object is said to be "known" when an appearance arises in the consciousness corresponding to the external form. But here, consciousness does not proceed in accordance with the external; therefore, it is established that the entire mind is devoid of an object and is erroneous.
Furthermore, the existence of a manifestor is not logical, especially in the case of something eternal; therefore, cognitions are not differentiated by the sound (dhvani) according to its refinement.

For just as a lamp restricts its power to the manifestation [of objects] for the purpose of perceiving a jar and so forth by means of the eye, so too does sound [restrict its power] in the ear for the perception of words. If a word is established by nature as being fit for perception by the ear, why is it not perceived even when that ear is unrefined? If it were perceived due to the presence of a suitable cause, then that would indeed occur at the time when a refined ear exists, just as it does for him. If it is not fit for perception, how could it become so later on? And if it were to possess fitness upon arising, the word would have to be something else produced anew. Alternatively, if the subsequent cognition does not arise through the power of that [original word], then its production is described as resulting from the refinement of the hearing organ and other such factors.
In this way, sound would be ungraspable because it is of no use in that regard; for indeed, there is no distinction whatsoever between it and taste and the other [objects of sense].
Or rather, this knowledge—whose nature is the comprehension of words—is produced by those [causes] such as the hearing of refined speech, which do not themselves depend upon words.

That which consists of both the cognition and the object of cognition follows along with that [word]; thus, for you, there would be a persistence of the word even within that cognition. Otherwise, if the cognition were not persistent while it is the word that persists as the object of that cognition, then your position would be subject to a further contradiction. For those two, having the natures of cognition and the object of cognition, are bound together as if by a chain; since they are invariably concomitant, the existence of one entails the existence of the second.
For it is clearly implied that cognition is connected precisely with the knowledge produced by hearing the refined [language], even when there is no refinement of the auditory organ.

If that object of knowledge were not of the nature of sound, like taste and so forth which are not of its nature, then auditory cognition would not have the nature of cognizing it; such being the case, [it would follow that] it is not [auditory].

What indeed is the relationship between cognition and the word, by virtue of which [the former] is held to be of the nature of the understanding of that word? It cannot be identity (*tādātmya*), because they are distinct. Nor can it be origination from that (*tadutpatti*), because the word is not a producer [of the cognition]. If there were such origination, then by necessity that [cognition] would always exist; thus, the cognition having that as its object would either always arise or never arise at all. This being the case, the postulation of an embellishment of the auditory organ (*śrotra-saṃskāra*) is futile.

For if the impression (*saṃskāra*) were merely occasional, then the possibility of cognition would occur only occasionally; thus, the postulation of an impression would be plausible as something "occasional. Furthermore, the impression—characterized as a potentiality—is to be inferred from its effect, which is cognition. Now, if that cognition either always exists or never exists at all, how indeed could it indicate an impression that is itself occasional? Therefore, the subsequent claim that [the cognition] arises from an impression of the auditory organ has not been satisfactorily demonstrated.
If a capacity is imparted to the auditory organ—whether it be non-different from space or from the quarters—then their eternity would be lost due to that production.
Furthermore, because it is not distinct from existence, even that which is conditioned would result in being eternal; consequently, cognition of objects would occur at all times.

If, however, there were a difference [between the sense organ and its power], the relationship expressed as "of that" (tasya) would not be tenable; furthermore, the auditory organ would lack agency because cognition arises from the power.
Just as, despite the commonality of mere non-attainment, there is no apprehension of everything [by a magnet], because the restriction of capacity is established in the case of iron by a magnet.
If there is attraction even there due to reaching the light of the magnet, then indeed that light is not seen; how, then, is it known to exist?

Why does that light not draw toward itself wood and other objects that are in contact with it? If you say it is because its power is restricted [to certain things], then the same would apply even in the case of those things it does not reach.
Objects situated at a distance, in the middle, or nearby are perceived simultaneously; for immediately following the application [of the sense organ], cognition arises for all of them.

Just as a form is perceived clearly or unclearly according to distinctions such as distance and proximity, so too in the case of sound, there would be the perception of intensity, dullness, and so forth.

If cognitions that appear as distinct have a single object, how is this objection not equally applicable to those who maintain the existence of external objects, namely, that the cognitions of forms [also] possess a single object?

But according to the view that [the auditory organ] grasps what has reached it, there would be no cognition of the sound as being "uninterrupted" in the case of the sound of thunderclouds and the like, just as in the case of the inner part of the ear.

Because it produces cognition of that [object] even when separated from it, the ear must be non-contacting (aprāpyakārin), just like the mind; otherwise, it would be like the skin and other sense organs.

For those who assert that the mind, too, functions by reaching its object, it is not logical for them to maintain that consciousness perceives an object situated at a distance of even a moment’s duration.

As for the argument that being an external sense organ and so forth proves the quality of reaching the object (*prāpyakāritva*), that is inconclusive because it is contradicted by its opposition to things of a different class possessing different properties.

Since [the atoms] were previously separated and distinct from conjunction and disjunction, and because air is non-momentary, it is not logical that they are non-distinct. For this very reason, due to the lack of any distinguishing feature, motion is not possible for it; and because of the absence of momentum, it does not continue to abide as long as the momentum lasts.

If [the sound], having reached the space of the ear, produces a sensation in the auditory organ, then why does that [sensation] not occur in the cognition of the sound, just as it does from the stroke of a whip? To say that "the attention to the sound obstructs the sensation" is incorrect; for one who knows the difference between the stroke of a whip and the wind, the sensation occurs in both cases alike.

The claim that there is an illusion of simultaneity despite the existence of a sequence due to rapidity is of no consequence at all, because in this case, the wind is not perceived in any way whatsoever.
Furthermore, even if air is described as being beyond the senses, as by the followers of Kaṇāda, then for you as well, how could there be the attainment of touch (*spraṣṭavya*) therein?

(2534) Or, let air be beyond the senses; nevertheless, for that which is conjoined with various [objects], its touchable quality—whether hot, cold, or otherwise—would be perceived, just like color (*vidanyavat*).

Furthermore, if it is argued that there is no cognition because of the lack of contact with the ear-cavity, then how can it be understood that the sound has not reached the space within the ear? Therefore, this conception based on the view of the Vedic ritualists is groundless; it does not lead to the satisfaction of the wise, and thus it shines only among the ritualists themselves.
Against those who assert that space is partless, the faults previously stated should be understood as equally applicable even if the auditory organ were a single, partless direction.

In the view that space (*ākāśa*) is a single, all-pervading entity, spatial division cannot be postulated; for that space is indeed one and the same, being the substratum of the conditioned [auditory organ] and nothing else. The auditory organ (*śrotra*), whose nature is the single ether, does not exist as something unconditioned by the ear-cavity (*śaṣkuli*). Therefore, the restriction of its conditioning is established through the difference in its physical bases (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Consequently, it must be accepted that the sense organ, having received its conditioning in a single base, is the cognizer in all locations where consciousness arises. It must be accepted that consciousness arises within the bodily regions of persons. However, because space is one, there is no separation of primary locations for you. Furthermore, even though our self (*ātman*) is partless and perceives everything in its entirety, it is still said to "grasp" [objects] only within the body; even when stated thus, this position is flawed. By this very reason, the lack of a fixed order regarding deafness and so forth is explained: it is not logical that the same thing should be incapable of being experienced by another person, since there would be no distinction [between them].

For if its original form is not abandoned and no specific modification arises, how indeed could your auditory organ (*śrotra*) not be an object of experience for another? Since it is eternal and independent, the auditory organ, being the ether (*nabhas*), would necessarily be an object of experience for everyone at all times. Indeed, the ether can never be assisted by merit (*dharma*) or demerit (*adharma*); and since it lacks the status of an effect due to its eternity, what kind of subjugation (*vaśīkriyā*) could there be of it?

Furthermore, how could that which is to be experienced become [new] again through the power of mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth? For, being eternal, it does not attain any distinction from them.

If, even though the substratum is impermanent, there is no momentary impermanence [of its qualities], then deafness and so forth would not be possible, because it would be impossible for those qualities to produce excellence within that substrate.

Or let there be some excellence (atiśaya) in that [organ]; however, such an excellence does not exist in space (vyoman). Nor can it arise through a connection with a substratum (adhiṣṭhāna), because space is eternal and independent. Therefore, deafness and the like cannot be attributed to space even by means of that [organ]. Even if space were composed of parts, this same argument would apply equally to its eternality.

In that very case, it is not logical for there to be a removal of your ownership as well, provided that even for him [the self], momentariness does not exist. For what excellence has arisen in him subsequently, by virtue of which he is deprived of ownership and would no longer obtain enjoyment?

And when such an embellishment (*saṃskṛti*) is not applicable to either the auditory organ or the sound—due to the impossibility of an embellishment through the conceptual alternatives of difference or non-difference—then: If the embellishment were distinct [from them], the auditory organ and the sound would not be embellished; nor would there be any connection whatsoever between the embellishment and those two. For a connection with a distinct entity can only be the relation of cause and effect. And in that case, this [connection] would exist at all times, because the cause would always be present. Even in the view that it is not a different object, that [embellishment] would likewise be eternal. Therefore, it cannot be produced, and consequently, it follows that cognition would be eternal. Thus, a restriction of the capacity of the wind and so forth is not tenable, because capacity itself is impossible when there is no object to be produced.

Therefore, since manifestation is impossible, this cognition of sound is the result [of its production], just like the cognition manifesting a jar or similar objects, which is invariably concomitant with the arising of the object to be grasped. Consequently, based on the presumption of an effect (*kāryārthāpatti*), there would be an equal difference in capacity everywhere between the two cases of effort and the desire to speak, regarding both production and manifestation.

Whatever logic Kaṇabhuj (Kaṇāda) employs to refute [the existence of] a portion of space should be understood by the wise to apply equally to a portion of direction as well. Furthermore, if the impression were upon the object, then only that single object would be impressed; since there is no restriction of capacity due to the object's non-existence [at the time of cognition], there can be no impression of the object.

If it were incapable of producing cognition, this word would never be perceived by anyone anywhere, because it would be of no use for that cognition. But if it possesses the capacity to produce cognition, then this word would always be perceived by everyone everywhere, since it stands as the cause of cognition.
For whether it be capable or incapable, that [nature] resides within itself by its very essence; what opposing or even auxiliary factor would be able to destroy its purpose?

Furthermore, this [sound] is capable of producing cognition only for certain individuals; therefore, while it is being produced, it is not perceived by everyone. Alternatively, if its refinement (*saṃskṛti*) occurs through sounds situated near it, then the word-sound is heard only by those very people, and certainly not by those situated at a distance.

For even in cases of proximity, a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is postulated as the cause; that same impression is equally present in those sounds situated at a distance. If it is claimed that a specific impression arises from the articulated sounds (*dhvani*), then the production of sound itself cannot be denied by anyone. For that specific impression is not distinct from the sound; otherwise, the sound would become unknowable. Therefore, the sound also must be produced.
Furthermore, once a word has been produced, it can never abandon that very self-nature; for if it were perceived as being subject to impermanence, it would have to be perceived at all times.

Even on the view that there are two types of formative forces (*saṃskāra*), it is true that the statement regarding the two faults holds; for there is no deficiency in either one, due to the persistence of the former.

For instance, those articulated sounds of the auditory organ which were previously manifested by manifestors have not perished, because they have not undergone destruction; otherwise, there would be the hearing of everything by everyone.
If the auditory faculty and the phonemes are both refined and fit for the restricted audition, then there can be no hearing for those who resort to other phonemes.

If those two [the organ and the object] are refined so as to become fit for the cognition of the person's color, then surely there would be auditory perception of those two as well, provided they persist in that very state.

If these auditory organs and phonemes are indeed distinct from one another upon their differentiation, how is it that they do not [permanently] reach [their respective objects]? Therefore, the hope for their permanence is groundless.
This single sun is not seen as having a manifold nature in water and other media; for all cognitions of reflections remain without an external objective basis.

In your own system as well, all cognitions are established as being formless (*nirākāra*), while the external object is admitted to possess form (*sākāra*). Furthermore, this reflection is observed as being situated within water and other such media, whereas the sun and other celestial bodies existing in the vault of the sky do not exist in that manner [within the water]. Why then does that very object appear in such a way? If you say it is due to an error (*bhrānti*), then for that very reason it is clearly without a real basis (*anālamba*), because it is devoid of an object possessing that [reflected] form. If it is argued that there is indeed the apprehension of that very object, then this is well said; however, if it is "that" appearing "otherwise," then everything would become the knower of everything. There could only be the apprehension of that very object if it were seen as it actually exists. But when there is the perception of another form, how can there be a vision of that [original object]? For even if cognition possesses a form, it is only when that form is not distinct from the known object that it is logical for the cognition to be its grasper. Only when the form exists [as the object] is it fitting for the cognition to be its grasper.

Let it be understood that the Reality, though handed down through tradition, is perceived by means of the downward-turned function; yet, even though it exists in the upward-turned state, it is conceived as being only in the downward-turned state. For it has been established that if this [Reality] were perceived exactly as it is situated, it would be so conceived, and not otherwise.

One does not, by means of that outward-turned activity, mistakenly perceive the face presented by the inward-turned activity as being "inward" (the Self). The cognition of the reflection does not have one's own face and so forth as its objective support; because it appears as something distinct from that [original object], like the cognition of taste, sound, and so on.

For in a mirror, an object appears smaller than it actually is; moreover, trees and other objects are perceived as inverted and submerged in water. Furthermore, the original object (*bimba*) faces the mirror, whereas the reflection (*pratibimba*) does not; this reflection is situated within the water and such media, while the original object stands at a distance. The reflection varies according to its substrate, appearing large, small, and so forth, whereas the original object does not. Therefore, the reason [adduced by the opponent] is not unestablished (*asiddha*).

If the cognition of an object were to occur even through a manifestation that is dissimilar [to it], then every mind—such as that directed toward color, sound, and so forth—would have all objects as its domain. Furthermore, that which is seen when the eye is slightly pressed by a finger—even though it is a single thing appearing as distinct—is likewise considered an objectless error. Moreover, the arising of a reflection in this context has already been refuted, because two corporeal things cannot occupy the same place due to their mutual resistance.
Or, even if a reflection exists while residing in multiple locations, its unity is not found at all because of its differentiation, just as in the case of the gross, the subtle, and so forth.

And this determination which occurs among men—namely, "The sun is situated above me"—is certainly an error; for all living beings perceive only one sun simultaneously, and never a second. Since no second discus exists here, and because it is not seen [as such], it is therefore determined that the sun is indeed one. But sound is not determined to be one in any way, because its plurality is perceived both successively and simultaneously. For when many speakers employ the phoneme *ga* and others at the same time, a difference is clearly perceived.

However, when this [cognition] is applied in succession, its difference is understood not only through perception, but also through an inferential mark (liṅga) by means of the intellect in a sequential manner.

Let its perception depend upon the manifesting sounds (*dhvani*); however, its apprehension must be of it as it actually exists. Otherwise, this apprehension would not be of that [word], because its true form would not be manifested. Indeed, a word does not appear as pervading the entire extent of space. Why then should the auditory perception conform to the different locations of those sounds? If it were manifested, it would appear by its own nature alone, like a jar or other objects. All of this has been stated merely as a formal analysis (*prakriyā*), and the reason given—the incapacity of manifesters—has already been established through the impossibility of manifestation. Furthermore, the cognition "that very same thing" which appears to be perceptual has already been refuted; thus, the fact that [the word] is distinct due to the difference in location remains uncontradicted.

Furthermore, whatever entity travels from one place to another does so by means of a succession [of moments]; it achieves its goal because of its momentary nature, for otherwise such movement would be impossible. Since the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) persists without being separated from its previous location, the attainment of another location is not tenable if that nature were stable.

Because space is devoid of any defining characteristics, its manifestation cannot be conceived; furthermore, because it is beyond the senses, this light does not exist in the sky, even though it appears as such.

Furthermore, manifestation is not tenable for the ether (ākāśa) in the same way it is for sound. For manifestation is indeed cognition, and this would have to be eternal because its cause [the ether] is ever-present. Just as a manifestor is in no way conceivable in the case of sound, so too here, when there is a cognition of sound, the notion that external conditions (paropādhi) [like length] belong to it is an error. Therefore, it is established that length and the rest are not properties of the articulated sounds (dhvani); for such [properties] would exist if the dhvanis were the manifestors, and that has been refuted.

It has been repeatedly discussed previously that even though these words and their objects are absolutely distinct, they are capable of producing a uniform conceptual cognition (*pratyavamarśa*). Therefore, a word is not a denoter by virtue of having a perceived relationship with its object; rather, it has been established that in reality, it is not a denoter through its own operation (*svavṛtti*).

For these cognitions produced by words appear falsely, since the relationship of signifier and signified is established only for universals (*jāti*), specific individualities (*svalakṣaṇa*), and so forth. Due to that delusion, speakers—despite the actual difference [between words]—regard the word "cow" as being one and the same, possessing a uniform cognition. Therefore, everything that has been stated by the twice-born [Bhartṛhari], who speaks much that is incoherent, while prioritizing the distinction between words, is without foundation.

For instance, there is no unity in the shaking of the hand and so forth, because of the difference in cognition; and its manifestation as fast, slow, and so on, has already been refuted. Furthermore, no single universal (sāmānya) is perceived therein that persists through them; rather, this [shaking] serves as a basis for understanding negation and other such meanings through convention.
It has been stated that words do not directly convey [external objects] because they are devoid of a necessary connection with them; rather, these [words] are indicators of the speaker's intention.
For those [causes] are ascertained as being its effects through perception and non-perception; therefore, the relationship of cause and effect is clear in this case.

And by whatever means the causal relationship has been ascertained through convention and so forth, that [relationship] conveys the speaker's intention through words, just like the movement of the hand.

This relationship of words, consisting of the nature of cause and effect with an object existing within the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*), arises when there is a convention (*samaya*). Therefore, it is called "conventional" (*sāmayika*); and because it is manifested by that [convention], the convention itself is also said to be their relationship, though not in a primary sense.
It is not something other than the two entities that exist as cause and effect; rather, it is those very two which, when joined in the state of being cause and effect, are designated as such.
And since those [individuals] are understood by the dull-witted as having a single, unitary nature, it is therefore held that their pervasion extends over the time of convention and linguistic usage.
However, in this case, a single real relation is not at all tenable; because objects are non-confused, there would be a lack of relation when they are distinct.

"The convention (samaya) is for every individual and for every utterance," and so forth—this was stated by one who did not understand the supreme system. For a convention is not a primary relation between those two [the word and its meaning], because they are properties of humans; rather, it is a relation in the sense that it "indicates" that [meaning]. Furthermore, others do not accept this [convention] as being established at every utterance, because a creator such as God has been refuted, nor was it established by Him at the beginning of creation.

And each individual relation, though appearing as if it were one and distinct due to momentary destruction, is not contradicted even in its diversity by the occurrence of a uniform conceptual reflection (*pratyavamarśa*).
And they say that the cognitions having that as their object clearly arise in succession; for otherwise, there would be no succession of those [cognitions].

When a convention is established for many [words] at one and the same time, no distinct convention is admitted, just as in the case of a single moment of blue or other [objects]. There is no relation of the speaker in the cognition that is different [from it], nor another belonging to the hearer; for that [cognition] has a single form, since it persists for both of them. To establish the relation for the hearer, the speaker first encounters that very [relation] which was previously perceived by him. Since his reflective cognition (pratyavamarśadhī) occurs in a single form, he therefore determines oneness even though the word and so forth are distinct.

The universal (*sāmānya*) has already been refuted even in the case of jars and the like. Indeed, no form (*ākṛti*) is accepted that is distinct from the qualities of the elements. Nor is the capacity for carrying water and so forth established as belonging to this form; for if those [qualities] were non-different from the form, they too would be eternal. If there were difference, there would be the fault regarding the relation [between them]; if their production were admitted, there would be non-eternality. Therefore, it is not logical that the capacity for carrying water and so forth belongs to the form. Even if the capacity were distinct from the jar and the like, these same faults would certainly follow; thus, its effect—carrying water and so forth—would result in being eternal.

If it is not held that the relation is indeed the power (*śakti*) itself and that its difference [from the word and meaning] is not admitted, then there would be a single power for words and meanings because of their non-distinction. Even if there were a distinction, there would be no relation whatsoever between that [power] and those two [word and meaning]; if it were produced from them, it would lack permanence, and there is no other possible state of affairs for a real entity.

When a word such as "cow" is uttered at the time of explaining a relationship, some understand the object through the cognition of that relationship, while others do not. This is because the object is perceived exactly as the relationship exists and is manifested. However, if the relationship were yours (the Mīmāṃsakas'), then everyone would ascertain the object. For you maintain that the relationship is nothing other than an eternal power (*śakti*). Is that power restricted and limited in its capacity to produce the cognition of the object, or is it unlimited? If it were restricted and unlimited, why would everyone not ascertain the object? If it is restricted, what is the cause? If you say it is the nature of the thing itself, then why does the cognition of one person alone arise there when the convention has not yet been grasped or is no longer remembered? That power must be established as restricted to the production of that specific cognition. Alternatively, if it is postulated that the power is restricted only when it is known, then if the known and unknown powers are distinct, its eternity is lost. If they are identical, on what basis is this distinction described?

Furthermore, by what means is the expressive power (*śakti*) held to be known? If it is argued that it is through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), then because this principle is established here: one perceives the word, the elder, and the object denoted through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); and one perceives the listener’s comprehension through inference (*anumāna*) based on their activity. Then, through the impossibility of otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*), one knows the power residing in both [the word and the meaning]. Thus, they understand the relationship, which is supported by three means of valid cognition (*tri-pramāṇaka*), through presumptive testimony.
Because it is established in a completely different manner, the [inherent] power cannot be understood; for from words that are merely conventional, comprehension occurs without confusion.

But on the view that the capacity (śakti) is eternal, it would not depend upon convention (saṅketa) and so forth; thus, the comprehension of word-meanings would occur at all times. Furthermore, even when other capable [words] are present, a sound (dhvani) would not cause the cognition of another meaning—just as in the case of words such as *kāli* and *mārya*—because its capacity is fixed. If a single capacity is postulated for the illumination of multiple meanings, or if capacities are distinct, then a single word would simultaneously become a knower of multiple meanings.

Furthermore, since the capacity to illuminate meaning is eternally established, the resulting comprehension of that meaning would likewise occur for everyone at all times. If it is argued that this capacity depends upon convention (*saṅketa*), then surely it must depend on something that assists it; yet that [capacity] is unchanging and cannot be assisted.
And because convention, which serves to illuminate meaning, depends upon human beings, there is the possibility of falsity even in a capacity produced by something other [than that convention].

Indeed, a single sound may possess the capacity to illuminate various meanings; however, all objects such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice and others are not applicable to every purpose. Since it is possible for them to illuminate even meanings contrary to what is intended, your postulation of an eternal relationship between word and meaning is pointless.

When there is dependence upon convention, why is this relationship—characterized by eternal capacity—nurtured as being causeless? For no function whatsoever is observed in that [relationship] which presents itself as already established, apart from convention, for the purpose of making the meaning known.
For indeed, this worldly convention is not observed to exist without a convention [of agreement]; therefore, the establishment of the relationship [between word and object] is a fruitless succession.
Since linguistic usage is possible even from a convention arising solely from mere human whim, [the claim that] yoga is established thereby is not tenable.

It is suspected that the linguistic usage [of the term "yoga"] cannot be explained otherwise; however, since yoga is beyond the senses, it is not perceived by human beings. Because no one is omniscient and because each preceding person lacked such knowledge, yoga is not established; why then is it postulated?
Therefore, words such as "cow" (go) and "horse" (aśva) possess an eternal relationship [with their referents], because they do not depend upon convention, unlike words such as "gāvī" and the like.

When the word *go* is present as the appropriate [denotative term], then even from words like *gāvī*, which are produced by incapacity for that [correct form], the cognition of a cow follows the original word (*mūla-śabda*). That is not so; because Śanakas and others do not understand the Sanskrit [original], how could there be a comprehension of the meaning by following the original word? Therefore, the relationship between word and meaning is not accepted as eternal; rather, it is logical that it is conventional (*sāmayika*), since its occurrence is possible in every way.

Regarding the dissolution that may occur in the form of the destruction of a region or the destruction of a lineage, or even that which is postulated by the unimpeded Buddhists and suspected even by Brahmā and others—in such a case, the supreme understanding of the Veda would be considered to have its root destroyed; false notions arising from delusion, intoxication, and the like, as well as contrary constructions, might arise. It is even suspected that the Veda itself might become something entirely different, having merely assumed the guise [of the original], as long as no subverting evidence is revealed.

Otherwise, even when there is a desire to act differently, the sound [of the Veda] would not proceed; for that very desire of men arises only in such a way and not otherwise. Thus, this Veda might be suspected of not having a nature different from its textual meaning; however, if activity proceeded from a desire for something else, no such suspicion would be dispelled.

Furthermore, the sequence [of words] is not accepted by all men as being established for all time; they also compose the sequence of words, sentences, and syllables independently. Otherwise, some composition would be non-artificial (eternal) like the Veda for you; thus, even in the case of a mere meaningless composition, the notion of authorship is destroyed. Just as he intends to speak this very same thing as it was spoken by others, there is no such lack of restriction; therefore, its beginninglessness is not like that of the relationship [between word and meaning].

If one were to have such an intention as "I am speaking what has been said by another," it would be due to a delusion arising from a similar reflective awareness, just as there is a distinction between actions.

When spoken by another, [the same phonemes] are not uttered with distinctness of pitch and other qualities; nor is this a property of the manifestor (vyañjaka), because they are perceived as being identical to the phoneme itself. Therefore, phonemes are seen to be different for each person, like jars and other objects. Since their difference is thus perfectly clear, why is its mark denied?

Furthermore, the indication of the conventional usage of jars and so forth by means of their genus has been previously refuted, because that [genus] does not exist and because it is incompatible with the individual.

Therefore, the universals (jāti) such as those of the palate and other articulatory organs are established as common to all persons; consequently, a speaker does not produce articulated sounds by first characterizing them through those [universals]. Thus, it is not the case that distinct universals serve as the causes for the manifestation of words, which persist only as long as the phonemes (varṇa) do, or that the individual manifestations (vyakti) associated with them [do so].

Therefore, for you, the sequence of sounds is not preceded by the order of conjunctions and disjunctions of the palate and other organs; nor is there duality of eternality through the universal (jāti), just as the parts of actions such as "revolving" are not characterized by a universal. In the same way, for us, there is no persistence of sequence belonging to the palate, the sounds, and the phonemes.

Even for individuals, there is no determination of the properties of the genus due to their subtlety; consequently, even though the castes are all-pervasive, there is no perception of their sequential order.
Therefore, the phonemes, following after all the qualities of the sounds which are established as eternal, would be the means for the cognition of different meanings.

Furthermore: "The various universals (*jāti*) are the causes for the manifestation of sounds; they operate as long as the phonemes (*varṇa*) persist, or else it is the individuals (*vyakti*) associated with them. Thus, because the manifestors exist, there would be a constant perception of the sound; therefore, for you, a sequence of phonemes consisting of a sequence of manifestations is not logical.

If universals are established as having forms connected to individuals, then the eternality of individuals also follows as unavoidable. Alternatively, if individuals are established as having forms connected to universals, then even against your will, the non-eternality of universals would result for you.
And since the impossibility of manifestation has already been established above, those phonemes, being thus stretched out [in time], would not be expressive.

Time, too, which is singular, all-pervading, and eternal, has already been refuted. Like the phonemes (*varṇa*), it is not manifested in all entities by anything whatsoever. Even if it were manifested in the phonemes, it could not serve as a factor for conveying meaning, because it would lack any distinction from other things, and its eternity would be untenable since it does not exist elsewhere. Therefore, the sequential order of phonemes, as well as their short, long, and protracted durations, are divisions of time; they cannot be justified as being conditioned by the manifesting sounds (*dhvani*). Consequently, there exists no such eternal property belonging to the word (*pada*). Thus, for those who maintain the non-eternality of phonemes, the word is established as non-eternal. Furthermore, even if it were a property of another, it would not be a factor [for cognition], just like the speed of a horse and so forth, unless a manifestation were postulated here through manifesting cognitions.

If, however, all [phonemes] were eternal, then the presumption (*arthāpatti*) [of their existence] would be refuted; for it has been established that the nature of the cognition of meaning resides in impermanent things. A phoneme arises from another intention (*vivakṣā*) produced by a preceding intention; its hearing occurs immediately after that. One who knows the preceding phoneme, whose hearing is not too rapid, subsequently produces a memory within himself by depending upon the memory of that [preceding phoneme]. This sequence among phonemes—whether as being produced with respect to the cognitions that originate them or as being the cause of those [cognitions]—is dependent on the person. Therefore, it is perfectly clear that the phonemes are distinct in every word due to differences in order, such as *dama*, *mada*, *latā*, and *tāla*. It is through such a sequence that these [phonemes] bring about the difference in meaning; for this very reason, the postulation of a *sphoṭa* here is also useless.

For that [sphoṭa] was indeed postulated by the grammarians for the sake of explaining the comprehension of meaning; yet since the phonemes themselves are capable of that, this postulation is purposeless. Furthermore, its non-existence is determined because it is not perceived despite being perceptible; however, if it were imperceptible, it could not serve as a communicator of meaning, just like an inferential mark (liṅga).

If it is claimed that because its causal status is established by its mere existence (*sattāmātra*), that [word] is intended to be a cognizer [of meaning], then it would produce cognition at all times, like the eye. Even when there is no understanding of the convention (*saṅketa*) and even when the phonemes (*varṇa*) are not heard, there would be cognition of the objects to be produced by it, due to the proximity of the capable cause. For this [word] is eternally existent and has no dependence whatsoever; nor can its manifestation (*vyañkti*) occur through sounds, conventions, or phonemes, because such is never observed. Indeed, they say that "manifestation" is cognition; yet that cognition does not exist [in the case of the word]. Therefore, the postulation of a manifestor (*vyañjaka*) for it is entirely useless.

"Sound manifests in the intellect when its ripening has been completed through repetition, together with the final sound in which the seed was deposited by the preceding sounds"—this too has been postulated by him here without any basis, for even in that [intellect], no other sound is observed to manifest.

Even for those who maintain that there is a sequence in the *sphoṭa*—whether it be produced (*janya*) or manifested (*vyajya*) by sounds occurring in succession—their position is contradicted. For neither manifestation nor birth can logically apply to that which is partless; since it does not transcend its single uniform nature, both [manifestation and birth] would necessarily occur all at once.

Just as phonemes, despite being composed of parts, convey meaning through a sequential order, why should the parts of the sphoṭa not function in the same way? Why have these unseen [parts] been postulated?

If the manifestation [of the sphoṭa] has been produced once by a single sound, they nevertheless employ other phonemes for the sake of achieving a complete manifestation; because its nature is difficult to discern, it is manifested again by subsequent phonemes that possess the same manifesting capacity.
Why does manifestation not recur again and again for that very same [entity], or for some other single one? For, in this way, there would be no distinction between them.
The individual manifestation, consisting of the objects, the sense organs, and the mental impressions, is like the phonemes; it too must be negated even when the mind appears as that [manifestation].

Therefore, that cognition which occurs prior to direct perception and consists of the knowledge of all the phonemes within the successive cognitions of the sequence is the cause of the cognition of the meaning.
For when the final phoneme is cognized, a simultaneous recollection of all the phonemes, produced by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), arises with respect to all the phonemes.
Regarding all these objects, the mental cognition of a synthesis (samuccaya-jñāna) is accepted by all theorists, even when those objects are known sequentially.
If this were not admitted, then indeed, in the case of things perceived sequentially, the perception of their aggregate in the form of "a hundred" and so forth would never arise.
Thus, although there may be a sequential cognition of the phonemes by means of the ear and the mind, subsequently, however, there occurs a simultaneous recollection of them.

Therefore, the phonemes mounted upon that [cognition] do not [directly] bring about the understanding of the distant object; rather, it is from the word that the cognition arises, and for this reason it is designated as such by worldly people.
All this is logically consistent only when consciousness possesses a formal aspect; otherwise, how could those [objects] which have perished appear in memory?

Now, if the phonemes were known previously as having their manifestation concealed, they would still be remembered as being merely present [in memory], because it would follow that they could not appear clearly.

Furthermore, the [theory of] persistence has already been refuted; for if that persistence were to exist, recollection would occur at the very same time as the cognition of the experience of the phonemes, due to having a single cause.

We do not at all deny that there is a single cognition [of the form] "cow"; rather, through the identity of the object grasped by it and the word itself, there arises the notion of oneness regarding the word.
Due to its rapidity and the smallness of the interval, that [distinction] might indeed exist in the word "cow" (go); however, in words such as "Devadatta," the difference is clearly perceived.

This cognition of an object arises from the phonemes, because it occurs immediately after the knowledge of them; for a cognition of fire arising from smoke and the like is indeed produced by that very [smoke].
There exists no cognition of meaning that arises immediately after a cognition of a word distinct from its phonemes; therefore, there is no other word that is expressive.

For positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), which are the basis for the linguistic usage of "being an effect," are indeed ascertained everywhere; therefore, pervasion (vyāpti) is established here by means of them.
Since it has been established that the capacity to signify belongs only to impermanent phonemes, and since both recognition and inference have been refuted as proofs for their permanence;

The injunction was made out of ignorance regarding the contradictions with one's own words and so forth; for all of those [contradictions] apply to you in the case of [the Veda being] eternal. It has been established that speech, being eternal, cannot be a communicator [of meaning]; this is because it lacks sequential order (*ānupūrvya*) and the like, and because it is not perceived as eternal.

The "unestablished substratum" (*āśrayāsiddhi*) that is alleged through the conceptualization of a difference in the subject (*dharmin*) arises from a lack of knowledge regarding the definition of inference; for the status of being a subject belongs to whatever appears in cognition. Whatever object, unexamined and established by common consensus, appears in cognition—even for a child—that much alone is declared to be the subject. Indeed, it is only with respect to that very [object] that this dispute among proponents has arisen; there is no dispute for anyone regarding a distinction constructed merely by one’s own whim. Therefore, when a subject is indicated without qualification, to introduce a conceptualization based on a specific qualification subverts the very operation of every inference. Even such an argument as, "The cognition produced by Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is valid, because it is produced by causes free from defects," is likewise subject to this conceptualization. If the thesis (*pakṣa*) is "the cognition produced by an injunction connected with an eternal object," then the fault of an unestablished substratum follows for the opponent.

Permanence is the state of remaining as it is, while impermanence is being other than that; for if the state of remaining as it is and its absence do not cease, what could possibly be said to persist?

And when the reason "being produced solely by the sense organs" is proposed here, no deviation [of the reason] is perceived, because the genus [of being produced by the sense organs] has already been refuted.
That which is the cause of sensory cognition appearing as its own [object] would be supersensible; however, it has already been established that causality does not exist in what is eternal.
And for everyone, this status as a cause of such a meaning is well-established; otherwise, this same conceptual construction would apply equally everywhere, even in the case of smoke and so forth.

Furthermore, for us who hold the conventional view, the capacity to initiate an effect that is a cognition immediately following effort is not established in the case of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṅkhyānirodha*) and the like, because they are merely conventional.

Furthermore, the two types of cessation (*nirodha*) are not admitted to be of the nature of destruction, because they are associated with the outflows (*sāśrava*). Pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha is the specific disjunction (*visaṃyoga*) [from each defilement]; the other cessation, apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha, is the absolute prevention of arising. Therefore, those who do not understand this established tenet float about, conceited in their delusions.
Neither its lack of intrinsic nature nor its own destruction follow immediately after effort; likewise, the collection of potsherds, light, and so forth, are the basis for such cognition.

Now, it might be argued that the perishability of flames and the like is unestablished; however, this is not so, for they perish at every moment. In such cases, the light particles (tejas-avayavas), being subtle, quickly move to another location. Indeed, a great mass of light remains concentrated in the region of the wick; as long as the preceding portion moves upward, it is perceived as a "flame. That which moves away even beyond that constitutes "radiance" (prabhā). But what moves further than that is not discerned due to its extreme subtlety.
Otherwise, what kind of eternal nature could that [capacity] have in relation to those [objects], given that a distinction between the capable and the incapable natures is firmly established?

Phonemes that are devoid of sequence possess no denotative power; therefore, such [phonemes] do not constitute a sentence, nor does a sequence exist among them. Because they are all-pervading and eternal, there is indeed no sequence of space or time for them, as is the case with letters [in writing], or with the distinctions between fruits, flowers, and so forth. If their sequence were inherent, the word *sara* would be possible, but *rasa* and the like would not, due to the contradiction with the established sequence. Furthermore, the letter *ra* and others, once established, do not arise again as possessing a different sequence; phonemes are described as being eternal and unitary. Otherwise, the recognition [of phonemes] which serves as the proof for their eternity and unity, would—as you yourself have stated—be fallacious, since it occurs even when there is a difference [in manifestation].

Nor is the sequence of individual manifestations the sentence, because manifestation is denied in the case of an eternal entity; since it lacks the fitness for being a sentence, its eternality is therefore untenable.

Just as words such as "vṛddhi" and so forth have meanings fashioned by human desire, and words such as "svarga" and "yāga" are likewise conceived [in that way], even so, in works such as dramas and prose narratives whose plots are invented, there exists no eternal, real, and intended relationship between word and meaning.
Even there, while the capacity is eternal, the injunction is non-eternal; it is solely due to that [injunction] that an error arises regarding the eternal capacity.

But surely, no external object exists there; in what sense, then, is an individual (vyakti) postulated? If it is argued that it is in the reflection of conceptual construction (vikalpa), then the same doubt may be raised regarding the Veda as well.

Who indeed can comprehend a potency that relates to objects beyond the senses? Therefore, even the *niyoga* (injunction) in the Veda cannot be conceived as dependent on human agency. Nor is there an understanding of it from elders, for they too remain inherently ignorant. However, comprehension may be possible through an explanation based on human [authorship].
Surely this objection applies equally to a scripture that is a human composition; for in that case, one acts out of faith, or even because of doubt regarding the matter.
When an object is established through perception or inference, [the cognition is valid]; however, this is not the case with Vedic speech, because it is self-evident.
Without considering that the teaching of the Dharma through discourses on generated objects is equal in its scriptural authority, others have here described this as being incoherent.

Apart from the beginninglessness of words and their meanings, there can be no other cause for the beginninglessness of their relationship; therefore, in the Veda, no such thing as a [new] relationship exists. As for the inference that the relationship was not created because it lacks any means [of production], let the inference that it was not taught be contradicted by what is actually observed.
Furthermore, the repeated practice observed among the elders is the means; thus, its abandonment regarding comprehension is unestablished.
All this would indeed be so if the determination of the meaning of the Veda were established as being non-contradictory even by comparison with the elders; otherwise, there would be a flaw.
Because it possesses a pervasion that encompasses all established [reasons], no counter-argument whatsoever can be formulated against the probans such as "being a composite" (saṅghātatva).

"Only phonemes (varṇa), when they are meaningful, possess distinct meanings, and are joined by a specific sequence, are said to be what are called 'words,' 'sentences,' and 'collections. Therefore, the possession of meaning, distinct meaning, and a specific sequence—which is precluded in the case of human authorship—is an unimpeded pervasion (vyāpti) [of non-human origin]."

If the subject is defined as "that which is denotable by Vedic study," there is no such ascertainment of pervasion; therefore, in this proof, the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is clearly doubtful.

When such a sequence of events is to be performed and it is certain that humans lack the capacity for it, this pervasion (*vyāpti*) cannot be ascertained here at all. Only if all human attributes were directly perceived could such an ascertainment occur; and that is possible only for an omniscient being.

Furthermore, the human origin of the Veda is clearly conceivable; for the practice of sexual misconduct, false speech, injury to living beings, and so forth, as well as qualities such as difficulty of pronunciation, lack of accentuation, obscurity, and unpleasantness to the ear—characteristics indeed observed in the Vedas—are seen even in the words of atheists and others. Moreover, whatever efficacy regarding the removal of poison or the attainment of prosperity is observed [in the Vedas], that same truth is seen in the recitation of mantras concerning Vainateya (Garuḍa) and others.
Furthermore, by this same reasoning, nothing whatsoever can be proven to be of human origin, since even the words of the Buddha could be inferred in this very manner.

Because its form is manifested by that [agent], it is said to belong to him; and even in that case, the recollection of the agent is based on the purpose [of the action]. If others do not accept this because the logical principle (*nyāya*) is the same, why is it not accepted? Let it not be so according to the desire of others, yet it is inferred in that way by virtue of the logical principle.

Furthermore, men are generally liars at all times; just as there is no trust in them today, so too there is none when they recount past events. By this logic you have stated, it is not established that any author anywhere, even while declaring his own work to be his own, could be trusted. Therefore, abandon this hope for truthfulness in non-human (apauruṣeya) texts, for the meanings set forth in them are indeed contrary to the meaning of the Vedas.

Moreover, in this way, only beginninglessness would be established, not reliance upon various [authoritative] sources. Therefore, if [the Veda] were uncreated, any other scripture would also have to be uncreated.
For instance, the customs of the Persians and others depend upon others; and the tenets of the nihilists (nāstikas) arise from the impressions of others.
And even if such non-artificiality were established, what benefit would there be for you? For this entire effort of yours is directed toward establishing the absence of falsehood.

In the case of [the properties] being time, being a person, and so forth, there is a doubt regarding the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), because—as in the previous case—the incapacity of the instruments [of knowledge] is not established for human beings.

Because it depends upon the instructions of Nara and because it is produced as a formal proof, there is no dependence on a speaker for its own meaning, nor is there any [dependence] regarding the subject or the example.

If the eternity and authorlessness of the sentence are [the probandum], then for both the subject (*dharmin*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the property of "arising from an eternal sentence" is clearly recognized as unestablished (*asiddha*). Thus, since the authorlessness of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) remains undetermined, the fault of being "unestablished due to doubt" (*sandigdhāsiddhatā*) applies to the subsequent reasons as well.

Furthermore, when momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) is established, scripture (*śruti*) is clearly contradicted: "The Self (*puruṣa*) is indeed eternal by its very nature; therefore, the cognition produced by it is [eternal]. And it is stated in scripture that "the Person does not perish. Thus, the contradiction previously mentioned is quite evident, as is its lack of proof. However, for one for whom the difference of place, time, and person is as perceptible as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand, the absence of such contradiction is determined by him through direct perception.

When the Veda remains thus, its form and meaning unknown and shrouded in darkness, the dull-witted feel an attachment to it just as they do toward their own customs, like the Persians. And because they do not understand its true meaning, due to the influence of the outflow of evil karma, they likewise engage in the defilement of harming living beings and other such acts.
Therefore, the authority of injunctions regarding Dharma is not established, because its meaning cannot be ascertained either from themselves or from others who are dull-witted.
Therefore, let this person, whose internal mass of darkness has been dispelled by the light of knowledge, be appointed as the instructor of the distinct meanings of the Vedic scriptures.
Therefore, let this person—whose internal mass of darkness has been dispelled by the light of knowledge—be appointed as the instructor of the distinct meanings of the Vedic scriptures.
And thus, when the human origin of the Vedas has been established, their intrinsic validity is also refuted without effort.
And thus, once the human origin of the Vedas has been established, their intrinsic validity is also refuted without effort.
Independence alone is the single basis for validity; for that very [validity] would be destroyed if dependence were resorted to.
For what person who speaks according to reason would adopt a position that destroys its own foundation—a position by which even the means for its own establishment is destroyed by its own statement?
For validity that is dependent [on something else] cannot be established anywhere; and what [means of knowledge], having an unstable cause, will establish the probandum?

If this is the meaning intended, then indeed it has already been established previously that the capacity (*śakti*) of all things is non-different from them. For the essential nature (*svarūpa*) which is capable of producing its own effect is called "capacity. If that [nature] were not of the essence of existence, then the entity could not exist as an agent of action.
If the intrinsic nature of the means of valid cognition attains manifestation through manifestors, then it initiates its effect while depending upon other conditions.
Since the manifestation of an eternal entity depends on other causes that are distinct [from it], there would consequently be a constant perception of its forms and effects.
Whether the power be distinct from it or possess a dual nature, nevertheless, that cognition must indeed be eternal, for it is conjoined with an eternal power.
Otherwise, it would not be eternal, because it lacks a constant uniformity; for at one time it is connected with the cognition of that [object], and not at another.
Regarding this, these wise followers of the Sugata say only this much: even though it resides in some form of cognition, it cannot be known by itself.

Who indeed, on account of being of the nature of experience alone, is capable of ascertaining the capacity [of consciousness] to attain the realization of the object to be known exactly as it exists, based on that experience alone?

Even though it is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), that [cognition] which, in the perception of a mass of hair and so forth, possesses the nature of experience while appearing with a vivid form [exists].

Therefore, whether it be the cognition of purposeful action or something else, another [cognition] is required only for the sake of ascertainment, and not for the production of that [ascertainment], as is the case with poison and the like.

For just as one determines that poison, wine, and so forth are not identical to other things because they lack immediate results and because their specific effects—such as fainting, perspiration, and delirium—are observed, so too, when cognition is determined by its effects, its capacity [to produce those effects] is understood through its identity with them.

Furthermore, you have stated that this validity, characterized as a capacity (*śakti*), is indeed beyond dispute and must be determined by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). Since the capacities of all entities are established through the presumption based on their effects (*kāryārthāpatti*), how is it not established that [validity] is established extrinsically (*parataḥ*)?

Furthermore, in this way, invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) would also follow as being intrinsic (*svataḥ*); for that which is non-existent by its own nature cannot possibly arise from anything else. Moreover, it can be stated without exception that "independence alone is the sole basis for invalidity," and so forth. Just as the capacity for non-correspondence (*visaṃvādana*) is ascertained from something else, so too is the capacity for correspondence (*saṃvāda*); therefore, in every respect, both are equal. Consequently, what superiority is observed in validity over its opposite, such that validity alone is held to be intrinsic while invalidity is extrinsic?
Since the validity of the means of knowledge is described as being intrinsic, it is also accepted that the operation [of those means] toward their own effects is intrinsic once they have arisen.

For when independent [cognitions] arise, their occurrence—being independent of their own causes—is for the sake of determining the validity of the object, just like [the production of] a jar or similar things.

A jar depends upon a lump of clay, a staff, a wheel, and so forth for its birth; however, it has no such dependence for the act of fetching water. In this same way, self-validity (svataḥ-prāmāṇya) must necessarily exist at the end [of the process]; for if validity were dependent on something else, an infinite regress (anavasthā) would result.

If intrinsic validity were required, then that [validity] would have to be established by another means of knowledge; and if one seeks that same thing in each subsequent case, we would never reach a firm conclusion. Just as the first cognition requires corroboration, so too must a corroborating cognition itself seek further corroboration.

As it is with the first, so it would be with the others; thus, as before, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Desiring such a process at every stage, we would never attain a firm conclusion. If you do not accept that the knowledge of qualities (*guṇajñāna*) has its validity dependent upon further qualities, then even the initial cognition of the object would not require the valid cognition of those qualities. Therefore, even after reflecting at great length, one must necessarily admit that validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*) somewhere; it is better to posit that very point of intrinsic validity at the very beginning.

By what superior reasoning could you claim that the cognition of the quality of correspondence depends on the first [cognition], by the power of which it would come to be? Therefore, self-validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) is established as the general rule (*autsargika*) everywhere; it is set aside only by the two [conditions]: the presence of a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-jñāna*) and the cognition of a defect in the cause (*kāraṇa-duṣṭatva-jñāna*). Even if this [validity] were dependent on another, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would not follow; for this dependence on another is itself established as being intrinsic (*svataḥ*).

For just as a means of valid cognition is not established by another means of valid cognition, so too invalidity is not established by that which is itself invalid. For if things of the same class were to depend upon one another, no firm foundation would be possible; however, when they belong to different classes, because they have distinct causes, they are firmly established.
The sublating cognition consists first of all in the ascertainment of the object's difference; because it possesses independent authority, it sublates the preceding cognition.

Even there, however, an exception might sometimes require further consideration; for one who has developed doubt regarding the previous [rule], that doubt is removed by even a slight [subsequent] statement.

If, while one is searching for another sublater of that [second cognition], yet another arises, then by the sublation of the middle one, the first alone possesses the status of valid cognition (*pramāṇatā*). Alternatively, if a thorough search is conducted with appropriate effort and no sublater of the sublater (*bādhakabādhaka*) is found due to the absence of its basis, then—because it is free from contradiction—that very [third cognition] is stronger and sublates the first; thus, the validity of the first is set aside. In this way, one does not transcend the triad of cognitions belonging to the investigator. Consequently, as long as no sublation has arisen, one should not suspect a further sublater.
For he who, out of delusion, imagines an obstacle even where none exists, will meet his destruction as one whose soul is filled with doubt in all worldly affairs.
And so, the nature of doubt has been censured by Vāsudeva: "Neither this world nor the next exists for one whose mind is consumed by doubt, O son of Kuntī."

To whatever extent a negation (apavāda) is conceivable within the mind regarding an object, and provided that upon investigation it does not arise, to that same extent one should remain with regard to that very object, thinking "it might perhaps be so," and not by cognizers who are driven by their own desires.
Differences of place, time, person, and circumstance are indeed established through conventional usage; therefore, those who seek to find a sublation must take these into account.

Due to being situated in a distant land, there may be an incorrect perception; in such a case, there might be some suspicion elsewhere. However, in that instance, the limit of the exception consists merely in going near [to verify]. But in other cases—such as differences in time, person, or circumstances—there is no dependence on that [verification], just like the cognition of a mirage and the like.
Thus, in a time of deep darkness, whatever doubt there may be regarding cows, horses, and so forth, or whatever erroneous determination occurs therein, its limit is the manifestation of light.
For instance, in cases such as the moon, confusion regarding directions, the Vedas, phonemes, and accents, one determines the error by questioning another person.

When an object is being known through sense faculties impaired by passion, hatred, pride, intoxication, hunger, thirst, and so forth, there occurs a misconception due to the absence of those [impairments] in the case of what is otherwise difficult to know.

Even in legal proceedings such as those concerning debts, when two parties are disputing, there is one statement from the defendant and two statements from the plaintiff. For fear of infinite regress (*anavasthā*), no further statement is recorded. Thereafter, the judge, the witnesses, and the members of the court shall deliver the verdict. Thus, in all transactions, it is held that there are only three cognitions; for this very reason, even the "threefold truth" of the gods is proclaimed. Therefore, since both [the cognition and its validity] are intrinsically valid (*svataḥ-pramāṇa*), there is no infinite regress; thus, validity and invalidity are established according to their respective conditions.

A statement that is ascertained to be eternal or composed by a trustworthy person is not corrupted in the slightest by either the listener or the speaker. Those who are teachers of knowledge and even fellow students there prevent its destruction; such persons are capable of preserving it. Therefore, the statement is not corrupted by defects, whether those defects are prohibited by its qualities or otherwise. Alternatively, in the absence of an author, those defects could not exist, being without a locus.

In that regard, two things are observed in the speech of a reliable person (āpta): the absence of defects and the presence of excellences (guṇas). It has already been explained how validity arises from excellences and how it does not exist [otherwise]. Therefore, because the speaker possesses excellences, there are no defects; they are excluded by those excellences. Consequently, the sentence is intrinsically valid, characterized by the absence of defects.
If the absence of defects in the words of a trustworthy person is understood from their virtues, then there would be that same infinite regress following upon the presence of those virtues.

This is not a fault, for at that time the knowledge of qualities is not required at all. It is not by being known that the qualities are there to assist; rather, by their mere existence, they are capable of excluding defects. While those qualities are present, no cognition regarding the defects of the person arises.
Validity is not sublated because it is not perceived by any defects; and since it is established as being unsublated, it remains self-evident here as well.

In the case of human composition, it is suspected whether defects exist or not; however, since there is no author for the Veda, we have no suspicion of defects whatsoever. Therefore, that which is called the intrinsic validity of the Veda due to its independence [from external corroboration] is established all the more easily even in the case of a work composed by a reliable person (*āpta*).
The fact that the meaning of the Veda is at all times inconsistent with other means of valid cognition is precisely what constitutes its authority; otherwise, it would be a mere restatement.

Even in the case of another [cognition] being a means of valid cognition, compatibility is not the cause; for among cognitions of the same object, validity belongs to only one through the process of exclusion (vikalpa).
Even where there might be a determination by subsequent means of valid cognition, it is certain that in that case as well, the object was not clearly ascertained by the preceding one.

Furthermore, there would be no validity regarding an object that perishes immediately after arising; moreover, auditory cognition that is not connected with the eyes and other senses would be invalid.

If its status as a means of valid cognition is established because it is connected with another auditory cognition, then the same would be established for the Veda as well, since it is connected with another cognition produced by it. However, for both [the Veda and the word], there is no cognition produced by a different means of proof; therefore, corroboration by a cognition produced by a different cause is not required.
Just as the connection with another cognition dependent on the same sense-organ is established as the cause for perception, so too should it be stated in the case of the Veda.

For when a correspondence with the fact is obtained through a single statement regarding different places, times, and persons, no other cause need be sought. Therefore, that cognition which has arisen firmly and does not contradict cognitions of other places and so forth is undoubtedly a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

The validity of verbal testimony and the other means of knowledge is not to be established by inference; otherwise, let it be that even the validity of perception is to be established by that same [inference], as there is no distinction between them.

If the validity of the means of valid cognition is established by another [means], then because that too must be established by yet another, an infinite regress (anavasthā) results. If, however, the validity of the establishing means were not established by another, then the validity of the things to be established would likewise be established in that very same way.

Indeed, perception and the other means of knowledge are not apprehended as being "means of valid cognition" in this way; and if they are not so apprehended, practical activity (vyavahāra) is not possible.

Prior to its apprehension, the means of valid cognition is established in its own nature; independent with respect to its own object, it is measured by other [cognitions] once that object has been cognized.

Just as all objects are grasped by the sense organs, such as the eyes, even though they themselves are not known, so it is not with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, in this context, being known (*jñāyamānatva*) is of no use for validity; the experience of the object is obtained from the [means of cognition] precisely when it is itself unknown.
Furthermore, an invalid cognition stands in regard to its own object as if it were a valid cognition; its falsity cannot be apprehended without another means of valid cognition.
