For the alteration of an object is not apprehended by the preceding [cognition] in the same way that its original state was; thus, in this case as well, falsity is grasped either through the cognition of the alteration itself or through the presence of a defective cause. It is by that alone that falsity is apprehended, and not by any other cause. This [cognition] is measured as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) only while it remains in its state of origination.
Therefore, even where falsity is demonstrated to others, both of these [points] must be stated there, and not merely a similarity of properties.

In this regard, those who lack wisdom rely on some mere similarity with invalid cognition to prove that all means of valid cognition are false. Such a construction of a proof serves only their own destruction; for even against another, a similar [refutation] arises by way of a reflection. And because it has been refuted by that [reflection], a proof that is not in accordance with reality is not capable of subverting the Vedic injunction (*codanā*), which possesses inherent validity.
To this it is replied: surely this systematic arrangement has a valid basis only for those things whose existence is admitted once they have been produced.

It is accepted that for jars and the like, dependence on causes is required for their own acquisition [of existence]; however, once they have acquired their own nature, their engagement in their respective effects occurs spontaneously. As for that cognition which you also maintain to be unstable immediately after its birth—what kind of operation could it possibly have after having acquired its nature and then ceased to exist?

For the operation of causes is indeed observed to be distinct from their birth; lest the same be thought to apply to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as well, its "birth" is specifically intended [as its definition]. Indeed, it does not remain even for a moment, nor is it born as something non-cognitive (*apramātmaka*), such that it might subsequently operate toward the apprehension of an object like the sense organs and other instruments.
Furthermore, if cognition is accepted as being non-momentary and eternal, this contradicts what has been previously accepted; thus, it is subverted by reasoning.
For every entity has already been established in detail as being subject to momentary destruction; since that which is eternal cannot be produced, what need has it for a cause?

And for this reason, it can be said that valid cognition does not function by itself; subsequently, it fails to engage in its own effects because it lacks a determinate form, like a sky-lotus. Or, let it be granted that non-momentary cognition functions by itself; yet, if it were for the sake of ascertaining its own validity, why would there be doubt and the like?
Since the ascertainment of validity arises from that [cognition] alone, once it has occurred, doubt and error find no footing.
Because of the relationship of sublated and sublator between the mind of certainty and the mind of superimposition, all certainty indeed functions upon the exclusion of superimposition.
Furthermore, for the sake of establishing the validity of the cognition produced by the Vedic injunction (codanā), the argument that it arises from causes free from defects is superfluous.

If it is maintained that once intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) is established, that [intrinsic nature] serves to ward off exceptions, even that is not so, because such a doubt is impossible. For that doubt persists only so long as certainty has not arisen; but once that certainty has arisen, how could there be any suspicion of invalidity? By what means, then, would an effort to remove it attain its purpose? Indeed, one who has ascertained the identity of a post does not suspect it to be otherwise.
When a determination of a certain form arises with respect to a particular object, the doubt regarding its opposite is dispelled by that very same [determination].
Just as when the existence of fire and so forth is apprehended through signs such as smoke, the exclusion of its non-existence follows from that very same apprehension.

In this way, let it be accepted that the exclusion of invalidity occurs by itself; therefore, a formal proof is not required for the removal of invalidity. However, if a doubt regarding two types of invalidity were to persist there, then the certainty of validity would not arise, because the object would be apprehended through error.
When an object is made the focus of cognitions characterized by doubt or error—just like a post—there is no ascertainment of its true nature at that time.
Just as a post, fire, or a person is determined by others through conditions such as the presence of crows, smoke, or causes like defects, so too [is the self known].
Since it has thus become an object of doubt and error, let it be understood that the validity of that [cognition] is known through something else.

Moreover, according to your own position, exclusion of another (anyavyavaccheda) occurs only in that sentence where the negative particle (nañ) is explicitly heard; elsewhere, its own positive meaning is understood. And here, in the statement "the cognition produced by an injunction (codanā) is a means of valid knowledge" (pramāṇa), there is no application of the negative particle; therefore, there is no exclusion of invalidity (aprāmāṇya).
Furthermore, if the validity of all means of valid cognition were determined by themselves alone, then why would there be a difference of opinion among proponents?

By some, such as the Prācyas, a restriction is asserted that [validity] arises from itself alone; by others, it is held that some [validity] arises from itself and some from another, while still others maintain there is no fixed rule.
Since dispute arises from error, and that error is sublated by certainty, proponents who ascertain reality would not dispute one another.

If the validity of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were determined intrinsically (*svataḥ*), then no one would ever be subject to deception, because they would proceed from a state of certainty. For it is by acting upon the notion that what is invalid is valid that one is deceived; however, through the understanding of intrinsic validity, no one could ever be the opposite.

Indeed, one who acts on the basis of what is not a means of valid cognition (apramāṇa) encounters non-correspondence with reality; the certainty regarding that [non-valid cognition] is held to arise from a subsequent sublating cognition (bādhaka-pratyaya). However, one who acts on the basis of a means of valid cognition does not encounter non-correspondence; and it is precisely for this [valid cognition] that we maintain the certainty of its intrinsic validity (svataḥprāmāṇya).

This is not due to a failure to understand the intended meaning; for this is what is intended here: that in the determination of the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of all means of knowledge as being intrinsic (*svataḥ*), there is no such certainty of intrinsic validity because of the restriction [of the conditions]. By the force of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), non-validity (*aprāmāṇya*) is understood therein, since it does not depend on the cognition of a discrepancy in the object or the cognition of defects arising from a cause. Because its non-validity is determined immediately after its birth, it is not logical to have a reversal of non-validity into validity in that which is invalid. Therefore, no one would ever act toward that which is inconsistent, because of the realization of its nature.

Furthermore, since jars and other such things are momentary, there exists no time for action distinct from the time of their birth; thus, the illustrative example [cited by the opponent] is unestablished.
For subsequently, since they do not depend on a potter or similar agents, but rather depend upon their own material causes and so forth, there is no spontaneous activity.

Nor does an infinite regress result from [the need for] another cognition, because it relies upon a means of knowledge. Therefore, the determination of intrinsic validity occurs in the cognition of causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*). Now, what excellence does this [cognition of efficacy] possess over the previous one, such that the latter is not accepted as being extrinsic (*parataḥ*) like the former? It is said: Validity is defined as correspondence with reality (*vastusaṃvāda*). And there is no definition of that [correspondence] other than the cognition of the repeated performance of causal efficacy. Furthermore, a cognition manifesting causal efficacy is clearly experienced, and it is ascertained by a mental reflection (*amarśana*) arising immediately after it. Thus, because its correctness and validity are determined intrinsically, a subsequent cognition apprehending the attainment of causal efficacy is not required. And since that first cognition—which manifests the effect—is itself a valid cognition, the determination of its validity follows from this very reason.

For in the first case—namely, regarding an object that is not [actually] present—the second [cognition], characterized by correspondence with the real object, would not arise, because its cause is impossible. Indeed, for one who determines a flame in a cluster of *aśoka* blossoms and the like, a cognition manifesting burning and cooking never arises. Or, if it were to arise, it would follow that it is not of a different class from fire, because the defining characteristic of fire is simply the capacity for those effects.

Therefore, as long as a cognition appearing as purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) has not arisen, a doubt regarding the invalidity of the first [cognition] arises due to the causes of error. Subsequently, the non-perception of the result, the observation of similarity, the dullness of the intellect, and so forth, constitute the causes of error here. However, once a consciousness manifesting the effect has arisen, this [doubt] no longer exists, because there is a direct perception of the activity intrinsically bound to the real object.
But when practice has become established, a distinct difference is perceived from the initial cognition which did not have that as its object, even though its fruit had not yet been attained.

But when the distinctness [of the object] is not perceived, there can be no ascertainment of validity for a cognition appearing as an effect, because of the suspicion that it might refer to an object of a different class. Even if validity exists in such a case, it cannot be ascertained; it is recognized solely through a subsequent cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). Therefore, the first cognition requires corroboration; yet, in that same manner, a further corroboration by means of another corroboration is not to be sought.

Because the cause of error does not exist, that [first cognition] possesses validity by itself; whereas there is aversion toward the first [cognition] only when it lacks such [validity], due to the possibility of error.

But surely, while that cognition’s status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) remains undetermined, how could a discerning person proceed toward it, since their desired object has not yet been attained?
It is said, O wise ones, that he proceeds by means of doubt itself; thus, no impairment of his wisdom follows from this.

Since its occurrence depends upon doubt, the ascertainment of its validity is the means for that [ascertainment]; therefore, it is a means of knowledge, and that [occurrence] exists even when there is doubt.

If, by acting out of doubt, I should attain the result, then the certainty of its validity will be known precisely therein; it cannot be otherwise. Nor is such an objection reasonable here as to why one should engage in a means, for there is no other way [to reach the goal]. Indeed, no one attains the end without the means; thus, even one who acts out of doubt does not forfeit their status as a discerning person.

But surely, even in a dream, there exists cognition appearing as purposeful action; yet neither that [dream-cognition] nor its cause—the first [waking cognition]—possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge.

For that state is not at all delusory, as it is entirely devoid of external foundations; in those states, no correspondence with external objects exists. Furthermore, since the mind and mental factors are self-cognized and indistinguishable from one another, the distinction between the two states is clearly perceived thereby.
It might be thought: "If its validity is determined by something else, it follows that it is an object of cognition (*prameya*). But is this not indeed non-contradictory?

For its validity is proclaimed as being dependent upon the object to be grasped; its status as an object of cognition (prameyatva) is established through its apprehension by another [cognition]. Thus, due to this difference in dependence, the distinction between the state of being a means of valid cognition (pramāṇatva) and the state of being an object of cognition is not contradictory, just like the relationship between cause and effect.

Thus, when the status of a means of valid cognition is ascertained through the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*), there is no infinite regress, because further expectation has ceased; this is established.

Even when a cognition has arisen, it is not yet ascertained as valid so long as the purity of its causes has not been apprehended through another means of knowledge. Regarding this point, the wise have said that there is no infinite regress, because that purity is recognized through a non-dependent, corroborative cognition. For in the case of a proximate object, the purity of the causes is understood without effort simply by observing the correspondence of the effect. In the case of a remote object, however, the cognition produced by those [causes] is a valid means of knowledge, precisely because it is produced by them, just like this [cognition] which has a proximate object as its domain.

Just as when a conch shell stands before one, through the attainment of the action to be accomplished regarding its whiteness, it is understood that "the cognition arising from eyes afflicted by jaundice is not [correct]," so too, when the purity of the cause has been established, if at that very moment a cognition of a yellow form should arise regarding a conch shell made of gold, the determination of its validity arises from the production of a cognition by means of a pure cause, just like the cognition of a white form regarding a conch shell whose function has already been fulfilled.
Because the author of the Bhāṣya has stated that [the body] is not afflicted by hunger and so forth, this objection regarding infinite regress is raised here out of delusion.

The validity of the first [cognition] is not apprehended due to the suspicion that it may be produced by a defective cause; therefore, the knowledge of its purity is considered to be an additional requirement.

Thus, when the purity of the cause is ascertained through the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*), this [cognition] which occurs toward an object that has not yet performed its purposeful action is appropriately established as being inexpressible (*avācya*).

If self-validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) were established as the general rule (*autsargika*) everywhere, it would be set aside by two things: the cognition of a sublater (*bādhaka*) and the cognition of a defect in the cause (*kāraṇa-duṣṭatva*). Thus, validity is obtained precisely through the absence of the cognition of a sublater and the absence of the cognition of a defect in the cause; and in this way, for you, the determination of validity would result from something else (*parasmāt*). For instance, this "absence" (*tad-abhāva*) is, in your view, another means of knowledge called non-apprehension (*abhāva*), whereas in my view, it is an inference (*anumāna*) known as non-perception (*anupalambha*).

By this very same reasoning, invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) might also be intrinsic (*svataḥ*). For in that case as well, it can be argued that such is the logical principle (*nyāya*): therefore, intrinsic invalidity is established as the general rule (*autsargika*) everywhere; it is set aside only by the absence of a sublating cognition (*bādhaka*) and the absence of knowledge regarding defects in the cause (*kāraṇadoṣajñāna*).

Thus, because the intellect (*buddhi*) consists of cognition, its lack of validity is established; however, this is set aside by the knowledge of excellences (*guṇa*) arising from causes that produce knowledge of things as they truly are. If invalidity were dependent on something else, there would indeed be an infinite regress (*anavasthiti*), for this [invalidity] is dependent upon a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), while that [validity] is self-established and not contingent.

For it is thus: you assert that validity arises from the absence of sublation (*bādhaka*). Yet, this very absence of sublation is itself accepted as another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) called "non-apprehension" (*abhāva*). The validity of that [non-apprehension] is also stated to arise from the absence of sublation. If one desires this for each subsequent case, no finality is reached. Since the status of being an independent means of valid cognition is not established in the case of a sublating cognition, it cannot therefore negate the preceding cognition.
Furthermore, if validity is desired even without the absence of sublation in some cases, then what is the reason for such hostility toward that same state occurring in the first instance?

This subverting cognition (bādhaka-pratyaya) sets aside the preceding knowledge because it possesses independent validity; if this were so, what room would there be for doubt here? Yet, if the very independence of its validity is doubted, then the subverting cognition is itself called into question. This is contradictory, for doubt does not arise regarding that which has been ascertained.

Even in the view that validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), since certainty arises by its own inherent force (*svarasena*), why is an effort made to establish the existence of a sublater (*bādhaka*)? For instance, in a case where the certainty of a means of knowledge does not arise by its own inherent force, the sublater is established there without effort through the very power [of that lack of certainty]. Therefore, what is the point of speaking here of three cognitions for an investigator? There is no room even for one, because [validity] is certain intrinsically. If a doubt should arise because of uncertainty even when no sublater is perceived—on the grounds that non-perception is not invariably concomitant with the absence of a sublater—then, this being the case, why have you been satisfied with only three [cognitions]? For even when [the sublater] is not seen, a sublation might still be suspected here, just as before. As long as there is no correspondence with the result (*kārya-saṃvāda*), the suspicion of a sublater does not cease; therefore, the restriction to three [cognitions] is fruitless. Consequently, even by one who has not experienced a sublater, a sublater must be suspected again; for the true nature of a thing never remains fixed by mere deception. A cognition appearing as yellow in a conch shell, though it arises throughout one’s life and is devoid of a subverting cognition, does not become a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Since there is no cause for purification, no sublation would arise; nor would it arise from any other cause. Therefore, doubt does not cease.

Therefore, this suspicion exists only where there is delusion; however, for one who perceives purity and consistency, no suspicion would arise in the mind of the wise. Such a person does not become characterized by doubt in any worldly transactions, for their intellect is free from doubt upon seeing purity and consistency. As for that dull-witted person who nevertheless continues to harbor suspicion even here, I consider his state of being prone to doubt to be contemptible.

When the determination of validity is conceived as depending on differences in place, time, and circumstances, then the ascertainment of validity is clearly [dependent] upon another [means]. For instance, when the absence of sublation regarding place, time, and so forth is well-ascertained by means of another instrument of knowledge, there is an ascertainment of validity for the preceding cognition.

However, a legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*) such as that concerning debts, which requires three statements, consists of such a locus [of dispute] and should not be cited when establishing valid cognition (*pramā*). In that case, the plaintiff and defendant, repeatedly recalling [the matter], do not obtain the opportunity to perform a subtle examination of the actual object. Indeed, valid cognition must be established according to the actual state of things, not through deception; therefore, this legal proceeding has been cited as being dissimilar to the subject at hand.
Even the threefold truth of the gods is not a cause for certain conviction; for if that [truth] were not established from the beginning as being real, it could not exist even subsequently.
Since these two subsequent statements belong to that very same person, what distinction is there between them and the others, given the absence of conviction regarding the first?
Therefore, by the reasoning previously stated, there is likewise an infinite regress in your own position, since validity and invalidity are established accordingly.

The eternality of the Word has already been refuted by us in detail. Furthermore, according to your tradition, there exists no authoritative person (āpta) whose defects have been entirely exhausted. How, then, can one whose veil of ignorance is not yet destroyed be considered authoritative? For it is possible that his speech might otherwise [be false] due to the presence of defects.

Even if an authoritative person (*āpta*) has been established, by whom can his multitude of qualities be known, such that there might be a definitive certainty regarding a statement composed by an authority? Even one who possesses super-sensory vision and perceives the excellence of his qualities—what need would he have for a statement composed by an authority? For he, being independent of verbal testimony, understands the matter for himself; whereas another, due to not knowing the authority, does not comprehend the matter from that [statement].
And in the theory of intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*), since it is impossible for a certainty produced intrinsically to be destroyed, for what purpose would there be any prevention?
A statement is indeed not corrupted by defects that have been set aside by excellences; however, because those excellences are not certain, it is impossible to ascertain it with certainty.
Furthermore, the authorlessness of the Veda has already been refuted; therefore, since there is no author, defects cannot be without a locus on that account.

It has been stated how validity arises from the excellences (guṇas) as is logically appropriate; yet, when the excellences are not recognized, the absence of defects is not perceived. To claim that a statement is intrinsically valid as characterized by the absence of defects is not tenable, for the absence of defects cannot be characterized if the defects themselves are not recognized.

For a person is not perceived as "possessing a staff" unless the staff is known; thus, the claim that such a [staff] is self-evidently a means of valid cognition is refuted. Since the absence of defects is established through a means of valid cognition by way of the absence of non-valid cognition, it is logical that this is the definition of a [valid] statement; therefore, the establishment of valid cognition is extrinsic (*parataḥ*).

Cognition whose object is human defects arises only when those defects are present; indeed, in the absence of defects, how could there be a cognition [of them], given that their qualities are not known?
Defects such as hatred and delusion are sublated by compassion, wisdom, and so forth; for if there is no certainty regarding compassion and the rest, how can their non-existence be established?
At that time, however, the excellences (guṇas) do not function by way of being cognized; rather, when the absence of defects is to be known, they are helpful merely by their existence. (3044)

If there were no such doubt, nor likewise a perverted cognition—namely, "Do faults exist in this person who is esteemed as authoritative, or do they not?"—then doubt and error would never arise for anyone in this regard, so long as he is not understood to be a repository of a multitude of virtues.

Even if there is an absence of defects, if there is ignorance [of them], the ascertainment of intrinsic validity would still not occur; likewise, as before, doubt would persist regarding the speaker in that case.

Furthermore, since the absence of defects is unknown, how can the non-existence of the two types of invalid cognition be apprehended, by means of which there could be a certainty regarding validity? If, on the other hand, validity were understood as being intrinsic even without the apprehension of the non-existence of the two types of invalid cognition, then there would be no disagreement [regarding this] as in the previous case. Is this statement a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or is it not? It must be non-valid for everyone, because of the certainty of intrinsic validity [in that case].
Therefore, in all three cases—the absence of defects, the absence of invalidity, and the presence of excellences—an awareness must necessarily be admitted as a rule.
Is it invalid or is it valid? Thus is this [subsequent cognition] deliberated. How could that which is a factor for the determination of an object as it truly is be invalid?

If validity is established extrinsically, how is the determination of that validity reached? Or rather, how is it understood that this cognition possesses the nature of being valid? If you say, "Because of the absence of a subverting cognition," then the same problem recurs here once again: is that [subverting cognition] itself valid or not?

If validity were established extrinsically (*parataḥ*), then the validity of the subject under discussion would likewise be obtained extrinsically. Or else, how could that which is non-valid be a cause for knowledge corresponding to reality? If it is argued that the validity of this [non-valid cognition] is also understood through something else, then one must consider: "By what is its validity known? To say it is due to the absence of a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*) leads to an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭā prasajyate*).

Therefore, from the [presence of] excellences (guṇas) comes the absence of defects (doṣas); from their absence, there is the non-existence of the two types of invalidity. Thus, the general rule (utsarga) remains unrefuted. If it is argued that validity is thus ascertained everywhere, then here too, the previously mentioned host of defects would follow, and an infinite regress (anavasthiti) would ensue.

If this negation—that the existence of valid cognition consists in the absence of defects—were to be postulated as a mere [negative] assertion, its establishment would not be possible at all. Its establishment cannot be conceived through the non-perception of non-existence, nor is it tenable on the basis of non-perception due to the fault of infinite regress.
The non-existence of the two—defect and error—is understood through non-apprehension; the non-existence of that apprehension [too] would have to be known by another, leading to an infinite regress.

If that [cognition] consists of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), then because one perceives something else distinct from it, the non-cognition of defects would consist of the cognition of excellences; and furthermore, it would follow that its nature is the cognition of the intended valid knowledge (*pramā*). Moreover, there would be a cognition of the non-existence of the two types of invalid cognition, which is distinct from that [valid knowledge]. Or, if the non-existence of the two types of invalid cognition is known independently, how could you have the certainty that "the remainder is the nature of valid knowledge"? If you say it is by "presumption" (*arthāpatti*)—namely, through the impossibility otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*)—then such a certainty would indeed arise from presumption, or from inference (*anumāna*), or from some other source.

For this very reason, by that same logic, invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) is also shown to be inherent (*svataḥ*), since it can clearly be stated even in that case: "Therefore, due to defects, there is an absence of excellences; from their absence, there is the non-existence of the nature of valid cognition; thus, the general rule (*utsarga*) remains unrefuted. Since this state of being a general rule is constructed merely by one's own intention, it can be clearly asserted even regarding invalidity, just as in the case of [the rule for] valid cognition. Because validity is initially attained by a cognition through its very nature of being non-contradictory (*abādhātmatva*), it is subsequently set aside by the cognition of excellences arising from causes that produce knowledge of the object as it truly is. And because excellences are not being cognized, invalidity is not set aside. Since it remains unrefuted, that [invalidity] is likewise established as being inherent.
Whether defects exist or not is doubted in the case of human compositions; however, since an author is established even for the Veda, we have no doubt regarding its defects.
Therefore, that which is asserted as the authority of the Veda on account of its independence is unestablished, since even that depends upon an author.
If there is no corroborating cognition, or if the purity of its cause is not ascertained due to the arising of doubt, then the Veda lacks authoritative status.
Even for any other [cognition] to be a means of valid knowledge, such a connection must be postulated as the cause, because certainty is dependent upon it.

For when its status as a means of valid cognition is already established, certainty is produced by this [subsequent cognition]; it is not that a previously non-existent state of being a means of valid cognition is generated for it by this [cognition].

Even in the case of an object that perishes immediately after arising, there is indeed the status of being a means of valid cognition; for even though [the object] is not ascertained, that [status] certainly exists, since ascertainment also occurs according to the sequence already described.

If the cognition of the purity of the cause and so forth constitutes certainty, and if the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*)—characterized by the attainment of water, fire, and the like—is directly obtained; or if there is a habitual engagement that is independent of the arising of a result, then [certainty exists]. But when one is devoid of all such means, there is no ascertainment of validity. Therefore, although validity may exist in that case, it remains uncertain; being as good as non-existent, it is designated as "not existing at all."

The manifest lack of connection between auditory cognition and the eye and other [senses] is even more evident. For form, sound, and so forth, depend upon a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*); because they are inseparable from one another, they exist as a continuum where each is the cause of the other. Thus, their relationship is indeed very clear. Therefore, by means of that [relationship], the cognitions of those [objects] also [stand in relation to one another], just like smoke and the transformation of fuel. Consequently, auditory cognition would be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for that [object], since it is not connected with the cognitions of others.
But this cognition produced by another means of proof is certain; therefore, it is desired that there be a correspondence with the knowledge produced by another cause.

Thus, in the case of perception, the connection with other cognitions dependent on various sense organs is established as the cause; however, such [a connection] is not observed in the case of the Veda.
For instance, first there arises a visual cognition of water produced by the eyes; then follows another, based on the tongue and the body, which manifests as drinking, bathing, and so forth.

Even by means of a single statement, however, no correspondence with reality can be found regarding place, time, persons, and so forth, because doubt arises in every case. For instance, the Vedic revelation is heard equally stating, "From the Agnihotra sacrifice, heaven results"; yet, being devoid of the factors for certainty, it is merely like the croaking of frogs following the sound of a drum. Furthermore, differences of opinion among Brahmins are observed even concerning heaven and other such matters; therefore, no correspondence with reality is found here regarding persons and the like.

In the case of knowledge produced by an injunction, firmness [of conviction] was previously cast aside; for the existence of the object as it is grasped remains doubtful due to its similarity with other things.

How could this have been determined by Brahmins who do not perceive everything—that the cognition produced by *codanā* is consistent with all things? Furthermore, it has been asserted that even perception possesses validity through inference, because it is produced from pure causes; therefore, it is a means of valid knowledge, just like any other such [cognition].

Furthermore, the validity of every [cognition] need not be established by means of another instrument of knowledge, because it has been proven that there is no error regarding the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*).
Furthermore, since the inference arises from a logical mark known as its own effect (kārya), which is certain and non-deviant, there is no error whatsoever in that inference either.
However, in some cases, an error arising through the power of various causes of delusion is dispelled by this [means], because there is no certainty regarding that [object].
An object does not become manifest through the manifestation of the unmanifest; therefore, just as in the case of another's perception, it must be admitted that knowledge is known.
But because it is itself insentient in nature, the objects are not grasped by the sense organs such as the eye; rather, those organs serve merely as causes for the arising of cognition.
Therefore, in this context, being known is useful for validity, because an experience of an object is never obtained if it remains unknown.

Even if there were apprehension of one's own consciousness in this case, because the causes of error exist, there would be no certainty regarding its being such [as it appears]. At that time, even the existence of an object is not determined by us at all, because through perception based on similarity, the superimposition of something else is possible.
Just as knowledge arising from repeated practice is understood to be valid by itself, so too some false knowledge remains non-valid by itself.
Even when there is knowledge of a subverting factor or a defect in the cause, the aforementioned infinite regress remains; by that much alone, it is not possible to apprehend its falsity.

This means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is cognized as being in a state of mere origination; it is not [cognized] first by itself, because it is non-conceptual and because self-awareness is not accepted [by you]. Nor is it [cognized] by another cognition, because at that time [the latter] is not present, and because that [other cognition] would also be unmanifest, or else it would lead to an undesirable consequence.

Even in the case of the Veda, a subverting means of knowledge (bādhaka-pramāṇa) has already been stated in the form of inference; therefore, by the refutation of the Self and other [entities] taught therein, it is not logical for that [Veda] to be a valid means of knowledge. Furthermore, since its human authorship is established, the possibility of defective causes must be suspected. Or rather, just as fire possesses an inherent power, the capacity for false cognition might exist [in the Veda] by its own nature. Consequently, the cognition produced by the Vedic injunction (codanā) is suspected of having defective causes; and because its defects are suspected, it does not differ from those whose defects are directly perceived.

Therefore, even for the Veda, intrinsic validity is not tenable; thus, it must be accepted that its validity consists in being composed and transmitted by one who is ascertained to be free from defects.

For indeed, the more the teachers are possessed of passion, hatred, and the like, the more they protect their own recitation; do they not? For who is weak in what part, who has recited a section before whom, who would maintain the purity of the accents, and who would break a word at an improper place? Since there are those who are thus zealous in searching for flaws, how could he—not being careful—recite the Veda free from defects? If the men who study the Veda were pure and indifferent [to such matters], others would surely have reported: "The Veda has been destroyed by them! Consequently, over a long period of time, the Veda, neglected and ruined, would become something entirely different, reduced to a mere semblance. But because those who destroy the Veda are restrained by those possessed of passion, hatred, and the like, the Veda has always been protected and will not lose its true form.

And it is maintained that the entire world has never been otherwise than it is now; nor is a so-called "great dissolution" known to exist in an ultimate sense. This may indeed be so, for the textual readings are identical; however, the realization of the true nature of their meaning cannot occur without direct perception.

He in whose conscious mind all persons, as well as the entirety of place and time, appear clearly like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand, is capable of understanding even the identity of recitation; otherwise, how could there not be disagreement due to differences in place, time, person, and circumstance?
Furthermore, you have no means of valid cognition here to prove that "the world is exactly like this"; nor is it logical to assert the non-existence of even Saṃvarta based on mere non-perception.

But according to the position that validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), the Veda produces certainty by itself regarding its own meaning and nature; therefore, there is no possibility of delusion or the like. Consequently, since it stands as a ground free from ignorance, doubt, and error, not even a single young Brahmin would require instruction [regarding it]. Furthermore, for that whose foundation is unknown, even destruction is impossible; what kind of destruction could there be for that which is eternal and surpasses even the thunderbolt? If it is argued that there might be a change in its manifestation, that has indeed already been refuted in the case of the eternal. Therefore, the wise consider even the preservation of this [Veda] to be fruitless.

Therefore, let it be accepted that there exists a creator who perceives supersensuous objects, whose internal mass of darkness has been dispelled, and who knows the distinctions among the meanings of the Vedas.

Therefore, let it be accepted that there exists a creator who perceives supersensuous objects, whose internal mass of darkness has been dispelled, and who knows the detailed classification of the meaning of the Vedas.
If the mere negation of knowledge of the Dharma is what is intended here, by what means can a person who knows everything else be prevented?

Moreover, even if there is some specific subject under discussion, such as oil, water, or ghee, by means of that [knowledge], let it be that he is omniscient; even so, he is not prevented from being such.

When it is said that the entire world consists of the nature of existence and non-existence, why would an omniscient person not be accepted as such in brief? Thus, even by relying on the totality [of the world] through the summary of being objects of knowledge and objects of cognition, if one is omniscient, who is capable of refuting him?

Furthermore, all those who have ascertained all categories (padārtha) in their entirety, by virtue of knowing them, would all be omniscient (sarvajña) simply through being knowers of those [categories] and their treatises.
Likewise, who indeed would not accept as omniscient even one who, by means of the six instruments of knowledge, possesses discernment regarding the six objects of knowledge?
But for one who imagines [the Buddha] as a special case, seeing all objects directly through immediate perception, that imagination of his is both futile and false.
Who is capable of knowing all the atoms within a single body, as well as all its hairs and body hair?
An investigation into the knowledge of every detail and individual instance of all things, being undertaken like an examination of a crow’s teeth, is useless.
Just as the claim that one perceives all entities with the eye is fruitless, so too is the proposition of being an omniscient perceiver of everything devoid of result.

For it is only when one knows merely the dharma and adharma of another that the acceptance or rejection of the scripture composed by him is established. Thus, in attempting to prove that [the Buddha] possesses knowledge of every subtle distinction in the entire world, people labor in vain through their zeal for treatises and debate.

Since the impure tastes and so forth of one who perceives them directly through immediate intuition are self-evident (*svasaṃvedya*), who indeed would postulate such a person? Furthermore, no statement by the Buddha or others is observed that brings about an understanding of the meaning of the Vedas, Upavedas, Aṅgas, and Praty-aṅgas; how then could he be [rightly] called omniscient in vain?
And when there are many omniscient beings who all teach contradictory doctrines, and all possess equal grounds for their claims, which one indeed can be definitively identified as the true one?
If the Sugata is omniscient, what proof is there that Kapila is not? And if both are omniscient, how can there be a difference of opinion between them?
Regarding a single portion such as mathematics, all beings—including the Jinas, Buddhas, and other sentient beings—are equally truthful; no distinction can be discerned among them.

By whatever very same reason the omniscience of one [Buddha] is established, that [reason], through mere attachment to one's own side, applies to another as well. The very same refutations that the Śākyas utter with vehemence against the proof of the omniscient Jina, the Jainas employ against them. In that situation, how can a definitive conclusion be reached by means of their unstable, divergent proofs and refutations, which are swallowed up by the arising of counter-reflections?

When those who resemble the Omniscient have thus been slain by one another, Vedavādin will slay all the remaining few. Just as any medicinal herb touched by the tip of a mongoose's tooth destroys all snake venom even when applied by those merely playing, so too any reasoning—whether worldly or Vedic—residing in the mouth of a Vedavādin removes the poison of the knowledge of the Śākyas and others. Who indeed would postulate such a person, whose characteristics—such as being knowable (*jñeya*), being an object of cognition (*prameya*), and being a real entity (*vastu-sattva*)—are capable of destroying [the opponent] through logical reasons? He by whom an omniscient being is postulated on the basis of a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) surely perceives all tastes and other objects with his eye alone.
Whatever kind of objects are perceived by whatever kinds of means of valid cognition, as is observed by people at present, so it was also in other times.

Even those men who are seen to possess excellence through their wisdom, intelligence, and strength do so only by degrees of slight difference, and not by perceiving objects beyond the senses. For even a wise man, though capable of seeing subtle matters, excels other men without ever transcending the limits of his own species.

Among sounds perceptible by the ear, the excellence of a person is observed through the perception of sounds that are distant or subtle; it is not [observed] from the perception of forms and other [objects]. Furthermore, even with the eye, the illumination of distant or subtle forms is performed through the attainment of excellence; however, the seeing of sound and so forth is not [performed by the eye].

Thus, a great excellence is observed in the investigations of the sciences; however, that excellence is not obtained merely by knowledge of other sciences. Having mastered grammar, one's intellect regarding correct and incorrect words is greatly refined, yet it is not so in determining the lunar mansions, lunar days, or planetary eclipses. And even an eminent astronomer, though he understands the eclipses of the moon and sun and so forth, is not capable of knowing the grammatical correctness of words such as *ādi*. Likewise, even one who possesses an excellence of knowledge in the Vedas, Itihāsas, and other texts, is not capable of directly perceiving the creation, the deities, or the *apūrva* (unseen merit).
He who can leap across a space of ten cubits in the sky is not able to travel a single league, even with hundreds of years of practice.
Therefore, even by means of extraordinary cognitions that have reached an extreme distance, one is able to know only something slightly more [than others], but not that which is beyond the senses.

Whatever perception arises for one staying in a single room, his power would extend only there, and certainly not to another room. And as for those objects separated by great distances—by lands, mountains, and oceans, or by other continents and regions—who here could see them while remaining right here?

While Nala and Ṛtuparṇa—both of whom were experts in the science of horses and dice—were traveling together in a carriage, this speech was uttered by Ṛtuparṇa: "No one knows everything; an omniscient being is not possible. There is no single person in whom knowledge is ever fully perfected."
Furthermore, perception possesses not even the slightest capacity to perceive the future; nor can inference and the other means of knowledge arise without their respective marks (liṅga) and so forth.
Therefore, there exists no direct perceiver of objects beyond the senses; he who perceives through the eternal Word, he truly perceives.

One who, unable to tolerate this, maintains that even the Buddha and others possess knowledge of supersensory objects based on another human-authored scripture—since he is identical to that [other person], his own statement lacks authority, and the unreliability of the person must also be asserted by the very same reasons previously stated.
Even if beginninglessness is postulated for such individuals, because they occupy a position of non-authoritativeness, it does not differ from that [non-authoritativeness].

Therefore, those who act like Mīmāṃsakas assert a commonality of beginninglessness for the Buddhas, just as they do for those who study the Vedas. However, because their lack of knowledge is of a specific nature, they do not attain equality with [the Buddhas]. For in this way, validity and invalidity would both be beginningless.

Indeed, those valid cognitions, their fallacies, virtues, and defects, though beginningless, do not all become equal merely by virtue of that beginninglessness. Just as gold, which has existed from beginningless time as a factor in worldly transaction, remains as it is, so too is illusory gold; but does that [illusory gold] therefore become equal to it?
Now, the distinction is being stated for those who claim that the omniscience of the Buddha and others is equivalent to the eternality of the Veda.
An omniscient being is not perceived at present by people such as ourselves; nor is any part [of him] observed, nor is there any logical mark (liṅga) that could lead to his inference.

Furthermore, there is no scriptural injunction whatsoever that makes known an eternally omniscient being; for how could such a person be established by means of either a created or an uncreated truth?
If the omniscient one is recognized by others solely on the basis of his own words, how can the establishment of these two be achieved, given that they are mutually dependent?
The statement is true because it was spoken by the Omniscient One; therefore, his existence [is established]. How could both of these be proven without another established root source?
But why do you not likewise understand that there is an omniscient being from your own words—which, being devoid of a [valid] basis, were uttered by one who is not omniscient?
Many omniscient beings must be postulated in order to establish the existence of even one omniscient being; for anyone who is not himself omniscient cannot perceive an omniscient being.

Indeed, even by those who understand him at that very time, it is impossible to know that "this one is omniscient," for they are devoid of the knowledge of his cognition and its objects. Furthermore, since he would not be understood by anyone [who lacks such knowledge], his words cannot possess authority for them, just like the words of others, because their source is unknown.

Even if one were to corroborate the objects known by all his disciples, he would not be omniscient because of the exclusion of objects known by other people; nor is it possible to corroborate all knowable things known by all men, for there is no meeting with the people residing in the three worlds throughout the three times.

For even one who knows only a little can delude a few people, so that they—whose minds are bewildered by devotion—might accept him as omniscient. Some, though devoid of knowledge of the Dharma and other truths, are capable of correctly describing what has been eaten, what has been thought of, or objects held in the closed fist through deceptive sciences. Likewise, some who are skilled in illusions, sorcery, and the like, delude ignorant folk so that they appear to be omniscient.

Even he who is celebrated in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas as the omniscient Brahmā and others, whose knowledge is said to be unimpeded and whose detachment is likewise proclaimed—he too must be described as possessing these qualities only in a secondary sense, like the statements found in mantras and arthavādas. Alternatively, his "unimpeded knowledge" refers to the unobstructed knowledge of the specific subjects under discussion, such as dharma; for although his knowledge is unimpeded regarding the four subjects at hand—dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—it does not have all possible objects as its domain.

For it is not by mere non-obstruction that the capacity to have all things as its object is asserted; rather, it is called "unobstructed" because it encounters no resistance even with respect to its own objects. Furthermore, this knowledge that yields results has as its domain only those factors (dharmas) that are relevant; there is no purpose whatsoever in knowing everything, such as trees and the like. To the extent that knowledge is useful, it is not obstructed; therefore, it receives the designation of "unobstructed cognition."
Alternatively, that knowledge which is directed solely toward the self through the practice of meditation is called "unobstructed knowledge" because of its very lack of resistance.
Even Śaṅkara, who is heard of as possessing the ten imperishable qualities—namely knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty—is himself possessed of knowledge by virtue of being a knower of the Self.
Indeed, that alone is true knowledge which is the vision of the pure Self; whereas that which pertains to the impure and its causes is called ignorance.

Furthermore, since Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara have the Veda as their body, they are omniscient because the Veda consists of all knowledge; what then of a mere human? Where are mortal beings such as the Buddha, and where are these three supreme gods? To claim that they too are omniscient out of rivalry with them is merely a deluded view.
Even in the eternal Vedic scripture, there is the mention of the triad beginning with Brahmā; and because of that [triad's] eternity, the eternity of the Vedas is not impaired.

For those [eternal deities] are eternally endowed with eternal qualities and eternal actions; since it is possible for them to be designated by the eternal Vedas, they are not contradictory [to the Vedic tradition]. However, for one who is non-eternal, such as Buddha, there can be no comprehension through an eternal scripture. Furthermore, if the eternity of the scripture is accepted, the postulation of an omniscient being is redundant.

It is better to understand the Dharma through the teaching of the Omniscient One than [to rely on] a Dharma whose omniscience is taught by the Vedas, because that [Vedic] Dharma has become obscured. Knowledge of the Dharma and other truths that is not obscured is what is truly distinguished. Thus, the status of being knowable through scripture cannot be established for an Omniscient One.
If someone similar to an omniscient being were seen at present, then the existence of an omniscient being could be understood through the force of analogy.

Having observed that all men of the present day are non-omniscient, one determines the non-omniscience of all others through the analogy of similarity. For the teaching of the Buddha and others concerning the domain of dharma and adharma would otherwise be inexplicable if he were not omniscient. Thus, even when perception and other means of knowledge have failed to establish an omniscient being, one who establishes an omniscient being solely through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) [is acting correctly].

Alternatively, the means of proof employed here is the "inference from general observation" (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*). It is stated that [this inference] regarding the Omniscient One proceeds on the basis of observing elsewhere that [instruction] is preceded by knowledge. For whatever instruction there may be, it is all preceded by knowledge; just as the instruction regarding the potencies of *abhayā* and other [medicines] is of such a nature. This instruction concerning *dharma* and *adharma* is an instruction, and it was composed by him; therefore, its being preceded by his knowledge is inferred from this.

Since this [teaching] can be accounted for otherwise, this presumption (*arthāpatti*) is not tenable; for this very reason, even this inference (*anumāna*) does not stand as valid. For the instruction of the Buddha and others can be explained otherwise—as seen in dreams and the like through delusion, or as heard from those who are mistaken regarding the truth of the Vedas and so forth.

For those who do not know the Veda, the [teaching] derived from the Veda is impossible; whatever teaching they provide arises solely from delusion. Whether for the purpose of deluding their disciples or out of mere delusion themselves, the instruction of corrupt teachers in the world proceeds by relying on what is not the Veda.

If this [teaching] were rooted in the Veda, then its teachers would have provided instruction only to those who profess the Veda, just as Manu and others did. But since they gave instruction to fools and Śūdras, it is known by that fact to be corrupt, merely conventional, and like a counterfeit coin.

But those perfected ones such as Manu and others, who are primarily authorities for those learned in the three Vedas, whose works are relied upon by the knowers of the three Vedas, and whose utterances originate from the Veda—[it is these that are authoritative].
Neither is it possible for them to compose a treatise nor to transmit it to their disciples without having seen the Vedic sentences or having shown them to their pupils.

If one were to employ a proof such as, "There exists some person who is omniscient" or "That omniscience [exists]," that would be inferior to the very thesis [one intends to prove]. The object which one desires to establish is not expressed by this [proof]; furthermore, there is no purpose whatsoever in proving what is already stated [by the opponent]. If omniscience is asserted for the sake of establishing the truth of a particular person's scripture, that [truth] is not obtained merely by establishing the existence of an omniscient being in general. As long as the Buddha is not proven to be omniscient, his word remains false; yet if an omniscient being is established in some unspecified person, how can the truth of [the Buddha's] word follow from that?

If there were another omniscient being, then the truthfulness of one's own word would depend on that other; for only through their coreferentiality could there be a relationship of mutual dependence between the two.

Whatever exists in this world is indeed perceived by someone, because it possesses the nature of being an object of cognition, an object of knowledge, and a real entity—just like curd, form, taste, and so forth. If one were to specify "mere cognition" [as the subject], the deficiency of the subject (*pakṣanyūnatva*) would result; for the one intended as "omniscient" is not established in that way. If there were some other person besides the Buddha who had attained omniscience, what use would his knowledge be for establishing the authority of the Buddha’s words?

Having reached the ten stages and with all passion and the like extinguished, he perceives everything through a knowledge that is like pure crystal. Even while absorbed in meditation and maintaining a mental retention (*dhāraṇā*) whose object is all things, and though thus pervaded by all objects, he is not capable of providing instruction.
And when one teaches some single thing like an ordinary speaker, that is a teaching sung by one who knows only a portion [of reality], and it would not be the speech of an omniscient being.

When he has entered that meditative absorption and remains like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), teachings issue forth even from walls and other such objects according to his will. Through them, human beings come to know all matters they desire to understand, and they swiftly attain their benefits according to their spiritual capacity. While such descriptions are fitting for those possessed of faith, we, being lacking in faith, seek logical arguments.

Furthermore, those [teachings] that have issued from the hollows of huts and the like cannot be considered instructions imparted by a reliable authority (*āpta*). Nor would there be confidence in them, for one might wonder: "By whom were these proclaimed? Could they be composed by the Buddha? Or perhaps taught by those deceiving Brahmins who play with distant echoes? Or were they uttered by invisible beings such as petty *piśācas*? Therefore, those who consider themselves wise should not place their trust in them.

Thus, omniscience in men is, by its very nature, without foundation. Furthermore, this must be considered: how is an "all-seer" (sarvadarśin) conceived? Is he one who knows everything simultaneously, or in succession; and does he know it all as having a single nature, or according to its primary characteristics, or through some power (*śakti*)? Knowledge of contradictory natures, such as the pure and the impure, cannot occur in a single cognition; nor are there ever different modes of apprehension [simultaneously]. Who could possibly understand, even in hundreds of years, each individual thing—past, present, and future—as they are infinite in number, if done sequentially? He who understands everything through an undifferentiated nature does not perceive the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all things. What is gained by that omniscient one being a knower of only a general form (*sāmānyarūpa*)? A thing is never understood through a cognition that has a different form [from the object]. Therefore, would that single-form cognition be correct or false? If it were correct, then all perceived diversity would result in non-duality (*advaya*). Consequently, for you, the disciples, the Omniscient One, dharma and adharma, and their teachings would not exist, because their distinct forms would not be determined. If that single cognition were false, then the Omniscient One would be deluded; his word would not be trustworthy, being like the speech of a madman or the like. If he is desired to be the Omniscient One because he knows all actions along with their causes through a supernatural knowledge born of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), then there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—whether perception, inference, or verbal testimony, whether produced by him or otherwise—for his existence; thus, such a person does not exist. Whether simultaneously or in succession, how can there be an inference without an effect? Nor is there any capacity [to know all]; for if he were capable, then everything would be known, and all individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) would be masters in perceiving everything. Yet they do not perceive the whole, because their means are fruitless. It is without proof that there is some one person among all men who, having obtained a unique means, is the Omniscient One. Since no such omniscient being is logically possible in this way, human speech is not the cause for the comprehension of Dharma. Thus say the Mīmāṃsakas, who are devoted to the independent Veda. And the human origin of the Vedas has been established in detail. Therefore, there exists only a direct seer of supersensuous objects; no one perceives them through eternal speech, because that is impossible.

The capacity of an eternal word to produce the cognition of its own meaning arises neither from itself nor from anything else, because of the contradiction between successive and simultaneous production.

Therefore, [acts such as] sacrifices for heaven and so forth were revealed after being known by [the author] himself. You too must have such an author of the Veda, one who perceives objects beyond the senses, who knows the purpose of both Pradhāna and Puruṣa, or indeed one who knows all dharmas. Otherwise, in the absence of such a person, the authority of the Veda would not exist. Thus, by this acceptance of a knower of dharma obtained through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), this negation of yours—which was formulated at length—is sublated.

Furthermore, this which has been stated—that "O wise one, command is bestowed by power"—is indeed without reason. How could one possibly know the number of hairs on the head and body? To this, it is said that there is no contradiction in the statement that someone, by means of the lamp of stainless and unshakable knowledge, becomes one for whom all things are illuminated.
Nor can the non-existence of a thing be determined by mere non-perception, because perception is neither the cause nor the pervader of things.

In this context, the cessation [of an effect] is logical when there is an absence of its cause or its pervader; for that which possesses a cause and that which is pervaded arise from the same state of being, just as smoke and mangoes cease to exist in the absence of fire and trees. Otherwise, they would lack a cause altogether, and the consequence of their being unrelated would follow.

And when there is a certain determination regarding all objects through your own perception arising from some cognition of yours, you yourself would then be established as a knower of all things without effort; therefore, why do you harbor such hatred toward yourself, who are inherently omniscient?

For this very reason, this omniscient being is not established for you as an object of perception; for if he were an object of perception for you, then omniscience would belong to you effortlessly. How could he whose knowledge has all things as its object be an object of perception for you, unless that knowledge having all things as its object belonged to you as well?
Therefore, because the nature of causes, pervaders, and the self is by its very essence visible, that which arises from a specific non-perception cannot be established for an omniscient being.

And this threefold view proceeds in all its various forms through the application of distinctions such as those between various contradictions, non-attainments, and attainments. Once its powerlessness has been established against the Omniscient One in its form of primary divisions, the other [views] fall away without effort.

The relations of cause and effect, pervader and pervaded, and contradiction are established only when there is visibility; and since the omniscient Self is not visible as something possessing specific attributes, these [logical reasons] are incapable of negating it, nor is there any other factor for negation.
If an omniscient being is refuted merely on the grounds of not being perceived by you, then you would also have to refute the marriage of your own mother and other such matters.
If the existence of that cause is understood through the observation of its effect called "sound," then surely its effect is observed in some cases even in the absence of that [cause].
If its non-existence is not understood from the perception of something else, then how is that perception of another established as having that [non-existent thing] as its object?

Is this [reliance on instruction] not found in the case of an omniscient being as well? Furthermore, why is this other statement of your own not considered here: "Men are generally speakers of falsehood at all times; just as there is no trust in them today, so too there is none in their reports of past events"?

Or let there be no such instruction, or let it lack authority; nevertheless, you have all reached this certainty: "An omniscient being is not perceived. For such a certainty would indeed arise from perceiving the nature of all sentient beings. And it has been described that upon seeing that [nature], one becomes omniscient.

Otherwise, doubt is appropriate even regarding non-perception, as in the case of [the existence of] living beings. For it is suspected that some who are omniscient do indeed know [him]; he, being the light of the self, perceives himself by himself through his own nature. Since this too is suspected, the non-perception of all [beings] remains uncertain.
For indeed, by the word "all," all living beings are intended; and since he (the person) is not excluded from that "all," his non-perception remains unestablished.
If that alone were to be abandoned, what obstacle would there be here? For one's own passion and so forth do not cease simply because others are unaware of them.

Even some of limited vision perceive [the truth] through inference; for indeed, the intellects of certain individuals are occasionally sharp in specific matters. For instance, the proof of the momentariness of the Vedas, the earth, and so forth—which was previously stated with great clarity—was not noticed by the dull-witted. Thus, due to such doubt, even the absence of knowledge regarding this [truth] is not certain; for it is only those classes of people who are free from doubt that perceive non-existence.
Even in the absence of an inference, there is no certainty regarding non-existence from that [absence], just as fire and other causes exist even when their effects, such as smoke, have not yet begun.

Indeed, doubt regarding an object that has been perceived at some time is appropriate, as in the case of a post; for such a doubt relies upon two possible alternatives. Since both a post and a man have been seen at some time, it is reasonable for doubt to arise there. However, an omniscient being has never been seen in this manner.
O wise one, by this very same method, it follows without any doubt that for you, the non-existence of your mother’s marriage and so forth would result.
In this regard, we describe doubt even when there is an absence of valid cognition (pramā), because of the cessation of means of knowledge regarding both the existence and non-existence of things.

For when there is a defect in the eyes or other sense organs, there is no valid cognition even though the object exists; and even when those organs are unimpaired, [there is no cognition] due to the absence of the object, as in the case of a jar or the like. Therefore, since non-perception alone is observed in two ways, it is better to maintain doubt regarding an omniscient being even on account of the absence of such valid cognition.

For even though it exists, it would not be perceived by the dull-witted, just like any other conceptual construction; nor does it produce an effect, like fire that is directly hidden within iron, a ball, or charcoal. Or rather, its effect is invisible, like the passion born of another’s conceptualization. Even if its effect were visible, no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with it could be recognized. Since the knower of all things is always invisible to those of dull intellect, his existence cannot be established through inference. Furthermore, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been stated that is neither a cause nor a pervader of this entity; therefore, since its presence is seen even when that [means] is absent, there remains doubt regarding it.
Therefore, there is no means of valid cognition whatsoever that subverts the existence of an omniscient being; rather, the proof for his existence will be set forth in detail.
Even though the means for attaining the complete knowledge of all objects may be fruitless, the wise followers of the Sugata nevertheless exert themselves with a different kind of mind.
It is understood that there exists one who knows the means for attaining heaven and liberation; not only is he directly perceived, but he is also recognized as omniscient.

Therefore, when there is an absence of sublation and a clear proof exists, why do those of dull intellect disagree regarding the Omniscient One? Or, even if there were no proof for him, since a sublation is not ascertained, doubt would arise; but what is the basis for this certainty they hold?
The restriction that "only an injunction (codanā) is capable of making known [dharma] and nothing else" is indeed logical, provided that the non-existence of any other means is firmly established.

For the sake of establishing the one who knows the purpose of both Pradhāna and Puruṣa as the knower of all things, that means of knowledge has been declared first, and others will be explained later. Therefore, in the effort to establish the reality of the one who knows the subtle distinctions of the entire world, people do not labor in vain through the agitation of composing treatises or engaging in debate.

Since perception and other means of knowledge connected with all cognizers do not exclude [the existence of merit and demerit], it is not established that merit and demerit are cognizable solely through scripture. Furthermore, the effort made by others to refute the existence of an omniscient being—even though the position of the Mīmāṃsā school remains unproven by this much—is due to their extreme happiness and stupidity.

But those who, while not having destroyed their ignorance regarding the nature of dharma due to its unsevered roots, claim that there are omniscient persons—they have merely revealed their own cleverness.

If the tastes of wine, impurities, and the like were perceived through a connection with the sense organ of taste, then at that time they would indeed be objects of censure for him. However, by means of the mental consciousness alone, which arises from the cultivation of the true nature of reality, even those things censured in conventional truth are perceived without being actually reached [by the senses].

Precisely because the speech of the Protector (Tāyin) is not seen to propound the meanings declared in the Vedas and other such texts, he alone is conceived as omniscient; for he maintains a state unique among all non-Buddhist teachers, whereas [the Veda] speaks falsely regarding the self and so forth, having been studied through negligence.
The gate of Śiva is non-dual and terrifying to those with wrong views; therefore, selflessness was clearly taught by him for the benefit of those to be trained.

It is known to be unsuitable for those in saṃsāra, the remover of all misfortunes, and the supreme mine of jewels of virtue for those engaged in its practice. If even poets recognize such a supreme reality, who would not regard them as omniscient, knowing the primary goals of human existence?

And this knowledge of selflessness belonging to Vardhamāna and others is of such a kind; for all other sectarian teachers have perished through their adherence to the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). The [doctrine] of those by whom much that is improper has been stated—such as the existence of a permanent self (*syādvāda-akṣaṇika-ātmā*) and so forth—is contradicted by perception and other means of valid cognition (*pratyakṣādi-pramāṇa-bādhita*); how then could they be omniscient? How can the clear comprehension of supersensuous matters (*atyakṣa-adhigama*) be attributed to those who stumble even over this perceptible object well-known to the people of Vāhīka and elsewhere? In this way, their very lack of omniscience is clearly understood, because they are possessed of false knowledge and because they teach what is contrary [to reality]. Just as another person, deluded by the notion that a post is a man, acts upon that misconception, [so do these teachers]. [Omniscience] is to be known through all methods of investigation based on the establishment of the reason (*hetu-siddhi*). One is "all-knowing" (*sarvavit*) due to the correct knowledge of the true nature of all things. Therefore, the reason is not to be considered one whose negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful.
If the statements of these [Jainas] regarding the theory of manifoldness (syādvāda) and so forth were merely intentional, then what is intended by them as the actual nature of all things?

If it is argued that [the Buddha taught] selflessness, momentariness, and so forth because the All-Seeing One directly perceives the true nature of all things, then let him be [considered omniscient]; for he remains in agreement with all [sages] since they do not proclaim mutually contradictory meanings as the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

Because they directly realize the reality that has been explained and which pervades all things, the Sugatas are all-seeing. And for them, in such knowledge, their state of being a Sugata is not differentiated; for it is characterized solely by the possession of such praiseworthy knowledge.

Although an omniscient being has been established in a general sense as being possible, it is the Sugata who is specifically determined [as such], because he is invariably concomitant with that definition.
Even without specific qualifications being stated, some omniscient being may exist—one who knows the entire world exactly as it is, in its nature of being selfless and so forth.
When selflessness has been directly realized, no fault finds a footing, just as darkness cannot persist before a blazing lamp, for it is diametrically opposed to it.
And because of the specific nature of his direct realization, no defect remains along with its latent impressions; therefore, omniscience is established through liberation from all obscurations.
And this is accepted by the Sugata because he proclaimed selflessness at the outset; therefore, the Tathāgata stands at the head of all founders of religious systems.

Therefore, for that yogi who perceives reality in accordance with valid cognition, there is no equality of causal basis with others who teach contradictory doctrines. For those whose speech is agitated by the sublation of their claims through valid cognition, any connection to the power of suprasensory knowledge is indeed far removed.

It is coherent, possesses appropriate means, declares the goals of human endeavor, and is not contradicted in the slightest by the two means of valid cognition even with respect to perceptible objects.
Like pure gold, which undergoes no alteration when tested by heating, cutting, or rubbing on a touchstone, that which remains unchanged when examined in such ways is [the true].

The jewel of the Tathāgata’s word, which arises in accordance with the destruction of the darkness of all false doctrines and is not obtained by those with much defilement—therefore, those possessing supreme intelligence declare the Sugata alone to be omniscient; and they call him the best of physicians, for he knows the primary goal of human endeavor. Thus, the Sugata is the omniscient one, while Kapila is not; this proof has been clearly stated immediately above, yet it has not been perceived by the deluded.

Even the distinction [of these places] is determined from within what has already been stated: [they are] superior to the false shrines of Ṛṣabha and others because they bring about the destruction of Smara.

For what fool would consider one who knows the reality of the meaning of all scriptures to be ignorant simply because of their knowledge of common meals or their mastery of the alphabet? Therefore, whatever reason is used to establish the omniscience of one person does not apply to another, because that specific causal basis is absent in the other case.
The Digambaras are incapable of those very criticisms that the Śākyas, free from agitation, utter against the teaching of the omniscient Jina.

That reality which has been established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through proven logical necessity (*pratibandha*) is established in the Buddhist doctrine, but not so in other systems. Therefore, let a definitive conclusion be reached sufficiently by means of their respective distinct proofs and refutations, which are like reflections that have emerged and then vanished.

But for omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), there exists no contradiction whatsoever—whether direct or otherwise—with [the properties of] being an object of knowledge and so forth; because it is established as being an object of knowledge through its exclusion of non-objectivity and the like, whereas that [omniscience] does not have a fixed characteristic through its exclusion of omniscience itself.
Furthermore, this omniscience does not have its causes fully present anywhere; for when qualities such as existence arise later, that which had previously occurred ceases.

Moreover, when that which is not contradictory [to the subject] is enjoined, the exclusion of something else is not logical; for while the presence of one form is established, the absence of another taste is likewise understood.
