In this regard, concerning the status of being a speaker implied by the word "etcetera," whoever conceives of a certainty regarding its exclusion [from an omniscient being] based on mutual contradiction—thinking that while there is speech in the case of conceptualization (*vikalpa*), an omniscient being is free from conceptualization, and that an object is not apprehended by a cognition permeated by verbal expression—even those who conceive of the speakerhood of an omniscient being as following upon discursive thought (*vitarka*) do not [accept it] when the possibility of speech is considered; nor is an omniscient being admitted to exist through the operation of conceptual cognition. For at the very moment of such conceptualization, the status of being a speaker is not established.

It is not logical that this [scripture] was composed by one who is not omniscient; rather, because it implies omniscience, it must be consistent with reality. Just as someone, having personally experienced heat, later speaks of it, there is no contradiction with the actual object because the speech arises from the experience of that object. Therefore, at the time of [the Buddha’s] omniscience, this reason (hetu) is unestablished; however, at the time when the discourse occurs, it would be the establishment of what is already established.

Even if you were to exclude the capacity for cognizing all objects, the flaw of a doubtful negative concomitance (*saṃdigdhavyatirekitva*) would still persist in that very state. Even if the capacity for verbal expression and activity is accepted as the reason (*hetu*), the defect of a doubtful negative concomitance continues to follow.

"By means of the momentum of the accumulation [of merit and knowledge], teaching proceeds even for the Protector who is free from conceptual construction, through the mechanism of the spinning wheel"—those wise ones who say this [must also face a problem]. For even with respect to them, the status of being a speaker is not established, since what is considered by the world to be "speaking" is merely a matter of mental determination (*adhyavasāyika*). In such a case, the reason would possess a doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatirekitā*). Now, on whose view would there not be the fault of the reason being unestablished (*asiddhatā*) here, given that [the opponent's position] is untenable?

It is said: If you consider "the state of being a speaker" (*vaktṛtva*) to be an independent probans (*sādhana*), then it would be either unestablished in its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*) or unestablished due to doubt (*sandigdhāsiddhatā*). Since there is doubt regarding this matter, its unestablished nature due to doubt is certain. Therefore, you must state such an argument as a *prasaṅga-sādhana* (reductio ad absurdum). In that case, the property (*dharma*) is revealed by means of scripture alone; however, there exists no further indicator (*jñāpaka*) for establishing its actual existence.

Thus, who would not conceive of that [Self] for whom reasons characterized by perishability, substantiality, existence, and so forth, are powerless to strike? Such reasoning—whether worldly or Vedic—residing in the mouth of the Veda-proclaimer is incapable of removing the poison of the fierce serpent that is the Śākya; for in this world, even when bitten by sight-poisoned snakes, a dull-witted Brahmin of little power may survive, but reasoning residing in the mouth of the Veda-proclaimer, though virtuous, is ill-fated, like a necklace placed upon one's feet due to its location on an inferior support.

It is impossible to say that smoke is non-deviant from fire, because according to his view, smoke exists elsewhere; since it has the nature of a single entity, it exists even upon the ocean. If fire is present there as well, then what would be the basis for negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)?

Or else, why should there not be a cognition of an effect possessing that same form even in that case? Or, if the self-nature is indeed different, let there be a real distinction between the entities.

It is postulated that the mental cognition which arises through the power of the repeated practice of reality as connected with all things is the sole means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). But [if this were so], visual and other sensory cognitions would not be means of knowledge; therefore, why is this said? "Surely he perceives all tastes and so forth with his eye. Furthermore, mental cognition consisting of the experience of form and other objects is established; there is no dispute even for the opponent regarding this much of a matter. For by him (the opponent), memory is described as having form, sound, and so forth as its domain, and in dreams, mental cognition consists of the experience of all objects. Therefore, if an omniscient being is postulated on the basis of a mental cognition whose objects are unrestricted, why would he perceive tastes and so forth with his eye? This fault would indeed arise if that [omniscience] were postulated as being purely visual. However, in brief, one knows taste and so forth by means of the mind alone. Even where excellence is observed, it does not exceed its own specific object; it may exist in the perception of distant or subtle things, but not in the function of the ear regarding form. Thus, such undesirable consequences as stated by others do not apply to us, because we maintain that excellence in mental cognition occurs precisely without exceeding its own object. Just as the perception of certain types of objects by certain types of means of knowledge is seen among people now, so it is for us at another time as well.

Or perhaps knowledge may be entirely pure, having all things as its object; for some excellence in the cause is expected to produce some excellence even in the fruit. It is not the case that because *āmalaka* fruits are seen to be small in the desert, they must all be of that same nature in reality elsewhere as well. From this [principle], the scriptural statement that "serpents hear with their eyes" is also possible; for the karmic powers of sentient beings are indeed diverse.
He for whom every object existing in the three times appears with its capacity thus determined is truly fit to speak in this manner.

By whatever types of means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) people of the present age perceive objects of such-and-such a kind, so it was in other times as well. Even now, the capacity of the world cannot be known by you, who are a mere living being, because all capacities remain undetermined. Alas, omniscience would consist in knowing the capacities of all sentient beings without exception; nor can this be established through inference, for there is always the suspicion of its being otherwise.

The possession of qualities such as wisdom by persons is also perceived through the application of knowledge of objects beyond the senses; for there exists a science known as *īkṣaṇikā* and the like, which, when well-cultivated within the field of knowledge (*vidyā*), brings about the thorough comprehension of another's mind even in this very life. Furthermore, they know and speak of things—whether past, present, or future—that were neither heard, inferred, nor seen in this life. Men possessed here by the power of various mantras, lordly serpents (*nāga*), demons (*rakṣas*), spirits (*yakṣa*), and so forth, manifest their speech in accordance with reality. Even if one thinks, "Let it not be seen," and so on, there is no subverting evidence here; thus, the non-existence of such [powers] is not established.

And since the author of the Veda has been established by the manner just described, you must necessarily admit a person who perceives objects beyond the senses. Therefore, a wise man would be capable of seeing subtle matters; even while remaining within his own class, he would surpass other men by transcending them. Just as the power of the ear and other senses is distinguished with respect to their own respective objects, so too would it be for the mind through specific qualities such as the practice of yoga.
For instance, a form situated at a great distance is perceived by vultures, and likewise, hidden treasures and the like are seen through the use of perfected eye-salves and other such means.
Thus, through the distinction of their respective destinies, gods and others may perceive things that are subtle, concealed, and so forth, in accordance with the nature of their own rebirth.

Furthermore, due to the excellence of the practice of yoga, the mental cognition of yogis becomes preeminent; there is no contradiction in this. If, however, it is argued that even in the absence of [extraordinary] movement, yoga, and so forth, there might still be an excellence in knowledge, this is rejected, for a fruit cannot exist without its cause. Just as the knowledge of other scriptures is not obtained by means of that [knowledge] alone, so too, in the absence of each successive cause, there can be no excellence.

Nor is it claimed that omniscience exists merely from the knowledge of one part, such that through the knowledge of the Vedas and so forth, there would be direct perception of heaven and the like. Rather, since an increase is observed through the practice of wisdom, compassion, and other qualities, another excellence is understood to arise from that which is thus increasing. Because these are qualities of the mind, their attainment of a final limit is possible; due to great practice, they reach a culmination in the cognition of all objects, just as with the quality of cruelty. For wisdom, by its very definition, consists in the comprehension of dharma and artha; if even a single [object] is not fully known, it remains incomplete.

Or, those things which proceed from seeds of a similar kind possess the nature of ultimate growth due to the specific excellence of their refinement (*saṃskāra*), like rice and so forth; and compassion, intelligence, and the rest are likewise capable of such growth, possessing the aforementioned properties, whereby, upon their increase, there arises omniscience.

Those things which possess the nature of being subject to diminution will undergo absolute diminution when their antidote is present, just like the impurities in gold. Likewise, these afflictions, cognitive obscurations, falsehoods, and so forth, are understood to possess the aforementioned characteristics; thus, upon their abandonment, the intellect becomes stainless. Or, if it is possible that these things possess the aforementioned properties, then an antidote capable of uprooting them utterly must likewise exist.

Because it is bound to the vision of reality (*tattvadṛṣṭi*), an absolute diminution of this internal darkness is understood to occur, just as in the case of external darkness. When that [darkness] has been diminished, great and unimpeded knowledge proceeds independently throughout the entire sphere of the knowable.

Those qualities which reside in a stable substratum and have been cultivated in some way, require no further effort for their maintenance once they have become established, provided there is no obstacle. Through the excellence of refinement, these qualities reach their ultimate limit, as clearly as the purity of gold. These qualities—wisdom, compassion, and so forth—possess the characteristics just described; and when they reach their ultimate limit, omniscience becomes radiant. There is no deviation from this rule in the cases of jumping or the heating of water; for jumping does not result merely from the act of jumping itself, but rather from strength and effort.

Or perhaps even leaping (*laṅghana*) reaches its ultimate limit through the specific power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), speed, and so forth, arising from its own causes. Thus, there is authoritative tradition regarding the attainment known as "mind-swiftness" (*manojava*), according to which a master travels even great distances by mere thought. Nor is its non-existence established merely by a lack of observation; furthermore, no one is capable of stating any subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against this.

A young royal swan is not yet able to depart even from its own nest; yet, through the distinction of practice, it reaches even the far shore of the ocean. Just as its movement arises from the distinction of practice conditioned by its support, why should a movement even greater than that not be possible for one of such a kind? For while in the stage of a Bodhisattva, he is not yet able to attain such a state of motion; but once he has attained a distinguished meditative absorption (*samādhi*), the Sage would be capable of it.
If one can leap across a space of ten cubits, such power would exist for that person even when traveling a great distance, because of that same cause.

When water is brought to heat, its destruction occurs because its substratum is unstable; therefore, for what [quality] could there be excellence in what [substratum]? However, the continuum of the mind is the substratum for mental qualities; because it functions through connection with that support, it never ceases in any way.

To the extent that the flood of qualities turns toward this [mind], to that same extent it becomes increasingly more luminous. This mind is luminous by nature, having the realization of reality as its essence; since it abides thus by its very nature, the defilements are considered to be merely adventitious.

If the mind were indeed restricted to another cognition as its object, then, because there would be no apprehension of [that other] unestablished entity, the cognition of the object would be impossible. Therefore, the mind possesses the nature of self-cognition because it is luminous; and this self-awareness remains established as having an unimputed form.

Therefore, once one has become habituated to the path, there can be no overcoming of it by those defects such as passion and hatred, for they were already weakened beforehand. And because the path—which washes away and destroys all [defects]—has become second nature, its loss does not occur without effort; yet effort does not arise without seeing its virtues. Thus, the Jina is understood to be omniscient, adorned with a multitude of qualities that are stainless and unshakable, his self being imperturbable against the winds of defects.

Furthermore, whatever things are intensely meditated upon appear with perfect clarity once that meditation reaches its consummation, just like the objects of desire and so forth. And all phenomena are meditated upon for a long time and in manifold ways by the Great Beings (*mahātman*) in their true form—namely, as empty, selfless, and so on. O one of great intelligence, the reality of the form consisting of emptiness, selflessness, and so forth has been established; therefore, that [cognition] is held to be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it arises from the cultivation of the actual nature of things.

Direct perception is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it manifests clearly and accords with the reality of the object, like the appearance of blue and other colors arising from the basis of the eyes and other senses. Since a clear manifestation of all phenomena can occur simultaneously within a single cognition, let it be understood that this is the case for everything. Because they are thus being vividly contemplated—just as in the cases of a woman, one’s own son, or a thief—even meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), which arises through the mere power of intention, is not difficult to achieve.

All phenomena are clearly manifested by a single cognition that reaches the pinnacle of cultivation, because they possess the nature of real entities, existence, and so forth, just like a beloved person and the like. Thus, for whomsoever there exist reasons—characterized by substantiality, existence, origination, and so on—that are capable of establishing it with certainty, who would not prove him to be the Omniscient One? Herein, he is established as the All-Knowing One, who encompasses the entire circle of objects of knowledge within a single moment of cognition, and who has become the crest-jewel upon the heads of gods and asuras.
Indeed, those [qualities] such as dharma were known by you even without anyone's instruction, because they were taught by the True Self, just like the purity of gold and other [precious substances].

Once the human origin of the Vedas is established, the proof is already proven; for there can be no true instruction regarding what is unknown, as such would be merely accidental on the part of a man.

The extraordinary power of mudrās, maṇḍalas, mantras, and so forth—seen in the liberation from piśācas and ḍākinīs, the removal of poison, and the like—is the stainless direct knowledge of the Sage, Tārkṣya, and others; for if that did not exist, how could it have been described?
Nor can there be knowledge [of it] through inference, because it has not been previously perceived; for that reason, the observation of the relationship of the inferential mark (liṅga) is impossible.

Having heard this, and because it has not been stated by anyone else due to an identical line of inquiry, and because such a thing is not of a nature that arises by chance or contradicts [the truth], it is cultivated in this way; this teaching is indeed for the sake of this [liberation] alone, and no other cause should be imagined. For if the activity were produced by another cause, then indeed such a doubt would arise. Just as for one whose mind is distressed by thirst while approaching a river, the occurrence of finding coral is considered a matter of chance.
This was not spoken for those of deluded minds whose hearts are distracted; for this is a definitive, unspoken [truth], which is preeminent and brings about the fruit.

He who reveals a truth not heard or inferred, being intent upon that goal and having directly perceived its nature, is a teacher of such a kind—just as another person who has directly seen water and the like is a communicator [of it]. The Best of Sages spoke of the truth not heard or inferred, which pertains to his own goal, concerning the seals (*mudrā*), mandalas, ritual procedures (*kalpa*), and so forth, which transcend the senses and whose efficacy is unknown to others, through his firm certainty.
Therefore, by means of superior cognitions that operate through the power of skillful methods, everything—even that which transcends the senses—can be known by those who possess them.

The perception that arises for one situated in a single room has its power restricted to that very place, and not at all in another room. This [conclusion] is appropriate for you to determine only when there is an experience of the capacity residing in all sentient beings; otherwise, what would be the basis for it?

If, by using oneself as an example, one were to determine the absence of capacity in others based on reasons such as "being a person" and so forth, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the effect [of inference]. For in that case, once your own dullness is established, all the wise would become dull-witted by the very example of yourself.

"There is no finality of knowledge in any person whatsoever"—this statement as well has been uttered merely as a word, without any basis. Or rather, such a statement was proclaimed by Ṛtuparṇa with reference to beings equal to himself—those who are dull-witted and of impure intellect. Furthermore, the proof for the possibility of an omniscient being has been stated in detail, and the refutation previously advanced by others against him has been rejected. Alternatively, even if that proof of his possibility were not stated, his existence is understood simply through the removal of refutations. For when no refutation is seen and no proof is revealed, doubt arises; by means of that doubt, he attains the status of being possible. And when he is thus rendered possible, the restriction—that "Dharma is characterized by the Veda alone, which is independent"—is thereby established.
And so too would there be the capacity for direct perception regarding future objects of knowledge; this has been stated by the Yogins in their examination of the three times.

Alternatively, through the power of yoga, the mental [cognition] of yogins may become vivid, appearing as if it were already present though not yet born, and free from dependence on signs or inference.

The cognition of the manifestation of its own nature has that specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object; because it is experienced as a clear manifestation, it is accepted as perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, there exists a direct seer of supersensuous objects; however, because an eternal word does not exist, no one perceives [them] by means of it.
The wise declare that the Sage’s cognition of objects beyond the senses arises from the aforementioned inference, and not from any other source, such as a fabricated scripture.

The lack of beginning (anāditva) is not asserted for agents, artificial sentences, or [human] utterances for the sake of establishing their validity; for that [lack of beginning] exists even in what is invalid. For instance, there is no validity for the atheists and others, nor for their words, nor for the Vedas and their expounders, despite their being without beginning.
Indeed, the beginninglessness of the artificial words of speakers is asserted [by others]; we reject it not out of rivalry, but solely for the sake of establishing their lack of authority.

The speakers [of the Vedas] are equal to the authors [of other texts], and the authority of the Vedas depends upon them; for the cognition of their meaning arises from explanations composed by those very authors.

Therefore, the Vedic sentences do not possess authority because of their dependence [on others]; nor does such authority belong even to those speakers who themselves perceive *dharma*, for they too are dependent. Even if one were to postulate that such speakers have no beginning (*anāditva*), this would not differ from the position of an atheist (*nāstika*) and the like, since they remain situated in the same state of non-authority. Because there is no distinction between their ignorance and the ignorance of others, everything here becomes equal; thus, neither authority nor non-authority could be beginningless in this way.
Or rather, there is indeed this distinction regarding the Sage and his words: he himself perceived the Dharma and, being filled with compassion, spoke it.
That from which the accomplishment of worldly prosperity arises, and from which the highest good arises—that is defined as Dharma by all wise men.
As it has been said: "From the performance of the rules regarding mantras, yoga, and so forth, according to the prescribed method, even visible results such as wisdom, health, and power arise."

From the vision of the selflessness (*nairātmya*) of all phenomena, as revealed by that [vision], there is the cessation of the flood of afflictions (*kleśa*) arising from the view that effects pre-exist in their causes (*satkārya*). The view of a sentient being (*sattvadṛṣṭi*), which takes the form of the perception of "self" and "mine," proceeds; and when there is the conceit of "I" and "mine," every affliction proceeds. That demonstration of selflessness is the adversary of the view of a sentient being. When that [demonstration] has become habitual through practice, the [view of a sentient being] ceases. And the mass of afflictions rooted in that [view] is eliminated due to the absence of its cause. When that [view] does not exist, existence (*bhava*), which is caused by it, is not born again. Liberation (*apavarga*) is proclaimed to be the absolute release from that. Therefore, the vision of selflessness is the peerless door to auspiciousness (*śiva*). All non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) desire liberation through the cessation of the ego-conceit (*ahaṅkāra*); yet, as long as the existence of a self (*ātman*) is maintained, the ego-conceit does not cease. This is because the efficient cause remains present and the object [of that conceit] is not refuted. If that object were refuted, however, [the conceit] would be absent, and a cognitive inversion (*viparyāsa*) would result.
It is not logical to say "I do not exist" if indeed an "I" exists; for by necessity, one who knows reality would attain nirvana, or else [the claim that one does not exist] is false.

Therefore, although in other religious systems there may be a slight attainment of worldly prosperity through the abandonment of the ten unwholesome actions, there is not even the slightest attainment of liberation; for, being characterized by the view of a self, the root of the afflictions has not been uprooted.
Furthermore, those ten wholesome paths of action which were proclaimed by the Protector become exceedingly powerful when embraced by right view.

But those who are enveloped by the view of a self (sattvadṛṣṭi) are possessed of error; therefore, being impure, a pure fruit does not arise from them. Thus, regarding the Supreme Sage, the teacher of the reality of phenomena (dharmatattva), who would a person of sound mind say that he does not himself see the Dharma?

The protectors [the Buddhas] proclaim that the omniscience of the All-Knowing One and the eternity of the Veda are equal; however, the wise do not accept this, because such eternity is impossible. For it has been stated that there is a sublation of that [eternity], due to the contradiction between succession and simultaneity. It is not logically tenable in any way for cognition and the like to be its effect.

"Is it because you yourself do not see an omniscient being now? Or is it because [he is not seen] by all?"—if this is what was stated, the refutation here has been explained in detail. For your non-perception (*anupalambha*) alone is inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*). Furthermore, the exclusion of others who possess different vision is doubtful and thus not a valid proof. Nor can the conceptualization that "he did not exist" be established in the same way as his negation; for such a claim is improper, since even regarding the past, it is impossible to effect such a total negation.

It might be thought: "That which has passed away is empty according to you, the All-Seeing One, because it is time, just as the present time is perceived. This is not a valid proof, because its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful; for it is not certain that this present time is empty [of a perceiver].
Furthermore, because the causal complex is absent, that which is called "past" does not exist in the present; yet, as in the case of Rāma and others, why should it not be possible in a past time?

And having established that wisdom and the other [faculties] possess the nature of being the subject (dharmin), the gender has been declared; yet no such gender is observed there, nor is existence (sattā) established as something to be proven.
However, we do not establish the existence of an omniscient being through scripture; for when the previously mentioned inferential mark exists, who indeed would speak of it on the basis of scripture?

But if you accept that the Veda is the source of valid authority, then why, O fools, do you not understand the Blessed One’s omniscience? For it is clearly recited in another branch [of the Veda] by learned Brahmins that the Blessed One, the best of sages, is omniscient by name as the "Nimitta."

He who, having manifested himself in a dream as a six-tusked white elephant, was born as a Bodhisattva, an ocean of virtues; he shall become one whose fame is proclaimed everywhere, an omniscient one, compassionate by nature, a pure one who has attained the state of immortality, and indeed the father of all the world.

Now, if it is claimed that this other recension (*śākhāntara*) is not accepted as being included within the Veda, then no reason for this can be determined here except for your own prejudice. Furthermore, those characteristics such as accents and so forth, which are well-known from the revealed scriptures (*śruti*), can be established even here [in this recension], since they arise solely from human intention.

But surely, no scripture that is eternal can be found here that has as its primary purport the prohibition of falling; for if it were eternal, it would be a mere explanatory eulogy (arthavāda), whereas if it had that as its primary purport, it would lack eternity.
And once the eternity of the scripture is established, the postulation of [a creator] is useless; for from that [scripture] alone, men will come to understand dharma.

Indeed, even in this well-known Veda, there is no eternality, since its result consists of cognitions that arise immediately after effort and cognitions that occur in a temporal sequence. However, once the authority of this well-known [Veda] is admitted, it follows for you that authority must also apply to other branches, because they too possess the nature of the Veda.
Alternatively, you must certainly establish through reasoning that it is not the Veda; otherwise, for you, its status as something not stated in the Śruti would remain doubtful.

Let the Veda be eternal and let it have that [dharma] as its purpose; however, if it were directed toward that [purpose], why would it not be non-eternal? Because it would be subject to destruction upon the completion of its purpose.
If this is so, how can clarified butter, wild rice, gold, matted hair, and the like—which are impermanent—be said to exist by means of that which is an eternal self?

If it is argued that even in that case [the word] "genus" (*jāti*) is eternal, then that too has been refuted. Furthermore, if the word denotes only that [genus], there would be no cognition of clarified butter (*ājya*) and so forth from the word. If the word were to denote that [substance] as well, why would its eternity not be lost? Therefore, let there be a form (*ākṛti*) even in the case of the Omniscient One; by that, the eternity of that [form] is established.

And at that time, the determination of the meaning of Vedic statements would have to occur independently—either from the Veda itself or from another person whose mind is overcome by delusion and the like. Consequently, regarding the Vedic revelation, "One who desires heaven should offer the Agnihotra," what proof is there that its meaning is not rather that "The Jina is omniscient"?

Because he clearly teaches only heaven and liberation, and because he possesses complete knowledge of the primary goal, he is understood to be omniscient. Of what use is his knowledge of the number of grains of sand in the ocean? Therefore, what is the point for us in perceiving his knowledge of other such matters?

"He too must be spoken of only in a secondary sense, because he possesses the nature of a mantra or an explanatory passage (arthavāda). This restrictive rule would hold true only if an omniscient being were refuted; however, since the absence of the previously mentioned subverting arguments has been established in detail, this restriction regarding a secondary sense remains doubtful, as the primary meaning is also possible.

If the non-obstruction of the mere cognition whose objects are phenomena and so forth is described as being accompanied by its fruit, then clearly the world has been conquered by the Buddhas; for it was previously established that their unobstructed knowledge, along with these [qualities], is the primary cause for both worldly prosperity and liberation, and is exceedingly clear.
Furthermore, that cognition which occurs within oneself alone, set in motion by the practice of meditation—its non-obstructed nature has already been established by them previously.

This indeed is that knowledge which is the vision of the pure self, because of the realization of "mind-only" (cittamātra) as it is free from adventitious stains and devoid of [the duality of] stain and the stained. It has been previously established that cognition (buddhi) possesses neither the form of the object known nor the subject who knows; and it has been revealed by the Fully Awakened Ones to be empty of the affliction of duality. By this, those of great intelligence are proven to possess a wisdom not common to the cycle of existence (saṃsāra), since their teachings continue to shine even today through the power of their sovereignty.

In the mind, which is luminous by nature and unstained by the forms of duality, who—being one whose self is not deluded by those dual forms—could conceive of it otherwise? Furthermore, when there is the realization of the selflessness of both [subject and object], the defects such as passion and hatred, which arise from conceptualizations of women and so forth, are extinguished without effort. This is that supreme reality which the Proclaimer of Truth taught; it bestows all prosperity and is beyond the reach of Keśava and others.

For it is known by others that the stable self is like a pure crystal; yet that [notion] of theirs is an error, because of the refutation of a permanent self. If the cognition grasping a self were to arise from the self itself, then it would follow that there would be simultaneous cognition of all selves. Alternatively, if it did not arise from that [self], or if it is admitted to be eternal, then it could not have that as its object, just like the mind of another person.

Because it has been extensively established that the characteristic of being an object of apprehension is absent, this very cognition is not [the self], since the vision of the pure self is like the sky. Furthermore, even if the nature of the self is accepted as being of the form of cognition, there would still be no such apprehension because of the existence of a distinction between the seen and the seer. If it is maintained that that cognition is of the nature of self-luminosity, then self-awareness (svasaṃvitti) follows, and the intellect would become something directly perceived (pratyakṣa).

Furthermore, there is no connection whatsoever between Brahmā and the others and the Veda, because they are distinct, because [the Veda] is eternal, and because it lacks dependence on them—just like anything else. Consequently, the claim that Brahmā and the others have the Veda as their body is inconsistent; likewise, the claim that the Veda consists of all knowledge is untenable, since its meaning cannot be definitively determined. Moreover, the Buddha has been established as omniscient through his own independent authority; he is not, however, postulated as having the Veda as his body in the manner of Brahmā and the others.
Because they exist outside the cycle of existence consisting of the five destinies, Buddhahood is not considered by us to be mortal; rather, it is regarded as such a transformation-body (nirmāṇa).
In the delightful city of Akaniṣṭha, which is devoid of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, the perfectly awakened Buddhas attain enlightenment; it is their emanation that awakens here in this world.

But how can you determine their mortality independently? For that is not possible through the scriptures of others, as such [scriptures] do not exist for them. Nor do we assert that they are omniscient out of rivalry with them; for who would conceive a rivalry between sky-flowers and things that are real?

For it has been established that [entities] are devoid of form due to their lack of all causal capacity; therefore, the Śiva-triad and others postulated by our opponents do not exist among eternal things.

Furthermore, their cognition is inverted because of their view of a self and so forth; however, that of the Buddhas is non-inverted, as has been established in detail. Therefore, they do not engage in rivalry with those [Buddhas], because of the vast difference between them. For who would seek to rival those with cataracts with a man whose vision is healthy?
Since the eternality of the qualities, actions, the Lord, and so forth, as well as that of the Vedas, has been set aside, we do not accept that scripture is eternal.

The existence of an omniscient being is not sought to be established through analogy (*upamāna*), because it has been stated that [analogy] is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*); therefore, the establishment of existence does not follow from it. For when existence is already well-established, similarity can be understood; however, this present proof is precisely for the sake of establishing the existence of the All-Knowing One. Thus, there is no establishment by means of analogy, and the refutation [of such a proof] is rendered fruitless. Furthermore, if you have observed all men to be non-omniscient, then you yourself would be omniscient, because you perceive what is distant and hidden, and because you perceive the power of knowledge connected to other mental continua.

Even if a person were standing right before you, how could you have the certainty that "this man is not omniscient," given that you yourself are one who perceives what is beyond the senses? If you say that the certainty regarding the non-omniscience of all other persons follows from seeing the non-omniscience in yourself—provided there is no perception of a sublation (bādhā)—then we reply: even when [the proof] has been stated, the suspicion of sublation does not differ from the mere non-perception of sublation. [In other words, the absence of perceived sublation remains the same whether the argument is stated or not.]
Who else, out of dullness or delusion, would contradict that faultless discourse on the paths to heaven and liberation, which has been established by the Buddhas?
Even while perceiving worldly prosperity as well as the supreme pacification of mental afflictions, those who attain these through that [practice] have been utterly deluded by it.

Furthermore, this teaching of the Buddhas is not rooted in the Vedas; for that [Vedic teaching] is said to be flawless, whereas this [Buddhist teaching] is, on the contrary, flawed according to the Śruti.

Their instruction is not of such a kind for the sake of accomplishing their own self-interest; rather, this entire undertaking is of such a nature as to act for the sake of others. Therefore, those who are compassionate by nature and consecrated to bestowing welfare upon the world, because they are friends without a cause, declare that state [of liberation] for all beings.

For those who are under the sway of greed, fear, hatred, envy, and the like—those pitiless souls—their teaching is merely partial. But those who are governed by compassion and perceive the reality clearly, being free from all hesitation regarding criticism, have given their teaching everywhere. Just as people may be corrupted by defects such as ignorance and so forth, even so does the compassion of the Protectors flow toward them. Indeed, they do not desire any connection such as marriage or alliance; rather, benefit must be rendered. Therefore, this is sung by the virtuous: "The wise look with an equal eye upon a Brahmin perfected in knowledge and conduct, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and even an outcaste."

When birth has been refuted in hundreds of ways, what is the point of pride in birth? And if no excellence superior to that [birth] is established, why is that [birth] considered "distinguished"? If all those who are the substrata of qualities such as mastery (*vaśitva*)—whose every stain has been destroyed—are here without distinction, then even those of different births would become distinguished when endowed with those [qualities]. If they were to be established as distinguished by virtue of relying on those [qualities], then their distinction would not exist otherwise, just like the case of the hunter and the Brahmin castes.
Those well-known rites such as the birth-ceremony (jātakarma) and others are like other things; for those practices are merely conventional, as they occur even in the case of artificial [beings].

A vast period of time has passed, and women are exceedingly fickle; therefore, it is impossible even to determine [your] Brahminhood. Indeed, there is no one among you who knows things beyond the reach of the senses, nor has even the eternal Veda declared the purity of your lineage.
Therefore, even Manu and others would not have provided instruction to the twice-born regarding these [cases], because their caste-status was unknown and thus remained undetermined.

"I suspect that Manu and others must have reached this certainty from some source—that Brahmins are devoid of reasoning, incapable of understanding the meaning of the Vedas for themselves, rendered dull by the mere rote study of the Vedas, and thus unfit for critical inquiry; therefore, they surely received their instruction on the Vedas and other matters from those very Brahmins."

"The Purāṇas, the Dharma of Manu, the Veda with its auxiliary limbs, and medical science—these four are established by authority and must not be undermined by reasoning. I believe that this threat was issued by them against the dull-witted; for otherwise, how could their status as being "established by authority" consist of anything more than mere words?

Furthermore, those great-souled ones who have clearly ascertained the logical consistency of their own words and possess the capacity to communicate them to others—having thus cast away all fear—they roar the lion’s roar, which brings about the exhaustion of the rut of the intoxicated elephants that are the false teachers. "O monks, my words should be accepted by the wise after they have examined them—like gold through heating, cutting, and rubbing on a touchstone—and not out of respect. And those who are true brahmins because they have cast off evil, having practiced the stainless selflessness, exist only within the teaching of the Sage. For this reason, the ascetic is proclaimed here to be of four kinds; indeed, the doctrines of others are empty of true ascetics and brahmins."

It has already been established that even such arguments as "there exists some person who is omniscient" are flawed by the defect of a deficient thesis (*pratijñānyūnatā*). For, as was stated previously: "Even though the proof for the complete knowledge of all things is fruitless, the wise Buddhists nevertheless exert effort [toward it]," and so forth.

"But that which is sung by one who knows only a single part cannot be the speech of an omniscient being"—regarding this point as well, it was previously stated [by us] that "it follows from the connection with all knowledge. Just as a person of limited vision, having experienced objects such as sacrifices and the like, subsequently projects them into his mind and speaks of them based on that experience; and yet, that speech of his does not fail to arise from knowledge of those very things. In the same way, the speech of an omniscient being would exist; however, it differs due to a difference in its cause: while the knowledge of all things has become the cause for [the speech of] him, the knowledge of only a small portion of objects remains the cause for that [speech of the limited observer].
If conceptual construction is impossible for him, what kind of intention to speak could he possibly have? For, because his conduct has been abandoned, conceptual construction no longer occurs in him.
For such an intention is not defiled, since for him there is no obscuration and it is exhausted; but by whom can that which is wholesome and conducive to the welfare of the world be prevented?

Nor does he determine that conceptual construction to possess an objective reality; for he knows it to be without a basis, being like a magician. Just as a magician knows that the mind which perceives objects such as horses is without a real object, and therefore he does not become deluded by it.

Such statements as these, when proclaimed, appear only beautiful to those possessed of faith; they have not been stated by the twice-born (the learned) in accordance with the subject at hand. Furthermore, [if one argues that] he is not pervaded by all objects and thus lacks the capacity for instruction—this is indeed the relevant point here—and regarding this, the great-minded ones say: "If he lacked the capacity to instruct, what would then follow? From that, you must conclude that there would be no scripture (āgama). To that they reply: "Let it be so; but have you ever seen him speaking? If this undesirable consequence is urged by means of a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum)—namely, that if speakerhood were not admitted, there would be no acceptance of scripture—then, since the author of the scriptures is accepted, his speakerhood must likewise be admitted.

If such a principle is well-known among those who propound logic, then in a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) proof, the property [of the subject] would be accepted by others based on faith alone. Furthermore, if it were established through reasoning, it would constitute an independent proof (*svatantra-sādhana*). And since such a thing is desired by the opponent, that scripture (*āgama*) must have been composed by him. Due to the momentum of his accumulations (*sambhāra*), teachings issue forth from walls and other objects at will, like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), for that person. Therefore, he is called the "author" by virtue of his sovereign influence (*ādhipatya*). Consequently, it does not follow that his authorship is accompanied by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). However, we, being lacking in faith, seek logical arguments; this was said by one who did not understand the purpose of the *prasaṅga*.
And why would those [sounds] emerging from a hut or similar structures not be considered taught by a reliable person (āpta), given that their production occurs through the influence of that [person]?

How could those [teachings] be composed by playful beings such as Piśācas, since they are devoid of frivolous talk, violence, and other base matters? In them, there is no instruction on frivolous talk, violence, or other base matters, nor any activity characteristic of playful beings or Piśācas. That [teaching] is held to be in agreement with the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding its entire subject matter; not even the slightest contradiction by these two means of valid cognition is observed therein. Furthermore, although it concerns that which is extremely beyond the senses, it is free from internal contradictions between earlier and later parts, and it serves as the motivator for all persons to generate qualities such as compassion. It is endowed with all excellent attributes, sets forth virtuous conduct, and brings about various forms of prosperity for fortunate ones both in this world and the next. It proclaims the antidotes to the entire mass of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and breaks open the gate-bolts of the city of Nirvāṇa. If such a work were the word of playful beings or Rākṣasas, then let them alone be the Perfectly Awakened Ones (*Sambuddhas*), for they abide in all those characteristics. Indeed, the nature of a thing does not change merely through the invention of another name. One who applies the designation of the uncultured to a distinguished person would be censurable by the wise.

When unrefined actions—characterized by sexual misconduct, false conduct, violence toward living beings, and so forth—are revealed by a particular word, that [word] is suspected of being composed by a libertine, a piśāca, or similar beings; for such speech is indeed conceivable from those who delight in such activities.
The simultaneous cognition of contradictory natures, such as the pure and the impure, by a single consciousness is observed; for those [contradictions] are not incompatible with awareness.

Alternatively, contradiction among them may consist in their being defined by existing through mutual exclusion, such that they cannot coexist in a single location. However, there is no contradiction for those things that appear in a single cognition, because pure and impure objects, or a snake and a peacock, are seen simultaneously by the eye.

As for the fact that there is no simultaneous cognition of the distinctions between pleasure, pain, and so forth, this is not contradictory; it should be understood as resulting from the absence of causes or their non-proximity. For [colors] such as blue, yellow, and white, which do not contradict one another despite differences in location or nature, are not perceived simultaneously.
Since the Omniscient One has indeed been established as one whose entire circle of objects of knowledge is pervaded by a single moment of cognition, a sequential process is therefore not accepted.

Whatever he wishes to know, that he knows with certainty; such is his power, for he has abandoned all [unwholesome] conduct. He attains [knowledge] either simultaneously or sequentially according to his own will. Having attained knowledge, the Lord indeed perceives through moments of consciousness (*citta*) and so forth. Or else, through sixteen moments of consciousness, he knows everything that is to be known, which consists of the nature of the Four Truths; therefore, he is called "All-Knowing" (*sarvavit*). In such a cognition, there is no need to consider even a mere fraction of time for the Lord, much less a duration of hundreds of years.

He who understands everything through an undifferentiated intrinsic nature (svabhāva) understands the very essential forms of all entities. That specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa), which is excluded from what is non-self, non-momentary, and so forth, is here called a universal (sāmānya) because it serves as the cause for tranquility and conceptualization. And the cognition that grasps that [universal], which arises through the power of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā), is manifested for the lords of yogins; its objective domain is the specific characteristic.
That universal which is postulated by others as being indefinable in terms of identity or difference and so forth—its apprehension does not occur through this yogic consciousness.

The mind of that Lord of Yogins is free from conceptual construction and unerring; otherwise, it would follow that it is overcome by conceptual construction and error in its apprehension of that [object].

And that universal which is proclaimed to be of the nature of conceptual construction and inexpressible—that which has the form of a constant concomitance—is demonstrated to be devoid of any real form.

He who, through supramundane knowledge born of meditative concentration, knows action along with its causes and its fruits, is designated as omniscient. His existence has been established previously by means of inference; since there exists a valid means of cognition for his existence, such a person indeed exists.
Whether simultaneously or in succession, his knowledge—and likewise his capacity—is revealed through the effects [of his teaching], when he performs the instruction.

This stainless teaching, in which the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) has been well-practiced, has been established in all scriptures and remains uncontradicted by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). It is a knowledge unsuitable for worldly beings, beyond the reach of Keśava and others, and is honored with their heads according to their capacity by those who are exceedingly wise. It brings about the destruction of the entire host of enemies that are all misfortunes, and is the cause for the attainment of various prosperities and *nirvāṇa*. Having obtained an uncommon means, characterized as distinct from all other men, He alone is the Omniscient Lord; this is established through valid proof.
Thus, when some omniscient person indeed comes into existence as the cause for the realization of Dharma and so forth, then his word is of human origin.

But considerations such as whether [the cognition] is formless (nirākāra) and so forth are of no use regarding the Omniscient One; for just as your own knowledge [is held to be] with respect to some object, so too is that of the other. Thus ends the Examination of the Person Who Perceives Beyond the Senses. The *Tattvasaṃgraha* composed by Śāntarakṣita is completed.
